Matoma is now touching triple digits with his fastball and sitting 95-98 mph with ease. He looks like a reincarnation of Yordano Ventura, a supreme little athlete with arm speed that breaks the sound barrier.  He showcases a loose arm with a very projectable frame that might come into even more velocity as his body matures and adds strength. His command is far from precise, but Matoma throws enough strikes to warrant optimism that he can be developed as a starter, and the way his fastball plays won't require him to be super fine with his location. His slider’s quality is very volatile pitch to pitch. He often gets on the side of it, which hinders the spin tightness and the authority of its break and results in the 85-89 mph offering varying greatly in shape. The best ones have short,  three-quarters shape with late tilting action.
The foundation of a high-leverage relief prospect is already here, but we have no idea how to account for the way Matoma's baseball background might leave room for all kinds of development on top of what he's already doing. He's athletic enough to be optimistic that he'll eventually have a good changeup, too. This is a volcanic profile, a very talented athlete with huge arm speed who is great to have in the system. If you dropped a prospect like this into the draft, Matoma would get a $2 million bonus or more, which is why he's FV'd in line with a second round pick here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has never been a player from Uganda to make it to the big leagues, though there is a growing baseball presence in the African nation. The Dodgers signed two Ugandan players in 2022, Ben Serunkuma and Umar Male, and since then the Pirates have inked two more, most recently Armstrong Muhoozi and Matoma, who received $20,000 in January 2023. Matoma got his feet wet in the Dominican Summer League that summer but really jumped on radars when news of his arm strength spread and he put up outstanding numbers, albeit in a small sample, in the Florida Complex League. Matoma may only be a six-footer, but he has a super-fast arm and tons of arm strength. He's touched triple-digits with his fastball and routinely is in the 97-98 mph range, though he does tend to fatigue pretty quickly. His 87-88 mph gyro-like slider could be a true out pitch in time, one that already misses a good amount of bats, and when he can keep his heater at the high end of his range, there's good velocity separation there. He has an upper-80s splitter, but it's a distant third pitch that doesn't kill enough spin. Considering that Matoma has played so little baseball, he's done an impressive job throwing strikes consistently. He has a reliever-like mindset, with a slow heartbeat, but the Pirates don't want to limit what he could become. He showed up this spring more physical with much more muscle on his frame, which could help him maintain his stuff as he takes his next step.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked in the top 20 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the 2021 signing period opened, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million. After an impressive debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing, his first taste of life in the United States and the Arizona Complex League did not go as well. He was middling along with a .707 OPS when he was sent to the Reds at the 2022 Trade Deadline for Brandon Drury. While the numbers in his first full season with his new organization weren’t eye-popping, he more consistently showed off his solid tools with the move to the Florida State League. A switch-hitter, Acosta has shown the ability to swing the bat well from both sides of the plate with quick hands and bat speed, though he was a bit better from the left side with Daytona last year. While he keeps the strikeouts relatively in check and draws walks, he can get overly aggressive at times because he has such strong contact skills. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but there were some good exit velocities coming off his bat in 2023, and he has the chance to find his way to some extra-base thump in the gaps. The hope is that Acosta, who is an above-average runner, will be able to stick at shortstop, and the Reds will likely keep giving him reps there for as long as possible. He has a decent arm and actions, but some see a move to second base eventually becoming necessary. How far his offense advances will determine if he can profile as an everyday guy at one spot in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Acosta was thought to be one of the better prospects available on the international amateur market when the 2021 signing period opened, with the Padres swooping in and signing him for $1.8 million on the opening day (Jan. 15). He made a strong first impression that summer with an OPS over .900, but he was having less success in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in the Brandon Drury Trade Deadline deal in 2022. In the early stages of his pro career, Acosta has shown some acumen for getting on base and making contact from both sides of the plate. He has quick hands and an aggressive approach, but he’s shown a willingness to see pitches and draw walks. There hasn’t been much power to speak of, and he needs to add strength to his frame, which could help him translate his contact skills into more extra-base authority. Acosta is a good athlete who runs well and possesses all of the defensive tools -- range, arm, footwork and instincts -- to stick at shortstop. He’ll keep getting reps on both sides of second base to potentially provide defensive versatility down the line and also to make sure he gets the at-bats he needs to reach his offensive ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the No. 19 prospect in the 2020-21 international class, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million on Jan. 15, 2021. The early returns were promising as the Dominican Republic native flashes five-tool potential and hit .285/.431/.484 over 56 games in his Dominican Summer League debut, though he was having less impact offensively during his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League when he was sent to the Reds in return for Brandon Drury at the Trade Deadline. A switch-hitter, Acosta boasts an impressive set of tools. The teenager has quick hands and is an aggressive hitter with a swing-first mentality. As a result of the aggression, he handles fastballs better than off-speed pitches, though that’s not all that uncommon in young hitters. He doesn’t hit for a ton of power yet, but still has time to grow into his 5-foot-11, 170-pound frame and there’s hope he’ll tack on a bit more power as he develops. A projectable athlete, Acosta has the athleticism to stick at short, but could also wind up at second base. Above-average speed, which helped him steal 26 bases in 56 games last season, gives Acosta the range to make all the necessary plays up the middle, though the accuracy on his throws isn’t always consistent. He does, however, have plenty of arm strength and could develop into a middle of the diamond star if everything goes well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arguably the prize of their 2020-21 international haul, Acosta signed with the Padres for $1.8 million out of the Dominican Republic. He’s clearly worth dreaming on. Acosta boasts five-tool potential and is a twitchy athlete with lots of projection. A switch-hitter, Acosta has extremely quick hands, which should make his swing play from both sides of the plate. As he grows into his frame and perhaps adds an inch or two – at 16, he stands 5-foot-11, 170 pounds – the Padres envision Acosta growing into a bit of power. He’s raw at shortstop but can probably stick there, considering his athleticism and excellent arm. Acosta is a classic projectable athlete, and San Diego has had success in the past developing middle infielders. It’s unclear what position Acosta might end up playing, but he has all the tools necessary to stick up the middle somewhere. If his bat develops too, the Padres might have another big-time athlete to plug into the mix.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Acosta, who was acquired from San Diego a couple years ago for Brandon Drury, continues to track like a fringe 40-man infielder based on his defensive ability and versatility. He now has experience at three infield positions (third base was new in 2025) and is a capable shortstop with a huge arm. It's possible he may be exposed to the outfield at some point in the future because versatility is going to be an important aspect of his rosterability. Acosta is a fine contact hitter but has so little power that it's tough to consider him anything more than the last infielder on a bench. But when prospects can play defense like this, especially at shortstop, they tend to find their way onto a big league roster at some point, even if it's just in the Sergio Alcántara, "Have Glove, Will Travel" role.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Acosta, who was acquired from San Diego for Brandon Drury, continues to track like a fringe 40-man infielder. He's a well-rounded shortstop defender with a plus arm. He has experience at both middle infield positions and should probably be exposed to third base, and maybe the outfield, at some point soon because versatility is going to be an important aspect of his rosterability. He hasn't slugged over .400 since his first season in pro ball and likely won't make enough of an offensive impact to be a big league regular. But Acosta has a compact swing and a fairly effective, conservative approach to contact form both sides of the plate. Still, while he posted roughly average BABIP-aided lines in the lower minors, his underlying data (especially his chase, despite above-average walk rates in the past) indicate looming regression. He's a gap-to-gap singles hitter without a plus tool, but he does a little bit of everything and should be on and off many a roster throughout his prime.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Acosta, who was acquired for Brandon Drury at the 2022 deadline, posted a .251/.364/.354 line at Low-A in 2023. He continues to track like a switch-hitting utilityman. Acosta's bat drags through the zone from the left side, making it tough for him to pull the ball. Though he has posted above-average walk rates throughout his pro career to this point, his underlying swing and chase rates suggest his OBP will dip as he climbs through the minors. He's a sound defensive shortstop with just a little bit of experience at other positions. Stocky and relatively lacking in physical projection for a prospect this age, Acosta is on pace for a post-2025 40-man add and a debut somewhere in 2026 or 2027, when he's needed for depth purposes.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: His profile is heuristically pleasing, and at times Acosta will show you flashes of ability that make you think he could be an everyday player, but with a well-rounded collection of 45- and 50-grade tools, he's more likely a switch-hitting utility man who is still about a half decade from the bigs. As is often the case for a switch-hitter this age, Acosta's two swings are fraternal rather than identical twins and vary in their efficacy. His barrel drags through the zone from the left side, making it hard for him to turn on pitches and causing him to pepper the opposite field, while his righty swing lacks vitality. In both ways he is similar to D-backs shortstop Geraldo Perdomo, who has scuffled with the bat against major league pitching. They're also mechanically similar, though Acosta is a bit more compact than Perdomo. Acosta is a dynamic athlete with the range and arm strength to play anywhere on the infield. He has plus defensive feet, hands, and actions, making him a likely long-term fit at shortstop and giving him a relatively high floor for a teenage prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: As is often the case for a switch-hitter this age, Acosta's two swings are fraternal rather than identical twins and they vary in their efficacy. His barrel drags through the zone from the left side, making it hard for him to turn on pitches and causing him to pepper the opposite field, while his righty swing lacks vitality. But Acosta is a dynamic athlete with the athleticism and arm strength to play anywhere on the infield. He has plus defensive feet, hands, and actions, making him a likely long-term fit at shortstop, though he saw some time elsewhere in big league spring games (due to the lockout, teams' extended spring training groups often played the last few innings after minor league camp broke before big league camp did). There are still paths to an everyday big league role for Acosta, but based on early backfield looks, they just aren't likely to be carved by his hit tool. Instead, he'll have to punch above his weight from a power standpoint, which is feasible given how explosive the little Acosta seems to be. He's more likely a switch-hitting utility man.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: As is often the case for a switch-hitter this age, Acosta's two swings are fraternal rather than identical twins and they vary in their efficacy. His barrel drags through the zone from the left side, making it hard for him to turn on pitches and causing him to pepper the opposite field; his righty swing is more generic. But he gets the bat to the ball from both sides and, though small, is a pretty dynamic athlete who might grow into some pop the way D-backs shortstop Geraldo Perdomo has. Acosta has plus defensive feet, hands, and actions, making him a likely shortstop. If he can make even average contact while playing a good defensive middle infield, he'll have a long big league career. (International Signee)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid Georgia high school prospect, Simmons struggled at the plate a bit during his senior year in 2018 to hurt his Draft stock. The Phillies liked the power potential and overall athlete enough to take him in the sixth round that June and go over-slot to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment for $750,000. It’s been a slow development process since, though he did lead the New York-Penn League in slugging percentage in 2019. He did show some glimpses of his offensive upside in his full-season debut in 2021, but injury, a pitch to the helmet and COVID-related shutdowns limited him to just 46 total games. Simmons has always had considerable raw power from the right side of the plate; the question since his high school days was if he’d hit enough to tap into it. He’s had flashes of bringing a solid approach to the plate, with a willingness to draw walks, but he does strike out a fair amount. When he does make contact, it’s loud with good exit velocity and the ability to hit the ball over the fence, especially to the pull side. The Phillies believe his bat is trending in the right direction. The high school shortstop has played three infield positions professionally, but as his body continues to get bigger and stronger, it doesn’t look like he’ll be able to play short long-term. He’s probably best suited for third, where his strong arm plays well, but will continue to get plenty of time at second base as well.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Simmons was so raw that he swung and missed a ton even during high school varsity play, so his 2019 statistical success in the Penn League was surprising and impressive. But an extended look at Simmons during his Australian Baseball League run (which included him struggling to hold on to the bat), has me backpedaling on his placement. It's rare to find infielders with this sort of bat speed but I think it's pretty unlikely that he hits, both due to his breaking ball recognition and a lack of bat control. (Fall Instructional League, Australian Baseball League)

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Not yet 21 on draft day even though he's a true junior. Defense-first prospect. Incredibly twitchy for a catcher. Great at framing around the edge of the zone. Explodes out of his crouch on throws to the bag; routinely pop 1.9ish even though his arm is only fair, exchange is that fast. Ball-blocking needs work but isn't terrible. Offense might be. Well below-average bat speed, twice as many strikeouts as walks as a junior. Backup ceiling is probable here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing sparingly as a freshman and putting up middling numbers as a sophomore at Nebraska, Caron took off as a junior, finishing with a .968 OPS and 16 homers, hitting six in six Big Ten Conference Tournament games to earn tourney MVP honors. That allowed him to become a bigger fish in a small sea of college catchers, landing in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft to the Mariners, who sent him to full-season Modesto for a brief pro debut. As someone who was young for the Draft (just 20 as a college junior) and from a cold-weather region (he went to high school in Wisconsin before heading to Nebraska), Caron might have more ceiling that he can catch up to. There’s some rawness to his bat, with his rhythm and timing at the plate not great compared to other college juniors, though his swing works pretty well, and he has pretty decent pitch selection, though he can be prone to being over-aggressive and pull-happy. He’s physical and strong with a good amount of power to tap into and he swung the bat very well in helping Modesto win its second straight California League title. Caron already has a strong arm, and there might be more than met the initial eye defensively as well. Nebraska’s coaches were very regimented in how they told their catchers to set up and receive depending on the count. A decent athlete who runs well for a backstop, Caron could take a step forward in his overall receiving when given the reins to his own protocol behind the dish. If it all clicks, he could develop into a power-hitting regular in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Targeting projectable, tooled-up prospects at premium positions, the Mets handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to Dominican amateurs in 2017, signing both shortstop Ronny Mauricio and Hernandez, a center fielder, on July 2. While Mauricio was widely viewed as the better prospect and therefore received a higher bonus, Hernandez signed for $1.5 million after he ranked 19th on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list. Hernandez is a premium athlete with a strong frame who has a high-energy style on the field. An aggressive hitter, he has terrific bat speed and outstanding raw power from the right side of the plate. That pop shows up more on the pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields and should tap into it more consistently as he refines his approach at the plate. Hernandez's plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball. Hernandez is a center fielder for the time being, but there's the chance he could grow and develop more into the prototypical athletic right-fielder mold down the road. Hernandez's power-speed combination has earned him comparisons to Jose Guillen from some scouts, and the Mets would be thrilled if he become that caliber of player.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Like Desmond Lindsay, who is further down this list, Hernandez is muscular, explosive, tightly-wound, and suffered a severe soft-tissue injury (a torn hamstring) that cost him most all of 2019. He wasn't part of New York's 2020 instructs contingent, so we have basically no new information from the last two years. Healthy Hernandez ran well enough to stay in center field and had sizeable raw power for a teenager. The cement on the bod is pretty dry, and while I think that means limited power projection, it also probably means Hernandez's chances to stay in center field may be a little more stable, assuming he has his pre-injury speed when he returns. While his 2018 slash line was strong (yeesh it feels scary to write that -- it's been a long time since this guy has played), there were some underlying swing-and-miss issues that might rear their ugly head in a more meaningful way in 2021. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Just because the Reds were limited in their international spending during the 2017-18 signing period does not mean they didn’t find any good players. Case in point is Cerda, a toolsy outfielder who signed for $100,000 in July 2017. After a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2018, Cerda struggled when he first came stateside, though he still hit for power in the rookie-level Appalachian League. He tapped into it with more consistency in his full-season debut in 2021, earning a late promotion up to High-A and getting added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. Though he’s still far away from the big leagues, the Reds thought Cerda’s tools were loud enough to warrant protection on the roster. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate, but has yet to maximize it in games due to inconsistency in his approach. There’s plenty of bat speed, but he chases too much, leading to high strikeout rates, though he is willing to draw walks to help offset that a bit. While Cerda has above-average speed, he hasn’t been much of a basestealing threat. And while he’s largely been a center fielder in the early stages of his career, most think he’ll be best suited for right field, where he played after his promotion to High-A. He could be a more controlled version of former Reds outfield prospect Jose Siri at the plate, one who fits the corner outfield power profile well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds weren’t allowed to spend over $300,000 on any player on the international market during the 2017-18 signing period. They think they may have found a steal in Cerda, who signed for $100,000 at the start of the signing period and then posted a very respectable .841 OPS during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. Aggressively jumped to the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019, he couldn’t replicate that success, though his power was still on display. Big, athletic and projectable, Cerda’s raw power is his calling card on the offensive side. The raw pop is plus from the right side of the plate, but there are questions about his ability to make enough contact to get to it. He uses a narrow stance with a high leg lift and hasn’t always been on time, contributing to a 26.6 percent strikeout rate in his brief career. He does offset the swing-and-miss somewhat with a willingness to draw walks (11.9 BB rate). Cerda might have a tick above-average speed and combines that with good instincts to give him every chance to play center field for a long time. He’ll flash an above-average arm that might be plus in time, so he could profile as a power-hitting right fielder should he have to shift over to a corner.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Heavy sigh Even though he had obvious swing-and-miss issues, Cerda was absolutely stuffed on this list last year because he's kind of a freak physically. He's built like an NFL wide receiver, has huge pull-side power, and still had room to grow into his frame at age 22. Somehow still listed at a comical 6-foot-3, 170 pounds, he's probably closer to 6-foot-5, 220 now, and has enjoyed all the raw power that comes with that extra size and strength. After swatting 17 homers and nearly 40 extra-base hits in just 87 games in 2021, Cerda followed that up with 24 homers combined between High- and Double-A in '22, though he hit just .198 at the latter stop in a 62-game sample. He is a career .233/.367/.470 hitter and trending down in the batting average department because Cerda has a very immature approach to hitting, trying to yank everything to his pull side (if you had this kind of raw power, you'd be tempted to do that, too), and he struggles to stay with pitches on the outer third of the zone. When he runs into one, though, holy cow. Visual evaluation of the quality of Cerda's at-bats (bad) does not match up with his chase data (good), and the multi-year track record of above-average walk rates should probably trump subjective scouting in this case. There is a contingent of scouts who think he's passable in center field (he's pretty good at going back on balls) but most do not (he's not good at coming in and makes frequent situational errors), and it's rare for an athlete this size to stay there. It would certainly help support a big league profile of some kind if Cerda could play out there for the long haul. In either case, he should remind Reds fans of two recent prospect friends, Jose Siri (the center field version) and Aristides Aquino (the right field version), both of whom ended up on the roster fringe.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
While new, very young players with big, projectable frames have begun to percolate up through the lower levels of the Reds system, don't lose sight of Cerda, who has become a giant. Cerda is still listed at a comical 6-foot-3, 170 pounds but he's probably closer to 6-foot-5, 225 now, and has enjoyed all the raw power that comes with that extra size and strength. He hit 17 homers and nearly 40 extra-base hits in just 87 games in 2021, and has a .250/.373/.488 career line since 2018. Cerda has ferocious bat speed, and his swing finishes with a helicopter swirl over his head, similar to Miguel Andújar's. 
Also like Andújar, Cerda lacks great pitch recognition and often seems uncomfortable in the box. The visual evaluation of his plate discipline doesn't corroborate his on-paper performance, as he's posted double-digit walk rates at every level. All but 21 games of his career have been in rookie ball (where you're going to walk a lot) or with Low-A Southeast automated strike zones, which appear to have inflated peripherals in 2021. Based on that, we're inclined to lean more heavily on eyeball scouting opinions, and see this particular issue as making Cerda a rather risky prospect. Perhaps there were extenuating circumstances for it, but the Reds made a mistake in not sending Cerda to the Arizona Fall League or instructs. It would have given them an intimate look at how he'd fare against a curated contingent of pitchers prior to them adding him to the 40-man. We buy that Cerda is so talented that he was a must-add in any case, but fall activity against either the select talents of instructs or the advanced pitching of the AFL (at least compared to what he'd seen) would have given the team a longer runway to evaluate him, and primed him for a quick move to Double-A in 2022, his first option year. There is volatility around Cerda's hit tool, but star-level power output lurking if he can even be a 40- or 45-grade contact hitter.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The Reds skipped Cerda over the AZL and sent him straight from the DSL to the Appy League for his age-19 2019 season. He responded by hitting .220/.360/.470 there, albeit with a troubling strikeout rate. He has a three true outcomes vibe, assuming Cerda's frame, which is that of the typical high school pitcher, fills out and enables him to grow into more power. He already has quite a bit, and an electric uppercut swing, but a corner outfield future means that unless he develops elite power, the amount of contact Cerda makes will need to increase for him to profile. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: A lot of big-framed college boppers have suspect hit tools, but Vradenburg's junior year ascent seemed much more balanced. He posted equal walk and strike out rates (13%) while driving the ball to all fields, and slashed a cartoonish .400/.492/.721 leading up to the draft. At his size, Vradenburg's swing inevitably has length and he struggles to turn on velocity. It was something to watch as he left the Big Ten and entered pro ball, and so far Vradenburg has struggled very, very badly at Low-A, where he's striking out nearly 30% of the time. His power is not yet actualized in games, despite his college slugging percentage. First base prospects need to rake all the way up the minors to have prospect value and Vradenburg is doing the opposite of that so far. Barring a profound late-season turnaround, he won't be on the next Marlins list update.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: A lot of big-framed college boppers have suspect hit tools, but Vradenburg's junior year ascent was much more balanced. He posted equal walk and strike out rates (13%) while driving the ball to all fields, and slashed a cartoonish .400/.492/.721 in his draft year. At his size, Vradenburg's swing inevitably has length and he struggles to turn on velocity. That's something to watch as he leaves the Big Ten and enters pro ball. Vradenburg's power is not yet actualized in games, despite his college slugging percentage. He hits the ball on the ground a ton and will likely need to alter his angle of attack to profile at first base. If/when he does that, whether or not it impacts his hit tool will probably dictate his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts largely ignored Vradenburg during his California high school career and first two seasons at Michigan State, and he wasn't on their follow lists heading into 2023 even after leading the Coastal Plain League with 48 RBI in 32 games the previous summer. Then he exploded last spring to slash .400/.492/.721 with 13 homers, becoming the second player in Spartans history to earn athletic and academic All-America accolades in the same season. After signing for $916,000 as a third-rounder, he batted .236/.368/.291 in Single-A. Despite his hulking 6-foot-7, 230-pound build, Vradenburg's hitting ability overshadows his power. He doesn't chase pitches out of the strike zone and focuses on smacking them from gap to gap, though his strikeout rate did spike from 13 percent in his final college season to 28 percent in his pro debut. There's some question as to whether he can provide more than 15-20 homers per season because his pop comes more from strength and leverage than bat speed in his left-handed stroke, and the Marlins will try to help him add more muscle and explosiveness. Vradenburg moves surprisingly well for his size, recording average run times from home to first and showing solid quickness once underway. He doesn't have much twitchy athleticism and may not have the hands and footwork to remain at first base, where he made five errors in 26 pro starts. With his speed and fringy to average arm strength, he may be able to handle left field.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Rincon had something of a breakout in 2023 when he managed an 88% in-zone contact rate, and 81% rate overall, in A-ball while playing a good shortstop. In the following two seasons, he has hit under .200 while dealing with some pretty serious injuries: a severe hamstring injury in 2024 and a broken hamate in 2025. His carrying tool is his shortstop defense, which should allow Rincon to wear a big league uniform for fits and starts of his physical prime. He has average range but plus hands and arm strength, and he's an above-average defender overall at short, with the physical ability to be plus at the other infield spots, though the Phillies haven't deployed him anywhere else just yet. Rincon is entering his 40-man platform year, and it would take an unforeseen offensive surge to net him a roster spot after this season. He's squarely on the 40-man fringe and will likely be on and off various orgs' rosters during his peak as a glove-first mercenary.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: After his breakout 2023, Rincon had a rough 2024 and was either injured (a hamstring injury cost him three months) or striking out way, way more than he was the season before. He K'd at a 25% clip at Low-A and a 31.4% rate at High-A. Rincon went to the Arizona Fall League after the regular season to pick up some of the reps he lost due to the hamstring injury and continued to struggle there. He was at or under the Mendoza Line all year when he was healthy enough to play. How much of this was rust, or related to discomfort and tightness that preceded the IL stint, and how much is related to Rincon's talent? His underlying contact rates dipped from 88% in-zone and 81% overall in 2023 to 81% in-zone and 74% overall in 2024. Rincon looked better at shortstop the further away he got from his hamstring injury, and was good there in the AFL, but the same was not true of his hitting hands, which were still a little slow and stiff. A year ago, it looked like Rincon would have the skill set of a Geraldo Perdomo type of second division regular. Now he's looking more like a lower-impact reserve whose best skill is his plate discipline.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
As far as Phillies go, it appears that the biggest gap between industry evals and my own from last cycle was right here with Rincon, who is rumored to have been a popular trade target during the last year or so. The slick-fielding, zone-controlling Yinzer high school draftee has plus defensive hands and actions, and is a virtual lock to stay at shortstop. He's compactly built and not especially strong, but Rincon tracks pitches well, rarely chases, and moves the bat around the zone from both sides of the plate. His swing isn't always well connected from the ground up, especially his right-handed swing, which often features an awkward weight transfer; in Rincon's lefty swing, his hands have a late move that sometimes causes his whole operation to be tardy. The latter issue is small enough to project that it will get cleaned up with time. Otherwise, Rincon's cut is short and to the point but still has a fair amount of natural lift. 
A high-probability utility prospect in the Geraldo Perdomo mold, Rincon has terrific soft skills, and his ceiling will be dictated by how much stronger he can get. Because we're not talking about a super projectable frame in this case, I'm not inclined to forecast a huge uptick in that realm, but the progression of Rincon's measurable power from 2022 to 2023 (16% hard-hit rate to 25%, with a max exit velo that rose nearly 10 ticks to 108 mph) was pretty substantial.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: The slick-fielding Rincon has plus-plus defensive hands and actions and is a virtual lock to stay at shortstop. It will be imperative for him to add strength as he matures. Rincon's feel for contact and (especially) for the strike zone are both pretty good, but he doesn't impact the baseball with anything close to the ball-striking quality of a big league hitter. Because Rincon is so compactly built, it's not a given that he'll grow into viable strength, but we're talking about a 45 FV utility type if he does.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies scouting department did fine work finding Rincon, who had moved to the Pittsburgh area from Venezuela for high school. The Phillies liked Rincon, who played his high school ball at Shaler Area High and committed to San Jacinto Junior College, and his defensive actions and upside enough to take him in the 14th round of the 2022 Draft, knowing he was eager to begin his pro career. He had a solid first full season in 2023 but has had trouble gaining traction since, missing much of 2024 with hamstring issues, then hitting the injured list again in 2025 with a broken hamate. Both times, he made up for lost at-bats by going to the Arizona Fall League, though he didn’t swing the bat well there. Thus far, all of Rincon’s value comes from his glove. He’s a no-doubt shortstop for a very long time, with plus actions, hands, footwork and more than enough arm for the premium position. Even though he’s not a burner, his defensive instincts give him plenty of range. He’s only played shortstop thus far, but he could easily slide over to other spots on the dirt if he ends up in a utility role. While his defense gives him a decent floor, what his ultimate role will be depends entirely on how much, if any, offensive impact he can find. There are some tools to build with for the switch-hitter. He swiped 40 bases thanks to excellent instincts on the basepaths, and he actually doesn’t swing-and-miss or chase all that much, doing damage when he swings. But his strikeout rate jumped to nearly 29 percent in 2025 because he got too passive and didn’t swing enough. If he can find any production in his age 22 season, he could rejuvenate his prospect luster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Venezuelan native headed to the Pittsburgh area for high school, the Phillies took Rincon, previously committed to San Jacinto Junior College, in the 14th round of the 2022 Draft. He jumped on the prospect map in 2023 with a performance that allowed him to reach High-A in his first full season. He wasn’t able to build off of that in 2024 as he missed three months with hamstring injuries, though he did return to action at the end of the regular season and made up for some lost reps by competing in the Arizona Fall League. While Rincon’s overall numbers as a pro don’t jump off the page (a career .711 OPS heading into 2025), he does bring some solid offensive traits to the table the Phillies are hoping he can get back to with a clean slate. The switch hitter makes a ton of contact with low miss and chase rates, and he draws a lot of walks. The hope is with continued added strength and healthy legs under him, he can provide enough contact and on-base skills to fit regularly into a big league lineup. What will get him to the big leagues -- and gives him a very high floor -- is his defensive ability at shortstop. He has excellent hands, footwork and plenty of arm for the premium position, and thanks to his instincts, he’ll have more than enough range, especially the further removed from those hamstring issues he gets. He may always be a glove-first guy, but he’s one who could do it as a starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon grew up in Venezuela but came to the Pittsburgh area to live with an uncle and play baseball for Shaler High School. He had committed to San Jacinto Junior College had the Draft not worked out, but the Phillies took a low-risk chance in Round 14 and signed him for Day 3 slot ($125,000). While his numbers from his first full season, in which he reached High-A, weren't amazing, he showed off a ton of skills that should continue to translate as he moves up the ladder. He shook off a very slow start this spring back in High-A and was performing better in May when a hamstring injury ended his 2024 season. Playing at age 20 for all of 2024, Rincon has a very high floor thanks to his defensive ability. His hands, range and footwork are excellent and play up because of his plus instincts. He has more than enough arm for the premium position, and even though he’s not a burner speed-wise, he should be able to play shortstop for a very long time. There’s optimism that Rincon’s offensive skills will continue to develop as well. He’s a switch-hitter with outstanding contact skills, rarely chasing and limiting strikeouts while drawing a good amount of walks. He’s continued to add strength and there could be more power to come in the future as well. The Phillies feel there could be some Bryson Stott in him in terms of him playing above his tools and becoming an everyday middle infielder in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What's better than one member of the De Los Santos family in your system? Two. The Pirates signed Yordany De Los Santos in 2022, then circled back to sign his younger brother Johan in 2025, who was No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's Top 50 International Prospects list for that signing period. After getting $2.25 million to join his brother in the system, Johan had a very strong professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, hitting .353 with a .911 OPS while not turning 17 until late July. He came stateside and got off to an equally solid start in the Florida Complex League in 2026. Swinging the bat from the left side of the plate, De Los Santos has a feel for the barrel with a line-drive approach and solid bat speed. He's athletic and twitchy in the box, and while he's hit-over-power, he could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with impact to come. He's an above-average runner who has already shown he likes to be aggressive on the basepaths. Primarily a shortstop as an amateur, De Los Santos has the actions and an above-average arm to give him a chance to play the premium position going forward. He's been splitting time between short and second base thus far in his blossoming pro career, as the Pirates like to encourage versatility to their young prospects, giving them options if De Los Santos' bat develops like it looks like it might as he rises through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The De Los Santos family must be doing something right. At least the Pirates think so. In 2022, they gave Yordany De Los Santos $1.2 million to sign. Three years later, at the start of the 2025 international signing period, they signed his younger brother Johan for $2.25 million. The younger De Los Santos ranked No. 23 on MLB Pipeline's 2025 Top 50 international prospects list and was one of the youngest players in the class, not turning 17 until late July. A left-handed hitter with a feel for finding the barrel, De Los Santos has a line-drive approach with a sound swing and bat speed. He's athletic with twitchy actions and could add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame with perhaps more impact to come, though he's likely to always be a hit-over-power type of offensive performer. He has good speed with the chance to make plays on the basepaths. With good actions and an above-average arm, De Los Santos has largely played only shortstop and will likely get plenty of reps at the premium position as he embarks on his professional career. The Pirates like to introduce multiple positions to players at a young age to encourage versatility, so don't be surprised if the younger De Los Santos sees some time at second base in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: The brother of Yordany De Los Santos, Johan is speculatively projected to center field here due to his sketchy infield look at the U18 WBSC tournament in August 2024. He ran a jailbreak 3.8 and 4.0 (meep meep) at that tournament, though. That speed will play in center if development on the infield doesn't occur. On offense, De Los Santos' hands are really lively and he rotates with verve through contact. His hands load low and his swing has a late hitch, and it might need adjustment against pro velocity. It's also possible things will simplify for him with strength and maturity, and that it won't take a mechanical overhaul at all. He's a Roman Quinn type prospect who signed for $2.5 million in January.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 50 | Splitter: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Only three players have ever been drafted out of Cary-Grove HS in Illinois, and just two have ever signed. Both enter the 2026 season as Brewers: Major Leaguer Quinn Priester (2019) and Dorchies. The latter was much less heralded coming out of the prep ranks than his predecessor and went in the 10th round of the 2024 Draft before signing away from a University of Illinois-Chicago commitment with a $162,500 bonus. Only 17 on Draft Day, Dorchies came flying out of the gate in his first full season, blowing past the Arizona Complex League and reaching Single-A Carolina by mid-June. He finished with a 2.74 ERA, a 1.05 WHIP and 89 strikeouts over 82 innings between both spots. Dorchies checks in at 6-feet-5 and uses that size to generate around 7 feet of extension, putting his five-pitch mix right on top of hitters. His four-seamer and sinker only sit in the 90-93 mph range right now, but the ride on the former and the run on the latter help them play beyond the velo. Still only 19 for all of his second full season, Dorchies could stand to add strength and get that heat closer to the mid-90s with regularity in time. His low-80s, low-spin splitter dives late to generate whiffs at his best rates, but he’s been more focused on throwing a low-80s sweeping slider as his most-used secondary. An upper-80s cutter serves as a bridge pitch. The teenager’s walk rate inflated about four ticks once he got away from the complex, but he doesn’t overthrow and should deliver a decent amount of strikes, especially if that strength comes around. Dorchies already displays desirable traits and promising future projection for a 10th-round pick and could become one of Milwaukee’s better development stories by the time he reaches The Show.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Dorchies, a lanky, 6-foot-5 UIC commit from Cary, NC, signed for just $162,500 in 2024 and had a good first full season in which he reached Low-A and posted a 2.74 ERA and K'd a batter per inning in 82 total frames. This is an athletic developmental project who, for us, has separated himself from the other mid-six-figure bonus high schoolers from Milwaukee's 2024 draft class by virtue of his delivery and physical projection. Dorchies gets way, way down the mound and generates over seven feet of extension even though he looks like a fairly generic athlete. His slider has promising depth but below-average bite at present due to a general lack of velocity. He has a shot to develop an impact fastball/slider combo at peak, but a lot of other stuff has to happen (third pitch, better command) for him to project as a starter. Those things are within the realm of possibility, but they're still more in the deep horizon of his development than they are imminent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2009, the Giants used a fifth-round pick on a college first baseman whose hitting ability and plate discipline stood out more than his power, finding a long-term starter in Brandon Belt. They see similar traits in Wyatt, who replaced two-way star Brandon McKay (the No. 4 overall pick in 2017) at first base at Louisville and ranked third in NCAA Division I in walks in each of his two seasons as a starter, including a school-record 72 in 2019. Signed for a well-below-slot $997,500 in the second round last June, he reached low Class A in his pro debut. Wyatt has a sound left-handed swing, good feel for hitting and an extremely patient approach that borders on passive at times. His strength gives him at least solid raw power and 20-homer potential, but he won't tap into it unless he attacks more pitches and drives them in the air more often. After he produced a lot of rolled-over, weak ground-ball contact in his debut, San Francisco is trying to help him become more aggressive while still maintaining his discipline. Wyatt is a better athlete than his well-below-average speed might suggest. He moves well enough at first base, displaying soft hands and decent arm strength. Some evaluators who scouted him as an amateur thought he might be able to handle playing some left field.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Wyatt has a fantastic idea of the strike zone (he walked 20% of the time in college) and his hand path is super short back to the baseball. The combo of the approach and hitting elements make him a notable prospect but Wyatt is also a maxed-out first base-only prospect with 50 raw power and his swing doesn't allow for that power to totally manifest in games. I think he'll end up hitting enough to be a pre-arb 1B/DH stopgap but I'm not betting on him being an everyday guy. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The condor-like Smith creates really tough angle on his pitches (a Brewers pattern of acquisition) by virtue of his extreme height, and he executes his plus changeup with remarkable consistency for a 40-grade athlete. He was a high-priority senior sign in the 2021 draft and ended up getting $1 million, projecting here as a quick-moving reliever. The Brewers shut him down after the 2021 draft and started Smith in the rotation in this season. While he'd show you 95 mph at peak, Smith was sitting 88-91 before he was put on the IL in August with elbow inflammation (he had a TJ in college). He picked up innings in the 2022 Fall League and was wild throughout but was back to sitting about 92. The changeup quality and the possibility of a velo bump out of the bullpen if/when he moves there still has Smith firmly on the big league prospect radar as a reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Smith creates really tough angle on his pitches (a Brewers pattern of acquisition), will show you 95, and executes his changeup with remarkable consistency for a 40-grade athlete. He was a high-priority senior in the 2021 draft and projects as a quick-moving reliever. He was shut down after the draft and has yet to make his pro debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith already made a name for himself as an amateur as the Most Outstanding Pitcher at the 2016 Area Code Games but had a strong commitment to TCU that caused him to drop to the 38th round in 2017. He made six starts for the Horned Frogs as a freshman but missed all of 2019 due to Tommy John surgery and much of 2020 due to the pandemic. Pitching in his fourth collegiate season last year, he posted a 3.83 ERA with 101 strikeouts and 20 walks in 82 1/3 innings, prompting the Brewers to select him in the second round. Smith signed for below slot at $1 million. The first thing that stands out about the southpaw is his height at 6-foot-7. He puts that to good use by creating good extension and a tough angle on his 89-93 mph fastball. The heater, which can touch 95, also plays up because he commands the pitch well within the zone. His mid-80s changeup gives him another above-average offering because of its tough fade. A low-80s slider rounds out the package and was trending in the right direction before the Draft. Smith’s ability to pitch in the zone and avoid free passes differentiates him from other big hurlers, who typically thrive on throwing hard with little command. The lack of a true plus pitch won’t make him an ace, but the rest of the package makes him a potential back-end starter.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text:
A powerful, tightly wound righty from the Midwest, Miller had among the best present arm strength/breaking stuff combinations of the 2022 draft's high school pitchers, and the Marlins gave him $1.7 million to eschew a commitment to Louisville. He hasn't had his peak velocity so far in pro ball. Rather than sit 92-95 mph and bump 97 like he would in high school, Miller's fastball is averaging closer to 92 mph the last few seasons. This is pretty typical for high school pitchers whose throwing schedule and innings count become more labor-intensive as pros, and the hope is that through physical maturity, they can at least maintain their high school velocity, if not improve upon it. Because Miller isn't the most projectable young guy, this is less likely to happen for him. 
Miller's secondary stuff is generating slightly above-average swing-and-miss. His slider and changeup both reside in the 80-84 mph range most of the time, and the slider is a nice east/west complement to Miller's two-seamer. His arm stroke has a little downward stab in the back and makes it a little tougher for Miller to repeat than is ideal, but he's still tracking like a starter, though likely a depth option rather than a rotation mainstay.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text:
A powerful, tightly-wound righty from the Midwest, Miller had among the best present arm strength/breaking stuff combinations of the 2022 draft's high school pitchers and the Marlins gave him just shy of $1.7 million to eschew a commitment to Louisville. So far in 2023, he hasn't quite had his peak velocity. Rather than sit 92-95 mph and bump 97 like he would in high school, Miller's fastball is averaging just shy of 92 mph. This is pretty typical for high school pitchers whose throwing schedule and innings count become more labor intensive as pros, and the hope is that through physical maturity they can at least maintain their high school velocity, if not improve upon it. Because Miller isn't the most projectable young guy, I'm anticipating this to be less likely to happen for him. 
Miller has already shown development in other areas, though. The length and consistency of his arm action changed a couple of times during the last few years but was dialed into a compact, repeatable stroke during his senior season, and remains so. His fastball has better ride than it did in high school when it appeared more tail-oriented to my eye, and Miller's changeup, while clearly a tertiary offering, is flashing bat-missing action and sink. His money pitches remain his two breaking balls, which can run together in the 77-84 mph range but are consistently above-average. The length and break is accentuated on his slower curveball, which is playing a little better than his slider so far because it appears to mesh better with his fastball. There are a lot of starter ingredients here but probably not big upside unless Miller shows an unexpected rebound in velocity.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: A powerful, tightly-wound righty from the Midwest, Miller has among the best present arm strength/breaking stuff combination of the draft's high school pitchers. The length and consistency of his arm action changed a couple of times during the last 18 months of his prospectdom, but was dialed into a compact, repeatable stroke during his senior year. His fastball velocity has been enough for him to pave over high school hitters, but Miller's fastball shape has more sink and tail than ride, which tends to miss fewer bats in pro ball. Some of his fastballs are so nasty, though, that they look like they're going to miss to the glove side of the plate, then run back over the outside corner. Miller's money pitches are his two breaking balls, which can run together in the 77-84 mph range, but are consistently plus. His slider has late bite and significant depth for a high school breaker in the low-80s, and the length and break is accentuated on his slower curveball. Miller isn't so projectable that you'd bank on him adding more velocity in pro ball, but enough that he should sustain his current range. Miller didn't throw many changeups on the showcase circuit, but a few of the ones he did had sink and tail. The pitch shows enough promise that Miller could end up with four average-or-better offerings (depending on how his fastball plays in pro ball), with the two breaking balls near locks to be impact pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller dominated as an Ohio high school senior in 2022, hitting 97 mph with his fastball in his first start and winning Gatorade's state player of the year award. His combination of stuff and polish made him one of the most attractive prep pitchers in the Draft and landed him a $1,697,900 bonus in the second round. He was rarely at his best in 2023, battling diminished velocity and missing six weeks at midseason with a shoulder impingement, though he returned to help Single-A Jupiter win the Florida State League championship. Even when Miller sat at 91-95 mph with his fastball in high school, there were some concerns about its mild armside run and pedestrian metrics, and hitters teed off on his heater when it parked at 88-90 early in 2023. He has switched to a sinker this year and it has operated in the low 90s with more life than his four-seamer. He always has shown good feel for spin, generating high rpms and plenty of depth on an upper-70s curveball and a tighter mid-80s slider. His mid-80s changeup has some fade and sink but needs more velocity separation from his fastball. Miller's high-three-quarters arm slot creates atypical angle and helps him stay on top of his curveball and slider, which he commands better than most youngsters can. His delivery has a short arm action and he repeats it well enough to provide regular strikes. Without a true plus pitch, he may not reach his original ceiling as a No. 3 starter, but he has enough pitches and control to be a No. 4 or 5.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller impressed scouts by popping 97 mph with his fastball in his first start last spring and never took his foot off the gas en route to winning Gatorade Ohio High School Player of the Year honors. His combination of velocity, secondary stuff and pitchability made him one of the top prep pitchers in the 2022 class and earned him a $1,697,900 bonus in the second round. After limiting him to 5 2/3 innings in his pro debut, Miami will turn him loose in Single-A this season. Miller worked on adding strength and velocity before his senior season and came away with a four-seam fastball that sits at 91-95 mph with some arm-side run but pedestrian metrics. He generates high spin rates and impressive depth on each of his breaking balls, a 78-82 mph curveball that dominates hitters more consistently than his tighter 83-87 mph slider. He has impressed the Marlins with his feel for his fading 82-86 mph changeup, which could become a solid offering as he uses it more often. Miller missed nearly two months of his first full pro season with shoulder soreness but returned at the end of July. A tough competitor, he likes to challenge hitters and has the ability to land his curveball where he wants. His high three-quarters arm slot creates difficult angles and helps him stay on top of his breaking pitches.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Kopp is a slow-twitch, long-levered giant. Inevitably there’s some length to his arm path, and despite an otherwise low-effort delivery, he’s never thrown strikes. The stuff is plenty good: He'll touch 97, his height and release give it an unfamiliar shape, and his best sliders have devastating late break. Because he’s left-handed and relatively young, teams are going to do all they can to get him to 40 control. The Dodgers recently added him to their 40-man roster, which speaks to the way even the best club will try to find room for an arm like this. We see mid-leverage upside if Kopp is a late bloomer, though it’s more likely that he’ll bounce up and down from the minors for several years.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: The quality of Kopp's stuff and control is wildly inconsistent from outing to outing, and he's walked at least 14% of opposing hitters since entering full season ball in 2022. It's very difficult to envision him ever being trusted in high-leverage spots, but Kopp's stuff has always been able to miss bats, even when he isn't operating at peak velocities. His size and vertical attack give his fastball tough-to-square angle. He rips it past hitters in the upper half of the zone, while Kopp's 87 mph slider plays best beneath it. It's a pretty typical middle-inning pitch mix hindered by Kopp's stagnant feel for location.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
There was a stretch when high school Kopp looked like a potential first round pick, as at the time, he was an extremely projectable 6-foot-4 lefty who was already reaching back for mid-90s heat. But Kopp's ability to find the strike zone evaporated during his senior year, his velocity regressed as he desperately aimed for the zone, and he de-committed from ASU, opting instead to go to South Mountain Junior College, where these issues continued. Fresh eyes got to watch Kopp throw in the MLB Draft League and at the Combine, and rather than fixate on and grow fatigued by his persistent issues, they saw a lefty with huge arm strength and a potentially good breaking ball. Now pro scouts can't believe Kopp signed for just $125,000. 
He spent the bulk of his first two seasons working as a starter for three innings at a time before the Dodgers put Kopp in the bullpen at the end of the 2023 regular season and Fall League. Kopp sits 95-98 and will occasionally touch 100 in relief. His north/south arm slot should theoretically impart big vertical depth on his breaking balls, but the shape and velo of those offerings is inconsistent, nasty at times and hittable at others. Kopp is only 21 and long-levered leviathans like him usually take a while to hone their command. He likely won't develop enough to be a starter, but he has a good shot to be a late-inning bullpen weapon if he can tighten up his breaking ball consistency.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: There was a little while during his pre-draft summer coming out of high school when Kopp looked like a potential first round pick. He was an extremely projectable, 6-foot-4 (now 6-foot-6) lefty who was already reaching back for mid-90s heat. But Kopp's ability to find the strike zone evaporated, and he struggled to throw strikes against even Single-A varsity hitters in Arizona during his senior year at a little school in Scottsdale. His velocity regressed as he desperately aimed for the zone, and not only did area scouts start to develop fatigue here, but Kopp also de-committed from ASU and instead opted to go to South Mountain Junior College, where these issues continued. Fresh eyes got to watch Kopp throw in the MLB Draft League and at the Combine, seeing a young, projectable lefty with huge arm strength rather than fixating on his issues. Now pro scouts can't believe Kopp lasted until the 12th round. He spent 2022 working two and three innings at a time mostly at Low-A Rancho, where he sat 94-97 mph with a routinely plus slider. Kopp is still quite wild and will need to progress in the strike-throwing realm to have any sort of regular big league role, but his stuff is consistent with a late-inning lefty reliever. He's a FV tier behind pitchers with similar stuff because of his distance from the big leagues, and because his command is a bit more tenuous than the Sheehan/Henriquez types.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: There was a little while during his pre-draft summer coming out of high school when Kopp looked like a potential first round pick. He was an extremely projectable, 6-foot-4 (now 6-foot-6) lefty who was already reaching back for mid-90s heat. But Kopp's ability to find the strike zone evaporated, and he struggled to throw strikes against even Single-A varsity hitters in Arizona during his senior year at a little school in Scottsdale. His velocity regressed as he desperately aimed for the zone, and not only did area scouts start to develop fatigue here, but Kopp also de-committed from ASU and instead opted to go to South Mountain Junior College, where these issues continued. Fresh eyes got to watch Kopp throw in the MLB Draft League and at the Combine, seeing a young, projectable lefty with huge arm strength rather than fixating on his issues. Now scouts can't believe Kopp, who is still 19, lasted until the 12th round. The extreme wildness is still often a part of the operation, but Kopp is a 19-year-old lefty sitting 95-97 mph with a routinely plus slider. He has high-leverage relief potential if the walks can get to an acceptable place.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kopp projected as an early-round pick after winning Gatorade's 2019 Arizona high school player of the year award as a junior, but he went unselected in 2020 after regressing as a senior. He was erratic again at South Mountain (Ariz.) CC but helped his cause by standing out as one of the best arms in the inaugural season of the MLB Draft League in 2021, prompting the Dodgers to sign him for $125,000 in the 12th round. One of the more unhittable lefties in the Minors, he limited opponents to a .178 average while striking out 220 in 136 2/3 innings during his first two-plus pro seasons -- though he also walked 94 and has yet to last longer than four frames in a game. When Kopp is dialed in, both his fastball and slider can be plus-plus weapons, and his 36 percent strikeout rate last year ranked second in the Minors among pitchers with 70 or more innings, trailing only fellow Dodgers farmhand Kyle Hurt (39 percent). His heater typically parks at 94-97 mph and peaks at 99 with riding action, while his slide piece can devastate hitters with its mid-80s velocity and sweep. But he also struggles to command his fastball and land his slider for strikes, which reduces their effectiveness. More physical than athletic at 6-foot-7 and 250 pounds, Kopp has difficulty keeping his long limbs and his delivery and sync and has no track record of providing strikes. He also continues to search for a reliable third pitch, dabbling with a slow curveball, a very raw mid-80s changeup and sometimes turning his slider into a harder cutter. Los Angeles began deploying him as a reliever in the final month of the 2023 season and in the Arizona Fall League, and that's a more realistic role unless his control somehow improves dramatically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2019 Arizona high school player of the year as a junior, Kopp baffled scouts with fluctuating velocity and diminished control as a senior and went unpicked in the shortened five-round Draft in 2020. Originally committed to Arizona State, he instead went to South Mountain (Ariz.) CC and stood out as one of the best arms in the inaugural 2021 season of the MLB Draft League. Signed as an 12th-rounder that summer, he had a .170 opponent average with 108 strikeouts in 62 1/3 innings between stops at Single-A and High-A in his first full pro season, but he also walked 43. There aren't many left-handers with better pure stuff than Kopp, who operated at 95-97 mph and touched 99 with riding life on his fastball in abbreviated outings in 2022. His slider can be a wipeout pitch with mid-80s velocity and sweep, though it lacks consistency and he can struggle to land it in the zone. The Dodgers have had him scrap a splitter in favor of a more traditional changeup that's still quite raw but has some fade. Kopp's huge 6-foot-7, 250-pound frame creates a difficult angle for hitters, though he's much more physical than athletic. He struggles to keep his delivery in sync and has no history of throwing strikes. He's still young enough that it makes sense to develop him as a starter, but it's probably more realistic that he becomes a high-leverage reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Tresh has above-average pull power and plus raw arm strength. His pop times are often in the 1.9s but his throws tend to sail on him rather than be on the bag, so his effectiveness in stopping the run game plays down a little bit. While Tresh has big power for a catcher, he struggles to cover the outer third of the plate and swings inside a lot of pitches in the strike zone, as well as over the top of a lot of breaking balls, and he's likely to end up as a 20- or 30-grade bat, which is basically par for the course at catcher. Tresh receives on one knee even with runners on base, in a style similar to former Phillies catcher Carlos Ruiz, where Tresh is very low, almost in a half split. This sometimes makes it harder for him to block balls in the dirt but aides his ability to frame low pitches. While he needs polish, Tresh projects as a power-over-hit backup catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: A catcher with plus-plus raw will always appeal to scouts, but many evaluators have put 40 or lower grades on his hit tool, and a lack of accuracy mitigates his plus arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A hamate bone injury caused Tresh to miss the start of his 2020 collegiate season, but he put himself back on the radar at North Carolina State in 2021, when he homered 15 times in 56 games and helped the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. The Royals selected him in the 17th round and gave him a high bonus – $423,000 – to sign him away from returning to school. Tresh posted an .828 OPS between High-A and Double-A in his first full pro season in 2022, with 14 homers and 54 RBI. Tresh is a strong hitter who generates impressive exit velocities with his raw power and bat speed. He made more contact in 2022 with a 24.3% strikeout rate between both levels. Tresh is still aggressive, and there are still improvements to be made in his approach, especially with pitches on the outer part of the plate, but he has a lot of power potential. Behind the plate, Tresh showed significant improvement with his receiving last year. He has a plus arm and should become at least an average defender. Tresh receives high marks for his ability to run a pitching staff, a quiet competitor who leads by example. How far he goes and what his ceiling ends up being depends on whether he can continue his improved approach and contact at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At North Carolina State, Tresh caught sparingly behind Patrick Bailey, the No. 13 pick in 2020, and Tresh missed the start of the 2020 season with a broken hamate bone in his left hand. He put himself back on the radar and filled Bailey’s void in ’21, homering 15 times in 56 games last spring and helping the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. It felt like a steal when the Royals selected him all the way down in the 17th round, but Tresh stuck to his signability and wasn’t afraid to go back to school if needed. The Royals were able to sign him for $423,000, roughly the slot of a fourth-round selection. Tresh posted a 1.143 OPS in six games in Rookie ball after he was drafted, earning him a quick promotion to Low-A Columbia, where he struggled more in 10 games. Tresh has obvious raw power and consistently high exit velocities thanks to massive strength and bat speed. He’s aggressive at the plate and will need to do a better job of consistent contact, but the Royals see room for improvement as he spends more time with the hitting development program. Behind the plate, Tresh is inexperienced for a college catcher, but he showed significant improvement as a receiver in the fall. He has a plus arm to keep the running game in check and should become at least an average defender if the Royals keep him at catcher. Tresh earns praise for his leadership, ability to run a pitching staff and his quiet competitiveness. He still has a lot of ceiling for a college player, which was appealing to the Royals in the Draft. How far he will go depends on his improvement with contact and time behind the plate.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Prosecky is a fun watch. He’s a high-slot guy with a Bugs Bunny sinking change and a slow curve that practically takes a nap on its way to the plate. Arm strength is an ongoing concern here, as he touched 95 at times but was sitting in the upper 80s by the end of last season. His fastball doesn't have bat-missing shape, but he does hide the ball well, so it’s a viable weapon if he can just keep it in the 90s. While his command isn’t bad, it isn't sharp either, and the result is a lot of nibbling and more fastballs leaking over the heart of the plate than he can afford. It’s the skill set of a crafty lefty who isn't quite crafty enough to start. He projects as a spot starter or swingman, roles Prosecky will likely be ready for by 2027.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: After pitching out of the Louisville bullpen for his entire college tenure, Prosecky's pro career got off to a great start in the Fresno rotation in 2023. He began 2024 on the shelf with elbow inflammation, but he was good when he returned: 14 games, 48.2 IP, 78 K (but a 1.42 WHIP). Prosecky only sits 91-93 mph, but hitters don't seem to pick it up. The southpaw has a short, vertical arm stroke that helps his heater play as an in-zone bat misser despite below-average velocity. He hides the ball forever and it appears to jump on hitters very quickly. He throws a classic 12-to-6 curveball off of that, a pitch that's virtually indistinguishable from his fastball until it starts to bend with huge, bat-missing depth. Those two pitches give Prosecky a lower-leverage reliever's foundation. Prosecky's arm stroke isn't always well timed, and his strike-throwing results have been mixed during this try as a starter. In the 2024 Fall League, Prosecky was working with a second breaking ball, a slider in the 82-84 mph range that looked below average. There's definitely more variance here than is typical for a guy who sits 92, but Prosecky is tracking like a low-leverage lefty.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: After pitching out of the Louisville bullpen for his entire college tenure, Prosecky's pro career got off to a great start in the Fresno rotation last season, but he began 2024 on the shelf with elbow inflammation. The southpaw has a short, vertical arm stroke that helps his heater play as an in-zone bat misser despite average velocity. He hides the ball forever and it appears to jump on hitters very quickly. Off of that he throws a classic 12-to-6 curveball, which is virtually indistinguishable from his fastball until it starts to bend with huge, bat-missing depth. Those two pitches give Prosecky a reliever's foundation. He's a bit of a short strider and his arm stroke isn't always well-timed, but so far Prosecky has thrown enough strikes to continue developing as a starter. His third pitch is currently a changeup, which is still below average but has long-term ceiling because of the whip of Prosecky's arm stroke. It's perhaps more likely that his ability to spin it leads to a second type of breaker, like a two-planed slider. Either way, Prosecky is probably just scratching the surface of a third offering because of his collegiate role. The median projection for Prosecky is that of a backend starter.
