He'll flash a power upper-80s changeup and has precocious slider command. If one of them becomes plus, then Ortiz should be a fine reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Puerto Rico, Ortiz slid over to Florida’s IMG Academy for high school ball as a two-way player who was initially known more as a shortstop. The Nationals took him in the 20th round of the 2022 Draft, as a pitcher, but he opted to head to junior college instead, playing both ways for Chipola. The Reds took him as a draft-and-follow in 2023, then saw enough progress on the mound back at Chipola to sign him for $225,000 that May. He got his feet wet the summer after signing, then threw over 90 effective innings with full-season Daytona in 2025. An athletic six-foot right-hander, Ortiz continues to get better the longer he’s been focused on pitching only. His fastball is gaining velocity and he throws it mostly in the 90-95 mph range with some armside run, and there could be more consistent velo to come in the future. The Reds feel his 84-87 mph changeup is ahead of his 83-86 mph slider but not by much, and there’s conviction he could end up having three above-average pitches down the road. In addition to the stuff ticking up, Ortiz used his athleticism to find the strike zone more consistently in 2025 and it’s not difficult to believe that he will eventually display average command. He has full-time starter upside with the organization excited to see how he handles a climb up the ladder and a heavier workload.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
At the plate, Duran’s strong bat-to-ball skills are allowing him to make good contact despite a couple of visual cues that give me pause. He’s a late lander with bat speed that's just fair, a looping hand load, and a somewhat grooved upper cut swing. He keeps his hands back well, though, and while he’s a little vulnerable to spin, he’s still often capable of adjusting off the fastball and doing something to spoil a tough pitch; there’s some hit skill here. The power is fringy, however, so while he’s got a chance to be competitive against big league pitching, he projects as more of a playable hitter than a good one.
Defensively, Duran projects as an average backstop. He’s not a huge guy, but he's built well enough to withstand the rigors of the job. He’s a quiet receiver, and while he doesn't have the world’s strongest wrist, he gets low and his movements are so small that he’s pretty good at stealing strikes. His control of the running game is just fair. He gets the ball out quickly, and his high transfer looks natural and smooth, but the ball sails on him as often as not. The whole operation looks great when he times everything up and delivers a strike; perhaps he'll be able to do so more often with reps. 
As a strong framer with competent but otherwise unremarkable skills and tools, Duran is the kind of player who seems likely to be hurt by ABS. He still projects as a solid backup, but the league has narrowed his most viable path to exceeding that forecast.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Duran is a backup catching prospect who was acquired from Miami as the PTBNL in the trade that sent Jordan Groshans to the Marlins for Anthony Bass and Zach Pop. He has performed well from a strikeout and walk standpoint in the lower minors, but realistically, the undersized Duran's offensive output is going to be meager. Still, Duran (who catches from a traditional crouch with runners on base, an endangered species) can really throw (he's remarkably accurate) and has sensational hands. He needs to get stronger at the catch point to improve as a framer, but Duran's throwing and ball-blocking are both plus. He had modest success as a hitter in Low-A (97 wRC+) in 2024. The 2025 season is his 40-man platform year, but Duran is going to be a slower burn who is more like two or three years away from being rostered.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Curley is a highly entertaining little (Georgia) bulldog righty. He spent two years at Virginia Commonwealth and was drafted in 2024 but opted to transfer to Georgia, where he moved from the bullpen to the rotation during the year. He has a max effort drop-and-drive delivery with a powerful lower body. He sat 95-96 in his starts and has touched 100 mph in relief. 
Curley has a couple breaking balls. His strike-stealing curveball has the most consistent shape and is more of a strike pitch in the 75-80 mph range. His slider/cutter is much more variable in terms of movement and location, but has the best chance to miss bats. Both can be nasty even when they're not located well. He’s athletic enough to start but frankly at his size and effort level, the injury risk seems pretty high in that role. Curley could move quickly in relief, and his feel for the zone could also facilitate a hybrid role.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Highly entertaining little bulldog righty whose size will likely limit him to the bullpen in pro ball. Spent two years at VCU and was drafted in 2024 but opted to transfer to Georgia, where he moved from the bullpen to the rotation during the year. Max effort drop-and-drive delivery with powerful lower body. Sitting 95-96 and up to 98 as a starter, touched 100 in relief. Throws a couple different breaking balls. Strike-stealing curveball has the most consistent shape in the 75-70 mph range. Slider/cutter is much more variable in terms of movement and location, as hard as 91 mph. They're often nasty even when not located well. Quick-moving power relief mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It should come as no surprise that Cleveland's biggest international signing in a deep 2026 class was another switch-hitting shortstop. Reinoso fits the bill after signing for $820,000 out of the Dominican Republic, although he is more physical than some other recent signings and is already listed at 6-foot, 200 pounds. It's quite early, but his raw tools, particularly on offense, are exciting. Reinoso was initially just a left-handed swinger but learned to switch-hit and is making rapid strides from the right side. He controls the zone well for his age and has a good feel for contact. He already does a good job of putting the ball in the air, so there's a chance for above-average power as he physically matures. Cleveland's system is full of middle infielders, so Reinoso will likely need to move around the diamond, but he'll have a chance to stick at shortstop. His arm is plenty strong for the left side of the infield, and he's a pretty fluid mover despite not being overly speedy. If he does have to shift to the hot corner, there's reason to believe he'll have the bat to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding big lefties with good stuff isn't always so easy, so Eaton got plenty of attention during his time at George Mason University. He worked out of the Patriots' rotation for two years, missing bats but with poor command. The Rockies thought he was worth a flier with their sixth-round pick in the 2024 Draft, and after sending him out that summer as a reliever for a brief pro debut, there was a lot of internal talk about putting him in the bullpen. That thinking has been shelved, however, after Eaton made 27 starts and amassed 140 innings while reaching Double-A in his first full season of pro ball, leading the organization in strikeouts, K/9 and strikeout percentage. Eaton is now showing an ability to throw three pitches for strikes and that, along with showing acumen for finishing hitters, gives him a chance to start. His fastball sits around 93 mph and he can reach back for 95-96. He'll carry his velocity deep into starts, and the pitch has occasional cut or tail to it. His mid-80s slider is his best pitch, eliciting a miss rate north of 40 percent last year. He'll manipulate its shape, sometimes throwing it with sweep, sometimes with the tilt and depth of a more traditional slider. A big reason for his success thus far has been his conviction in throwing his low-80s changeup more. The big left-hander struggled with the strike zone throughout his college career, a big reason why the Rockies weren't the only ones thinking he belonged in a bullpen. It's not pinpoint command, but he's around the zone enough where the organization thinks he might have the ability to stick in a rotation for a long time.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Eaton has a well-rounded mix of average stuff and strike-throwing. He has both fastballs, and while he touches 96 mph with the four-seamer, both have round-down shape limits their utility. His change and slider are both average and play a little ahead of that grade due to his ability to move them around the plate. The southpaw is also good at some of the old school stuff, like sequencing and changing speeds. In my looks, his control tended to be great right until it fell apart completely, and between that and the lack of an out pitch, he looks like more of a one-time-through guy than a reliable starter. There’s also a chance everything plays a half-grade better than this projection in short stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers broke with their track record of spreading out international signing bonus money across several players to make some big-money deals for a few years. One such example was Santana, whose $2.95 million bonus was a franchise record when the 13th-ranked prospect of his class signed in January 2021. Santana showed some intriguing stretches over his first couple years in the organization to suggest he was worth the attention, reaching Single-A Lakeland at age 18. Then came 2023, a campaign that saw the 19-year-old move all over the infield, bat .156 over 97 games and draw nearly twice as many walks (91) as hits (48). Santana signed with reports of an advanced bat for his age, yet nearly half of his plate appearances ended with walks (21.7 percent) or strikeouts (27.7). He produced 12 home runs in 97 games at Lakeland, including seven at spacious Joker Marchant Stadium, and half his hits went for extra bases, yet he averaged exit velocities in the 80s across a variety of pitch types. He produced a high walk rate but still chased too many pitches out of the zone, a trend he’s working to reverse. He bulked up his frame last year in search of power, but he might have outgrown the shortstop position, at least on a full-time basis. The Tigers still like Santana’s talent and are willing to let him figure things out, but are nonetheless nearing decision time with other infield prospects making their way up the system. He’s still just 20 years old and is determined to play his way back into top status, but he needs to reshape his game as a hitter to give himself a chance, especially if he has outgrown becoming a full-time shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers thought enough of Santana coming out of the Dominican Republic to sign him for a franchise-record $2.95 million bonus as part of their international class in January 2021. MLB Pipeline’s 13th-ranked international prospect didn’t need long to make an impact, tearing up the Dominican Summer League later that year and then making a quick impression in the Tigers’ Minor League mini-camp the following spring. He skipped the Rookie-level Florida Complex League and went to the Single-A Florida State League, where he received enough of a challenge at age 18 to slow his lofty comparisons but showed flashes of what many still believe is impressive potential. Not surprisingly, Santana’s raw power dropped some as expected in a Major League Spring Training park in Lakeland. He still used his strong lower body for an uptick in line drives while better using the whole field. He shows a smooth, quick swing and advanced plate discipline for his age at the plate, reflected in a 15.9 percent walk rate last year, but his strikeout rate also ticked up. His speed has yet to translate into stolen bases or triples. Santana moved around the infield in Lakeland as part of a rotation with Manuel Sequera and Peyton Graham. His speed and quickness enabled him to hold his own at short, but he reportedly gained weight over the offseason in search for more power and the Tigers have moved him around in his return to the FSL with looks at second and third. The Tigers have a logjam in the middle infield at the lower levels of their farm system, but a slow start back in Lakeland has kept him in Single-A for 2023. Santana made an in-season adjustment regarding the position of his hands in the box and his swing path, and the changes have led to a late-season surge. He still has many parts of his game to smooth out, but his raw talent is some of the best in the organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For years, the Tigers spread out their bonus money on the international market for several small- and mid-level signings, rather than throwing big money into any particular prospect. They changed course a few years ago for players like Santana, who received a team-record $2.95 million bonus when he signed with Detroit in January 2021. He ranked No. 13 on MLB Pipeline’s prospect list for his international class at the time, then backed it up by posting a .942 OPS as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League later that year. Santana has very strong legs, which provide both the strength of his right-handed swing and the low center of gravity that helps him move smoothly and quickly at short. His above-average bat speed and efficient swing allow him to turn on power pitches and make him difficult to pitch inside. He isn’t afraid to stand up on the plate and was hit by 15 pitches over just 54 games in the DSL. For his power, he doesn’t chase as often as others his age, and he can recognize breaking pitches. He might not make highlight plays at short, but he has the potential to be a reliable defender, earning him comparisons to Jhonny Peralta, though his current build brings some comparisons to former Tigers prospect Willy Adames. Santana has good speed with his leg strength but is still learning how to utilize it on the basepaths. Detroit’s recent investment in the international market has resulted in a class of talented players with Santana at the top, but the Tigers have historically avoided rushing their international prospects. They’ve changed up tactics a bit for Santana, who has spent much of his age-18 season with Single-A Lakeland. It’s been a growing experience for him -- one with plenty of walks but a relatively low average -- but the establishment of some stateside success is good for his future development.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers have spent more aggressively in the international market the past few years, with Santana as the latest example. The Dominican shortstop ranked 14th on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list when he signed with Detroit for a team-record $2.95 million bonus in January 2021. The Tigers scouted Santana for nearly three years. One evaluator believes he has the natural ability to become an impact hitter once he grows into his body frame. MLB Pipeline’s scouting report compared him to Jhonny Peralta, who played four seasons in Detroit during a 15-year Major League career. He has above-average bat speed with an advanced approach and raw power that should improve with maturity. He’s a steady if not flashy defender with quick feet and an average arm. He has the quickness and speed to be a plus runner. Like slugging outfielder Roberto Campos, Santana faces a long path to reach the big leagues. Also like Campos, his upside sets him apart from others at this point in the system. His bat skills should allow him to chew up lower-level pitching once he gets more experience.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Santana was billed as one of the more advanced and complete hitters in his international class, but in parts of three pros seasons, he's been more of a power-over-hit type who has begun to share time all over the infield. Some of that is due more to the presence of Peyton Graham on the Lakeland roster than his own issues at shortstop, though Santana has become strapping and thick in his lower half very quickly, and his defensive projection shifted off of shortstop more than a year ago. Along with Santana's strength has come impressive power for his age, but his feel to hit has simply not been what was hoped when he was an amateur, especially his slider recognition. Santana had a concerning 25% strikeout rate in the 2022 FSL and was out of the gates slow early in 2023 when he was put on the IL with a left knee contusion suffered during a game in mid-May. The strikeout issues have been bad enough for long enough now to stop forecasting Santana as a potential everyday player. Unless he continues to develop much more power than is projected here, the hit tool is going to prevent that from happening even if Santana stays at short. He's now in a hopeful role-player bucket behind some of the similar upper-level hitters who are better shortstop defenders.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Among the most polished hitters in the 2021 international class, Santana went to the DSL in 2021 and posted a great line, slashing .269/.421/.520 with nine homers in 54 games. His swing is compact but dynamic throughout the hitting zone, he has natural feel for all-fields contact, and his swing's gentle loft creates power without compromising much contact. He was generating Placido Polanco comps as an amateur, billed as an ultra-polished wunderkind hitter more than a guy who was going to be among the DSL leaders in tanks. Santana did not come stateside for Detroit's (limited) fall instructional activity and is among the higher-priority 2022 spring targets, as we're still living off his amateur report with no compelling reason to shift away from those fairly lofty expectations.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Among the more polished hitters in the most recent international class, Santana's swing is compact but dynamic throughout the hitting zone, he has natural feel for all-fields contact and his swing's gentle loft creates power without compromising much contact. He's this year's Placido Polanco comp, projecting to play second or third and hit enough to profile there. (International signee)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was the Royals’ top international signee in 2021 and signed for $1.5 million out of the Dominican Republic and the club sent him to Single-A Columbia right away in '22 as an 18-year-old. It has been a slow progression from there, spending three seasons in Columbia before making it to High-A Quad Cities in ‘25. He slashed .260/.333/.351 across 116 games, which also included six games on a rehab stint in the ACL and five games at the end of the year in Double-A Northwest Arkansas. Vazquez was the Royals’ best hitter in the Arizona Fall League, though, with a .928 OPS in 22 games and nearly as many walks (19) as strikeouts (20). Vazquez has always been a solid defender, but his bat has been slower to develop. It’s coming along, though, with harder contact recently. He’s gotten a lot stronger in the past year or so and really grown into his 6-foot-2 frame with broad shoulders. Vazquez is starting to have an understanding of the zone and hasn't been so fooled by breaking balls, allowing him to make more contact. He’s a potential plus defender with good hands and instincts with a strong arm to boot. Some think that as he’s filled out, he might be better suited for second base or even third, but you’d like to see a little more pop if you move him to the corner. An above-average runner with good instincts on the bases, Vazquez has the profile of a utility infielder if he can continue the positive trend with his bat. He was in big league camp this spring, which allowed him to learn a lot about the Major League routine.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals’ top signee in the 2021 international signing period, Vazquez signed out of the Dominican for $1.5 million. The team was aggressive with him early, sending him right to Single-A Columbia in 2022 as an 18-year-old. He has spent three seasons there making incremental progress with his game. In 2024, Vazquez slashed .253/.353/.289 with a 13.2% walk rate, 22.2% strikeout rate and a 99 wRC+. He missed about six weeks with a hamate injury and finished his season in the Arizona Fall League, hitting .298 with a .744 OPS in 14 games. Vazquez has always been a defense-first shortstop with good hands, instincts and agile movements that make the Royals believe he can stick at the position. Offensively, Vazquez has made slow but steady progress just with his hit tool and really increased his line-drive rate in ‘24. He’s in a better neutral position with his swing, which helps, and he’s also stronger and more physical after four seasons in pro ball. Vazquez flashed raw power when he was an amateur and still has good bat speed now, but the power has yet to show up in games. It might be more extra-base hit potential than anything. Vazquez has a strong arm and is an above-average runner. After three years, Vazquez headed up to High-A Quad Cities for 2025. His defense plays, and the Royals will stick with him as a shortstop, but he’ll have to show just a bit more offensively to reach his ceiling, which is likely as a utility player who can get on base unless he really finds something with his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez was in high demand during the 2020-21 international signing period because of his tremendous upside, and he signed with the Royals for $1.5 million. He came to the United States a year later, which was ambitious for his age-18 season, and he was overmatched at Single-A Columbia in ‘22. He returned in ‘23 and made modest gains, with a .618 OPS, 15 doubles, 32 stolen bases, a 13.2 percent walk rate and 22.7 percent strikeout rate in 113 games. Vazquez is a glove-first prospect right now, although some evaluators still believe the power is coming because of the capability to add strength to his athletic frame. He shows good actions on the left side of the infield, makes agile movements and exhibits a plus arm with accurate throws. More repetitions will lead to fewer mental mistakes and make him a reliable defender over a flashy one. Vazquez had a line-drive profile when he first signed, and he’s slowly starting to get there with his smooth and repeatable right-handed swing. He needs to show improvement in his swing decisions to make the most of his physical gains. Still young with upside, Vazquez has had a slow start to his pro career, and the Royals knew they were being aggressive when they pushed him to Columbia. His defense will play, so it’ll be his hit tool that will determine his role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vazquez received comps to Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado during the 2020-21 international signing period and was coveted by teams because of his enormous upside. The Royals were able to sign him for $1.5 million and brought him over to the States a year later, where he went straight to Single-A Columbia in 2022. The Royals acknowledged that was ambitious for his age-18 season, and it wasn’t without struggles: Vazquez slashed just .195/.262/.229 with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate, 10 doubles and no homers in 77 games. He’s been sent back to the Carolina League for 2023 and has shown modest gains with the bat but still hasn’t been league-average. Vazquez looks the part with his athletic frame that has only added strength since he became a Royal. His defense wows with agile movement, exceptional reads, quick hands and good footwork. He profiles as a starting shortstop, but it remains to be seen what the Royals have with Vazquez offensively. He has a smooth, repeatable swing that should produce line drives as he matures. He’s shown nice rhythm and timing to his at-bats, but little has come into focus with the results. Vazquez looked overpowered and overmatched in Columbia last year as an 18-year-old facing a lot of older pitchers. The Royals were impressed with how Vazquez held himself despite the struggles last season. His tools give scouts something to dream on. Vazquez is still all upside in his projection and will need to show some offensive breakthroughs to be able to understand what kind of player he could be.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2020-21 international signing period, Vazquez received comps to what Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado looked and played like when they were teenagers. The Royals signed Vazquez, who was ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list, in the early days of the signing period for $1.5 million. After spending his first season in the Dominican Summer League, Vazquez skipped right over the Arizona Complex League and moved to Single-A Columbia for his age-18 season. Results with the Fireflies have been hard to come by, but the Royals maintain the teenager is just getting going with plenty of room to grow. Vazquez has already put on strength since he was signed, and that led to improved impact at the Dominican Academy last summer; despite the lack of results, reports mentioned how much louder the ball sounded off his bat. His smooth, repeatable swing makes a healthy amount of contact, and he should add more extra-base hits as he matures. He has average speed with above-average baserunning skills, and he’s an excellent defender with exceptional reads, a quick release and good footwork. He should remain at shortstop, and the Royals have yet to play him anywhere else in his first two seasons. Scouts see the long, lean and athletic prospect hitting at the top or even near the middle of the order as he develops, and he has a solid ceiling as a well-rounded player. Even with Vazquez’s 2022 struggles, Kansas City officials continue to point out that he moved to the Carolina League at the same age as an American high-school senior. A full-season breakout could be on tap for 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 12 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 International Prospects list in 2020-21, Vazquez is built like a young Fernando Tatis Jr. and compares favorably to a teenage Manny Machado. The Royals were able to sign the Dominican amateur in the early days of the international signing period, which was pushed back to January due to the pandemic. Long, lean and with an athletic frame, the 16-year-old Vazquez has a lot of room to grow. A smooth and repeatable swing makes consistent contact, and he projects to have average power. Some believe he will be able to hit around 15-20 home runs while hitting at or near the top of the batting over, and he has solid speed with projected above-average baserunning skills. Vazquez should remain at shortstop to start his pro career, with quick hands and great instincts. He gets exceptional reads on ground balls, features a quick release, has the ability to throw from all angles and shows good footwork at the position. Vazquez has reported to the Royals’ Dominican academy, and game action will determine more of a plan for his development. The projection is there but there’s still a long way to go for the young player. His hit tool and defensive ability give him a carrying asset.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
Kansas City's top 2021 international signee, at this point Vazquez could probably give you a good restaurant recommendation in Columbia, as 2024 is his third straight year with the A-ball affiliate. He tallied just under 800 plate appearances for Columbia between 2022-2023, striking out 24.2% of the time and slugging under .300. That being said, those were pretty aggressive assignments and Vazquez is still slightly young for the level. Although his bat still lacks extra-base power, he’s at least hitting for average and getting on base in his third look at the league. 
What was once a high-effort swing has been tamped down to a much quieter operation with fewer moving parts. While the swing is more under control, he’s still chasing frequently enough for it to hinder his hit tool projection. When he does connect, he's spraying his contact to all fields. Vazquez is playing shortstop exclusively and is developing into a solid defender up the middle with his body control and soft hands. He has elements of quick-twitch in his movements and moves well laterally, which will enable him to cover more than enough ground to stay at short. He’s still prone to inaccurate throws across the diamond, which he'll need to shore up to reach his defense-first bench utility projection.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Kansas City's top 2021 international signee, Vazquez really struggled with a 2022 full-season assignment at age 18 and was sent back to Columbia to start 2023. He's hitting the ball harder than last year, but he hasn't made any bat-to-ball progress and is still more of a magmatic collection of twitch and projection than he is clearly a prospect at this point. He won't be 20 until December and is already very physical, he will show you plus bat speed, and he has a cannon when he steps into a throw. But a slow exchange and tight hips prevent him from making a lot of odd-platformed throws cleanly or quickly, and Vazquez's swing features a ton of effort and he doesn't track especially well. There are meaningful tools present here but still a long developmental road ahead.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Parrish is a lefty with a plus changeup and starter-caliber command, so he’s extremely likely to play a big league role of some kind, but whether or not he can seize a rotation spot for the long haul may be dictated by how his breaking ball develops. It’s an extremely slow, lollipop curveball in the 69-72 mph range, almost an Eephus-style curveball in the Zack Greinke and Vicente Padilla mold. It would be a cute fourth or fifth option if it were allowed to function as a get-me-over surprise a few times per start, but it’s Parrish's third pitch. It’s possible the Royals will help him parlay his natural ability to spin the ball (his curveball spin rates are often in the 2600-2700 rpm range) into a firmer slider, but that hasn't happened yet. It’s encouraging that they've done something similar with Jonathan Heasley, who had a below-average curveball in previous years and has added a really hard, upper-80s slider in 2022. Parrish only sits in the low-90s but his short, deceptive arm action and his fastball’s carry make it a viable offering, and help it miss bats in the strike zone. Lefties with a changeup this good tend to be valuable big league contributors either toward the back of the rotation or as a swingman/spot-starter type. The key variable here is whether Parrish can find a breaking ball sufficient for the upper part of that range of outcomes.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Parrish is a lefty with a pretty good changeup, and those guys tend to wind up having big league careers, even if it's just as upper-level depth. His velo was on the rise just before the 2019 draft, averaging just over 90 mph for the first time in his career, but in the postseason he was back to 87-91 when he had to rely more on his secondary stuff. That's probably the approach he'll need to take going forward, as both his changeup and curveball are better offerings than the heater. He projects as a fifth/sixth starter barring an unforeseen bump in velocity. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Florida State, Parrish did enough to warrant the Royals’ attention in the 2019 Draft, when they took the southpaw in the eighth round and signed him for slot at $184,700, shortly after he dominated Arkansas in the College World Series. After the 2020 season was canceled due to the pandemic, Parrish shoved in Double-A Northwest Arkansas last year, striking out 95 in 83 innings with a 3.36 ERA across 18 games as one of the most consistent starters in the Royals’ system. He even earned a spot with Team USA’s Olympic Qualifying team. Parrish might have been overlooked in the Draft due to his 5-foot-11 frame and lack of velocity, throwing in the high 80s for most of college, but he’s up to low 90s consistently now -- and even flashed 94-95 mph in 2021. Parrish’s headliner is his changeup, an upper-70s pitch that consistently misses bats. He didn’t have to use his curveball much as an amateur, but he’s significantly improved the pitch to be at least average. Parrish doesn’t have a fast arm, but it’s extremely efficient. He can spot the ball to all four quadrants and walked just 25 batters in 83 innings in 2021. Parrish’s ceiling may be limited because of his velocity, but Royals officials love the way he pitches and his overall craftiness. His dominance last season also proved that velocity isn’t everything. A back-end starting role is an attainable goal, but Parrish could end up filling a lot of roles for the Royals -- starter, bulk pitcher out of the bullpen or a middle-inning reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Hartle came over from Pittsburgh as part of the infamous Luis Ortiz trade. His slender frame, low release, easy-going delivery, glove tuck, and high socks all bear an uncanny visual resemblance to Andrew Heaney, though the youngster’s arm path is longer and he’s not quite as deceptive overall. Like the recently retired soft-tosser, Hartle sits in the low 90s and isn't going to blow anyone away. The angle and shapes on his fastballs are unusual enough to miss barrels, but he'll need to rely on his slider and change to punch tickets. As was the case for Heaney, Hartle’s low slot is perfectly geared to throw a late-fading cambio, one that should help him limit platoon splits. He deftly suppressed hard contact in High-A last year, but his secondaries aren't so good as to think he'll be able to do so against big leaguers. He projects as a no. 5 starter, a lite-beer version of… well, you can probably guess by this point.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Hartle was a 6-foot-5 lefty who had a ton of profile in high school. He wasn't throwing hard then, but you could dream on his build and delivery, especially under the tutelage of Wake Forest’s pitching dev program. It looked like Hartle was making the leap as a sophomore, even without increased velocity, but his performance backed up during his junior year and the Pirates signed him for $850,00 in the 2024 third round. During the offseason, he was traded to Cleveland as part of the Spencer Horwitz shuffle, and he opened 2025 at High-A Lake County. Hartle still isn't throwing especially hard, but his mechanical consistency, balance, and ease for a pitcher his size are still remarkable. He has platoon-neutralizing weapons in his changeup and curveball, while his cutter and slider act as a way to keep hitters from hammering a mediocre heater. It's not the high-variance/high-upside profile of his high school days, as Hartle now projects as an innings-eating fifth starter.

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Hartle arrived on campus with a ton of profile because of his super projectable frame. It looked like he was making the leap as a sophomore, even without increased velocity, but his performance backed up during his junior year. Because of Wake's reputation as a pitching factory, there's concern that if there were better stuff here, they'd have unlocked it. All the elements that made Hartle an exciting high school prospect are still here (broad-shouldered 6-foot-5 frame, very repeatable delivery, starter-quality repertoire depth and command), but his fastball averaged 90 mph in 2024 and he gave up a lot of hits. He features a five-pitch mix and mostly lives in the bottom of the zone. His sweeping breaking ball and changeup (both low-to-mid-80s) generated roughly average miss in 2024, while his fastball and cutter were way, way below average in that regard. Hartle has grounder-getting (60% GB%) fifth starter stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Hartle is a lanky lefty with 40 present stuff but huge projection. He has fairly advanced feel for locating but there's arm deceleration on his changeup right now. Because he didn't have a velo spike as a senior, he may end up going to Wake Forest where they tend to get guys to throw harder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hartle was one of the top prep lefties in the 2021 Draft class and entered his junior season at Wake Forest as perhaps the top college pitcher, but his stuff and control backed up and caused him to slip in the '24 Draft. He ended up signing for $850,000 as a Pirates third-rounder before the Guardians acquired him and fellow southpaw Michael Kennedy for Luis Ortiz. The North Carolina native made it to Double-A in his first full pro season and earned High-A Midwest Pitcher of the Year honors after logging a 2.35 ERA with 100 strikeouts and a 1.05 WHIP in 103 1/3 frames for Lake County. While he doesn't have overpowering stuff, Hartle throws strikes with a deep repertoire and creates unique angles from his 6-foot-6 frame and horizontal release. His best pitch is a slurvy slider that gets plenty of chase against lefties, and his changeup gets a decent amount of chase and miss but rarely lands for strikes. Hartle has a four-seam and two-seam fastball that each sit in the low 90s, although he could add more power as he fills out his 207-pound frame. He often works with his upper-80s cutter in the zone and limits hard contact on the pitch. Hartle repeats his delivery well and throws plenty of strikes. He profiles as a back-end starter currently, although the Guardians have had success developing this type of pitcher in the past. He's done a great job of preventing hard contact -- and home runs, in particular -- to date, but without velocity gains, that will be difficult against more advanced hitting. Hartle's 2025 season ended two weeks early with a shoulder injury, but he's unrestricted heading into 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Some clubs rated Hartle as the best left-hander in the 2021 prep class, but he went undrafted because he was set on attending Wake Forest. Following an All-America sophomore season, he entered 2024 as a consensus first-rounder before all four of his pitches and his control regressed. The Pirates drafted him in the third round, then sent him to the Guardians five months later as part of a package for Spencer Horwitz. At his best, Hartle exhibits advanced feel for a plus slider, solid cutter and average fastball and changeup. His heater sat at 89-92 mph and topped out at 94 with less life and command last spring, and he became reluctant to throw it when it got pounded. His low-80s slider and upper-80s cutter weren't as sharp as in the past, and his sinking mid-80s changeup rarely landed in the zone. As a sophomore, Hartle used his athleticism to repeat his easy delivery and spot his pitches wherever he wanted. Diminished stuff with less command was a recipe for disaster in 2024, when he also gave up four runs and recorded just five outs in his lone pro outing. He once looked like a lock to be at least a No. 4 starter with the upside of a No. 2, and now he's a reclamation project for an organization renowned for its ability to develop pitching.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: A little infielder with plus-plus wheels and gap power, Wilson still has questions on his hit tool, but his athleticism and ability to play multiple positions could land him as high as the second round.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Playing at Alabama is a family affair for the Wilson brothers, with the oldest, Parker, playing football for the Crimson Tide, and Ross and Peyton playing baseball. The Royals drafted Peyton 66th overall in 2021, and he spent his second full season at Double-A Northwest Arkansas in ‘23, where he was the everyday second baseman and slashed .286/.366/.411 with a Texas-League leading 33 doubles in 128 games. He finished the year with a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League, posting an .822 OPS in 21 games. Small but mighty at 5-foot-8, Wilson has a strong frame with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact from both sides of the plate. However, it’s not power contact -- he’s not going to be hitting a ton of balls over the fence. Wilson is pretty aggressive in the strike zone for as little power as he has, although his 18 percent strikeout rate was the lowest of his career last year. What Wilson loses in power, he makes up for in speed as a plus runner who easily stretches singles into doubles. He has the speed to swipe more bags than he has so far, but that comes down to instinct. Defensively, Wilson’s above-average arm strength should allow him to play in the infield and outfield, but the Royals had him almost exclusively at second to get repetitions and settle in there. Wilson’s work ethic and makeup are off the charts, and there’s no question he’s mentally going to be able to move around to different positions in the field if that’s what the Royals need. He doesn’t possess the hit or power tool of an everyday player, so he could use more experience as a utility man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton comes from an athletic family, with his oldest brother, John Parker, a former Alabama quarterback and other brother, Ross, a former Crimson Tide baseball player. Peyton followed in Ross’ footsteps at Alabama, playing center field as a freshman and moving to second base in ‘21 before the Royals selected him in Competitive Balance Round B that summer. Wilson got off to a slow start because of a hamstring injury, missing about three weeks in April and running cautiously until later in the season. He finished strong with a .268/.359/.456 line at High-A Quad Cities. Wilson has a small frame at 5-foot-8, but he’s strong with a short, compact swing that makes hard contact as a switch-hitter. His best tool is probably his speed, which he can use on the bases and in center field. Wilson’s arm is plus-plus, too, which allows him to play center field without a problem, but he's gotten more time at second base, where he can also be a great defender. He’s still getting a feel for the strike zone and what pitches he can do damage on, so if he tones down the aggressiveness, he could unlock a high average with some sneaky pop. Of Wilson’s 14 homers in 2022, eight of them came in August and September last year, and of his 23 stolen bases, 15 of them came in the final two months of the season, too. So he and the Royals were looking forward to seeing what he can do over a full season, and he's been about league-average in the box in the Texas League in 2023. While center field has taken more of a backseat, he can still be a future utilityman for the big-league club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peyton was the third Wilson brother to star at Alabama; John Parker set records as a quarterback, and Ross still shares the freshman home run mark with 15. After catching and playing center field as a freshman, Peyton moved to second base in 2021 and hit .290/.353/.460 with nine homers in 58 games. The Royals selected him with the 66th overall pick and signed him for exactly slot at $1 million, and Wilson made his professional debut last summer, posting a .733 OPS between rookie ball and Low-A Columbia. At 5-foot-9, Wilson’s strength is deceiving, and his short, compact swing makes hard and loud contact from both sides of the plate. He has a chance to hit a lot of extra-base hits because of his speed, which earns plus-plus grades from scouts. If he tones down the aggressiveness he showed in college ball, he profiles as a leadoff hitter, allowing him to cause havoc on the bases. More toolsy than the typical second baseman, Wilson has great instincts and range at the position, and he has a well-above-average arm that has served him well as he’s gotten looks in the outfield this summer. With his athleticism, speed and overall scrappiness, Wilson fits the mold of a typical Royals player. After bouncing around as much as he did in college, the Royals’ plan is to get him as much time as he can at second base in full-season ball, and as he slows the game down, the organization will likely begin to move him around the field. If he can’t stick at one position, Wilson has the ability to play almost anywhere on the field as a utilityman.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Tanner performed on paper in parts of three seasons in the SEC, slashing .285/.385/.476 during his career. Like a lot of the 2021 CWS champions, he didn't have quite as strong of a 2022. Tanner tends to spray good velocity to the opposite field and crush hanging breaking balls to his pull-side. He's strong enough to put balls out in either direction, and has a big, physical, prototypical catcher's frame. Defensively, Tanner has improved as a receiver but has a 40 arm (it was better early in the 2021 college season), though he's a gung-ho ball blocker and field general. He has flashed everyday offensive ability but that trended down in 2022, and some of his defensive issues remain. He has started to track like a backup (he's FV'd like a high-probability backup here), but at his amateur peak he looked like he could be more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Tanner hit 15 homers as a sophomore at Mississippi State, including one in the game that clinched a 2021 College World Series title against Vanderbilt, he was more known for his work behind the plate. He didn’t hit as well as a junior in 2022, but his glove work was the main reason why the Reds took the Bulldogs standout in the second round of last year’s Draft. Tanner is always likely to be a defense-over-hit backstop. He loves to throw and who can blame him, with one of the strongest arms in the Minors. It’s plus-plus with some amateur scouts hanging an 80 on it, the kind of hose that can shut down a running game. A good leader behind the plate who works well with pitchers, Tanner is a solid receiver and blocker, giving him all he needs to catch in the big leagues for a long time. How often he’s able to do that will depend on how his bat develops. There’s strength and bat speed from the right side, with a solid knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to draw walks, although he needs to get the ball in the air more to put that raw power to better use. In his brief pro debut, he was a little pull happy; the Reds think an emphasis on staying in the middle of the field, trusting his hands and believing he has the goods to stay on the fastball away and breaking stuff moving away from him to go opposite field will serve him well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers saw a chance to build organizational depth and some offensive upside at catcher when they drafted Crouch in the 11th round in 2021 following a breakout junior season at Central Florida. But even they weren’t expecting how well he adjusted to the pro game. After two strong weeks at Single-A Lakeland, Crouch moved to High-A West Michigan and helped lead a Whitecaps turnaround, taking ownership of a young pitching staff while providing clutch hits. That earned him a September promotion to Double-A Erie following a season-ending injury to Dillon Dingler. Crouch doesn’t really have one standout tool so much as he does a lot of things well. He’s sneaky athletic behind the plate with a strong enough arm to control a running game. He improved his receiving skills as the season went on but still has a lot of room to grow there. Similarly, he has enough power in his quick swing to punish mistakes but is more effective as a situational hitter. He batted .346 with 51 RBIs with runners in scoring position at West Michigan despite just eight extra-base hits. More impressively, he struck out just 14 times in those situations. Crouch was one of the more intriguing players in the Tigers system for some evaluators, thanks in part to his sudden emergence. With a strong work ethic and an effort to get stronger, he has a chance to reach the Majors in time, likely profiling as a backup. It’ll be interesting to see how the Tigers move Crouch and Dingler, who aren’t far apart in the system.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: A catcher named Crouch who receives from one knee is an ironic injustice for those of us in the nominative determinism crowd. Crouch is an athletic catch-and-throw guy with a quick exchange. He does a little bit of everything on defense, enough to project as an average big league defender. Crouch is also a career .268/.338/.401 hitter in the minors, with most of that coming at High-A West Michigan in 2022. Of medium build, Crouch's swing is super simple and compact. His footwork is so conservative that at times it looks unnatural and imbalanced. It's a little beneath Crouch's level of athleticism to have such a simple swing, but it's kept him on time routinely enough for him to hit .268 so far. He can spray stuff up and away from him into the oppo gap and hook pitches on the inner third down the left field line for doubles. Everything here is pointing toward a high-probability 40-man spot as a team's second or third catcher. He's gone back and forth between Double-A and High-A early in 2023 depending on Detroit's needs due to Dillon Dingler's injury. He's a post-2024 40-man add and the Tigers don't appear to be pacing his promotion ahead of that schedule, so look for him to compete for the backup job in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It looked like Hettiger, who starred on the Los Angeles high school scene, was going to head to Oregon for college ball as the 2023 Draft wore on and he didn’t hear his name called. The Phillies had other ideas, using some extra bonus pool money when Day 3 started, going over slot to sign him for close to $400,000. He hasn’t put up big numbers as of yet, but he made some progress along the way in a rough first full season with Single-A Clearwater, then earning a promotion to High-A Jersey Shore while finishing the year in Double-A in 2025. A former switch-hitter who is now only hitting left-handed to help simplify things at the plate, Hettiger does have the makings of a solid approach at the plate, seeing a lot of pitches and drawing a lot of walks as evidenced by his career walk rate north of 16 percent heading into 2025. He finds the barrel a lot, and there’s some power for him to get to, but while he limits chase, the swing-and-miss is concerning (29.1 percent K rate). When he first entered pro ball, there were questions about Hettiger’s ability to catch long-term, especially because he hadn’t played much behind the dish in high school. He continues to get reps at first, but he’s become one of the better defenders at the position in the organization, with more than enough arm. If that continues, he could end up catching in the big leagues one day, getting at-bats against right-handed pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the first two days of the Draft came and went in 2023, Hettiger may have thought he was headed to Oregon for college ball. But the Phillies hadn’t quite used up their bonus pool money over the top 10 rounds and were able to nab Hettiger in Round 11, going over the Day 3 slot ($150,000) to sign him for just under $400,000. He made his very brief pro debut in the Florida Complex League last summer after signing. A switch-hitter, Hettiger appears to be better from the left side than the right, though he sees the ball well and has good at-bats from both sides of the plate. He’s used a small trigger in his swing in the past, but tends to be on time and has an advanced approach with excellent pitch recognition. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into, and that shows up more when he’s hitting left-handed. Strength gains this offseason could start showing up at the plate during his first full season. Hettiger didn’t catch a ton in high school, as the solid athlete moved around and played the infield corners quite a bit. There’s work to be done on his receiving, but he sets up well behind the plate. He’s already shown that he has more than enough arm to remain behind the plate, throwing out several potential basestealers in the FCL, with the Phillies having a bit more faith that he can stick there.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
An Oregon commit from the northwestern part of Los Angeles, Hettiger signed for just shy of $400,000 in 2023 and hit .195 at Clearwater in his first full pro season. In 2025, he gave up switch-hitting and slashed .232/.330/.389 in Lakewood, good for a 117 wRC+ in the South Atlantic League. 
The hitting environment in the Sally masked Hettiger's power, his carrying tool. This guy can really swing it. His hands are explosive and generate blood-thirsty pull-side launch, with Hettiger showing average big league power as a college-aged prospect with room on his frame for more strength. Hettiger also has a real approach and tends to target high pitches, the ones he's suited to crush. He's probably going to strike out a bunch (he K'd at a 29.1% clip in 2025) because he runs deep counts and sells out for power when he swings, but his feel for contact also might improve some as he focuses solely on hitting left-handed. 
Lefty-hitting catchers with this kind of bat speed are uncommon, and that's what is giving Hettiger some prospect value here. Though the Phillies gave him a shot of espresso at Double-A in September, Hettiger is still very much a developmental prospect, especially as a defender. His receiving and pitch framing are sushi raw, and some of the pitchers in Reading were visibly frustrated by his struggles at the very end of the season. Hettiger has also played a lot of first base; it wasn't until the last month of 2025 that the Phillies really dedicated Hettiger solely to catching. He's athletic enough to have a shot of sticking back there, though it's probably going to take several years before he's good enough to handle the duties of a big league job.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Payne's breaking balls are dominating the FCL, as both his 76-79 mph curveball and 80-85 mph slider are generating an absurd rate of miss. Both have plus depth and bite coming from Payne's higher arm slot. His fastball features below-average velocity and downhill plane, but Payne is throwing it for strikes consistently even though his delivery looks rather effortful. He doesn't have great changeup projection, but his curveball might be good enough to play against righties, and Payne is a very physical dude who looks like he'll be able to withstand a starter's workload. This was a nice pull late in last year's draft. It only took $235,000 to keep Payne from going to George Mason, and a year later, he looks like a guy who should've gotten closer to a million.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: High school pitching can be one of the riskiest demographics in the Draft, but occasionally a late-round flier can emerge as a true gem. That appears to be the case with Payne, whom the Marlins signed away from his George Mason commitment for $235,000 as a 2024 18th-rounder and now looks like a bargain. The southpaw cruised through the Rookie-level Florida Complex League by striking out more than a third of the batters he faced and ended the year with six solid Single-A outings. Payne can really spin a pair of breaking balls and leaned on his low-80s slider and high-70s curve to rack up whiffs and chases. Both pitches have significant downward movement from his higher three-quarters delivery, which has helped mitigate platoon concerns. His fastball is still a work in progress, though, with a 91 mph average and sinking shape in 2025. He was more consistently hitting 95 over the offseason and has the build to add more velocity. Payne has a little-used cutter and a changeup with splitter-like movement that have had modest success in the mid-80s, but the breaking balls remain his meal ticket. The Marlins tried to ramp up his stuff at the cost of his control early on, and it will be key to see him throw more strikes to avoid bloated walk rates. Still, Payne has No. 4 starter upside thanks to his workhorse size, repeatable delivery and breaking balls -- or perhaps more if his added velocity sticks.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: German is a medium-framed middle infielder who signed for $400,000 in 2025. He spent his first pro season as the DSL team's leadoff man and offensive catalyst, a well-rounded switch-hitter who also has the actions to develop at shortstop. German has better bat speed from the left side of the plate and enough pull power to yank out the occasional mistake. He's fairly small but is built well enough to layer on more strength without sacrificing athleticism, though we're probably talking about strength that leads to big league viability rather than big power, similar to Geraldo Perdomo. This is definitely the biggest "arrow up" prospect from Washington's 2025 DSL class to this point, though he likely doesn't have overt ceiling due to the limitations of his size.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: German signed for $400,000 last year out of the Dominican Republic, giving him the joint fourth-highest bonus of Washington’s 2025 international class but well behind the seven-figure deals for Brayan Cortesia ($1.92 million) and Daniel Hernandez ($1.1 million). Only year later, the switch-hitting infielder has surged in stock to become the best prospect of the group at this very early stage of his career. German was a Dominican Summer League mid- and post-season All-Star with a .283/.479/.513 line, eight homers and 33 steals in 53 games. While many of his age can be undisciplined at the plate, German showed an advanced approach from both sides of the plate, leading to a 42/43 K/BB ratio. He shows better ability to slug from the left side to this point -- all eight of his dingers came against righty pitchers – but that might also speak to his lack of gametime against southpaws (only 49 plate appearances in 2025). German stands only 5-foot-10, but what he lacks in stature, he makes up for in his early tendency to lift and pull the ball, helping the pop show in games. By getting on base so much, German gives himself plenty of chances to steal bags, and he certainly took advantage by showing off his above-average wheels in the DSL. That athleticism has helped him stay up the middle on the dirt to this point, and he has the arm strength to make that a defensive asset as well. Nationals instructors have been impressed by his teenage work ethic and aptitude with the glove early on, and he should be a priority middle infielder at the Florida complex when he arrives stateside this spring.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
After the Dodgers dropped sixth-round money on Patick, a slender left-hander from their backyard (West Covina, CA), he didn't pitch at an affiliate in his draft year and injury kept him out of action until the second half of the following season. His 92.1 innings in 2025 felt like his full-season professional debut, and a successful one at that; he posted a 17.2% K-BB with no drop-off in a late-season, two-start cameo at High-A. He settled into a 92-95 mph (touch 96) velocity band over 25 appearances, working exclusively as a starter after April and making use of a contact-heavy high-80s cutter to lessen the burden on his heater, which has below-average ride.
While his heater doesn't have compelling raw action, Patick’s unique delivery opens with a big leg kick and counter-rotation that sets up every pitch in his arsenal to come from a high, crossfire angle. It’s a big movement that he struggles to time up with his arm stroke. That, along with his lack of a reliable changeup or a demonstrated ability to land his curveball for strikes — it generated goofy whiff numbers in A-ball, but mostly projects as a device to throw off hitters from timing his slider — drives a relief projection at this juncture. But the extra tilt allows his slider to flash above-average potential, with left-handers ducking out of the way of some of the benders he lands for strikes and Patick showing some nascent feel for landing it backfoot to righties. Despite Patick's slender frame, there's not much projection left. Still, he has the tools to be a death-to-lefties reliever at present, with the velo, spin talent, and early performance to keep pushing toward a back-end starter future.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: It took a little less than $350,000 to sign the broad-shouldered, narrow-waisted Patick away from a UC Santa Barbara commitment, and in his second full season, he's out the gate throwing much harder than in 2024. Patick will show you 94-96 mph in long relief and bend in the occasionally great two-planed slider. These often spin around 2,700 rpm, and some of them have enough lateral wipe that you could justifiably classify them as sweepers. He also has a cutter in the 88-92 mph range. Patick's arm stroke tends to be late, and his command can waver, which has been especially true so far in 2025. He's a risky young lefty, but he has burgeoning arm strength and good natural breaking ball quality, giving him an eventual lefty relief projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patick stood out more with his projection than his present stuff when the Dodgers made him an 18th-round pick out of a suburban Los Angeles high school and signed him for an over-slot $347,500 in 2023. An illness requiring hospitalizing sidelined him for what would have been his first Spring Training and limited him to 31 2/3 innings in 2024, but he bounced back to successfully navigate Single-A last year. His 27 percent strikeout rate ranked third in the California League among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 85 1/3 innings. Patick's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with more downhill plane than life, and he uses it to set up a wide variety of secondary pitches. His best offering is a mid-70s curveball with depth that confounds both lefties and righties but also makes it difficult to land for strikes. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with plenty of sweep that he can turn into a tighter cutter that climbs as high as 93 mph, as well as an 85-88 mph changeup with some fade. Patick has good feel for spinning the ball and mixing his pitches. He creates deception by utilizing a big leg kick, rotating his upper half and throwing from a crossfire angle, and that doesn't stop him from throwing strikes. He has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter and his ability to neutralize hitters from both sides with his breaking pitches could make him a useful bullpen piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: “A person’s a person, no matter how small,” is, of course, a quote from the Dr. Seuss classic “Horton Hears a Who?” Now, that wasn't about this Horton, a shortstop who ranked No. 9 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list and signed with the Angels for $2 million when the 2026 signing period opened in January. But the Dominican infielder is 5-foot-9, so perhaps the passage is apt after all. Hailing from the same town in the Dominican Republic that produced big leaguers like Hanley Ramirez, Horton is a super-athletic left-handed hitter with all the tools to stay up the middle. He has a smaller frame, but he’s already shown in competition that he has good balance at the plate and a natural feel for finding the barrel. He has a solid approach with above-average contact skills and has sneaky pop. It's more gap-to-gap right now, but he could grow into double-digit home run power in the future. Horton’s speed and twitchy athleticism are assets on the basepaths and in the field. He has the ingredients to stick at shortstop, with smooth actions. The Angels think he has plenty of arm for the position, with the chance to be a premium defender, but in a worst-case scenario, he slides over and becomes a plus second baseman. He gets very high marks for his makeup and high energy style of play.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: This one is from Eric’s overview of the 2026 international class: Horton had a $2.5 million deal with the Yankees that was broken in February of 2025, and he ended up getting $2 million from the Angels. He is an amazing little athlete with a chance to be a special infield defender. He swings hard for someone his size, which makes scouts apprehensive about projecting on his contact ability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One would be hard-pressed to find another pitcher in Seattle’s system who has endured as many obstacles since Draft Day as Carlson. Since being selected in the second round in 2017 out of a Minnesota high school, the righty underwent Tommy John surgery one year later, then came back in an emotional return in Spring Training in ‘20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. More than one year after that, he finally began his first full pro season. That topsy-turvy start to his career gave him a more grounded mental approach, and in his first full season, he impressed by making every start. The quirky Minor League schedule actually helped ease him into a no-limits workload, and he reached 100 innings over 19 starts with a 4.77 ERA. Essentially, everything was finally consistent for the 23-year-old, who is in the same age range as some of Seattle’s other top arms, such as George Kirby and Emerson Hancock, who were drafted after him. That gives Carlson a good outlook and strong upside. Before the shutdown in 2020, Carlson had added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which allowed him to reach back into the high 90s on his fastball. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above-average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. There’s a lot to like about his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carlson was always going to be a case of patience for the Mariners, who selected the righty out of high school in Minnesota in the second round in 2017, given that he was raised in a cold-weather state. But they didn’t anticipate that he would weather the significant setbacks, with just three professional innings so far. He underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2018 and was sidelined all of ’19, but returned in Spring Training in ’20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. But Carlson enters 2021 completely healthy – and that will be the biggest thing for the 22-year-old. Beyond the physical toll, there’s the mental factor of being back on a field again consistently. It understandably will take time for Carlson to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence that it all will eventually come back. Before the shutdown, he’d added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which gives the Mariners optimism that he’ll be able to get back up to the 93- to 97-mph range he showed on his fastball as a high school senior. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. Carlson is likely headed to High-A Everett or Low-A Modesto to start the regular season. He'll need time to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Carlson was a revered two-way high school prospect committed to Florida even though he was from Minnesota. He spent the summer before his draft year sitting in the low-90s and working with a better changeup and better command than is typical for a cold-weather, two-way player. His big, strapping frame portended more velocity. The following year, that velo arrived, and Carlson sat 93-97 for stretches of his pre-draft spring. Seattle drafted him in the second round, gave him $2 million, and Carlson made two starts in the AZL before he was quickly shut down. He had Tommy John and had a season wiped away by the pandemic, all of which piled up to nearly four years between when Carlson threw his last pitch in affiliated ball in 2017 to when he threw his next one, at Low-A in early 2021. His peak velocity has not returned, and Carlson has been more in the 91-93 range, topping out at 94, with some carry and tail. His arm action is still fairly long, his delivery has some head violence, and at a physical 22-years-old, I don't consider him a likely candidate to add velocity. His new-ish curveball has good back-foot angle against lefties and enough depth to miss bats, while his changeup remains a fair offering with tailing action. The entire package looks like a fifth starter (a 40) right now, but the way individuals in baseball either round up or down on that projection depends on what part of Carlson's prospectdom they choose to look at. Look at his draft pedigree and there's hope for more than that; look at his actual performance track record and there's skepticism. He needs to pitch well enough to be added to the 40-man this offseason and nobody is sure how his stuff and health will respond to a full-season workload after he's never even come close to pitching deep into season. I'm inclined to take the under on the hype and justifiably good feelings surrounding his return. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies like Williams and his upside so much, they acquired him twice. They first took the Colorado high schooler out of their own back yard in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, signing him for $450,000. He hadn’t thrown a competitive pitch when the Rockies sent him to the Reds that offseason as part of the deal that netted them Robert Stephenson. He was making his pro debut in the Reds system when he came back to the Rockies in the Mychal Givens trade close to the 2021 deadline. He took a developmental step forward in 2022 across two levels of A-ball before finishing with a 12-strikeout exclamation point in Double-A. Still only 21 for all of the 2023 season, Williams’ projection is looking like it’s starting to turn into performance. The Rockies think he has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix, with all of them being at least average. He’s commanding his low-90s fastball better to both halves down in the zone and showing he can pitch up with it. He’s also learned that he can’t just blow away hitters with his heater and is mixing his pitches much more effectively. He’s always been able to spin a breaking ball with an outstanding power curve and there are makings of a distinct slider. He also started showing conviction in throwing his changeup more consistently. With his delivery more under control, Williams is developing beyond just a thrower, learning to execute his pitches. The next step will be command within the zone but his improved stuff, pitchability and added physical maturity have led to an up arrow next to his name.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams was the top high school player in Colorado for the 2020 Draft, though no one got to see him pitch leading up to it because the coronavirus pandemic shut down the season before it began there. So teams interested in the big, physical right-hander had to mostly go on what they saw over the summer. The Rockies saw enough to take the prepster out of their own backyard in the fourth round of the shortened Draft, and they signed him for a below-slot bonus of $450,000. They never got to see him throw a competitive pitch, as they sent him to the Reds, whose scout team Williams played on in the Area Code Games in the summer of 2019, as part of the deal that saw Jeff Hoffman join the Reds and Robert Stephenson head to the Rockies. Williams has all of the elements of a future big leaguer, but they’re a bit raw and undeveloped at this point in time. The Rockies saw a fastball in the 92-95 mph range coming from his 6-foot-3 frame. His secondary stuff is all inconsistent, but he has a good feel to spin his breaking ball with the chance to have a plus curve down the road. He had not thrown his changeup much in high school, so that will be an area of focus developmentally for him as he starts his pro career. Big and physical, Williams is a solid athlete who should be able to eventually command the baseball well enough to give him the chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter. Patience will be key as he’s not logged many innings on the mound, knowing that there have been pitching success stories out of the Colorado high school ranks – Roy Halladay, Kevin Gausman and Kyle Freeland as the prime examples – but that Gausman and Freeland went on to college and it took a while for Halladay to figure it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017-18 international signing class for the Rockies may always be known as the group topped by Ezequiel Tovar, who led with his $800,000 bonus. Carreras has been in that shadow, starting with signing for just $15,000 in February 2018 and continuing as the pair progressed together, with Tovar jumping ahead developmentally. Carreras started making more of a name for himself in 2022, shaking off a shoulder injury that hurt him in 2020 and '21, reaching Double-A for the first time and getting added to the 40-man roster. Rangy and athletic, Carreras has always exhibited some positive offensive traits with good bat speed and the ability to make hard contact out front. He’s been overaggressive to a fault, however, and will need to make better swing decisions and be more selective to reach his offensive ceiling. He did start using the leverage in his swing to tap into some of his raw power, and there’s reason to believe that the doubles he was hitting in bunches could turn into more home runs if he can refine his approach. Carreras can play a solid defensive shortstop, with good instincts and plenty of arm for the position, and he’s also shown in the past that he can handle sliding over to third base, something that might have to happen with Tovar establishing himself at short. Even if it’s eventually as a utility type, Carreras is the type who is already showing leadership and other intangibles to make him a valuable big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carreras signed with the Rockies for just $15,000 in February 2018 as an 18-year-old, which is a touch old for the typical international prospect. He went out and hit well in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 (.867 OPS), then turned in a solid debut stateside with a .294/.369/.466 line in the Rookie-level Pioneer League the following summer. Both the pandemic and a shoulder injury limited his development time in 2020. Surgery required to fix that issue delayed his 2021 start and hampered his overall production as he moved to full-season ball. Tall, lean and athletic, Carreras has shown excellent bat speed from the right side of the plate with an ability to make hard contact out front when he’s healthy. There’s leverage in his swing and as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame, there should be a good amount of power to come. He was a bit tentative with his swings after coming back, but the pop showed up at times and the next step for him tapping into that power is to make more adjustments and eliminate his tendency to chase. Carreras has played mostly on the left side of the infield, with more than enough arm to stay there, and opinions are split over whether he can play shortstop or third regularly. The latter puts more pressure on the bat to develop, but his makeup and intangibles point to him maximizing the tools he has.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the very top of the 2017-18 international signing period, in terms of bonuses, stood Wander Franco, now the game’s No. 1 prospect, who got $3.825 million to sign with the Rays. Close to the other end of the spectrum was Carreras, who received just $15,000 in February 2018 to join the Rockies. He’s looked like a bargain find so far, hitting well both in the Rookie level Dominican Summer League in 2018 and during his United States debut in the Rookie Advanced Pioneer League in 2019. A left shoulder injury limited his time on the field at instructs in 2020, but he’s been given a clean bill of health. Carreras provides an exciting combination of size, strength and athleticism to both sides of the ball. He has plenty of bat speed with present leverage to his right-handed swing and when he grows into his 6-foot-2 frame more, there’s bound to be more power to come. Carreras is able to extend and make hard contact out front, all while showing a solid approach at the plate. The 21-year-old infielder creates buzz with his defense as well. He has quick reactions and one of the best infield arms in the system. Carreras has shown the ability to play second, third and short capably, but given his physical and offensive projection, he might profile at third base the best in terms of a long-term home, though the Rockies love positional flexibility from their infielders.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Carreras' excellent defense should carry him to a low-impact utility role. He has fantastic defensive footwork, his hands, actions, and transfer are all lightning quick, he has a flair for making acrobatic plays around the second base bag, and his arm (if a little inaccurate at times) is very strong. As he enters his age-25 season, Carreras remains rather thin and has plateaued with gap doubles power, which he struggles to get to because he tends to chase. It's the skill set of a glove-only nine-hole hitter. On a good roster, Carreras would be used as a defensive replacement.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Carreras' carrying tool is his defense. He has fantastic defensive footwork, his hands, actions, and transfer are all lightning quick, he has a flair for making acrobatic plays around the second base bag, and his arm (if a little inaccurate at times) is fantastic. For a bit while Carreras was in the low minors, it appeared as though he might grow into meaningful power, but that hasn't happened and he's still a relatively skinny, light-hitting offensive player whose propensity to chase is also a bit of a problem. There probably won't be sufficient offensive impact for Carreras to be a regularly or even oft-used complementary player, but his defense will very likely make him a bench infielder who provides a late-game defensive upgrade.
