He makes a reasonable amount of contact and can do damage against breaking balls, but his plate discipline slipped when he moved from High-A to Double-A last summer. Bericoto is a below-average runner out of the batter's box but is closer to average when he gets going. He has divided his time between the outfield corners and first base, getting most of his action in right field. He exhibits decent range and average arm strength, though he'll need to keep improving his reads and routes to stay in the outfield.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
A high school infielder who became a reserve catcher during his underclass seasons at Stanford, Rios didn't really get consistent reps until his junior year when he moved into a vacant spot in the outfield. He responded by slugging a jet's worth, hitting .384/.485/.707. 
Rios doesn't have the prototypical offense of a corner outfield prospect, and his best chance to profile is by improving at the catcher position. He's catching about a quarter of the time so far in 2024 and looks predictably raw. He's a one-knee, bottom-up receiver, and has a tendency to stab at pitches that miss the location where he's set up. This needs to quiet down, and Rios' ball blocking needs to improve. There are amateur scouts who liked Rios' bat enough to give him a shot in an outfield corner. He was especially good at getting on top of high fastballs in college, but his hand path, which is remarkably similar to Keston Hiura's, is not the kind for which this is typically true. It's possible Pac-12 pitching just wasn't good enough to expose the upper-zone hole in Rios' swing (which seems to be true early on in 2024 as he K's north of 30% of the time). If it turns out his hit tool can hold water, then Rios is going to be a doubles machine capable of playing a part-time corner role, but we think it's more important for him to catch.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: A high school infielder who became a reserve catcher during his underclass years at Stanford, Rios didn't really get consistent reps until his junior year when he moved into a vacant spot in the outfield. He responded by slugging a jet's worth, hitting .384/.485/.707. Rios doesn't have the prototypical power of a corner outfield prospect, with his best chance to profile there coming via his excellent feel for contact. Rios was especially good at getting on top of high fastballs in college, but his hand path, which is remarkably similar to Keston Hiura's, is not the kind for which this is typically true. It's possible Pac-12 pitching just wasn't good enough to expose the upper-zone hole in Rios' swing. If it turns out his hit tool can hold water, then Rios is going to be a doubles machine capable of playing at least a part-time corner role. If not, then it would be interesting to see if he can catch as a pro or play an infield position again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rios was the Pac-12 Player of the Year in 2023 after finishing with an OPS of 1.191 while helping Stanford reach the College World Series. This was an amazing development given the fact that Rios appeared in eight games combined over his first two years in college. He became one of the more intriguing college bats on the West Coast last year and the Angels were piqued enough to take him in the third round of the Draft. It was a small sample, but he struggled out of the gate during his pro debut, mostly with Single-A Inland Empire. Even though his résumé was light, amateur scouts had some conviction that Rios would hit at the next level. The right-handed hitter is short and quick to the ball and he displayed a very advanced approach, drawing a ton of walks, as well. The combination of pitch recognition, discipline and finding the barrel enabled him to use his raw power consistently, with 18 homers last spring. For Rios to make it, he’s going to have to hit because he doesn’t have a real defensive home. He played left field at Stanford but the Angels started working with him behind the plate -- he spent a lot of his non-playing time catching bullpens in college -- and they liked his leadership and his good hands behind the dish, though his arm is below-average. He’ll still get some reps in the outfield, but he’d obviously have more value -- and there’d be less pressure on his bat -- if he can catch.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Fifth in the NCAA in hits in 2021, Boissiere is a low-ball-hitting corner outfield prospect who sprays to all fields. He projects as a platoon piece.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Branden Boissiere (third) entered the spring with less of a profile than other Wildcats and then had the best statistical season on the team and led Division-I in hits. He has a good shot to be the larger half of an outfield platoon, at least.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boissiere arrived on the University of Arizona campus in the fall of 2018 and never stopped hitting from there, finishing with a .355/.434/.488 line over 117 career games with the Wildcats. His best numbers (.369/.451/.506, five homers) came as a junior, prompting the Nats to select him in the third round and sign him for below slot at $600,000. Boissiere stumbled out of the gate at Low-A Fredericksburg, going 17-for-85 (.200), but that’s not unheard of for a college player settling into the pro game after a long spring. Boissere earned solid reviews in the Grand Canyon State for his impressive approach against collegiate pitchers. He posted near-equal K/BB ratios all three years, an indication of his willingness to work a walk while limiting his punchouts. His slugging numbers won’t open any eyes on their own, but he’s capable of above-average raw power from the left side. It’s pop that plays to all fields too, so he could see 15-20 homers in the Majors at his peak. The left-handed thrower, who will be 22 for the entire season to come, had some experience as a corner outfielder in his early NCAA days but was a full-time first baseman in college and the pros last year. He possesses the agility to be an above-average glove at the cold corner, adding another way he can provide value. He’ll still need to fulfill every bit of his hitting potential and maybe squeeze a little more power to meet the offensive requirements of the position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tampa-area native looked like he was heading to the University of South Florida until the Orioles took him in the 2022 Draft and signed him for $440,000. Showalter lasted barely a year in the Baltimore system until he was traded to the Cardinals at the 2023 Trade Deadline as part of a big return for Jack Flaherty. He returned to Single-A Palm Beach for his age-20 season in 2024 and was a Florida State League end-of-season All-Star as a reliever after posting a 2.62 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 34 1/3 innings. His season ended early in August due to shoulder issues. Showalter’s dominance comes down almost entirely to his fastball. The 6-foot-2 right-hander gets low down on the mound, hides the ball behind his body until the very last moment and then unleashes the heater from a tough release angle. The pitch may only sit 90-93 mph, but with its extreme vertical approach angle, it cuts under a ton of bats in a way that’s almost reminiscent of Craig Kimbrel’s heater (albeit with less velo at this stage). Showalter also works with an upper-70s sweeping slider that can get slurvy and a barely thrown mid-80s changeup. Showalter averaged more than a walk every two innings, and given his control and limited pro workload, there is a temptation to keep him in relief full-time. But under new player development leadership in 2025, the Cardinals will consider giving Showalter starting looks since he’s still relatively early in his development, knowing that he could go back to bullpen domination at any point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hailing from just north of Tampa, Showalter had a commitment to the University of South Florida and looked like he was heading to the Bulls out of high school until the Orioles selected him in the 11th round of the 2022 Draft. Baltimore signed the right-hander for $440,000 ($315,000 of which counted toward its signing pool) to enter pro ball. Showalter got his career off to a solid start with 41 strikeouts over 30 1/3 innings between the Florida Complex League and Single-A Delmarva when the O’s moved him to the Cardinals at the 2023 Trade Deadline in the four-player Jack Flaherty deal. He made one appearance for Single-A Palm Beach but was shut down afterward. He returned to the Florida State League as a reliever in 2024 and has dominated in the role with K-heavy appearances. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has a fastball that can touch the mid-90s but is generally 91-93 mph. However, he hides the ball well -- essentially keeping it behind his back until rushing forward with arm speed -- and he dips so low at the time of release that the heater comes in almost flat with an incredible vertical approach angle. That can make for an explosive look, and it gives low-level batters fits, leading to a high usage rate around 80 percent. His mid-70s breaking ball shows sweep and depth that could help make it an above-average pitch with further development. Improving Showalter’s mid-80s changeup should also be a focus after lefties posted a .316/.438/.474 line against him last year. The effort in Showalter’s delivery has led to the occasional wildness, and before the Draft, some evaluators believed the righty was headed toward the bullpen eventually. That shift has come to pass, but it's clear early on that the fastball alone could really work in short spurts.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Showalter was part of the return for Jack Flaherty. He pitches heavily off of a sinker/four-seam combo that sits 90-93 mph and occasionally touches a tick or two above that. The offering plays drastically above the velocity, though, due to his upshot angle and his ability to hide the ball for an extended period of time thanks to his quick, compact arm action. The breaking ball is a bender that will regularly show average tightness, but it's also susceptible to backing up on him and losing the authority in the spin. Still, it has big potential movement and is a favorite of folks who take a data-oriented approach to scouting. He projects to be a single-inning middle-relief type whose deception allows his stuff to punch far above its weight.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Hertzler is a certified big boy (6-foot-4, 235 pounds), but he's smooth mover who spent part of his time at Liberty as a two-way player before the Astros dropped nearly $400,000 on him in 2024. The surprising agility hasn’t kept him healthy for more than 21 innings since turning pro, with a forearm strain ending his 2025 season after four starts. He was carving up until that point, though (16 innings, 34.4% strikeout rate, 9.4% walk rate). His fastball has good carry out of a super vertical slot but sits 91-94 mph, and his command of a suite of secondaries stands out more than any one weapon. Hertzler’s changeup has racked up nutty miss rates in a tiny sample and clearly doesn't lack for deception, but it has below-average drop and will require careful command. There’s back-end starter potential here, but he’s already dealt with the level of injury that will shrink his window to avoid a shift to relief.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: A former two-way player at Liberty and a high school rotation mate of Blue Jays first rounder Trey Yesavage, Hertzler’s 6-foot-4, 235-pound frame doesn’t present much projection, but there’s room to grow given that pitching has only recently become his sole focus. His low-90s heater is protected by a suite of secondaries with downer action out of high-three-quarters slot, but he only got in three starts this year before a forearm strain shut him down. Hertzler’s pro career has shown flashes of big-time bat-missing potential limited to under 20 innings of in-game action due to injury.

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Hertzler has a large, athletic frame that is already well filled out. He has a clean, medium arm path and throws his four-pitch mix from a high three-quarters slot. His fastball sits in the low 90s and regularly touches higher when he needs it; the pitch has carry through the zone when elevated that allows it to punch up. He throws two breaking balls, with the curveball is a deep downer, while the slider is also heavy on the vertical plane but mixes more horizontal action in than the curve. He maintains his fastball arm speed when throwing his mid-80s changeup, which has late fading action and flashes depth. His 9% walk rate in 2024 was a drastic improvement over his 2023 mark, and if it keeps trending that way, he could evolve into a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hertzler teamed with Trey Yesavage at Boyertown (Pa.) HS ,and after three years of college, he went four rounds behind him in the 2024 Draft, joining the Astros as a fifth-rounder. A two-way player in his first two seasons at Liberty, he focused on pitching as a junior and became the Flames' No. 1 starter. He has worked just 21 innings as a pro because he sprained his forearm last April and made just one more appearance five months later. Hertzler's best offering is a low-80s changeup with significant fade. It helps him maximize the effectiveness of a fastball that sits at 91-94 mph and tops out at 97 with carry and armside run. He showed better feel for his tight mid-80s slider than his 78-82 mph curveball during his brief action last season. With a 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot, Hertzler's pitches come out of a higher release point than usual. His control and command improved as he got more experience at Liberty, and he has no problem providing strikes. He'll need to show he can handle a starter's workload after totaling just 142 innings in the last four years but should be fully healthy for 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyertown (Pa.) High's 2021 pitching staff featured two arms who would go early in the 2024 Draft -- Blue Jays first-rounder Trey Yesavage and Astros fifth-rounder Hertzler. A two-way player in his first two college seasons at Liberty, Hertzler became the Flames' No. 1 starter when he focused on the mound last spring. His pro debut consisted of two brief appearances at Single-A. In his lone season as a college starter, Hertzler showed the ability to get chases and miss bats with four average pitches. His fastball operates at 91-94 mph and touches 97 with carry and armside run, and it could become a solid offering if he finds more velocity. His fading low-80s changeup is his best secondary pitch, followed by a tight mid-80s slider with occasional depth and a low-80s curveball. Hertzler's strong 6-foot-4 frame and high arm slot created a higher release point than hitters are accustomed to. As he got regular innings in 2024, he did a good job of cleaning up his delivery and providing strikes. He has more untapped potential than most college pitchers and could develop into a No. 4 or 5 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Powell has a cannon for an arm and incredible raw juice (116.2 mph max exit velocity), and he saw most of his playing time at shortstop in 2025. Yet his hit tool issues are so pronounced that sliding off short – and his hands looked rough enough last year that he didn't play there down the stretch – could be a big blow to his prospect status. Despite missing seven weeks with a left hamate fracture, Powell managed a .239/.344/.404 line at Low-A in 2025, but he loads his hands very late in a max-effort swing and he whiffed on heaters at twice the big league rate against younger competition. He’s big, strapping, and athletic, with the physical tools to mature into an excellent defensive third baseman, but his 62% contact rate was already meaningfully lower than any qualified big leaguer last season, so the odds of him whiffing too much to surface as a power-oriented corner reserve remain high.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Last year’s JUCO Player of the Year is far more toolsy than the typical Low-A utilityman, as it’s rare to see someone with above-average present exit velos bouncing between three infield spots at Fayetteville. Lean and 6-foot-3 with long levers, Powell has more than enough arm strength to throw across the diamond, but he's more accurate when he can set his feet, rather than when he's rushing his play clock as he needs to when he's asked to play short. He both has so much raw pop that his air-pull rate is but a quibble, and is swinging and missing in the zone so much (he has about a 64% contact rate) that accessing the juice that allowed him to hit 32 bombs in his last year Seminole State feels far off. Statistically, Powell has swapped excessive chase for excessive in-zone whiff this year (bad trade). Visually, he’s working very hard to stay closed and cut down length in his swing path by keeping his hands close to his body, but he struggles to keep his head still and track pitches, leading to exceptionally poor performance against spin so far. With the Astros preparing him for a multi-positional future, he’s trending toward an infield version of Michael A. Taylor, but Powell’s hit tool issues might be too extreme for such an outcome.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Powell got just 35 at-bats as an Oklahoma freshman, prompting him to transfer to Seminole State (Okla.) JC, where he became the national junior college player of the year as a sophomore in 2024. He topped NJCAA Division I in slugging (1.088), OPS (1.649), homers (32) and RBI (104) before giving up an Oklahoma State commitment to sign with the Astros as sixth-rounder. He slashed .264/.331/.442 in Single-A before breaking his left hamate last May, then missed two months and hit just .209/.358/.358 afterward. Powell features well above-average raw power, the product of a fierce right-handed stroke and an aggressive mindset that looks to crush balls to his pull side. He exhibits reasonable plate discipline and hits balls extremely hard when he makes contact -- but there are major questions about whether he can do so consistently against advanced pitching. He had a swing-and-miss rate of 29 percent against the strikes he saw in 2025, including 33 percent against in-zone fastballs. While Powell is slower out of the batter's box, he flashes solid speed underway and stole 32 bases in 38 attempts (84 percent) in 84 games last year. He played mostly shortstop in junior college and spent the majority of his time there last year, but his quickness is better suited for third base. He was erratic at both spots in 2025, committing 16 miscues in 61 starts, and has average arm strength. The organization will focus on getting him reps in the outfield this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kevin Alvarez wasn't the only Astros outfield prospect to make a strong impression in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League last year. Signed for $472,500 out of Venezuela, Millan had a history of performing well at amateur events, so his easy transition to pro ball wasn't much of a surprise. He batted .279/.407/.419 with 11 extra-base hits and 13 steals in 42 games. More advanced than most 17-year-olds, Millan controls the zone and makes consistent contact. While he's not very physical at 5-foot-11 and 170 pounds, he hits the ball surprisingly hard for his size and generates plus raw pop. His right-handed-stroke is relatively flat, so he'll need to add some loft to fully tap into his 20-homer potential. A plus runner, Millan uses his quickness well on the bases and in center field. He has the instincts to steal bags and chases down balls from gap to gap. He also features solid arm strength and recorded six assists in 40 outfield starts.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Millan is an athletically built outfielder who signed out of Venezuela for a shade under half a million dollars in January of 2025, and thrived in his debut season, posting a .279/.407/.419 line in 42 DSL games. He’s slender with some room to add strength, and he already hits the ball quite hard at 17 (102 mph 90th-EV), but he stands 5-foot-11 and isn't a big projection case. Despite a simple and fluid setup and a really precocious approach (he swung at 92% of pitches over the heart of the zone in his debut), Millan's 72% contact rate was just OK. His plus speed has made him an effective basestealer and gives him a real shot to stay in center, where his power-over-hit skill set could play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2025 Delaware high school player of the year, Mitchell won a state championship at Cape Henlopen HS (Lewes), a program that has produced big leaguers Mason Fluharty and Zack Gelof. The Astros drafted him in the seventh round, making him the state's highest selection since 2012 Rangers second-rounder Jamie Jarmon. Mitchell signed for $797,500, tripling his slot value and breaking Jarmon's Delaware record of $601,500. More physical than most high schoolers at 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, Mitchell features plus raw power. He needs to learn to let that pop come naturally rather than hunting home runs, which leads to his left-handed stroke getting too long and uphill. He hits balls hard but doesn't have much experience facing quality pitching, so he'll have to prove that he can hit premium velocity and breaking pitches. As a catcher, Mitchell stands out most with solid arm strength that will play better once he improves his footwork. He needs to clean up his receiving and blocking and may need some time to adjust to handling pro pitchers. He's a below-average runner but not bad for his position.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: The Astros went under slot on three straight picks before giving Mitchell, a lanky 6-foot-3 Delaware high school catcher, almost $800,000 in the seventh round of last July’s draft. All prep catchers are long-term development projects and Mitchell exemplifies that, as his small state origins mean that he’s seen and caught very little pro-level velocity. His big, projectable build provides compelling raw power potential, but he also consistently ran a contact rate over 80% on the showcase circuit and showed good bend at the waist to stay on breakers. Reports on Mitchell’s raw arm strength are positive and he moves well enough to project him to stick behind the plate, even if the work to find mechanical consistency and develop his receiving to be able to handle pro-quality stuff offers a long, risky path to major league impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college athlete in the 2019 Draft, Bishop went 10th overall to San Francisco, signed for a below-slot $4.1 million and had a solid pro debut. But he barely played in the next two years because the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season in 2020, when he came down with COVID-19 during Summer Camp, and he strained his right (throwing) shoulder in his third game of 2021, limiting him to just 16 contests. He's the younger brother of big league outfielder Braden Bishop, who spent most of last season at the Giants' Triple-A Sacramento affiliate. Bishop's bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed swing produce well above-average raw power that plays to any part of the ballpark, but he has yet to show that he can make enough contact or stay healthy enough to take advantage of his pop. He always has come with swing-and-miss concerns, and they've worsened in 2022 as he's gotten more aggressive and pull-happy. He also missed another month of needed at-bats with an oblique injury. A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a recruited walk-on at Washington before deciding to concentrate on baseball at Arizona State, Bishop has plus speed and at least 25-25 upside. He's still learning to make the most of his quickness as a basestealer and a center fielder, and his inactivity hasn't helped. He should be at least a solid defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable and accurate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington, Bishop changed his mind and opted to play baseball at Arizona State. The younger brother of Giants Triple-A outfielder Braden Bishop exploded as a junior in 2019, batting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games, which prompted the Giants to draft him 10th overall and sign him for a below-slot $4.1 million. He recorded an .867 OPS in his pro debut, participated at San Francisco's alternate training site and in instructional league last year and missed most of the first three months this season with a right shoulder injury. Bishop had some of the best raw power in the 2019 Draft, with his bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed stroke enabling him to crush the ball out of any part of the ballpark. He did a better job of translating his pop into production once he settled down his approach, worked deeper counts and began using the opposite field, but he still comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He struck out in 27 percent of his plate appearances during his debut, though he also had an encouraging walk rate of 26 percent. Add in plus speed that he's still learning how to get the most out of on the bases, and Bishop has 30-30 potential. After playing the corners during his first two college season, he took quickly to center field in 2019 and should be at least a solid defender there. His arm is fringy to average but he makes accurate throws.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bishop’s exceptionally loud tools made him the 10th overall pick in the 2019 draft despite questions about his ability to make consistent contact. Nearly three years later, those questions remain, mostly because Bishop hasn't been able to get the necessary reps thanks to a global pandemic and a 2021 season that was mostly lost to shoulder issues. Bishop has plus-plus raw power and is capable of moonshots when he gets a hold of one, but that’s rarely been on display as a pro. While he’s exceptionally patient, at times bordering on passive at the plate, he has a grooved swing that just doesn't cover much of the zone and leaves him strikeout prone despite the fact that he rarely chases. He remains a plus or better runner who covers more than enough ground in center field, but his fringe arm dipped to disturbingly below average following his return to action. More than anything, Bishop just needs a full and healthy season to get his development back on track, but it’s now been three years since he was a dominant force, which he really only was for a few weeks of pre-conference play during his draft spring.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bishop changed his college commitment late (he was originally going to play two sports at Washington), and headed to ASU. After struggling as an underclassman, he arrived for his junior season with a better body and quieter swing, and exploded, slashing .342/.479/.748 in 2019. He sent many non-conference pitches rocketing into Phoenix's midnight sky before he started seeing -- and swinging over the top of -- Pac-12 breaking balls. He was hitting .450 when PAC play began, struck out in 26% of his plate appearances, and finished hitting .342. Whether this was a real problem was the subject of many draft room debates, as was Bishop's relatively short track record of performance. Because the 2020 season was banged due to COVID, we still have very little quantifiable idea of how Bishop will handle a better cross section of breaking balls than he saw early in his junior year. He crushed middle-in pitches at the alt site but continued to waive at back foot breaking stuff. If he can indeed learn to lay off of those or drop the bat head and hit them, then he's going to be a star. Bishop has rare physical tools. He's a plus runner and will post 70 run times to first on occasion, has solid feel for center field and huge, playable power. It's unclear why his arm strength dipped as a junior when it was an asset earlier in his career, but it's not a significant part of the skillset and I heard nothing odd about his pre-draft medical, so for now I'm looking the other way. He's a Pick to Click who just needs to generate a little more confidence in his hit tool. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A star on Panamanian youth teams, Sugastey signed for $525,000 in 2019 but had his pro debut delayed by the pandemic. He broke in by winning the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title (.358) in 2021 but has had his development further delayed by quadriceps and knee injuries the last two seasons. He's the best catching prospect in the system, though the Giants declined to protect him on the 40-man roster last November because he's not close to ready for the Majors. Sugastey stands out more with his defense than his offense. He moves well behind the plate and continues to improve as a receiver and game-caller, though he still needs more consistency. With well-above-average arm strength and a quick transfer, he'll be able to combat the increased reliance on the running game. Sugastey consistently puts the ball in play with his short right-handed swing, though he's going to have to make adjustments and add strength in order to do damage. He produces mediocre exit velocities and struggles to drive the ball in the air, so he may not produce double-digit home run totals. He has a soft-contact approach that yields some gap power and few walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring in international play for Panamanian youth teams, Sugastey signed for $525,000 in 2019. The pandemic pushed his pro debut back until 2021, when he won the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title with a .358 average. He found the jump to full-season ball more difficult, hitting .240 in Single-A last summer while dealing with a quadriceps injury. In a system full of aggressive sluggers, Sugastey stands out with his bat-to-ball skills and hit-over-power approach. He repeatedly puts the ball in play with a compact right-handed stroke, though he doesn't hit the ball especially hard and must add more strength. He did a better job of avoiding ground-ball contact in 2022, but still slugged just .334 and may max out at 10-12 homers per season. More athletic than most catchers, Sugastey still is learning behind the plate. His receiving improved last season but still has a ways to go. He combats the running game with well-above-average arm strength and a quick transfer, and he also shows promise as a game caller.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing a potentially special 2018 international class, the Giants landed another deep crop the following year headlined by shortstop Aeverson Arteaga. Sugastey landed the fifth-highest bonus ($525,000) in that haul after starring in international play on Panamanian youth teams. The pandemic delayed his pro debut until 2021, when he won the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting title by hitting .358/.405/.439 at age 18. Sugastey excels at putting the bat on the ball with a compact right-handed swing, though he almost does so too easily. He hits a lot of ground balls and displays average raw power at best, so even if he continues to add strength, he might top out at 12-15 homers per year. His ability to make contact also cuts into his ability to draw walks, so much of his offensive value could come from his batting average. Sugastey owns one of the strongest arms in the system, earning plus-plus grades from some evaluators, and threw out 30 percent of basestealers in the ACL. He's more athletic than most catchers yet still a work in progress behind the plate. He needs to clean up his receiving but shows promise as a game-caller.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
Sugastey is a talented but flawed catching prospect who has had moderate success through the mid-minors despite a wreckless, over-aggressive approach. He's an athletic mover in the batter's box, especially for a catcher, and has modest but meaningful thunder in his hands, which produce average bat speed. Sugastey does everything he can to prioritize contact. He has a fairly simple swing that becomes strideless and simpler with two strikes, and he tracks pitches well and works a ton of well-timed contact back into the middle of the diamond. He had a two-strike chase rate over 60% in 2023 and his walk rates have dwindled into a problematic range (less than 5%) of late. 
Sugastey is more "fine" on defense than very good. He's a fair one-knee receiver who works through the ball from the ground up, but he isn't strong or skilled enough yet to frame pitches in other parts of the zone. Sugastey also doesn't have great pure arm strength, but his exchange is rhythmic and consistent — he's a threat to hose you because of accuracy more than velocity. Even when catchers have monster tools, plate discipline this poor still creates risk and volatility — think Jorge Alfaro and Francisco Mejía. Sugastey isn't that toolsy, but he can hit pretty well for a catcher and has no significant flaw besides his chase, so he profiles as a streaky bat-first backup.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Sugastey moved up to High-A this season, and while he’s hitting and slugging more than he did last year, he’s walking much less and his chase rates have ticked up considerably, nearing 40% as of list publication. But Sugastey is still a young catching prospect with precocious bat-to-ball skills. Aside from his ball-blocking (which is very poor), his defense isn't much worse than the typical 20-year-old catcher's. He isn't especially twitchy, which also applies to Sugastey's look in the batter's box, but our rule of thumb is to let catchers burn slowly, especially if they have a meaningful offensive skill. Sugastey is still more of a hit tool flier at a premium position than he is an actual prospect, though. He's definitely not a postseason 40-man add. Instead, you hope he takes a step next year and pushes for a spot.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Sugastey was another member of the Giants' consequential 2019 international signing class. He spent 2021 on the complex, where his ability to hit consistently was on full display; he ended the season hitting .358 and striking out just 16% of the time. His catching is significantly less spectacular, but it’s fair to allow some runway as he develops new defensive habits under professional coaching. Despite being just 19, his frame is fully filled-out, leaving little in the way of body projection. But his bat is loud and he plays a position of extreme difficulty, one lacking offensive competence at the big league level.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: The Astros dropped over $800,000 to grab Taylor at the back of the second comp round in 2022, and after elbow issues cost him most of last year and slightly delayed his start to this season, it’s easy to argue the spindly 6-foot-5 right-hander hasn't had enough runway to develop as a starter. But he already sort of pitches like a reliever, using his high-slot, 20-inch IVB four-seamer nearly 70% of the time, and he has a high-maintenance, super-rotational delivery that has driven strike-throwing issues. Taylor is sitting 90-93 at present but has flashed 95 mph this year, and if he develops a more consistent downer breaking ball, it would really tie a single-inning reliever profile together.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: An elbow issue has kept Taylor out for most of 2024; as of list publication, a source familiar with the situation has indicated he's tracking to pitch again this season but is probably still a few weeks from throwing. Taylor pitched 84 innings in a piggyback role last season and struck out 34% of opposing hitters. His fastball shape is the key component to his profile, and as such, it’s the offering he relies on most heavily. While it only sits 91, it features 21 inches of induced vertical break from a very high release point. He tends to favor his secondaries (in order of usage frequency, his slider, curveball, cutter, and changeup) when he’s ahead in the count, letting their respective vertical shapes play off the life of the heater, though he’s had limited success with them, and instead has mostly garnered upper-zone swing-and-miss with the fastball. We like him as a reliever long-term.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Taylor’s fastball shape is the key component to his profile, and as such, it’s the offering he relies on most heavily. While its velocity tops out in the mid-90s, he spins the hell out of it, giving it upper-zone life that exaggerates the extension he creates with his 6-foot-5 stature and over-the-top release point. His mid-70s curveball and mid-80s slider both clock in around 18% in terms of usage, and he'll mix in a mid-80s changeup on somewhat rare occasion. He tends to favor his secondaries when he’s ahead in the count, letting their respective vertical shapes play off the life of the heater, though he’s had limited success with them, and instead has mostly garnered upper-zone swing-and-miss with the fastball. He's working in the standard Astros piggyback role and struggling with walks. We like him as a reliever long-term. No present bat-missing secondary keeps him in the same FV tier as at last year's draft.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Taylor's fastball has ridiculous hop, and it blows past hitters at the letters with impunity even though it only sits in the low-90s. He has three secondary pitches, but often tips them with a slower arm speed of varied release of some kind. He has an elite fastball characteristic and the rest needs to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts while winning Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore in 2021, then encored by breaking his own mark with 126 the following spring. The Astros selected him in the supplemental second round, making him the Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani. His strikeout rate (13.5 per nine innings) in his 2023 pro debut ranked fourth among Minor Leaguers who worked as many as his 84 innings. Taylor's low-90s fastball features outstanding metrics because he has a 6-foot-5 frame with a high arm slot and plenty of extension, plus he backspins the ball so well that it has tremendous carry up in the zone. He has added significant strength since turning pro, weighing closer to 225 pounds than his listed 190, and the Astros hope that results in added velocity that will make his heater even more effective. After throwing roughly 80 percent fastballs in college, he's trying to refine the rest of his repertoire. His best secondary pitch is his low-80s slider, though he'll switch to a tighter version after having difficulty controlling a sweepier version in 2023. Both his upper-70s curveball and low-80s changeup are fringy and leave him vulnerable against left-handers, who batted .313/.405/.458 against him last season. He repeats his delivery well enough but will need to provide more strikes to reach his ceiling as a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2021 Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year, Taylor set a Central Michigan record with 125 strikeouts and then broke the mark with 126 whiffs last spring. He left two starts early with elbow tightness but didn't miss a turn in the rotation and looked good in the NCAA regional playoffs against Florida. The Chippewas' highest pick since 1986 second-rounder Kevin Tapani, he signed for $804,700 as a supplemental second-rounder and will make his pro debut in 2023. Taylor's fastball sits around 90 mph and tops out at 94, yet it rarely gets squared up. His heater is an analytical darling because his high spin rates produce tremendous carry and he uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create plenty of extension that throws hitters off. He relied on his fastball roughly 80 percent of the time in college, with his seldom-used 78-82 mph changeup with fade and sink serving as his most reliable secondary pitch. The Astros will work with Taylor to improve his breaking pitches and add strength. His tight 78-82 mph slider is average at best, while his soft mid-70s curveball is more of a fringy offering. He does a good job of keeping his long limbs in sync and repeating his delivery, though he has battled the strike zone more than expected in his first taste of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2017, the Royals acquired a pair of pitchers via the Rule 5 Draft, Brad Keller and Burch Smith, with Keller moving into the Royals' rotation and being very consistent there. Kansas City was at it again in '18, getting McWilliams and Chris Ellis. The organization sees some of Keller in McWilliams, a big right-hander originally drafted and signed by the Phillies who has been traded twice prior to his Rule 5 selection. The 6-foot-7 McWilliams has always been intriguing because of his size and power projection. As a starter, he's proven durable, topping 130 innings in his last two seasons of full-season ball, though he struggled a bit with a promotion to Double-A in 2018. He'll throw both a two- and four-seam fastball, the former in the low 90s with sink and the latter climbing into the mid-90s with good running action. The Royals really liked his slider as they were evaluating players for the Rule 5 Draft, and his breaking ball took a step forward last year, enabling him to miss more bats. His changeup continues to be a work in progress. While not wanting to give up on him as a starter because of his durability and ability to fill the strike zone, his best chance of initially pitching in the big leagues will likely be out of the bullpen, a la Keller. There could be an uptick on his stuff if he becomes a fastball-slider reliever with an intimidating presence.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: McWilliams is on his eighth organization (ninth if you count his Mexican League stint) since he was drafted out of high school in 2014, and he has yet to make his big league debut. After bouncing around for years, he briefly retired in 2022 and did sales and player development activity for third party companies while he wasn't pitching; the Cubs even offered him a scouting job at one point. McWilliams was goaded into throwing in the Mexican League more or less on a lark, which then led to an opportunity in the Dominican Winter League, where he looked good enough for the Cubs to sign. He's currently enjoying his best bat-missing season since moving to the bullpen in 2021, striking out 14 per 9 IP as of list publication. He sits 95-97, tends to pepper the glove-side and high portions of the zone, and has a really hard upper-80s sweeper with inconsistent finish. Both pitches are playing like above-average offerings, McWilliams' body and athleticism look as good as they ever have, and he's throwing enough strikes to put himself in position to finally make his big league debut at some point in 2024.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Still only 25-years-old, the Mets are McWilliams' fifth org. Originally a frame-based projection high schooler selected by the Phillies, McWIlliams was traded to Arizona (2015, Jeremy Hellickson) then later to the Rays as one of two PTBNL in a bigger deal (2018, Steven Souza). Then he was selected by the Royals in the 2018 Rule 5 Draft, had a bad spring and was returned to Tampa. They eventually lost him for nothing as McWilliams became a six-year minor league free agent and landed a big league deal with the Mets for $750,000. He throws really hard (95-98 last year, 94-96 and touching 97 so far this spring) and his fastball has huge spin. McWilliams just has very little feel to locate and it impacts slider quality/consistency and makes him walk-prone. McWilliams' stuff is a middle relief fit but his command pulls him more toward an up/down option year role. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez’s signing, initially scheduled to take place in the 2018-19 international window, had to wait until June 2020 due to the pandemic and an age discrepancy. After joining the Cardinals for $525,000, he moved to Single-A Palm Beach in 2021 and couldn’t break past the Florida State League until '23 when he was promoted to High-A Peoria in late June after showing significant control improvements. Nunez finished with a 3.39 ERA, 65 strikeouts and 30 walks in 63 2/3 innings between the two stops and got in eight more appearances in the Arizona Fall League where he held his own. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has always been on the St. Louis radar because of his velocity. Despite leaving the club midseason, he threw 24 of the 30 hardest pitches for Palm Beach in 2023, topping out at 99.9 mph. He averaged 96-98 mph with the heater, which acts like a sinker, and the lack of rising movement makes it more hittable than the velo alone would indicate. His upper-80s changeup is better at generating swing-and-miss with nice armside fade, and FSL hitters chased it out of the zone 43.1 percent of the time. He’ll throw a low-80s slider too, but even low-level hitters knew to lay off it given his poor command of the breaker. Nunez worked on staying within his delivery, allowing for the overall control improvements last season, but it’s going to take more for him to move beyond 40 control. He has the present stuff to be a quality reliever, and last year’s results give him solid momentum heading into his Rule 5 decision year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez was meant to sign during the 2018-19 international signing window but was declared ineligible by MLB because of an age discrepancy. The Cardinals were finally able to sign him for $525,000 in June 2020, after a pandemic-related pause in the international market. The Dominican Republic native jumped right into full-season ball the following year and showed enticing stuff with lackluster results. There are two ways to best describe Nunez’s experience at Low-A Palm Beach. First, he threw the 109 fastest pitches thrown by Palm Beach pitchers as recorded by Statcast in 2021 -- all at 98.2 mph or above and topping out at 101.1 mph. Second, he walked 56 batters in 53 2/3 innings, nearly equaling his output of 59 strikeouts in the same span. It’s a lot of gas, very few brakes from the 6-foot-3 hurler. Nunez also sports a mid-80s curveball that can flash above-average with decent spin rates and an upper-80s changeup that he doesn’t sell very well just yet. The Cardinals like Nunez’s clean delivery and work ethic and believe his control struggles were the result of inexperience due to lost time and an aggressive assignment. The righty pitched almost exclusively out of relief in 2021, and that’s where his big-time velocity profiles best anyway. If he can even find just 45-grade control in the Minors, his future as a back-end reliever will become even clearer.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Nuñez, who signed for just north of $500,000 after he was suspended for a year due to an age discrepancy, has an explosive upper-90s fastball, but he ran a bloated ERA and walk rate in his first two pro seasons due to a total lack of mechanical consistency, which seemed to be worsened by poor conditioning. Some of that was remedied in 2023 when Nuñez suddenly looked much more svelte and his delivery became somewhat more consistent. He posted a 65-to-30 strikeout to walk ratio over 63.2 innings between Low- and High-A, as Nuñez's heater averaged 96. He's struggling to miss bats at Springfield early in 2024, but his fastball is capable of overwhelming hitters when it's in the zone thanks to its plus riding action. Between his arm quickness and Nuñez's projectable frame, he’s a candidate to have top-shelf velocity in the near future. He lacks feel for both of his secondary pitches, but he’ll tease you enough to believe both have a real chance at being effective offerings if he can ever learn to harness them. Right now, he has an up/down profile worth keeping tabs on, but he has a higher ceiling than most in this bucket because of the raw stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Nunez, who signed for just north of $500,000 after he was suspended for a year due to an age discrepancy, has an explosive upper-90s fastball. But he ran a bloated ERA and walk rate in his first two pro seasons due to a total lack of mechanical consistency, which seemed to be worsened by poor conditioning. Some of that has been remedied in 2023, as Nunez looks svelte, his delivery has been much more consistent, and he's nearly halved his walk rate. Despite its velocity, the shape and angle of Nunez's fastball causes it to play down from a bat-missing standpoint, but it's getting an above-average rate of groundballs (57%). While utilizing a fastball-heavy approach overall, Nunez's changeup has caught up to his slider in terms of usage and is now outpacing it in its effectiveness. With his new, more consistent arm stroke, it could be an above-average pitch. After floating toward the very bottom of the Cardinals prospect list for the last two years as an arm strength flier, Nunez looks more like he's on track to be in the 40-man mix as a reliever after the 2024 season. A mid-season promotion to Peoria would put him on pace to spend the back half of 2024 at Springfield, comfortably within range of a roster spot if he keeps throwing strikes.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Nunez, who signed for just north of $500,000 after he was suspended for a year due to an age discrepancy, has an explosive mid-90s fastball and has been up to 101 mph, but he has very little idea where it's going and his command has regressed along with his conditioning. Purely an arm strength flier at this stage, there's big relief stuff here but low big league probability unless Nunez finds mechanical consistency.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Núñez is your pretty standard teenage pitching prospect. He's a projectable 6-foot-3, his fastball sits in the mid-90s and will climb higher than that at its very peak, and he has good breaking ball feel and an athletic, picturesque delivery. He's a fantastic developmental ball of clay who has a much better chance to start than the host of single-inning relievers who occupy most of the rest of the 40 FV tier in this system. The Cardinals got him for just north of $500,000 after Núñez was suspended a year due to an age discrepancy, but as a prospect he's pretty comparable to recent high schoolers who signed for close to $1 million, like Matt Thompson, Carter Baumler and Andrew Dalquist. (International Signee)

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text:
After three years of struggling with control (and, last season, injury), Panzini was moved to the bullpen after he returned from the IL in the middle of 2024. He's been working in a swingman/piggyback role at Quad Cities so far in 2025 and is having a career-best season. His strikeout rate is just shy of 30%, while his walk rate is in the single digits for the first time. 
Panzini is still working four-plus innings in most of his outings, even when he comes out of the bullpen, and he could conceivably transition back to starting full-time. His repertoire, however, has not really been fleshed out. He is a fastball/curveball merchant whose slider shape is basically the same as his curveball. The good news is that Panzini's fastball (which has 20 inches of vert and at times a little bit of natural cut) and curveball (12-to-6 shape that mirrors his heater) are playing like above-average pitches, giving him the projection of a middle reliever, especially if he finds more velo in a single-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Panzini was old for the 2021 high school draft class and was already a very stocky young guy, lacking typical projection, but he was already throwing hard (sitting 93 mph and topping out around 95) and his fastball had underlying traits that helped it play at the letters. Panzini also has real secondary stuff, including the makings of two good breaking balls (his slider is the better of the two) and a changeup that he already has feel for locating. He was only sitting 89-91 mph during instructs but was back in the 91-95 range during 2022 extended spring training. His pitch mix is more switched on than the other two high school pitchers picked in the 2021 draft, and while his ceiling is likely the lowest, Panzini has a chance to move more quickly than either Ben Kudrna or Frank Mozzicato.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: He's old for the class and not at all projectable, but Panzini has real stuff, including a mid-90s fastball that plays at the letters and the makings of two good breaking balls.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panzini was part of the trio of prep pitchers the Royals took high in the 2021 Draft, with his selection in the fourth round following Frank Mozzicato (first) and Ben Kudrna (second). It took Panzini until 2025 to reach the upper levels of the Minors, mainly because of a lat/oblique injury that caused him to miss significant time in ‘24. He bounced back well in ‘25, moving up three levels from High-A to Triple-A and ending the year with a 3.39 ERA in 26 games (17 starts) and 109 innings. In Double-A, where he made 13 appearances (10 starts), Panzini had a 27 percent strikeout rate and an 8.7 percent walk rate. With the injury slowing him down some, it wasn’t until 2025 that Panzini looked and felt healthy, and his velocity started to pop. His above-average fastball sits comfortably in the mid 90s and flashes into the upper 90s with good vert. Panzini has two breaking balls: an upper-70s curveball that has good depth and grades as slightly below average right now but could be above average down the line, and a mid-80s slider that is average and gets sweepy at times -- he’s working on tightening it up. Panzini is still developing a changeup that he doesn’t use much. Alongside health, Panzini has really worked on his body the last few years and is taller, leaner and stronger. He moves better now, which has helped to smooth out his delivery. Panzini made so many starts in ‘25 because he needed to throw innings following the injury, and then the Royals needed more depth in Triple-A when he made it up there at the end of the year. But it’s likely that Panzini returns there this year and makes the reliever transition; that’s where he can make an impact at the big leagues, and it can be in multi-inning stints with his arsenal.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panzini became the highest Draft pick out of Red Bank Catholic High School in southern New Jersey when the Royals selected him in the fourth round in 2021 and signed him for well-above slot at $997,500. He fit right in with the two high school pitchers the Royals took in earlier rounds, Frank Mozzicato and Ben Kudrna, and the three pitched in instructional league together last fall. The Royals viewed Panzini as an under-the-radar pick based on how many arms were in the Northeast last year and were thrilled to get him in the fourth round because of his ceiling. Pitching largely off his fastball, Panzini hovers around 94-95 mph consistently and throws the pitch with plus life and high spin. Although there’s not much projection left in his 6-foot-3, 220-pound frame, some believe there is more velocity in there. Panzini has a slider that could be above average in time, and he mixes in a changeup, though not consistently. He threw that pitch in the Royals’ fall camp and flashed some deception with it, which should help him get through a lineup multiple times. Panzini will need to learn how to land his breaking balls for strikes consistently to eliminate the reliever risk some scouts saw during the Draft process. He could fill a bullpen role with his fastball/slider combo and aggressive mindset, but he also has a durable frame that will be able to log innings. The Royals love his quiet competitiveness and plan to start him, taking their time to see what they have, but he could be someone who does move quickly as things begin to click.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Sanchez looks like the same player he was when the Angels acquired him from Philly as part of the Noah Syndergaard trade, which is a positive in some ways and a negative in others. The good: Sanchez is a lean and lanky switch-hitter who has demonstrated above-average overall feel for contact. The bad: He's been rail thin for basically his whole career and has yet to get any stronger. Sanchez's 2024 statline was pretty terrible, but Tri-City is a horrible place to hit. Sanchez's lefty swing is beautiful and pure, and he can pull pitches on the inner third with power. It may end up being sexier looking than it is functional against big league velocity, but it's a good enough reason to stay on Sanchez as a prospect to some extent. His underlying contact numbers are a bit better than average, and Sanchez's build and bodily looseness indicate athletic longevity. His ceiling is capped by a lack of physicality, but there are still fifth outfielder tools here.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Sanchez looks like the same player he was when the Angels acquired him from Philly as part of the Noah Syndergaard trade, which is a positive in some ways and a negative in others. The good: Sanchez is a lean and lanky switch-hitter who has demonstrated above-average overall feel for contact. The bad: He's been rail thin for basically his whole career and has yet to get any stronger, and his performance has mostly come as an old-for-the-level hitter. Sanchez is 23 and still at High-A, and he needs to get stronger if he's going to have the power to play right field in the big leagues. We've kept him alive on the list because of his switch-hitting contact profile, but we'd really like to see him add strength.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The switch-hitting Sanchez is off to a very strange and statistically underwhelming start with Inland Empire in 2023. That's somewhat concerning considering he's 22 and, as a bat-first prospect, should be cruising through the Cal League in his second A-ball season. The eyeball reports here are pretty much the same here, however, and it sounds like Sanchez is the same hitter the Angels traded for last year as part of the Syndergaard deal with the Phillies — he's just dealing with tough ball-in-play luck so far. He has two simple, good-looking swings, he's tough to beat in the strike zone, and he can sneak up on you with decent pop to his pull side. There aren't big showcase tools here, like power or speed, but Sanchez is a potential plus-hitting switch-hitter who still has a shot to be a part-time outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The switch-hitting Sanchez has two simple, good-looking swings, he's tough to beat in the strike zone, and he can sneak up on you with decent pop to his pull side. Early statistical returns (just 28 games in 2021) indicate he may also have plus plate discipline, as both his walk and strikeout rate was better than the Low-A average, though the sample is quite small (because of the strike-calling situation in Southeast, it's a helpful rule of thumb to comp K%/BB% to league averages rather than the kinds of rates you're used to seeing baseball-wide). Sanchez slashed .297/.373/.446 over the course of July until a COVID outbreak in the Clearwater training facility resulted in the cancellation of a handful of games. Shortly thereafter came an IL stint, effectively ending Sanchez's season. He picked up reps in the Puerto RIcan Winter League, where his surface-level performance was poor, but he looked pretty good from a scouting standpoint. There aren't big tools here, but Sanchez is a well-rounded young player with a very short supporting statistical track record.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Phillies drafted Sanchez in Round 12 of the 2019 Draft and went over slot to sign him for $300,000, he had some difficulty gaining traction, playing in the Complex League after signing and starting again there in '21 following the lost year because of the pandemic. He had trouble staying healthy in 2022 and then was sent to the Angels with Mickey Moniak in return for Noah Syndergaard at the Trade Deadline. Sanchez stayed relatively healthy last year, playing in over 100 games in a season for the first time and putting up solid numbers overall while finishing things off with an aggressive assignment to the Arizona Fall League. Finally putting in a full season, Sanchez started to unlock some of his raw tools a bit more consistently. He shook off a rough April, when he hit just .209, to hit .304 for the rest of the season. He’s a switch-hitter who’s a little better from the right side, but he showed some ability in both boxes. He’ll draw some walks, rarely strikes out and he started getting to his raw power for the first time. A corner outfielder only, Sanchez has a very strong arm, but unlike many young players with hoses they like to show off, he combines it with very consistent accuracy, which helped him rack up 15 assists from right field in 2023. He may be a fourth outfielder who plays in either corner at best, but he also might just be figuring out how to be a productive hitter, with more projection to come.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Castañon had a huge chunk of his sophomore and fourth-year junior years knocked out due to injury and had his junior season disrupted by the pandemic in between. He raked when healthy, though, and Castañon has mostly continued to do so in pro ball, as he hit 23 bombs in 2022 and is on pace to have close to another 20 at Fort Wayne in 2023. Castañon has an athletic cut that gets a lot out of his compact frame. His big leg kick is sometimes tough to time, and he can go through periods of habitual lateness because his front foot isn't down in time. He has enough power to be dangerous to all fields and enough feel to hit to get to that power in games. His underlying data is quite strong — 75% contact rate, 45% hard-hit rate — and Castañon checks a lot of visual boxes as a hitter. He does, however, have a very stiff lower half (some of his college injury woes were hamstring-related), and this impacts him on both sides of the ball. He struggles to elevate low pitches and he isn't a very rangy defender. He was a below-average defensive second baseman at UC Santa Barbara and has moved to third base, where he is also below average. He's a step slow a lot of the time but has enough arm for third. Ideally there's another position in his bag at some point so Castañon can be the righty part of a multi-player platoon.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Castanon had a huge chunk of his sophomore and fourth-year junior years knocked out due to injury and had his junior season disrupted by the pandemic in between. When healthy, he rakes. He has fantastic hitter's timing and an athletic cut that makes the most out of his compact frame. He has enough power to be dangerous and enough feel to hit to get to that power in games. Castanon has a very stiff lower half and is a below-average defensive second baseman overall, though at times he shows you the slick actions he's developed in lieu of having typical middle infield athleticism. It's a tough profile, but we like Castanon's feel to hit enough to consider him a much more notable sleeper than the typical Day Three college draftee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Castañon broke out with a 1.208 OPS during his senior year at UC Santa Barbara in 2021 but was limited to only 28 games by a broken hand, hurting his Draft stock. The Padres picked the infielder in the 12th round that summer, signed him for $125,000 and have seen him hit at every Minor League stop since. Castañon was a California League end-of-season All-Star for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first full campaign, then slashed .287/.352/.491 with 13 homers in 77 games for High-A Fort Wayne to begin 2023. His numbers at Double-A San Antonio were much closer to average (.280/.335/.436) over a 54-game stint to end the year. The right-handed hitter has put up solid batting averages at every stop, staying on time with the ball even with a large leg kick. That leads to hard contact that helps fuel the numbers, despite below-average speed that would otherwise help pick up extra hits here and there. Castañon was especially good at elevating and spraying the ball to all fields at Fort Wayne but got more pull- and ground-ball heavy at San Antonio, hurting his power. There’s still potential for 15-plus homers though, if he can even out those approaches. Castañon needs to hit because he’s a major question mark defensively. His lack of agility makes him a rough fit for second base, and his lack of arm strength makes him a stretch for third base. Those have been his two primary positions in pro ball, and barring a full-time move to first base, there isn’t a great place to hide his glove. Castañon might be best at being a right-handed part of a DH platoon and bench infielder, provided he carries his previous results to the upper levels.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
Phillips had a huge velo spike during his 2022 senior spring. After sitting about 91 mph during his showcase summer, he was sitting 94-98 with relative ease during his draft year until he had Tommy John in early April. The Braves still saw fit to give him about $1.5 million in the second round. The Mariners used their amateur reports to inform their decision when they traded for Phillips as part of the Jarred Kelenic/Evan White contract swap. Phillips needed a second Tommy John before the 2024 season and won't be back until 2025. 
Healthy Phillips has a powerful, athletic delivery, though scouts have had varying opinions about the quality and consistency of his secondary stuff. Seattle has shown an ability to coax better secondary stuff out of George Kirby (who was also fastball-heavy as an amateur) and others. Phillips is a prospect of extreme variance. It's tough to value an arm strength-only prospect who will have gone several years between starts in an actual game, but Phillips has the talent to be a good reliever even if only one or two of his other attributes progress.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Phillips had a huge velo spike during his 2022 senior spring. After sitting about 91 mph during his showcase summer, he was sitting 94-98 with relative ease during his draft year until he had Tommy John in early April. The Braves still saw fit to give him about $1.5 million in the second round. Phillips has a powerful, athletic delivery and a slightly more mature physicality than the typical high school prospect, though scouts have had varying opinions about the quality and consistency of his secondary stuff. It made developmental sense for Phillips to sign rather than go to school since, for one, the Braves have shown the ability to augment secondary stuff during the rehab process, and that's the area where Phillips needs the most developmental love. The length of the pro schedule will also allow Phillips to get some late-summer work whereas the college schedule would not have. Phillips has some of the most extreme prospect variance in the Braves system. It's tough to value an arm strength-only prospect whose future is clouded by surgery on the same level as the near-ready big leaguers in the 40 FV tier, but if Phillips returns with peak arm strength, and especially if his secondary stuff has improved, he'll be in the 40+ FV tier by the end of 2023 baseball activities.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Phillips had a huge velo spike during his senior spring. After sitting about 91 mph during his showcase summer, he was sitting 94-98 with relative ease during his senior spring, until he had Tommy John in early-April. He has a powerful, athletic delivery and a slightly more mature physicality than the typical high school prospect, though scouts have had varying opinions about the quality and consistency of Phillips' secondary stuff. He may still sign and complete his TJ rehab as a pro. He'd be on pace for a late-2023 debut if he signs, whereas he might not pitch competitively until the year after that (the 2023 college season will be just about over at the 14-month mark of his rehab) if he goes to school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips’ raw stuff has intrigued evaluators for some time, but injuries have largely kept it in the mythical category. The Braves took him in the second round of the 2022 Draft because of his upside despite the fact he had Tommy John surgery in April of his senior year of high school. He spent the 2023 season rehabbing and then was sent to the Mariners in the trade for Jarred Kelenic and others. Phillips had an eye on taking the mound competitively in 2024 when he needed a second TJ leading up to Spring Training, so he enters the 2025 season without having an official professional pitch on his résumé. It’s hard to know exactly what Phillips might be because it’s possible he hasn’t been truly healthy since his junior year of high school in 2021. The Texas native has shown high-octane stuff, with a fastball that has good run and sits in the mid 90s, touching close to 100. His breaking ball is a bit of a hybrid, thrown with slider-like velocity around 85 mph, but with curveball depth. There is feel for a fading changeup, but he hadn’t used it much nor had time to develop it. All of Phillips’ grades are hypothetical and on-paper numbers at this point. The hope is to get him on the mound at some point during the 2025 season, and while it will likely be '26 before anyone will be able to get any sense of what kind of pitcher he might be, the potential that intrigued the Braves three years ago is still too good to completely forget about him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was high on the Mariners’ radar ahead of the 2022 Draft, but the Tommy John surgery he underwent in April impacted his status and led him to being taken by the Braves in the second round for $1.5 million. He wound up in Seattle’s system as the upside return in the 2023 trade that sent Jarred Kelenic to Atlanta, but then he underwent a second TJ leading up to Spring Training in ‘24 that will further prevent him from making his pro debut. Part of what may have led to his injuries is also what made him so enticing, which is the fastball with elite velocity that sits in the mid-90s, flirts with triple digits and features strong running action. His best secondary pitch is a power breaking ball that he gets up to 85 mph, a pitch that has curveball depth with slider velocity. With that type of combination, he doesn’t often use the changeup that he has in his back pocket that possesses good fade. The most notable comparison Phillips has drawn is to Nathan Eovaldi, who was also high on Draft boards back in 2008 as a Texas high schooler before sustaining an elbow injury. The focus for Phillips in 2024 will again be to get healthy after another brutally unfortunate setback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Phillips was rushing up Draft boards in the spring of 2022 as reports flowed in of the Texas prep right-hander hitting triple digits with his fastball. He seemed like he had a shot at being a first-round pick until the train was derailed temporarily by Tommy John surgery in April. He had been scouted regularly prior to the injury and the Braves felt comfortable enough to take him as their third straight high school arm in the 2022 Draft, signing him for $1.5 million as their second-round pick. He never threw an official pitch for the Braves, who sent him and fellow right-hander Jackson Kowar to the Mariners in the December trade that sent Jarred Kelenic, Evan White and Marco Gonzales to Atlanta. The hope is that Phillips will get back to the improved stuff he showed before the elbow injury. His fastball can sit in the mid-90s, reach the upper 90s and touch 100 mph with good running action. His breaking ball, a power curve with depth thrown up to 85 mph, could be a plus pitch. Like many prep hurlers with that kind of fastball-breaking ball combination, he didn’t use his changeup much, but he has shown feel for a mid-80s offering with fade. Compared by some to big leaguer Nathan Eovaldi, a Texas high schooler who blew out his elbow as a junior, Phillips’ improved strength has led to a repeatable delivery and more strikes. He’ll get his first true professional test in his new organization in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic when they stumbled upon Morel, whom they signed for $97,500 in 2023. He tore up the Dominican Summer League in his pro debut, hitting .344/.417/.644 and topping the Rookie-level circuit with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He continued to excel when he came to the United States last year, slashing .307/.407/.575 to rank third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in slugging and fourth in OPS (.982). Significantly larger and stronger than his listed 180 pounds suggests, Morel hits balls harder than most teenagers and has plus raw power. He has had less success tapping into it in 2025, when he hasn't launched balls in the air to his pull side as easily and his plate discipline has regressed. His right-handed swing can get too long at times and his aggressive mindset results in strikeouts. Morel draws comparisons to a more athletic version of Marcell Ozuna. He presently has solid speed and looks to make things happen on the bases, though he may slow down if he gets much bigger. His plus arm contributes to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts and effort need improvement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sebastian Walcott's $3.2 million bonus absorbed most of Texas' 2023 international bonus pool, but they also may have found a bargain in Morel, who signed for $97,500 and was discovered while the Rangers were scouting other players in the Dominican Republic. He batted .344/.417/.644 in his pro debut, topping the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League with 17 doubles, eight triples, 32 extra-base hits and 116 total bases. He puts on one of the best batting-practice shows in the system and draws some comparisons to two-time All-Star Marcell Ozuna. Morel has a quick right-handed swing, more strength than most teenagers and room on his 6-foot-2 frame to add more muscle. He has plus raw power and gets to most of it, already showing the aptitude to drive balls in the air to his pull side. He'll need to tighten up his plate discipline as he faces more advanced pitching, but he doesn't strike out excessively. Morel is fairly athletic but could slow down a bit as he matures physically. He's presently a solid runner but hasn't shown much feel for stealing bases. He has arm strength to match, adding to his right-field profile, though his defensive instincts need some work.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Morel signed for just under $100,000 in 2023 and has had two power-hitting rookie ball seasons, with a .307/.407/.575 line in Surprise last year. He's a very physical teenage outfielder who is still listed at a comical 180 pounds on his player page. In reality, he's pushing closer to 230 pounds already at age 19, and he has the kind of raw power you'd expect given a young hitter that size. Morel's hit tool is a bit suspect. He K'd at a 24% clip in his first two seasons and his strikeout rate has exploded in 2025 as he repeats the ACL. His ability to do damage is limited to a relatively narrow part of the zone. He could feasibly be a power-over-hit corner guy in the Nelson Velázquez mold, but we'd like to see him mash against upper-level pitching before declaring him any more than a power-hitting bench weapon.
