mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Venezuela native didn’t sign with the Mets until he was a 19-year-old in August 2021 but moved quickly, reaching Single-A St. Lucie the following year. New York used him as a reliever that first full season in the Florida State League with promising results: a 3.78 ERA and 54 strikeouts in 47 2/3 innings. Gomez generated a ton of buzz in his second Spring Training, averaging 100 mph during one backfields outing. He made three starts for High-A Brooklyn as the Mets hoped to see him transition into a rotation, but he needed Tommy John surgery after that and missed the rest of the season. Gomez’s fastball sat 96-98 mph before surgery and regularly touched triple digits. The heater had plenty of ride up in the zone too, making it more than just a radar-gun darling. He also showed an upper-80s slider that could break over two planes, leading to some buckled knees from anyone trying to time their swing on the fastball. An upper-80s changeup remained very much a work in progress, and that will continue when he returns in 2024. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s velo increase coincided with control issues as he walked nine batters in his seven innings with Brooklyn. The ability to limit walks was closer to average at the lower levels, and there’s hope it would have improved as the sample grew larger in the South Atlantic League. Regardless, Gomez had arguably the best two-pitch profile in the Mets system pre-injury, and he could be dominant in a move back to the bullpen when healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pham was a 19th-round pick in the 2021 Draft as a senior reliever out of the University of San Francisco and signed for just $25,000, so he wasn’t really on anyone’s radar when he broke out in 2023, leading Orioles hurlers in a host of major statistical categories and finishing the year at Double-A. He spent all of 2024 back at that level, and after getting off to a slow start, pitched to a 3.00 ERA with more than a strikeout per inning over his last 18 starts. Undersized and lacking huge stuff, the 5-foot-11 Pham makes up for those shortcomings and gets the most out of his ability with a deep arsenal of pitches and a bulldog mentality. He operates with a low-90s fastball that is average velocity-wise but can be difficult to square up because its high spin and Pham’s low arm slot give it the illusion of rising action. He supplements that pitch with an array of secondary offerings. None are plus pitches on their own, but Pham is effective when he mixes them up. He draws high marks for his makeup, competitiveness and moxie. He’s become a better strike thrower since transitioning full-time into a starter, though he struggled early last year when his walk rate began creeping back up. Whether he can reach his low ceiling as a back-end starter will hinge on his ability to command all of his pitches consistently and maintain his strength and stuff, both deep into starts and throughout the season. Anything less and he could emerge as a swingman type who is able to cover innings relatively soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Cutter: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Pham was a reliever for four years at the University of San Francisco and pitched out of the bullpen for parts of two seasons after the Orioles signed him for just $25,000 after selecting him in Round 19 of the 2021 Draft. Given the chance to start last summer, Pham put himself on the prospect map with a 2.57 ERA across 112 innings. He led organizational pitchers in ERA, xFIP (3.68), WHIP and K/BB (19.9 percent) and finished the year at Double-A Bowie. Undersized at 5-foot-11, Pham doesn’t have the typical build of a starter. But he has five pitches at his disposal and uses his height to his advantage, throwing from a low slot and angle that helps his hoppy fastball play up and makes him difficult to time. That fastball lives at 92-93 mph and can touch 96 with good spin. But his success comes from his assortment of secondary offerings, which all individually grade out as average but are effective when Pham mixes them up. His cutter and curve are his best pitches to lefties, his slider can be a plus offering against righties and he has an average changeup that he folds in on occasion. Pham didn’t have a huge track record of throwing strikes when converted into a starter, but he posted the lowest walk rate of his career (including college) last year and sliced it even lower after a midseason promotion to Bowie. Drawing high marks for his competitiveness and moxie, he was able to maintain his stuff as a starter, both over the course of five- to six-inning starts and six months of the season. Whether he stays in that role long term hinges on whether he can keep developing the feel for his secondary pitches and continue throwing all his offerings for strikes on a consistent basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After splitting time as a starter and reliever at Illinois, Lavender headed to the MLB Draft League with Mahoning Valley in 2021 for another opportunity to boost his stock. The Mets selected him in the 14th round, signed him for $125,000 and immediately gave him a full-time role in the bullpen. The southpaw appeared for all five domestic affiliates in his first three seasons, topping out at Triple-A Syracuse in 2023. After posting a 3.27 ERA with 67 strikeouts in 44 innings in the International League and ranking second among Mets Minor Leaguers (min. 50 IP) with a 36.9 percent K rate last season, Lavender was diagnosed with ligament damage this April. Lavender is the rare reverse-split reliever -- he held righties to a .164/.265/.336 line in 2023 compared to .241/.366/.374 for lefties. A big reason is the deception in his three-quarters-slot delivery. He hides his 90-92 mph fastball (touching 95) exceptionally well, and it sneaks up in the zone against righties, who missed on 48 percent of their swings against the heater. For that reason, Lavender went to the fastball 66 percent of the time against righties and 65 percent overall in 2023. His 78-81 mph changeup got an even better whiff rate (56 percent) against other-side batters because of the velo separation and way he sells it out of his hand, but its usage lags well behind the fastball. He also has a low-80s slider with some sweep, but it’s not nearly as effective as batters slugged .463 off it in ’23. The effort in Lavender’s delivery can get him off line at times, and he’ll run into some problems with location and control. That – and his lack of standout velo – may keep him from serving a prominent role in future Mets bullpens, but he’s essentially ready to get out Major League batters from both sides now.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Lavender, who was selected in the Rule 5 Draft last December, had the internal brace style of Tommy John early in 2024 and will start the 2025 season on the 60-day IL; he should be back in mid-to-late summer. In 2023, he struck out 86 hitters in 54.1 innings, and Lavender has a career K/9 of 13.7 even though his fastball, which he throws 65% of the time, sits just 91 mph. That’s because he has one of the more deceptive deliveries in the minors. He almost looks like someone who learned to throw with their left arm later in life. There are some Hideki Okajima elements to his delivery, including Lavender’s head whack, which prevents him from seeing his target at release. He gets way, way, way down the mound, generating seven and a half feet of extension. His arm action is also super whippy, and the line on his fastball is incredibly difficult for hitters to get on top of. The rest of his repertoire isn't great, but Lavender smells like an up/down reliever on the back of his fastball alone. If he can come out of TJ rehab with a good second pitch or more fastball velocity, look out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Only two pitchers cracked MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list in 2024, and the highest-ranked arm on the list came at No. 25 in Franco. The Dominican right-hander signed with the Cardinals for $800,000, and while he’s since been outshined by other members of his signing class in Rainiel Rodriguez and Yairo Padilla, it’s worth remembering that he was the one who received St. Louis’ highest bonus in 2024. Franco didn’t flash impressive numbers out of the gate with a 6.16 ERA, a 1.63 WHIP and 37 strikeouts in 38 innings in the Dominican Summer League, but he showed some of the promise that made him a notable addition in the first place. Officially 16 on signing day, Franco was all about projection when he first joined the St. Louis system, and his arsenal has already shown an upward trajectory in year one. After sitting 91-93 mph with his tailing fastball as an amateur, he’s closer to the 93-95 mph range now, and entering his age-18 season, there’s still likely more room for velo. He improved a high-70s slurve to be more of a low-80s sweeping slider while his mid-80s changeup needs more refinement. DSL pitchers are typically wild, and Franco was no exception with a 13.3 percent walk rate in year one. Harnessing his pitches will be just as important as improving their individual pitch quality, and that’ll be part of the process as he expands his professional workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2024 international class was much more heavy on bats than arms. In fact, only two pitchers featured among MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 international list this offseason, and the highest-ranked of the pair was Franco at No. 25. The Dominican Republic native signed with the Cardinals for $800,000 at the start of the signing window on Jan. 15, becoming the organization’s most high-profile addition of the period -- one in which it was down $500,000 in pool money after signing Willson Contreras in 2022. Having only turned 17 back in February, Franco is all about projection. He already stands 6-foot-3 and is expected to fill out as he heads toward and into his 20s. Even so, he already sits 91-93 mph with a tailing fastball that can help generate ground balls now, and considering his present arm speed, there’s a good chance he could be adding a few more ticks to that heater in time. He can sell his 85-87 mph changeup well out of his three-quarters arm slot, and he shows a high-70s slurve that he uses as his preferred offspeed weapon for now. The right-hander can pitch in the zone well from a fairly low-effort delivery at his current stage of development, though that deserves following if he does end up adding velocity. Creating better separation across his fastball and changeup will help too, but in general, he has the tools to be a potential Major League starting pitcher down the road.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Franco’s second year in the DSL got off to a late start and then built up slowly. Despite never getting a specific injury designation, he didn't make any starter-length outings until the end of the season and only covered 16.1 innings total, but he took another step toward wielding standout present velocity. The 19-year-old righty's fastball now sits 94-97 mph, and he throws an encouraging number of strikes with it (60% in-zone rate); he also has a mid-80s slider with decent length, such that it is overwhelming his current competition (50% miss rate). The rest of his arsenal is still pretty rudimentary and his short stride furthers the relief feel, but it’s easy above-average velocity from a teenager who bears watching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was working his way back from a knee injury in the spring, but despite not being scouted much, he still looked like the best Draft prospect out of Puerto Rico in the 2023 class. That status was cemented when he headed to the Draft Combine in June, and by Draft day, he'd established himself as MLB Pipeline’s No. 213 prospect in the class. The Padres liked him even more than that, selecting him in the third round and signing him for $550,000. Gonzalez became the first Puerto Rican catcher selected in the first 10 rounds since 2017 (Santis Sanchez, A’s). He opened with Single-A Lake Elsinore in 2024 and was traded to the Rays at the Deadline as part of a three-player return for reliever Jason Adam. There are plenty of interesting parts of Gonzalez’s profile, starting with his status as a left-handed-hitting backstop. The Combine was the perfect place for him to show above-average raw power with a steady rate of exit velocities above 96 mph, and there’s a chance he could add even more pull-side pop in pro ball. The biggest raves he earns are reserved for his arm strength, with one evaluator noting he has a “bazooka” behind the dish. His blocking and receiving skills could end up being solid with professional work, and therein lies the rub. Having only turned 18 in October of his Draft year, Gonzalez faces a potentially long developmental path, and the history of prep catchers isn’t terrific across the game. But the building blocks, in this case, are worthy of some early excitement and intrigue, and that’s what the Rays were buying into with this acquisition.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Unknown to FanGraphs until he showed up at the 2023 MLB Draft Combine, Gonzalez had one of the better high school BPs at the event and arguably the prettiest swing. He's a loose rotator with lovely natural loft, though his swing does have some length to it. His swing path and length lead to a lot of oppo gap contact and a general inability to turn on the ball. He has really struggled on offense at Lake Elsinore and might have a bottom-of-the-barrel hit tool because he won't be able to get around on pro fastballs. His receiving is also predictably raw, but the twitch and explosion from his crouch and Gonzalez's raw arm strength are both exciting. He's a dev project with extreme risk and variance, mostly on the main section of the list because of how we value catching.

fangraphs.text: Leeper had an extreme collection of injury issues as an amateur, including two Tommy John surgeries. He was totally healthy and throwing very hard during his last few seasons at Oklahoma State, but he still ended up being passed over in the shortened 2020 draft and signed as an undrafted free agent. Less than a year after signing, Leeper was at Triple-A blowing upper-90s gas past veteran hitters and working with a plus slider. He seemed poised to debut in Chicago either late in 2022 or sometime in 2023, but he blew out again this spring and had his third career TJ in April. A successful rehab will put Leeper back on the doorstep of a big league relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring as a Texas prep junior, Leeper underwent two Tommy John surgeries and an ulnar nerve transposition that limited him to 2 2/3 innings over his senior season and first two years at Oklahoma State. He persevered and eventually became the Cowboys' closer before signing with the Cubs for $20,000 as a 23-year-old nondrafted free agent in 2020. He made a spectacular pro debut last summer, recording a 1.29 ERA with 53 strikeouts in 35 innings between Double-A and Triple-A, though he was shut down in August with elbow inflammation. Leeper goes after hitters with two pitches. His four-seam fastball sits at 94-96 mph and touches 99, and it features a flat approach angle and riding life that make it tough for hitters to barrel. If they try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with an 86-88 mph slider that features tremendous depth. After averaging 7.0 walks per nine innings during his college career, Leeper more than halved that rate to 3.3 in his pro debut. His stuff is real and if his control is as well, he could help Chicago in the near future and eventually fill a high-leverage role. The biggest question is his health, as he didn't pitch on consecutive days in 2021 before missing the final two months, though the Cubs say his shutdown was precautionary more than anything else.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
It took a little over $1.2 million to sign Heubeck away from a Wake Forest commitment when he was a rail thin 6-foot-3 and had lovely natural breaking ball depth. He was seemingly poised to break out whenever he could add weight and velo, and shore up his strike-throwing. In the four years since he was drafted, Heubeck has added some arm strength and has been able to sustain it across (at most) 91 innings, but the command piece of his profile hasn't improved and he's had double-digit walk rates at every minor league level. 
Heubeck's delivery is similar to that of former Dodgers prospect Clayton Beeter. He has a drop-and-drive style, hides the ball for a long time, and has a nearly perfect vertical arm slot on release. It creates huge ride on Heubeck's fastball, which averages just over 20 inches of vertical break, but he doesn't command it. Both of Heubeck's breaking pitches — a truly beautiful 12-to-6 curveball and a mid-80s gyro slider — have tended to generate plus or better rates of swing-and-miss. Because Heubeck's slider feel is the best of all his pitches, he leaned on it more often as a strike-getter in 2025 and it wasn't as successful at missing bats. Rotator cuff inflammation curtailed his 2025 innings output and the Dodgers chose not to put him on their 40-man roster after the season. We think he'd perform in a relief role where his scattershot control would be less of an issue and allow him to use his slider for chase again.

Heubeck's feel for landing his slider is the best of his three pitches, and it might suit him to use it more often early in counts. The ship is close to sailing on Heubeck as a starter, as he's in his 40-man platform year and is once again struggling to throw strikes. His stuff is good enough to play in relief, even if Heubeck's velocity stays the same with the role change.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Heubeck brought a snappy curveball and projectable frame to the table as a high school draftee, and there was hope that he could really pop as a prospect if he could develop more velocity and find more consistent feel for release. After a rough 2022, that began to happen in 2023, as Heubeck righted the ship while repeating Low-A before struggling after a late-season promotion. Heubeck's fastball added a tick and a half of velo, averaging 93.5 mph across the entire season. He made more consistent use of two distinct breaking balls, both of which have lovely natural depth. Still skinny as can be — Triston McKenzie is a fair body comp and not a bad delivery comp, either — Heubeck has more room for mass on his frame and is still only 21 years old. His power pitcher's style of attack is inherently a little inefficient from a strike-throwing standpoint, but Heubeck's limber and loose flavor of athleticism, his physical projectability, and the strike-throwing strides he made in 2023 are all indications that his control will continue to improve. His slider and curveball are distinct enough to give him starter's repertoire depth. If he can maintain his Low-A performance across an entire 2024 season, he'll have put himself in position to be a 40-man add after the 2025 campaign. Of the many 20-to-22-year-old high-variance pitchers in the org, Heubeck has the best chance to start.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Heubeck brought a snappy curveball and projectable frame to the table as a high school draftee, and there was hope that he could really pop as a prospect if he could develop more velocity and find more consistent feel for release. So far neither has happened, and Heubeck struggled through 15 short, inefficient starts in 2022 once he finally left the complex and went to an affiliate. While his delivery is very loose and fluid, Heubeck doesn't repeat it consistently right now, working in the low-90s with carry at the top of the strike zone. That inconsistency extends to his curveball quality, which is nasty when Heubeck snaps it off right. The Dodgers have tended to be an organization that can help players like Heubeck tighten these things up and come closer to reaching their ceilings, but league-wide, for every long-term pitching prospect who hits in a big way, there are many more for whom things remain stagnant or go awry. This is the track Heubeck is on. He's list-worthy because of the hope that things will somehow click, which is still feasible at his age.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: We're being disciplined and resisting the urge to 40+ Heubeck here as we try to be consistent across the minors with how we grade this sort of profile. Heubeck has a real chance to pop as a mid-rotation, Top 100 prospect because the thing he needs to develop is premium velocity, and there are things about him (his on-mound athleticism and prototypical frame) that indicate he will. He is very loose and fluid but doesn't repeat his delivery consistently right now, working in the low-90s with carry at the top of the strike zone. He has inconsistent feel for creating vertical action on his curveball, but when he snaps it off right, it's a really promising, exciting pitch. The Dodgers have tended to be an organization that can help players like Heubeck tighten these things up and come closer to reaching their ceilings, which in this case is substantial. But league-wide, for every teenage pitching prospect like this who hits in a big way, there are many more who never actually develop more arm strength, or who do but struggle to sustain it, or who get hurt, and that has to factor into how we view Heubeck more than the bias created by Dodgers player dev pixie dust. And it isn't like Heubeck's velo instantly popped: he was still in the low-90s and somewhat erratic when Eric saw him this spring.

fangraphs.text: A plus athlete with a plus frame, Heubeck is more about stuff projection than perhaps any pitcher from the 2021 draft. He is very loose and fluid but doesn't repeat his delivery consistently right now. He works 90-94 with carry and pitches at the top of the strike zone, and he has inconsistent feel for creating vertical action on his curveball, but when he snaps it off right it's a really promising, exciting pitch. There is a sizeable gap between Heubeck's present ability and his ceiling, but he presents the DOdgers with really exciting raw material for their developmental staff to work with.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland High School Player of the Year in 2021, Heubeck offered one of the best curveballs and was one of the most polished pitchers in that year's prep class. Since the Dodgers signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment with an over-slot $1,269,500 bonus in the third round, he has gained velocity but lost some feel for pitching. He missed the last two months of the 2025 season with rotator-cuff inflammation, and his strikeout rate (28 percent) ranked fifth in the Double-A Texas League and his walk rate was the eigth-highest (12 percent) among pitchers who worked at least as many as his 66 1/3 innings. Heubeck's fastball operates at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with huge induced vertical break that helps it ride by barrels up in the zone. Both of his breaking balls grade as plus pitches and get lefties and righties out when they're on, though he also has difficulty landing his upper-70s downer curveball and tight mid-80s slider for strikes. He also struggles to locate a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Heubeck filled the strike zone as an amateur and should have at least average control given his athleticism and clean arm action. Instead of his letting his stuff play naturally, he'll lapse into overthrowing his fastball and overspinning his breakers. Though Los Angeles still hopes to develop him into a starter, it's more realistic to project him as a bat-missing reliever whose ability to throw strikes will determine what role he fills.

mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's Maryland high school player of the year in 2021, Heubeck stood out with one of the best curveballs and some of the best polish in that year's prep class. He posted a 3.05 ERA at High-A last year with the best average-against (.181) and second-highest strikeout percentage (30 percent) among Midwest League pitchers with at least 90 innings, but he also had the worst walk percentage (17 percent). Heubeck now operates with a 92-95 mph fastball that reaches 97 with huge induced vertical break that creates significant carry. Both his upper-70s downer curveball and his tighter mid-80s slider can be plus pitches that work against both lefties and righties when he lands them for strikes, which he hasn't done consistently in pro ball. He also has a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink that could be an average pitch if he learns to harness it. Heubeck has a clean arm action and an athletic delivery that should be conducive to at least average control. He sometimes overspins his breaking balls and needs to find a better balance between trying to create nasty stuff and throwing strikes. The Dodgers still think he could develop into a No. 3 or 4 starter, even if takes longer than they expected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heubeck earned Gatorade's 2021 Maryland high school player of the year award after leading Gilman School (Baltimore) to the state Class A title, fanning 15 in a complete-game victory in the semifinals and saving the finale. The Dodgers drafted him in the third round, making him the Old Line State's highest prep pitcher pick since 2005, and signed him away from a Wake Forest commitment for an over-slot $1,269,500. He quickly stood out with his aptitude during his four-inning pro debut and in instructional league, with one club official describing him as \"plug and play.\" Heubeck already possesses a plus curveball with upper-70s velocity and legitimate 12-6 break. It plays well off his fastball, which sits at 90-93 mph and tops out at 95 with good induced vertical break and carry up in the strike zone. He also shows promising feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink. With a clean arm action and athletic delivery, Heubeck should provide at least average control. His strike-throwing and velocity should improve as he adds some much-needed strength to his skinny 6-foot-3 frame. A potential No. 3 or 4 starter, he could move through the Minors more quickly than most high school pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like his father, Eric, the 1992 National League Rookie of the Year, Karros played collegiately at UCLA before turning pro with the Dodgers. He pitched just 41 innings in three years with the Bruins because of the pandemic and persistent back issues that sidelined him for all of 2022, when Los Angeles drafted him in the 16th round. He has filled the strike zone while climbing from Single-A to Double-A the past two seasons, though he missed nearly three months last summer with mild flexor soreness. Karros' fastball parks at 91-93 mph and reaches 96 but stays off barrels because his 6-foot-7 frame creates an unusually high release point and plenty of extension. He'll spot his heater where he wants, then catch hitters off balance with a solid low-80s changeup that he leverages down in the zone. He also can miss bats with a low-80s slider that has depth and occasionally will flip in a fringy upper-70s curveball. Karros stands out more for his pitchability and deception than his pure stuff. He repeats his simple delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes, though he nibbled at the zone a bit too much when he got hit harder in Double-A. He has a high floor and could become a back-of-the-rotation starter.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Eric Karros has two boys in pro ball (Jared and Kyle), and they're set to have concurrent big league careers, as Kyle has already debuted and Jared has a chance to do so soon if he can stay healthy in 2026. Jared is the oldest, a spot starter with plus command and a much improved changeup. Injuries and missed reps add risk to his profile, but also they give him late bloomer characteristics. The pandemic knocked out just about all of his freshman season at UCLA, while a nagging back injury limited him to seven appearances as a sophomore and wiped out his entire junior season. In pro ball, Karros missed roughly 10 weeks of 2024 with a flexor strain, and his 2025 ended in June due to a forearm muscle injury. 
When healthy, Karros looks like a command-oriented innings-eater. He has rare size at 6-foot-7 and has a high arm slot, giving him a release height of about 6-foot-9. It creates huge downhill plane on all of his pitches, aiding the effectiveness of his well-commanded breaking balls, which have a little extra depth as a result. He employs a slider-heavy approach against righties and a fastball/changeup mix against lefties. In 2025, Karros was more consistently creating sink and tailing action on his changeup, which has become his best pitch from a miss and chase standpoint, though none of his pitches are overtly plus. Uncommon mechanical consistency for a pitcher his size helps him throw starter-quality strikes, which is the bedrock of his fifth starter profile. Karros' injuries slid him further down in this FV tier than he would have been had he stayed healthy for all of 2025.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text:
Eric Karros has two boys in pro ball (Jared and Kyle), both of whom are pretty likely to play in the big leagues. Jared is the oldest, a potential back-of-the-rotation starter with a rapidly improving changeup. The pandemic knocked out just about all of Jared's freshman season at UCLA, while a nagging back injury limited him to seven appearances as a sophomore and wiped out his junior season. In pro ball, Karros has climbed to Double-A Tulsa and been relatively healthy, save for a flexor tendon injury that cost him about 10 weeks of 2024. 
Karros is 6-foot-7 and has a high arm slot, giving him a release height of about 6-foot-9. It creates huge downhill plane on all of his pitches, aiding the effectiveness of his breaking balls, which have a little extra depth as a result. Karros commands his mid-80s slider to the glove side of the plate, and at the start of 2025, he's been more consistently creating sink and tailing action on his changeup, which has been his best pitch so far this year. Those two pitches are average and above on pure stuff, and play a little better thanks to Karros' command. Karros will pepper the top of the zone with his fastball to get ahead in the count, and then work his secondaries to the corners, with the occasional dirt-bound curveball rounding out his repertoire. His heater has played like a below-average pitch to this point, which might be more of an issue against big leaguers, especially if it means Karros needs to more frequently pitch backwards early in outings. Aside from his injury history, he's a stable backend starter prospect on track to debut at some point next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Belgrave's lack of polish led to him redshirting in his first college season at Maryland and recording a 6.79 ERA with 51 walks in 51 2/3 innings during the next two. The Marlins still saw enough promise to draft him in the 15th round last July and he posted a 2.16 ERA in Single-A during his pro debut, though he still battled the strike zone. He allowed one run in three playoff appearances during Jupiter's run to the Florida State League championship. Both of Belgrave's pitches looked better than ever during his brief debut. His primary weapon is a late-biting slider that sat at 86-88 in his first taste of pro ball after parking at 82-84 mph during the spring. His fastball also jumped form 93-95 mph with the Terrapins to 95-97 with the Hammerheads, and its heavy life induces groundouts. Belgrave has a short arm action and considerable effort in his delivery, so he has trouble repeating his pitches and throwing strikes. He's going to work on adding a changeup as Miami considers trying him as a starter, but he's probably going to wind up as a two-pitch reliever. If he can improve his control and command, he could be a seventh- or eight-inning option.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text: Belgrave and the other Pensacola players wore custom Player's Weekend-style unis recently and the back of Belgrave's jersey read "Stuff Plus." This is a big-framed, 6-foot-4 righty who uses a short stride down the mound and a sidearm slot. His fastball finishes with tail in the up/arm-side corner of the zone, but Belgraves' best pitch is easily his slider. His lower slot creates big lateral wipe on that pitch, and Belgrave can throw it for strikes much more consistently than his fastball at this stage. He also shows you a cutter every once in a while, though he's only using it 10% of the time right now. He's tracking for a late-2026 debut in an up/down relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles under Mike Elias love to draft college players, and the 2024 Draft was no different, with Baltimore taking each of their first six picks from the collegiate ranks. But they tend to break that pattern once or twice per Draft for a prep player they really believe in, and in 2024, that was Layton. An athletic infielder from Charlotte Christian HS in North Carolina, Layton was the only high schooler the Orioles took in the top 10 rounds when they made him a sixth-rounder. They then went more than twice over slot to sign him away from his commitment to Southern Miss for $715,800. The Orioles decided to wait for 2025 for Layton to make his pro debut. But they are bullish on the athletic switch-hitter with a few interesting raw tools. He’s shown some ability to make consistent contact from both sides of the plate, and he uses all fields with a gap-to-gap approach and a solid swing. Layton’s athleticism plays on both sides of the ball, and on the basepaths, he has the kind of speed that should make him a basestealing threat. Layton was clocked at up to 93 mph as a prep pitcher, plus arm strength that would help him play anywhere in the middle of the field. Though he was drafted as a shortstop, he lacked defensive polish and area scouts weren’t convinced Layton had the chops to stick there. Even if he gets the chance to prove them wrong off the bat, Layton’s speed, athleticism and arm strength may be best suited long-term for center field, where those raw tools can play more freely.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Layton was an over-slot sixth-rounder who signed for $715,800 last year. He’s filling up the stat sheet in Delmarva, where he’s hitting .295/.446/.432 (150 wRC+) with enormous walk and strikeout totals. For good measure, he’s 11-for-19 on the bases and has started at four positions, including short and center. He’s a switch-hitter with a long, upper-cut swing from both sides, and while he seems to track and identify pitches reasonably well, right now he’s having a lot of trouble hitting anything in the upper third of the zone. There’s enough athleticism and hit skill to stay on him for now, but he'll either need to turn it loose earlier or shorten up. Defensively, Layton has been at least fair at a bunch of different spots and has middle-of-the-diamond speed, if a light arm for short. He looks like a potential super-sub type if he can get the swing-and-miss under control.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohn immediately claimed a role in Mississippi State's bullpen as freshman before missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery. He showed average stuff when he came back as a starter and went undrafted in 2024, then improved his stuff and strike-throwing as a redshirt junior last spring. One of the best fourth-year collegians in the 2025 Draft, he went in the fourth round and will make his pro debut this year. Though Kohn's fastball has pedestrian velocity at 91-95 mph, hitters don't see it coming out of his low three-quarters arm slot and flat approach angle, and he has the aptitude to work it with carry up in the zone or spot it down at the knees. He also has advanced command of a sweeping low-80s slider that he can locate on either side of the plate. While he works almost exclusively with those two pitches, he does show a promising low-80s changeup with fade that could give him a third solid offering. Kohn improved his athleticism in 2025, allowing him to get down the mound better and repeat his delivery more consistently. That led to improved extension and deception as well as control and command. He has a high floor as a three-pitch lefty starter with advanced feel for his craft and strong mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Spence spent his first two college seasons at Black Hawk (Ill.) CC, where he batted .368/.442/.600 while also seeing action on the mound. He continued to play both ways at Southern Illinois-Edwardsville, where he won the Ohio Valley Conference batting title (.385) in 2024 before the Astros signed him for $150,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He reached Double-A in his first full pro season, hitting a combined .244/.368/.403 with 10 homers and 27 steals in 116 games between three levels. Spence rarely chases pitches and could fit at the top of the order with his on-base skills and basestealing ability. While the left-handed hitter doesn't miss fastballs, he struggles to make contact against breaking balls and changeups and has been overmatched by southpaws in pro ball. He has some sneaky pop but also hits a lot of grounders, so he'll probably top out at 10-12 homers per season. Though there's some question about how much offense Spence can provide, he can help a team win in a variety of ways. He knows how to use his plus speed to reach base, steal bags and chase down balls in the outfield. He's a solid defender in center with plus arm strength that translated into a low-90s fastball in college.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Karpathios played both ways in his one season at Maryland’s Harford Community College in 2022, and the Padres (via area scout Danny Sader, who scouted Jackson Merrill from the same area) preferred his bat. Looking to go pro rather than stay in school, Karpathios signed with San Diego as a nondrafted free agent that July, just one month after his 19th birthday. While he was a decent performer early in his career, his big breakout came in 2025, when he hit .249/.357/.413 with 15 homers and 73 walks in 124 games between High-A and Double-A. Karpathios ended the year with time in the prospect-rich Arizona Fall League. The Pennsylvania native stands tall from the left side of the box before getting into a leg kick. He rarely chased pitches outside the zone during the 2025 regular season despite increasing his overall swing rate a tad. His exit velocities were loud with a 90th-percentile EV of 105.8 mph, leading to a jump in home-run production. He can hit the ball well to all fields too, although he went the opposite way more than he pulled the ball once he reached Double-A. Getting the barrel out front more often will be a focus when he returns to the upper levels, or else he’s probably limited to 15ish homers per season. Karpathios also whiffs at high levels against non-fastballs, and he swung and missed more across the board in the Fall League (albeit after a long summer). A below-average runner, he has experience in all three outfield spots but is the best fit in right, thanks to his above-average arm strength. Ahead of his Rule 5 decision year, Karpathios is trending toward a lefty bench bat/fourth outfielder, and that’d be a nice development win for an NDFA signing.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bergolla is a twitchy, slick-fielding shortstop with pro ball bloodlines, as his father played for over a decade and got a cup of coffee with the Reds in 2005. The younger Bergolla is a polished player with a smaller frame, but he's got advanced feel for contact and is explosive enough that his size may not be a problem. He has a well-rounded skill set and a chance to move quickly because of his precocious baseball feel and instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees' decision to select Jackson in the fifth round last July drew criticism after reports surfaced that he drew a swastika on the dorm room of a Jewish student when he was a freshman at Nebraska in 2021. He transferred to South Mountain (Ariz.) CC as a sophomore and spent his final two college seasons at Utah, where he was charged with impaired driving in 2024. He batted a combined .363/.455/.577 and earned first-team all-conference honors in his two years with the Utes before signing for a well below-slot $147,500. A left-hander who made consistent hard contact college despite an aggressive approach in college, Jackson was unusually passive in High-A during his pro debut. He usually crushes fastballs but had trouble making contact against in-zone heaters last summer, though he may have been overwhelmed by his challenging assignment. He has the ingredients for at least 15-homer power, especially if he can learn to elevate more pitches. Jackson was more impressive defensively in his first taste of pro ball. He displays smooth actions, solid range and plus arm strength, leaving no doubt he can remain at shortstop. He has average speed with good baserunning instincts.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Cedeno is a twitchy, compact middle infielder with good feel for contact from both sides of the plate. He's short but swings hard and is currently whistling balls over the heads of opposing infielders. He tracks pitches well, has precocious barrel control, and extremely short levers, which all combine to make him a potential plus or better bat. Cedeno lacks the frame and physicality typical of big leaguers but the quality of his fall contact, how hard he swings, and how well he controls the swing even though it features a lot of effort all excite me enough not to worry about how little he is right now. The broad strokes of his profile -- smaller frame with sneaky strength, switch-hitting, 2B/3B look on defense -- compares a lot to Tommy Edman. Out to start 2021 due to a meniscus injury, further evaluation of this sleeper favorite of mine will likely have to wait until the AZL begins. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Hechavarria is a 22-year-old Cuban righty who signed for about $250,000 in 2024. He’s a loose athlete with good body control and a clean, if slightly long, circular arm swing. His pitchability jumps out, as he has advanced command and control for a guy his age. He’s adept at locating his fastball at the top of the zone, can run his slider on and off the plate, and, most impressively, has a knack for pulling the string on the change in just the right spot to miss lefty barrels. Lower-level hitters have been overmatched: In 135.2 career innings, he’s notched a 2.12 ERA with 139 strikeouts and only 39 walks and 10 homers allowed. 
The road will get bumpier soon. Hechavarria’s fastball should play, as he touches 97 with average carry or a tick more, but his breaking ball looks fringy to my eye and I'm skeptical it’ll miss a ton of bats. The strike-throwing foundation is enough to project him as a starter, but he looks more like a backend guy than an impact arm.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Núñez is your pretty standard teenage pitching prospect. He's a projectable 6-foot-3, his fastball sits in the mid-90s and will climb higher than that at its very peak, and he has good breaking ball feel and an athletic, picturesque delivery. He's a fantastic developmental ball of clay who has a much better chance to start than the host of single-inning relievers who occupy most of the rest of the 40 FV tier in this system. The Cardinals got him for just north of $500,000 after Núñez was suspended a year due to an age discrepancy, but as a prospect he's pretty comparable to recent high schoolers who signed for close to $1 million, like Matt Thompson, Carter Baumler and Andrew Dalquist. (International Signee)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kouba spent his first two college seasons at North Central (Texas) CC and opened 2021 in Dallas Baptist's bullpen, pitched his way into the rotation by midseason, earned all-Missouri Valley Conference honors and became a 12th-round pick. He doesn't dazzle anyone with his stuff but compensates by being the best strike-thrower in the system. He was named Double-A Texas League pitcher of the year in 2023 and finished the season in Triple-A. Kouba's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and tops out at 94 but doesn't get hit hard because he has all the traits the Astros target with pitchers: low release height, flat approach angle, significant extension in his delivery. It also plays up because he keeps batters off balance with his best pitch, a solid low-80s changeup with fade and sink. He has a pair of ordinary breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider he uses vs. righties and an upper-70s curveball he employs against lefties. With his combination of deception and control, Kouba could be a No. 5 starter. His stuff works better than it grades because he mixes his pitches well, commands his fastball and throws his secondary offerings for strikes. He was in line to get an opportunity if Houston needed rotation help in 2024 before missing two months with an elbow injury that didn't require surgery.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
At $275,000, Almonte was a fairly big signing for a pitcher on the international market. He’s a big, physical righty, a little tightly wound and not especially twitchy, but strong with an innings-eater's build. He has a long, circular arm path, loose enough to project on his command, though he’s a little wild right now. 
Almonte has four pitches that all at least flash average. He touches 97 with the fastball and sits 93-95 early in starts. He has average carry or a tick more on the four-seamer and can also hit the box with a sinker. The slider is his best secondary, a sweeping, low-to-mid-80s offering that ran a 40% miss rate in the DSL. While his curve can run into the slider and the change doesn’t consistently have a ton of fade, he’ll execute often enough to project four viable offerings at maturity. He’s eons away and a lot can go wrong, but you can dream on a no. 3 or 4 starter, while the arm strength and slider feel give him a relief fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big league caliber talent can be found just about anywhere and Diaz has the chance to prove that true. Taken in the 27th round of the 2019 Draft out of Michigan State, where he relieved for a year after two years at Iowa Western Community College, Diaz put himself on the map in 2021 with a huge full-season debut that saw him earn a promotion from High-A to Double-A and strike out 16.6 per nine for the year. He wasn’t as dominant post-promotion and he struggled to find the strike zone during his time in the Arizona Fall League, a trend that continued in Double-A in 2022. Diaz is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who profiles as a reliever only. He can get his fastball up to 97 mph, but typically sits around 92-93 mph. It plays up because of its carry in the zone and his extension coming down the mound. His power breaking ball can get slurvy, and it has good depth, but because of the mid-80s velocity, it plays more like a slider. Diaz generally had shown a penchant for throwing strikes somewhat consistently, generally attacking the zone and going right after hitters, but his walk rate continued to climb with Mississippi in 2022. He doesn’t need pinpoint command to fill a prominent role in a big league bullpen, something he should be able to do once he shows he can handle the upper levels of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Saladin still didn’t see the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic and repeated the level after becoming a starter in 2022. He moved stateside in 2023 and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 with a 2.62 ERA that ranked second among St. Louis Minor League full-season qualifiers. He also struck out 134 and walked 33 over 123 innings between Single-A and High-A. He was Rule 5-eligible in the offseason but went unprotected and unpicked due to his distance from the Majors. Standing only 5-foot-11, Saladin still stands out for his fastball that comes out of a low release height and has a flat vertical approach angle, causing more swing-and-miss than expected for most four-seamers. The pitch played in the 92-94 mph range in the Florida State League but lost some steam late with Peoria, understandable considering Saladin’s workload. His mid-80s changeup comes with enough armside run and deception off the fastball to get some whiffs too and hold lefties relatively at bay. A low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball aren’t at the same standard. Saladin kept his walk rates fairly low at both levels in 2024, and while he relies on some chase on all of his pitches (particularly the changeup), he has the control to remain a starter. Despite his Rule 5 status, the hurler is only entering his age-22 season and should get heavier 40-man consideration if he enjoys repeat success in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing as a 17th-round pick from a Puerto Rican high school in 2023, Rodriguez spent his first three seasons in pro ball in Tampa. Minor injuries limited him to 90 plate appearances in 2023-24 with the Yankees' Rookie-level Florida Complex League team there, and he returned to the FCL to start last year. He earned a promotion to their Single-A Florida State League affiliate after six weeks and slashed .237/.342/.392 with two homers in 30 games before missing the final month with a sprained wrist. Rodriguez has a quick left-handed stroke, makes reasonably good swing decisions and generates a lot of contact and promising exit velocities. Overly pull-conscious in his first two years as a pro, Rodriguez settled down his approach in 2025. He began to understand that he doesn't have to launch every pitch he sees to right field, which resulted in fewer rolled-over grounders, and he should develop 20-homer pop as he continues to get stronger. Rodriguez possesses solid speed and some basestealing savvy. He has spent most of his early pro career on the outfield corners, where he's a solid defender with average arm strength. He may be quick enough to handle center field and should get more of an opportunity to show what he can do there in 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Carela was first acquired at the outset of the White Sox's teardown, when they flipped Keynan Middleton to the Yankees at the 2023 trade deadline. Originally seen as a kitchen sink low-90s righty, Carela pitched well down the stretch at Double-A Birmingham in 2024, even touching 95-96 mph while starting the Barons’ Southern League championship clinching game. It was enough to earn the 24-year-old a surprising 40-man selection as potential starter depth, but he blew out the following spring and has since been released and re-signed on a minor league deal. 
Carela is a lean and high-waisted athlete, but there's some stiffness to his lower half, and he arguably commands his above-average slider better than his sinker. Reps are probably the key, as Carela throws it more often than anything else, showing some feel for varying its speed and shape. The approach gives him a reliever look and his platoon splits concur, and his TJ rehab keeping him out until midseason could be another nudge toward the 'pen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Kahle first got to the University of Washington in 2017 after playing his high school ball in Southern California, he got to learn under the wing of Joey Morgan, who ended up being a third-round pick of the Tigers that June. Kahle took over as the Huskies' everyday backstop the following year, then led the team in all three triple-slash categories (.339/.506/.532) during a breakout junior campaign before signing with Milwaukee as a fourth-round pick in 2019. Kahle's uptick in production during his sophomore and junior years has the Brewers believing that he'll at least hit for average in pro ball. He's shown the ability to catch up to good fastballs with solid bat speed and recognizes breaking stuff well. He has an advanced approach and takes his share of walks, giving him strong on-base skills on the top of the natural hitting ability. While Kahle’s power plays mostly to the gaps, he does stay inside the ball well and shows some ability to turn on pitches for some over-the-fence pop. Short and stocky, Kahle is a below-average runner and doesn't have that much agility behind the plate. But he has improved his receiving and blocks well, and while his arm strength is fringy, it's accurate. Whether Kahle can unlock all of his hitting ability will likely determine his ultimate role. If he can make the necessary offensive gains, Kahle has the chance to play a long time, with a floor as a very good backup and the chance to be a solid regular if everything clicks.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 Draft Board and was selected 24th overall, where he got a $2.3 million bonus to forego his commitment to LSU. At the time, scouts viewed him as one of the draft’s more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues persisted into 2024. He played well at High- and Double-A after returning to the field and reached Triple-A last season. He struggled there, hitting for some power but also striking out 30.2% of the time. So far this year, the strikeouts are under control but the power has vanished.

Let’s start with the positives. Romero has big raw power and generated plus measurable exit velocities as a 21-year-old last year. He does so with limited obvious effort, just a small hand loop for a load. Evaluators of all stripes love to see this kind of power in a controlled, fairly short-levered swing. Statistically and visually, though, there are a few red flags lurking here. Romero’s trouble with secondaries jumps off the page immediately, as he whiffed on spin more than 40% of the time last season. Swing-and-miss in general was a problem, as his contact rate was below 70% (the big league average is 75%). He’s also prone to chasing, particularly with two strikes. Visually, he doesn’t seem to get the A-swing off all that often. He lets it fly on pitches at the belt and lower middle in, but he otherwise tends to look off balance or use a gentler, sometimes inside-out cut on pitches on the outer half.

At third base, Romero’s hands are pretty good but the rest of the package looks light. At his speed, he isn’t especially rangy, and both his throwing accuracy and the time it takes him to get rid of the ball are below average. He’s also playing some second base, which redistributes some of the pressure from the latter issue onto the former.

Ultimately, Romero is going to go as far as his power takes him. It’s a potential carrying tool, and can play like one even if he’s an otherwise flawed hitter. That would require a big change in his approach, though, as he’s more of an aggressive hitter than a guy who militantly hunts his pitch. At 22, he’s young enough to take a step forward here, and perhaps positive walk and strikeout rates in Worcester are an early sign that he’s trending that way. He projects as a power-first utility player, with unusual thump for a guy who can cover second base.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 Draft Board and was selected 24th overall, receiving a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. High school Romero was viewed as one of the draft's more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues persisted into the start of 2024. When he was finally deemed healthy in the middle of May, the Red Sox effectively skipped Romero over Low-A (he only played there for a month in 2023) and sent him straight to Greenville. He hit well enough there to earn a late-season promotion to Portland, and all told in 2024, Romero slashed .271/.312/.509 with a terrifyingly low walk rate (5%). He's back in Portland and has a strong surface-level statline, including twice as many walks. 
Look under the hood and Romero is more of a mixed bag. While his baseline chase rate has backed off, he's still expanding at a 50% clip with two strikes, which is nearly two standard deviations worse than the big league average. He's also running a sub-70% contact rate as of list publication, which only a handful of qualified big leaguers carry each year (the major league average is 77%). He has issues covering the outer third, and swings underneath a ton of fastballs finishing away from him. Romero still has a good-looking low-ball swing and the explosive hitting hands that made him an exciting draft prospect. He has impressive all-fields power for a hitter his age and is pulverizing the ball when he actually makes contact. 
His build is fairly mature for a 21-year-old athlete, and Romero's mobility on defense isn't great; he takes quite a while to turn the baseball around to first base. His throwing stroke and accuracy also look a little odd (Romero has an over-the-top arm slot atypical of an infielder), and he takes a while to get rid of the baseball. There was a point last year when this could have reasonably been explained as rust coming off of injury, but we're a good distance away from that now. There's a chance Romero doesn't stick on the infield at all, and even if he does, he's going to be below average. There's enough lefty pop here to consider Romero a priority prospect, but he's got some risk indicators, both visually and from a data standpoint.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 draft board and was selected 24th overall, receiving a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. High school Romero was viewed as one of the draft's more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues have persisted into the start of 2024. When he was finally deemed healthy in the middle of May, the Red Sox effectively skipped Romero over Low-A (he only played there for a month last year) and sent him straight to Greenville. 
Romero still has a good looking low-ball swing and the explosive hitting hands that made him an exciting draft prospect. His mobility on defense isn't great, and he takes quite a while to turn the baseball around to first base. His throwing stroke and accuracy also look a little odd (Romero has an over-the-top arm slot atypical of an infielder), and he takes a while to get rid of the baseball. Whether this is just rust or is the result of continued back discomfort or physical changes caused by it, we just won't know until Romero gets more time to air out as a pro prospect. 
Romero's 40-man timeline is such that he and Boston have through the 2026 season to get things on track; that's still plenty of runway. If I were an actual team thinking about Romero from a trade standpoint, it would be tougher to rank him this highly; teams aren't falling over themselves to acquire a teenager with recurring back issues. But this is a "hold" on where Romero's FV grade was as a draft prospect. I am more inclined to let Romero's late-season look — once he's had an opportunity to fall into a routine and get some traction — drive any sort of FV update during the next list cycle.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: While not a lock to stay at shortstop due to middling range and actions, Romero had among the more advanced hit tools in the 2022 high school class, able to impact pitches all over the strike zone. He ranked 37th on the 2022 draft board and was selected 24th, where he received a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. Lower back stiffness has sidelined him for all of 2023 as of list publication, though Romero is expected to start playing rehab games on the complex shortly. He projects as a strong-side platoon infielder who's capable at second and third base.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: While not a lock to stay at shortstop due to middling range and actions, Romero has among the more advanced hit tools in the 2022 high school class, able to impact pitches all over the strike zone. Based on where hitterish middle infielders were picked in 2021, he fits near the comp round.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A true gamer who rose to prominence at Kansas State for his speed, discipline and defense -- he led the Big 12 in steals (40) and walks (55) as a junior while being named a Gold Glove finalist -- Jones signed with the Yankees for $150,000 as a 2024 12th-rounder. He's hardly missed a step in pro ball with 69 stolen bases and nearly as many walks (111) as strikeouts (130) across his first two seasons of pro ball, and ended 2025 at Double-A. The Marlins acquired him along with three other prospects in January for Ryan Weathers to add to their outfield depth on the farm. Jones holds his hands high and maneuvers his barrel around the zone to make frequent contact on all pitch shapes. He controls the zone well and rarely chases, taking pride in getting on base. The Tennessee native has not made much hard contact, though, and doesn't have much projection left in his 5-foot-10 frame. The Marlins hope a mechanical change will make him more powerful so he can at least fill a Brett Gardner-like role. Not only does Jones possess impact speed, but he's also highly efficient and isn't afraid to take an extra base. He's similarly an intellectual defender in center field -- and a quality defender in the outfield corners -- with a good sense of how to position himself and average arm strength. Jones is a high-character player who gets high marks for his motor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies targeted college pitching in the 2025 Draft, using 13 of their 20 selections on that demographic. Their first six picks were all college arms, with Tallon the last of the half-dozen. The big left-hander spent three years at Duke, almost entirely as a reliever, showcasing swing-and-miss stuff albeit without the ability to command it consistently. A 12.5 career K/9 rate for the Blue Devils stood out and the Phillies took a chance on his bat-missing arm in the sixth round, signing for right around slot. While there was some talk about Tallon being given the chance to start out of the gate, it’s looking like he’s going to be a reliever to kick off his pro career. The 6-foot-5 southpaw is all about his unhittable fastball, a pitch he threw more than 70 percent of the time last year at Duke. It sits in the low 90s and tops out at just 95 mph, but it elicited a miss rate of 34 percent and a 35-percent chase rate in 2025 thanks to a deceptive delivery and a low release height. He’ll need to improve his breaking ball, though his cutter-like slider did miss bats at times. Tallon did throw a mid-80s changeup now and again in college, but will likely focus on his top two pitches as a professional reliever. He needs to harness his command after walking 4.7 per nine last year, but if he can do that and improve his ability to spin the ball, he could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez left Cuba in 2024 but took a while to get cleared by Major League Baseball, so he didn't turn pro until January. He signed for $900,000, the second-highest bonus in the Cubs' 2026 international class. He stands out with his all-around ability and high baseball IQ. A switch-hitter, Martinez has a slight 5-foot-10 build that seems built more for contact than profile. While he does focus on lining balls to all fields and getting on base, he also hits balls surprisingly hard for his size. He won't be a slugger but could provide 15 homers per season once he gets stronger. Martinez has quick-twitch athleticism and plus speed that serves him well on the bases and in the field. He has good actions and solid arm strength at shortstop, where he should have no difficulty remaining. He also earns praise for his makeup.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Bullard was thought to have a strong commit to Texas A&M, which pushed him out of the top rounds of the 2025 draft where his talent belonged. Toronto plucked him in the 12th and signed him for $1.7 million, the largest bonus ever given to a player in that round. 
Bullard is a speedy center field prospect. He’s a switch-hitter whose quick, slashy swings look similar from both sides. While not narrow, he’s slim. He could develop relevant, wiry strength, but you can also imagine him topping out as a 30 or 35 power guy if he doesn't. This is an ideal alignment between player and team, as Bullard is as likely to max out on his strength and power in Toronto as anywhere else. While there’s no guarantee that the Jays can buff him into a power threat, the contact and defensive pieces here are the foundation of a fourth outfielder, one with everyday upside if the damage grade exceeds the forecast above.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 40 The sixth overall pick in the 2017 Draft by the A’s out of North Davidson High School in North Carolina, Beck positioned himself as a top-10 pick following a strong pre-Draft workout that continued his positive trend that started with an impressive senior season. Progressing nicely through the Minors in 2018, he remained stuck in the Class A Advanced California League in 2019. Beck did not receive an invite to the club’s alternate training site last year. Beck has struggled to live up to the high expectations that were placed on him. His combination of a strikeout rate over 34 percent in 2019 and inconsistent power in games at the pro level has hindered him at the High-A level. But the A’s still believe they have a good player in Beck, it’s just a matter of figuring it all out. He does have premium bat speed and worked hard on calming down in the box with the confidence that if he can make more contact, the power will naturally come. Although it doesn’t necessarily show up in the stolen base numbers, Beck has very good speed. It helps him play strong defense in center field, a spot where he has also shown a solid arm. He’s still young, and there are still some tools he’s working to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Corona Del Mar High School in California, Schwartz headed to UCLA, where he redshirted his freshman year and only saw 15 games in the shortened 2020 season. His big breakout finally came last spring when he hit .396/.514/.628 with eight homers and a 28/37 K/BB ratio in 44 games for the Bruins. Those numbers made him the Pac-12 batting champion and earned him a spot on the All-Conference Team. The Mets selected Schwartz in the fourth round and went slightly under slot to sign him for $475,000. He walked more than he struck out (13 vs. 12) but otherwise saw minimal results with a .195 average and a .576 OPS in his first 25-game trip to the Minors with Low-A St. Lucie. Despite standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Schwartz isn’t your typical slugging first first baseman. He’s shown an advanced approach everywhere he’s played over the last four years, including in summer-ball circuits, and as he proved in his final season on campus, he makes enough quality contact to sustain a good batting average. However, he doesn’t have a long history of hitting the ball over fences, and before the Draft, some evaluators were concerned that previous shoulder, knee and hip problems would keep him from showing even average power in games. Schwartz is first-base only on defense, and the Mets secured that by giving him all 24 of his defensive starts at the cold corner with St. Lucie. He faces a high offensive threshold there, and simply producing a solid average and OBP might not be enough to meet it. Schwartz is staring up at Pete Alonso on the Mets’ first-base depth chart, so he needn’t press to expedite his route toward Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Wisconsin high schooler with a big fastball, Snead started his college career at Wichita State, but then moved on to Tennessee where, as a sophomore, he helped the Volunteers win the 2024 Men's College World Series, picking up a key save and hold in the Finals. He came out of the bullpen again as a junior, but his combination of a full arsenal and ability to throw strikes could give him the chance to start, something the Angels no doubt were contemplating when taking him with their compensation pick following the third round of the 2025 Draft. There’s no doubt that Snead can throw hard -- he sat around 95-97 mph and touched triple digits. But the heater often lacked life, with sink over carry, so if he wasn’t locating it down in the zone well, it was very hittable. He’s already gotten to work on differentiating his two- and four-seamers (which often blended together), as well as improving his low-90s cutter. His low-80s curve evolved into his best secondary offering in 2025. There’s also a mid-80s slider and low-90s changeup in Snead’s bag of tricks, though he didn’t pull them out often. He has a bit of a slinky delivery coming from a low three-quarters slot, and while he finds the strike zone, it’s control over command. The Angels could give him a chance to start out of the gate, knowing that he could also develop into a late-inning reliever with better fastball characteristics.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners’ activity in the 2024 international signing period started with Dawel Joseph being the headliner, getting $3.3 million in January. Six months later, they added Shen, signing the Taiwanese right-hander, for $175,000 in July. Pitching at age 21, Shen was rolled out cautiously, making his debut in the Arizona Complex League last May. After 28 dominant innings over seven appearances, he earned a bump up to full-season ball for nine more starts. Right out of the gate, Shen displayed a feel for commanding all three of his pitches. His fastball sits in the low 90s, touching 95 mph now and again, and he throws it with sink to help get ground ball outs. His mid-80s changeup also gets weak contact on the ground and gets a lot of chase. He can spin an 81 mph slider decently, and it missed bats at the lower levels, but a little more power could make it even nastier. Shen filled up the strike zone in both stops during his debut, though he was getting too much of the plate during his time in Modesto. Some added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame would help not only that slider, but all of his offerings trend upwards. He has back-of-the-rotation potential based on his pitchability and projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Meola was named Atlantic Sun Conference Tournament MVP as a sophomore after homering three times in four games and earned ASUN defensive player of the year accolades as a junior in 2025. The cousin of former U.S. national soccer team goalie Tony Meola, he went in the fourth round, making him Stetson's highest-drafted position player since 2003 first-rounder Brian Johnson. He took over at shortstop for an injured Maui Ahuna at Single-A San Jose and helped win a California League title. With solid speed and quick feet, Meola covers plenty of ground at shortstop. His smooth actions, soft hands and strong arm help make him a plus defender at short. Factor in some sneaky power, and some Giants officials think he has J.J. Hardy upside. Meola hits the ball surprisingly hard for a 5-foot-11, 172-pounder and can drive the ball out of the park to all fields, giving him the potential for 15-20 homers per season. He does get overly aggressive and pull-happy, however, resulting in strikeouts and rolled-over ground balls. He's most effective when he focuses on driving balls from gap to gap.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Werner pitched and hit his first two years of college at Texas A&M before transitioning to hitting full-time in ‘22 and ‘23. Scouts were still intrigued by his 90-plus mph arm, and the Royals drafted him as a two-way player in the seventh round of the 2023 Draft. But he made his pro debut as a hitter with four games in the Arizona Complex League before heading to Single-A Columbia. There, he simply produced and produced some more. Werner won the Carolina League Player of the Month in September, when he had a 1.328 OPS and paced the league in hits (15), runs (12) and RBIs (14). There were some questions about the swing-and-miss in Werner’s game leading up to the Draft, and he did strike out at a 23 percent clip in the small sample at Single-A last year. Werner holds his hands high, and he’s not totally smooth in his setup or follow-through. But he’s done a good job of freeing up his swing with the work he did this offseason, and that should help to unlock his impressive power. Werner has athleticism and an ease with which he moves about third base, although he made eight errors in 20 games at Single-A. He has a cannon of an arm and should be able to stick there at least for now. Werner receives high praise for his work ethic and cerebral approach to the game, his routine and his preparation. He’s a physical presence at 6-foot-3 and 225 pounds. It certainly was a small sample size in Columbia last year, but it rightfully garnered some attention. Werner has some tools to work with, which excites the Royals long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After showing the ability to command his fastball and miss bats with his secondary pitches as a freshman at Cloud County (Kan.) CC and a sophomore at Nebraska, McConnaughey positioned himself as an early-round pick in 2025. But his elbow gave out after three starts last spring and required Tommy John surgery in March. He still rated as the top prospect in the Cornhusker State and went in the fourth round to the Rangers, signing for a below-slot $495,825. McConnaughey's fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 mph, though it plays up a bit because he can ride it up in the zone and sink it down at the knees. He can manipulate his low-80s slider, landing a tight version for strikes and getting chases by burying them in the dirt or sweeping them away from righties. He also has good feel for a tumbling 82-85 mph changeup that neutralizes left-handers. McConnaughey has an easy, clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to place his pitches where he wants. Pitchers often throw harder after adding strength during the Tommy John rehab process, and adding more velocity to his present polish would raise his ceiling. Scouts praise his mound presence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $30,000 out of the Dominican Republic, Arana has quickly emerged as the Marlins' top hitting prospect from the 2025 international class. It's no small feat that the converted outfielder took to the left side of the infield well in his debut season and made quick work of the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Across 52 games, he hit .297/.419/.476 with nearly twice as many walks (30) as strikeouts (18) and impressive underlying data. Arana uses a pronounced toe tap to time up pitches well and has outstanding contact skills from both sides of the plate. He has displayed strong swing decisions, and although more passive approaches can lead to plenty of walks in the DSL, he rarely whiffs, which portends continued strong results against more advanced pitching. Currently stronger from the left side, Arana hasn't shown a ton of pop to date but added almost 10 pounds in the offseason and could tap further into his power if he pulls the ball in the air more. Arana is a twitchy athlete who aggressively uses his plus speed on the bases, and a refined approach should help with his efficiency. He covers ground well at short and third base and should have plenty of arm for either position. If he continues to add weight, his bat should profile on the left side. If he remains more nimble, it's not out of the question that he could also play second base or center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres are one of the most heavily involved -- if not the most heavily involved -- teams in Mexico as part of the international signing process. That’s where the club headed to sign Serna in January, two months before the southpaw turned 17. Serna gained some international notoriety at the 2024 WBSC U15 World Cup in Colombia, where he struck out 12 and allowed only one earned run on one hit and four walks in seven innings against the host nation. He signed for $1 million. The 6-foot-3 southpaw throws free and easy from a smooth delivery, and while he only sits 88-91 mph with his fastball now, he has the size to add strength and get that velocity up to at least Major League average in the years to come. His best present pitch is an upper-70s slider with short, controllable depth, and it should help fuel any immediate Minor League success. There’s a feel for a low-80s changeup too, though he barely used it in the World Cup. Serna excelled on the international stage because he could hit his spots at an advanced level, and he was willing to go right after hitters. The Padres brought up his strike throwing on signing day as the most exciting part of the early profile, and if Serna can sharpen his stuff with physical maturity -- not a given considering the wide error bars on young arms -- he could be a midrotation option in the Majors in the next decade.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Jerzembeck missed his final two years at South Carolina recovering from a TJ and later a stress fracture in his elbow. He was nasty on the backfields this spring, executing a lateral attack with a tailing mid-90s fastball and late-biting slider. Jerzembeck's delivery has NC-17 violence and his recent injury history is severe, making him a likely reliever. Early this year he's done a mix of starting and long relieving at Myrtle Beach. His changeup has enough tail and sink to give him a third projected bat-missing pitch, and he can tweak his slider to play more like a cutter.
