There's a starter's mix here, and Jerzembeck (who is underdeveloped from a reps standpoint) has pretty solid feel for location, but his delivery is just too messy to project him in the rotation. He should be a reliable long reliever instead.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Cool Breeze" Corey was a reliever at Division-II Wingate who the A's began to stretch out as a long reliever and spot starter in 2024, before more solidly committing to developing him as a starter in 2025, when he worked 123 innings (including his Fall League frames). Avant still has some reliever risk because of his below-average control — he only walked 10.5% of opponents in 2025, but his underlying strike-throwing was worse than that, and he's tended to be in the 13% or above area dating back to college — but he is built like a starter at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-4, and he deserves a longer developmental runway since we're talking about a small school guy who barely pitched in college because he was deployed as a reliever. 
Avant throws hard; he was parked in the 93-97 mph range last year, though his fastball's downhill plane sucks some of the effectiveness out of that pitch. Conversely, the higher slot helps add depth to Avant's slider, which has great velocity for a standard gyro-style offering. Whether Avant can continue to start will depend on the development of his splitter/sinker, an 87-91 mph offering that he actually has decent feel for locating, but that lacks big movement. Automatic pitch tagging thinks a lot of his splits are two-seamers, so it's tough to tell exactly how many of them he threw last year, but the number is something like twice what he did in 2024, though still only 200 of them across the entire season. He looks like he takes great care of himself, and he's an engaged teammate who was often watching his fellow A's arms with intense focus as everyone got underway this spring. It's probably more likely that Avant is a reliever in the end, but even if that's the case, he'll be a draft-and-develop feather in the cap of the A's. They should continue with the starter track for another two seasons at least, and decide more about his path when his 40-man roster deadline arrives after the 2027 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez flew under the radar in the 2016-17 international class, signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela. He took a few years to find his footing, but he absolutely wowed in 2022, especially when making the jump to High-A Everett, where he slashed .342/.477/.583 with seven homers and 27 RBIs in 35 games to give him 27 homers and 114 RBIs (second among all Minor League hitters) in total. There’s a chance he taps out because of his speed and defense, but the Mariners are bullish on how he finished the season, which he capped off with time in the Arizona Fall League. The big focus for him into 2023 will be finding better counts to continue to do damage, which should help him better tap into his considerable raw power. He can be aggressive and expand the zone too often at times, though he offsets the swing-and-miss with a willingness to take walks. When he’s putting the ball in play, he’s found far more line drives and fly balls, a big reason why he surpassed his 2021 season home run total by June last year. Likely destined for first base, Perez has legit pop from the right side and the exit velocities to show for it, but he’ll need to continue raking to progress -- his big league trajectory depends on it, especially given the defensive limitations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most advanced prospect in Miami's 2022 international crop, de la Cruz turned pro for $150,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Making his U.S. debut last summer, he needed just two starts in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League to earn a promotion to Single-A. The only 18-year-old to work double-digit innings in the Florida State League, he held his own with a 4.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts in 43 1/3 innings. While de la Cruz still is refining his entire repertoire, both his fastball and curveball show the potential to become plus pitches once fully developed. His riding fastball parked at 92-95 mph and touched 97 before he tired late in his first full pro season, and he should add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-70s curveball has good shape with plenty of depth and some horizontal action but also would benefit from more power. De la Cruz's changeup has some interesting fade, though it gets too firm in the mid-80s and he needs to use it more often so he can refine it. He's not as physical as Edward Cabrera was as a teenager, but he reminds some club officials of their big league starter with his repertoire and delivery. His control was spotty versus much older competition in the FSL but should be fine as he adds more strength and experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green showed off an exciting power-speed combination across three seasons at Cal by swiping 45 bases and crushing 34 home runs in 151 games. The A’s had plenty of looks at those raw tools while scouting him just down the road over the years and were thrilled to land him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, going over slot value to sign him for $1 million. Getting his feet wet at Single-A Stockton last year, he hit .289 with an .832 OPS, three homers, eight doubles and nine stolen bases in 24 games. Green falls in line with recent A’s Draft picks such as Denzel Clarke and Henry Bolte who stand out for their exciting raw tools. The ball really jumps off the bat with his ability to drive it to all fields, and the A’s still believe there is more raw power he will tap into. The big concern has always been his lack of consistent contact, as his strikeout rate hovered around 30% in college, which could be attributed to his unorthodox mechanics at the plate. But the A’s have been encouraged by his improvements in that respect, and he has shown a decent eye by drawing a fair amount of walks. A plus runner who can cover a ton of ground with a solid arm, Green has a chance to stick in center field, though some scouts see an eventual move to left. The A’s saw Green as a first-round talent with a ceiling that is just about as high as any other prospect in the organization, but he will have to overcome the swing-and-miss issues that plagued him throughout his amateur career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairly anonymous when he signed with the Yankees for $30,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, Ramirez batted .319 in two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before attracting attention in his U.S. debut last year. He earned Florida Complex League All-Star accolades after ranking second in the Rookie-level circuit in hitting (.348) and on-base percentage (.447) and fourth in OPS (.960). The Marlins acquired him as part of a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. at the Trade Deadline last July. Ramirez employs a leg kick at the plate and makes consistent contact with a disciplined approach and a compact right-handed stroke. He's learning to turn on pitches but hits a lot of ground balls and may not provide more than 10-12 homers per season. Though he puts the bat on the ball with ease, he makes good swing decisions and draws a healthy amount of walks. Ramirez's solid speed plays better on the bases than in the field, though he's not a prolific basestealer. His average arm and range are best suited for second base, though he spent the majority of his time last year at third base, where he committed nine errors in 36 starts. He also has seen action at left field and shortstop and projects as a utilityman with a sparkplug mentality.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Geraldo received the sixth-highest bonus ($600,000) in the Cubs' 2026 international class, he may have a higher offensive ceiling and a stronger arm than any of his counterparts. A late bloomer physically out of the Dominican Republic, his stock was rising as the January opening of the signing period approached. Geraldo has the ingredients to develop 25-homer power. He has a quick right-handed stroke, a knack for barreling balls and room to add plenty of strength to his 6-foot-1 frame. He's an advanced hitter for his age who shows some ability to recognize pitches. An average runner who doesn't have typical shortstop quickness, Geraldo compensates with plus arm strength. Given the four of the five Cubs 2026 signees who landed higher bonuses also play shortstop, he likely will get some reps at second and third base when he makes his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He probably fits best at the hot corner in the long run and should have the pop to profile there.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
It’s important to scout well in your own backyard, even and perhaps especially when it’s a big one like “all of Canada.” Doing so puts you in a good position to take fliers on intriguing but raw guys like Piasentin, an Alberta native who signed for the fourth-largest bonus in Toronto’s 2025 draft class. He didn't play after the draft and hasn't faced a ton of good competition in his life, and is thus something of a wild card on this list. There’s very little footage of him available, and he’s the type of player who enters pro ball with a wide range of outcomes ahead of him. 
Piasentin is a strong kid, very well built for his age, and has a chance to grow into plus raw power. His swing is a little long, but he has the bat speed to make it work. We don't know how he'll handle pro caliber spin, but limited looks against decent velocity suggest he’s got a shot to develop a viable hit tool. Defensively, his actions aren't messy, but they aren't exactly quick either. He’s played a lot of third base as an amateur, a good fit for his plus arm if he proves rangy enough to stick there. Honestly, I don't have a great feel for where Piasentin should place on this list, but I'm intrigued enough by the power to stick him here for now; we’ll know a lot more soon.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Van Dam was a ninth-rounder out of NC State, a promising righty who slipped in last year's draft in part because Tommy John surgery wiped away the end of his sophomore and most of his junior season. It didn't take long for his modest draft position bonus to look out of step with his talent. 
Van Dam is an above-average athlete with good body control and a very loose arm swing. After throwing well in front of Eric last fall, he looked good again on the backfields this spring, sitting 95-96 with average carry and limited tail on his fastball. He flashes a plus curve, and while he doesn't throw his slider much, his feel for spin suggests he could have a pretty good one of those as well. Van Dam maintains arm speed on his change, which makes it projectable, even if he’s not yet generating the kind of movement likely to miss a bunch of bats. He isn't especially deceptive, as his arm stroke and delivery are long and timeable, and if I had one nagging thought about my in-person look, it was that hitters seemed to make surprisingly good contact against him. That could also just be a coincidence, because Van Dam’s stuff and control look big league-caliber. 
Kansas City is using him in a multi-inning relief role out of the gate, an understandable choice to manage his innings in his first full season after surgery. In the long run, Van Dam has a shot to start. It’s possible his fastball won't have the same zip or that he'll be too hittable in that role, but for now you can dream on a no. 4 with a mid-to-high-leverage fallback. Good scouting from the Royals here.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Between COVID and a medical redshirt season, Franklin was a sixth-year senior at Missouri in 2023 with ugly surface numbers and an uglier delivery when the Sox took a $10,000 flier on him in the 10th round. But his short-armed, vertical riding mid-90s heater has always piled up whiffs, and while the right-hander is entering his 40-man platform year at age 27, it also comes on the heels of a season that saw him strike out 35.3% of hitters in 56.1 innings while finishing the year at the end of the Triple-A bullpen. The Sox have added a Garrett Crochet-esque leg kick to keep Franklin’s weight back in his delivery, which has had mixed success in allowing his arm to get on time (11.2% walk rate). Given his heater's sub-70% in-zone contact rate, Franklin has been extremely fastball-heavy throughout his pro career, but most recently he has leaned on a mid-80s splitter as his primary secondary, which alternates gorgeous finishes and arm-side misfires.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Gomez is a stout lefty with a really strong lower body and a clean, deceptive arm action. Though he's a little shorter than most big league starters, the consistency and ease of his delivery gives him the look of a guy who can take the ball every fifth day. His arm stroke hides the baseball from the hitter until very late, when Gomez's hand appears from behind his head and suddely a 93 mph fastball is backspinning toward the dish. All of Gomez's pitches play up a tad because of his delivery, and his changeup has exciting long-term projection because of it. Though neither of Gomez's breaking balls is especially nasty, they consistently finish in effective (and different) locations. His pitch mix features weapons that finish in all four qudrants of the zone, and though he is definiely a control-over-command type, it's enough to consider Gomez a future backend starter. He won't turn 21 until the middle of 2026, but his build is relatively maxed out and he's more of a polished prospect than one with big long-term projection. The 2026 season is Gomez's 40-man platform year and the Guardians, who acquired him from the Mets in exchange for international pool space, might try to push him to Double-A at some point to see if he merits addition after the season.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Araujo is a bat-first catching prospect who had an awesome 2025 DSL debut during which he slashed .289/.377/.528 with 21 extra-base hits in 45 games. He's a medium-framed, short-levered hitter whose top hand drives the explosion of his swing, facilitating lots of loud pull-side contact. Araujo can flatten his bat path to cover the top of the zone or use a more uphill angle to scoop low pitches. 
Because of his youth and inexperience, Araujo is currently a very raw defensive catcher and is not a lock to stay back there. He played a lot of first base in 2025, too, though that was due as much to Philly's DSL catching depth as it was Araujo's own shortcomings. If he doesn't develop as a catcher, then Araujo's modest size (think Ty France's body) would likely cap his power and, it follows, his ceiling as a first baseman. For now, he's a talented young hitter who'll be tested by Florida complex arms as an 18-year-old in 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Hampu was a great find in the 2024 draft, as you don't normally get a flamethrower with a razor-sharp slider in the 18th round. There’s some effort to his delivery, and he can spray the ball around, but while he'll never have great command, he was actually a fair strike-thrower after a rough April last season. The former Governor is even a little deceptive, as a glove throw just prior to release is distracting and helps his already considerable stuff play up further. The developmental key going forward is getting his change and slider in good locations more consistently. Hitters did absolutely nothing with either of them last year, but he had too many noncompetitive misses to fully leverage their effectiveness. There’s work ahead, but Hampu has big league stuff, and modest improvements in his control will put him on track to reach his middle relief projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coley faced plenty of adversity in his college career at Rhode Island, striking out in more than half his at-bats as a freshman in 2019, losing most of the 2020 season to the pandemic, missing all of 2022 because of a school credit snafu and half of 2023 after breaking his jaw in a collision at first base. He homered eight times and stole six bases in 25 games last spring, graduated with a mechanical engineering degree and signed with the Marlins for $50,000 as a 17th-rounder. He made his pro debut by batting .265/.395/.480 in Single-A and helping Jupiter win the Florida State League title. Coley's bat speed and strength rank among the best in the system and create plus raw power. A right-handed hitter, he looks to make the most of it by launching balls to his pull side, though his approach also yields strikeouts and rolled-over groundballs. More raw than most 23-year-olds because he had only 305 at-bats in five years in college, he could do a lot of damage if he learns to be more selective. He didn't run much at Rhode Island but Coley possesses plus speed and swiped nine bases in 10 tries during his 33-game pro debut. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground of center field and he has solid arm strength that could improve a tick if he cleans up his throwing motion. Besides his tools, he draws raves for his intelligence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading the Big Ten Conference with 18 homers as a Maryland junior in 2021, Cowles signed with the Yankees as a 10th-rounder and had modest success in his first two full pro seasons. He boosted his stock by leading Arizona Fall League shortstops with a .956 OPS in 2023, a prelude to posting the best numbers of his career last year in Double-A. Five days after an errant pitch broke his left wrist, the Cubs acquired him along with Jack Neely in a July trade for Mark Leiter Jr., then protected Cowles on their 40-man roster in November. Cowles doesn't possess a better than average tool but offers a little bit of everything, offensively and defensively. He's a right-handed hitter who has enough pull power to generate 15 homers per season, while drawing his share of walks. He cut his strikeout rate from 28 percent in 2023 to 17.7 percent last year, improving his frequency and quality of in-zone contact. Cowles plays quicker than his average speed at times and has the savvy to steal a few bases. He shuttled between shortstop, third base and second base in 2024, fitting best at the keystone and struggling with the speed of the game at the hot corner. Getting the most out of his ability thanks to his strong work ethic and high baseball IQ, he profiles more as a utility man than a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sometimes buying low on a prospect can provide a huge payoff. That's what the Pirates are hoping they can get from Ager, who had dropped to the sixth round of the 2024 Draft after a subpar junior season at Santa Barbara. Considered one of the top college arms on the West Coast heading into the year after pitching for Team USA over the summer, his stuff and performance regressed, though he did settle in as the Gauchos closer. It turned out he had been trying to pitch through an oblique issue, so the Pirates are hoping a healthy Ager will rebound quickly in pro ball. When he was at his best, Ager had a solid four-pitch mix and the ability to throw strikes with all of them, with a fastball in the 92-93 mph range that topped out at 96. His low-80s slider flashed plus in the past, with the potential to miss a lot of bats. He uses a slower mid-70s curve as a get-me-over type of breaking ball, and while his changeup has been his fourth pitch, it has the chance to be an average offering. As a sophomore, Ager repeated his delivery and threw a lot of strikes, giving him the chance to start long term. He's 6-foot-6 with some projection, and the Santa Barbara program has a history of producing solid big league rotation pieces, with the Pirates curious to see what he might do now that he's 100 percent healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knipp spent most of his time over his time at Campbell University as a catcher, becoming the starter and putting up big numbers at the plate in 2024. He also returned to the mound to make four relief appearances that year, showing off tremendous arm strength that intrigued several teams. The Mariners initially announced him as a two-way player when taking him in the sixth round of the 2024 Draft, but it seemed like they were inclined to have him focus on the mound only. He didn’t make much progress as elbow trouble in Spring Training resulted in Tommy John surgery, and he missed the 2025 season. Not only is Knipp coming back to pitch at some point in 2026, the Mariners have decided to let him also get at-bats as a DH after seeing him swing it well last spring, taking since-traded prospect Jurrangelo Cijntje deep twice. As a hitter, he’s strength over bat speed with raw power and questions about him making enough contact to get to it. On the mound, he had been up to 96 mph with his fastball last spring, showing good ride and induced vertical break on the pitch to go along with an interesting sweepy 84-85 mph slider. It will be interesting to see how long the Mariners conduct this two-way experiment, with Knipp in his age-24 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Panamanian pipeline to Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.) highlighted by Guardians 2019 first-rounder Daniel Espino, Rodriguez was one of the older prep prospects (19 years, seven months) in the 2023 Draft. The Cubs didn't mind his age because they had some third-round grades on him, and they took him in the 13th round. His development has progressed more slowly than expected, but he finally reached Double-A at the end of last season. Rodriguez operates at 92-95 mph and touches 99 with his fastball, but he's often tentative with it because it lacks good shape and gets whacked when it grabs too much of the plate. He shows much better feel for strikes with his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Like the rest of his arsenal, his tight mid-80s slider plays as an average pitch. Rodriguez works solely out of the stretch with a low release height that creates some deception. He has improved his strike-throwing every season as a pro, though his control and command still need more work if he's going to succeed as a starter. He gets more ground balls than he misses bats and is more likely to wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz slugged .771 with 34 homers in his two years at Walters State CC in Tennessee and showed out nicely in separate stints in the Appalachian (2023) and MLB Draft Leagues (2024) to establish himself on the Draft radar. The Cardinals took him in the 16th round and dipped a little into their bonus pool to make him a JUCO signing for $200,000. Ortiz ripped through the Florida State League in his first full season with a .285/.406/.446 line and 10 homers in 77 games and produced a .938 OPS over 30 contests with High-A Peoria following a July promotion. The 6-foot-1 right-handed slugger has an interesting stance at the plate that starts with him leaning back and then launching forward with a leg kick. It’s a swing designed for contact in the air, and his 29.7 percent line-drive rate was highest among Cardinals full-season qualifiers, while his 29.3 percent ground-ball rate was lowest. His 105.3 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity in the FSL was also comfortably above average, and Ortiz could be a threat to hit 20+ homers pretty easily if trends hold. Ortiz was beatable with good velocity and sliders in the zone, however, and that will be a more worrisome trend against better arms in the upper Minors. The Puerto Rico native ran subpar sprint speeds in the FSL but picked his spots well against Single-A catchers, going 31-for-34 in steal attempts there. (That dropped to 8-for-14 in the Midwest League, perhaps a better sign of what to expect.) The Cardinals believe Ortiz has enough athleticism to keep getting looks at third base, where his above-average arm strength fits, but have already mixed in plenty of first. It’s likely he lands down the defensive spectrum and needs to keep his offensive production high to be valuable.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $42,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2024, Laroche pitched just three innings during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He returned to the DSL last year and stood out with some of the best stuff in the circuit, posting a 2.11 ERA with a 34/6 K/BB ratio in 38 1/3 frames. He'll make his U.S. debut in 2026 and could push his way to full-season ball at the end of the summer. LaRoche features an explosive sinker that operates at 93-95 mph and maxes out at 97, and he also uses a four-seam fastball with similar velocity and armside run. His tight 82-85 mph slider has the potential to become a solid offering. While he has yet to use it very often, he also shows some feel for a mid-80s changeup. Though Laroche stands just 5-foot-11 and doesn't have a smooth delivery, he's very athletic and deceptive. He flies down the mound, producing plenty of extension for his size as well as a unusually low release height. He has no problem filling the strike zone but will need to refine his command as he climbs the ladder.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Simon was a fairly ordinary pro prospect in college, a $150,000 signee out of Elon. He has picked up a couple of ticks and gone to more of a drop-and-drive delivery in pro ball, a combination that has allowed him to flourish as he’s ascended the system. After a solid few months at High-A last year, Simon dominated down the stretch at Binghamton, posting a 1.06 ERA with 28.6% strikeout rate and a 4-to-1 strikeout-to-walk ratio. 
Simon isn't tall, but don't call him undersized, as he’s a fit and powerful 200 pounds. That leg strength is the foundation of upper-90s heat, which has a little carry and missed a bunch of bats in the mid levels last year. He leans on the fastball, as his secondaries flash but aren't consistent. His change behaves like a soft sinker and his slider like a cutter. Sometimes he nails the location in a way that makes them look and play above average, but he doesn't always pull it off. He’s also a control-over-command arm, as he tends to fall off the mound and pull the ball with him — in the zone, but mostly to the glove side. Still, the fastball is good enough to form the basis of a middle relief projection, which he should reach if he can find a way to get one of his secondaries to a 55 more consistently.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Cruceta is a well-rounded young center field prospect with exciting physical projection and present contact skill. He slashed .291/.438/.373 in his DSL debut and managed a 77% contact rate. That low slugging percentage is indicative of Cruceta's strength and bat speed right now — he lacks both. But his hands work in an aesthetically pleasing way, he's a good athlete, and he runs well, and at a statuesque 6-foot-1, he could mature into that center field Goldilocks Zone where he adds power but stays rangy on defense. Cruceta looks a lot like the domestic high schoolers who get a $1 million bonus, give or take, and he has a non-zero shot to be an everyday player eventually.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Florida high school product, Hermann was headed to play college baseball at South Florida before the Yankees took him in the 14th round and gave him a slightly over-slot $135,000 bonus in 2021. Because he was the lightest player in the Draft at 160 pounds, they had him initially focus on adding strength before making his pro debut in 2022. He needed little more than a month before earning a promotion from Rookie ball to Single-A, where he recorded a 2.66 ERA in four starts. Hermann's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94, playing better than its velocity because it has a flat approach angle that produces carry up in the zone. He has advanced feel for a sinking 83-88 mph changeup that yields ground-ball contact, though it could use more velo separation from his heater. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with encouraging shape and spin rates that he can morph into an upper-80s cutter. While he lacks physicality, Hermann is athletic and has projection remaining. He has good extension in his delivery, allowing his pitches to appear quicker than they are, and he provides plenty of strikes. If he can get stronger and add more power to his stuff, he could become a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three years of relief work at Kansas State, including a junior season that catapulted him onto Draft boards, he went in Round 14 in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. Los Angeles challenged him with a Double-A assignment in his first full season and he responded. The left-hander led the Southern League in saves and was named its Reliever of the Year, missing a ton of bats and giving up very few hits in the process. Torres does it from a 6-foot frame and with average stuff, but his combination of a lower slot -- the ball looks like it’s coming from the first-base dugout -- and feel for using what he has helped him strike out 14.3 per nine innings and hold hitters to a .143 average in 2022. His fastball only sits around 90 mph, but the angle and carry up in the zone helped it elicit a 36-percent miss rate last year. His low-80s slider can also miss bats, a sweeping breaking ball that flashes above average. He continues to work on a changeup to give him another look for right-handed hitters, but no one squared him up from either side in the Southern League. The Angels love Torres’ athleticism and competitiveness on the mound, and while he could stand to cut the walk rate down a little, he’s around the zone enough to project future success. The overall stuff might mean he doesn’t get the ball in high-leverage situations in the big leagues, but he’s not far from getting the chance to impact the Los Angeles bullpen and he’s shown he is far from afraid of the spotlight.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher redshirted at Mississippi in 2020, helped Walters State (Tenn.) CC make the Junior College World Series in 2021 and cranked 18 homers (including two grand slams in one game) at Charlotte in 2022 but went undrafted because of worries about his stroke and strikeout tendencies. Then he set 49ers marks for single-season (30, third in NCAA Division I) and career homers (48), including a record six while winning MVP accolades at the Conference USA tournament, powering his way into the fourth round. He batted .273/.396/.500 with five homers in 31 games in Single-A in his pro debut. There's nothing subtle about Fisher's approach. He stands upright at the plate and looks to launch balls to his pull side with an uphill left-handed stroke. His combination of bat speed and strength, extreme pull-focused mentality and high exit velocities led one amateur scout to call him the mid-major version of Kyle Schwarber. Though he ranked fifth in D-I with 64 walks and generally makes good swing decisions, his mentality results in a lot of strikeouts and some difficulties against non-fastballs. Fisher isn't the prettiest runner, but he has surprisingly solid speed and succeeded on all 15 of his steal attempts between college and pro ball last year. His athleticism should translate into defensive ability as well, but he's just adequate as a corner outfielder with an average arm. A part-time catcher in junior college, he played mostly right field at Charlotte and in his debut but is better suited for left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-hander Nehomar Ochoa Sr. pitched in the Expos system from 2003-05 until falling off a horse and injuring his shoulder, and his son was born in Venezuela shortly before his career ended. The younger Nehomar moved to the United States at age 10 and blossomed into a physical and toolsy outfielder at a Houston high school before signing with the local Astros for $300,000 (double slot value) as an 11th-rounder in 2023. In his first full pro season, he slashed .222/.317/.359 with 10 homers and 17 steals in 103 games as the second-youngest batting qualifier (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Extremely physical at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Ochoa has a quick right-handed swing and at least plus raw power that plays mostly to left field because of his pull- and launch-heavy mindset. He has enough natural pop to hit 25 or more homers per season without swinging for the fences. He'll have to moderate his approach as he advances because he chases too much and is overmatched by breaking balls from righties. Very athletic for his size, Ochoa has average speed and is aggressive on the bases. He's still a work in progress as a corner outfielder, but he has the quick reactions to become at least an average defender and may get a trial in center field. He has plus arm strength, reaching 95 mph with his fastball as a prep pitcher and throwing out 12 runners in 76 starts in right field last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fontenelle bounced around during his college days, starting at the University of Washington in 2021, then moving to McLennan Junior College the following year and then on to Texas Christian for his Draft year in 2023. He went to the College World Series that year and finished with an OPS over 1.100, helping him land in the seventh round with the Angels. In a very unsurprising development for anyone who follows the organization, Fontenelle went up to Double-A to start his first full season and was playing well when his season ended after just 22 games after a slide into second caused both a dislocated ankle and fractured fibula. He made it back to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he really struggled to shake off the rust at the plate. A big switch-hitter the Angels think just fell through the cracks as teams focused on Horned Frogs teammate Brayden Taylor, Fontenelle has the chance to fit the corner-infield profile well offensively. When he’s healthy, he can hit the ball very hard with excellent exit velocities. He didn’t swing and miss much in college with a solid overall approach, and while his strikeout rate ticked up during his pro debut and in the AFL, it’s too small of a sample size to draw any conclusions there. Fontenelle has only played third with the Angels, and while he’s big and a below-average runner, he has good instincts (which help him steal some bases despite the lack of quickness) and actions, with enough arm to have a chance to stick at the hot corner. He’s played first base and even a little left field in the past, so there are some options should a move be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivas earned NCAA Division II All-America accolades at Indianapolis in 2022 before transferring to Mississippi, where he was the Rebels' best starter as a junior before missing all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. The Yankees still drafted him in the 16th round because they were intrigued by the deception of his pitches. He returned to the mound last year and recorded a 3.38 ERA with a .166 average-against and a 31 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Rookie ball to High-A. Rivas doesn't fool hitters with a riding fastball that sits at 90 mph and maxes out at 92, but he utilizes it well enough to set up a pair of baffling secondary pitches. He does an excellent job of killing spin on a low-80s changeup with splitter action that generated a 41 percent chase rate and 57 percent swing-and-miss rate in his pro debut. Hitters also consistently swung over the top of his tight low-80s slider. Though Rivas spent his first pro season as a starter, he profiles better as a tricky left-handed reliever. He has to nibble with his below-average heater and get chases with his slider and changeup, so only a third of his pitches landed in the strike zone last year. His competitive makeup also would work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez-Gomez pitched one season each at San Bernardino Valley (Calif.) JC and Temple (Texas) JC before the Cubs signed him for an under-slot $100,000 in the 10th round, using some of the savings to land since-traded Zyhir Hope with their next pick. Used primarily as a reliever as a pro, he got torched in his debut and spent most of his first two seasons in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2025 with a 1.46 ERA and 29 percent strikeout rate at two Class A stops, which may earn him a chance to show what he can do as a starter this year. The key to Martinez-Gomez's success was developing a low-80 splitter that's a weapon, as he does an excellent job on killing spin before it dives under barrels. The splitter plays well off his fastball, which parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with sink and armside run. He also spins a fringy slider in the low 80s. Martinez-Gomez's athleticism helps him get down the mound well and create extension in his delivery, though it hasn't helped him repeat mechanics well enough to provide regular strikes. He has a career 16 percent walk rate in pro ball before slicing that mark to 6 percent at High-A during last season's final month. If he can maintain average control, he might become a back-of-the-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds are always active players on the international market and it was no different during the 2024 international signing period. They focused much more on bats, with seven of their top bonuses – all six figures or more – going to hitters. Down the list was Torres, a six-foot right-hander who got $30,000 to sign with the organization when the period opened in January of that year. He was among the Dominican Summer League’s leaders in ERA, WHIP and batting average against, then came stateside in 2025 and was equally dominant over 38 1/3 Arizona Complex League innings. While a bit undersized, Torres is strong and stocky and his intriguing combination of feel for pitching and solid all-around stuff points to a future as a starter. He has three usable pitches, all of which are average but could be better as he progresses. His fastball sits in the 91-94 range, and he’s shown the ability to maintain his velocity throughout outings, he spins a low-80s curve very well and has good feel for an 85-87 mph fading changeup. All of his offerings play up because he’s shown a very strong feel for throwing them all for strikes, especially for his age. He’s walked just 1.9 per nine in his brief pro career heading into 2026, with the hopes of him having at least above-average command in the future. He’s yet to show he can answer the bell in a full-season rotation, but the Reds are bullish on his ability to start long term. Other organizations have definitely noticed his early success as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton played little in his first four seasons at Wright State, redshirting when he arrived, coming off the bench the next two years and having the 2020 season shortened by the pandemic. He finally got a chance to show what he could do in 2021, when he was named Horizon League Player of the Year and ranked third in NCAA Division I in runs scored (78) and OPS (1.306). Signed for a well-below-slot $47,500 in the fifth round that July, he slashed .308/.425/.508 between Single-A and High-A in his first full pro season before dropping to .206/.320/.341 in the final six weeks in Double-A. Hamilton has one of the best approaches among Astros farmhands, controlling the strike zone while making consistent contact and drawing a healthy amount of walks. His left-handed swing is geared more for hitting line drives than launching balls, but he has enough bat speed and strength to generate 12-15 homers per season. He handles same-side pitchers well, adding to his usefulness as a potential fourth outfielder. Hamilton has plus speed and uses it well on bases, swiping 27 bases in 31 tries last year. He possesses average range in center field, where he played most often in 2022, and could be a solid defender on the corners, where he also saw a lot of action. He has average arm strength, gets rid of throws quickly and registered 11 assists last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels gave seven-figure bonuses to outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus at the start of the 2022 international signing period, but they also brought in some intriguing young pitching talent. No one got a higher bonus than Encarnacion, who signed for $500,000 and then struck out nearly 11 per nine innings during his Dominican Summer League debut. A plus athlete on the mound, Encarnacion’s fastball currently sits around 92-93 mph and can touch 96. His slider is his best secondary offering, a low-80s breaking ball that has the chance to be better than average in the future. He’ll throw his changeup up to 87-88 mph, giving him a true three-pitch mix, though he could use some more separation between his heater and the offspeed offering. The two things Encarnacion needs to work on the most are his command and physicality. He walked 5.3 per nine in his debut and adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame will help him repeat his delivery, which in turn will lead to more strikes. There’s projectability here to go along with some intriguing stuff, giving him the chance to develop into a starting pitcher long term as he comes stateside for the first time in 2023 at age 18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting $600,000 to sign with the Pirates out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Terrero couldn’t play until 2021 because of the pandemic. He showed off a solid approach during his Dominican Summer League debut that year, then posted an .890 OPS in the Florida Complex League when he came to the United States for the first time. He was streaky during his full-season debut in 2023, fading down the stretch, but showing off some of his offensive potential. With a smaller frame, Terrero has yet to display a ton of impact from the left side of the plate. But there were some gains in terms of exit velocity last year, which gave the Pirates hope there could be more of that to come with some pop to his pull side. He’s made a ton of contact in his brief career, though his strikeout rate did climb a bit in Single-A Bradenton. He tends to have a consistent approach and draws walks, with a 13 percent walk rate in 2023. Terrero runs well enough to steal some bags, and it also gives him the potential to stick in center field. He’s an average defender there now who still needs to work on his reads and routes. He’s actually a plus defender in an outfield corner, but he’s not going to have the kind of offensive impact teams like to see from that spot, which could make him a bit of a tweener if center doesn’t work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he played on the same Goodpasture Christian HS (Nashville) as Tigers fourth-rounder Carson Rucker in 2023, Elkins flew somewhat under the radar because he was also an all-region running back in football who didn't spend much time on the showcase circuit. Teams recognized his tools but didn't have much history with him, allowing the Dodgers to land him in the eighth round with an over-slot $407,500 bonus. After making a one-game pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he returned there last summer and batted .285/.412/.457 with 20 steals in 57 games. Elkins has a strong 6-foot-1 frame and a quick right-handed swing that give him plus raw power with the potential for more. He has a pull-happy approach and looks to drive the ball in the air, enabling him to tap into most of his pop. He'll have to prove he can hit advanced pitching because he tied for the ACL lead with 80 strikeouts while whiffing at 35 percent clip, though he did show a willingness to work deep counts and take walks. Elkins may have the best combination of power and speed in the system. He's a plus-plus runner who's aggressive on the bases and in the outfield. Both his center-field defense and arm strength grade as at least plus, and the Dodgers have some internal 70 grades on both tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts went undrafted after his junior year at Utah in 2023, when he batted just .266 with three homers over 46 games, but he started to show out for Mankato in the Northwoods League that summer (.346/.476/.555), creating some momentum for himself. He built on that with a Pac-12 All-Conference nod after slashing .356/.430/.562 with seven homers in 55 games for the Utes as a senior. His 33 steals were most among Pac-12 players. The Padres selected him in the seventh round and signed him for just $10,000, but Roberts continued to show out with a .340/.414/.470 line in 24 games with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first taste of the Minors. Roberts cuts a stunning figure in the field at 6-foot-5, 205 pounds, and he moves exceptionally well for that size, notching 60-yard dashes in the 6.5-second range. He was a perfect 14-for-14 in steal attempts during that short run in the California League, and the Padres don’t have much doubt that his speed will continue to play as he reaches higher levels. With those wheels, Roberts is a comfortable fit in center field and has just enough arm for the position, too. That said, the left-handed hitter hasn’t been a huge power threat despite his size, though San Diego officials were intrigued by the good weight he put on during in his first offseason. He struggled to make contact against sliders and changeups as a senior and will need his speed to help run high BABIPs that can make up for some of the contact issues. Roberts already enters his first full season at age 24 and doesn’t have a long runway, but his best skills could be useful in the Majors in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heuer had some of the best physicality and projectable fastball velocity in the 2023 Draft, but he turned down the Guardians as a 16th-rounder to attend Texas Tech. He served as the Red Raiders' No. 1 starter and pushed his fastball to 98 mph last spring, but he also logged a 6.28 ERA as a Draft-eligible sophomore. That didn't deter the Yankees, who signed him for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round. Heuer operates at 93-95 mph with cut and carry on his fastball, which is effective up in the zone but gets pounded when he doesn't command it well. His mid-80s slider with sweeping action can be a solid offering when it's on, though he has trouble landing it for strikes and it sometimes flattens over the heart of the plate. His mid-80s changeup with fade and depth was his most effective offering as a sophomore, though he didn't use it much. Scouts don't love Heuer's delivery, which features a short arm action, high release point and some crossfire. He presently has fringy control and below-average command, which may make him more of a reliever than a starter in the long run. If he doesn't make it in baseball, he has his own livestock business with his brother and raised ewes that won grand champion titles at the 2020 and 2022 Georgia National Fairs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dumesnil looked like he could be a high-round Draft pick after an eye-opening sophomore season at Cal Baptist, including a .362/.440/.702 slash line with 19 homers, and an All-Star season in the Cape Cod League, hitting .311 and leading the circuit in steals (26). A difficult junior season changed his momentum, but the Tigers snagged him in the eighth round, signed him for $214,300 and immediately put him at Single-A, where he made an impact for Lakeland in the Florida State League playoffs. Strong and athletic, the 6-foot-2 Dumesnil showed the ability to hit with power in college, but his 2025 season came with struggles against spin, notably sliders, and inconsistent power. Both of those continued in Lakeland, where he hit fastballs well but not for much power while whiffing on breaking balls. He’s not a fluid runner but has enough speed and aggressiveness to swipe bases, which he did often in a small sample size for the Flying Tigers. Dumesnil’s speed does help him cover ground in the outfield and he’s shown he can be solid at all three spots defensively. Some feel he can play center long term, but others feel he’s best suited for a corner, with left being a better option because of his fringy arm strength. Even with the struggles he’s had, the Tigers will try to get him back to 2024 Cape form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you’re a high-ceiling high school pitcher who hasn’t heard his name called in the top 10 rounds and think you’re headed to college, the Angels can always give you hope. On an almost annual basis, extra bonus pool money is available to take and sign some prep arms. In 2025, they targeted a pair of intriguing high school lefties, taking Talon Haley in the 12th round and Mitchell a round later. Rather than head to Texas, Mitchell signed for $872,500, heading down a baseball path despite coming from a football family that includes an uncle who quarterbacked in the Canadian Football League and a brother who was a wide receiver at Arizona. After pitching for Team USA the summer before his senior year, Mitchell got off to a good start back at school but was shut down with shoulder fatigue after a month, so building up strength will be a key. He can sit 90-92 mph with his fastball, touching 94, and the fastball plays up because of deception in his delivery and carry up in the zone. He has a good feel to spin an upper-70s curve with depth that works well off of his heater. Like with a lot of high school pitchers, he hasn’t used a changeup much, but he’s shown glimpses of a decent cambio in the low-80s with fade and sink. Mitchell is athletic on the mound, repeating his delivery well and filling up the strike zone. There’s room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, which could help all of his stuff tick up as he gets his pro career going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2024, the Mariners signed Chia-Shi Shen out of Chinese Taipei. They hit that pitching market again in 2025, signing Lin for $460,000 when the signing period opened in January. A former two-way player who pitched well in international competition, Lin looked really good in Spring Training after signing, but then wasn’t able to make his pro debut because of a lat strain, though he did get some innings in the bridge league at the end of the year, once again raising expectations. Lin had played both the infield and outfield previously, and he brings that athleticism to the mound. The 5-foot-11 right-hander has the chance to have a full starter’s repertoire, with his splitter the standout pitch. It flashes plus and can fall off the table with excellent depth while also throwing a distinct changeup. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for more, and there could be more velocity in the future. He has some feel to spin with a more traditional slider, though it’s behind the other offerings, and there’s been some talk of adding a sweeper to his mix. Lin’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone consistently. His stuff may never wow anyone, but his feel for pitching and full array of offerings gives him the chance to start, with the Mariners getting to see what he’s like in competition this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Mason Martin, a former Pirates farmhand who ranked fourth in the Minors with 35 homers in 2019, Martin also stands out with his well-above-average raw power. Signed for an over-slot $250,000 in 2023 as an 11th-rounder from a Washington high school, he struggled for two years in Rookie ball before doing more damage in Single-A last year and drawing significant trade interest from other clubs. He earned Carolina League all-star honors after leading the Single-A circuit in extra-base hits (43) and ranking second in slugging (.440) and third in homers (12) and OPS (.783). Martin can drive the ball out of the park to all fields with an impressive combination of bat speed and strength, and he hits the ball harder and farther than most Rangers farmhands. In 2025, he did a better job of attacking hittable pitches in early counts and launching them in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make better use of his pop. How much he'll be able to tap into his 25-30 homer upside at higher levels will depend on his ability to improve his swing decisions and handle secondary pitches. Though Martin stole 15 bases in as many attempts last year, he has fringy speed with good instincts on the bases. He has limited range and below-average arm strength, relegating him to left field and diminishing his value outside of the batter's box. He's adequate at first base and can fill in in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the top 10 rounds of the 2025 Draft, the Phillies took nine pitchers, eight of them from the college ranks. The lone hitter in the group was Ferrara, a high school shortstop from Toms River East High School in New Jersey. The athletic middle infielder had shown off some tools on the summer showcase circuit and turned in a strong season in the New Jersey Shore Conference. The Phillies had some bonus pool money to play with in the ninth round when they took Ferrara, who signed for an over-slot bonus close to $600,000, or fourth-round money. The Phillies pushed the six-foot right-handed hitter to full-season Clearwater for a 15-game debut that did not go particularly well, though little should be read into thrusting an 18-year old kid from the Northeast into that level of competition. What was impressive was that even in the small sample, he was starting to make some small adjustments that should help him in the future. He wasn’t on time, launching his barrel too late, which led to poor barrel accuracy. When he got more synced up, his barrel accuracy and zone contact improved. He’s already added strength and physicality since signing, which could help him get to more impact. While Ferrara only played second base during his debut, the Phillies think his athleticism gives him the chance to stick at short. He’s an easily plus runner with decent actions defensively. He’ll continue to see time on both sides of second base, and it’s not out of the question that he gets some run out in center field at some point in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels clearly have a thing for two-way players. We all know about Shohei Ohtani, and Jared Walsh got to the big leagues in 2019. In 2018, they drafted William Holmes and are letting him both hit and pitch as a pro. They took Rivera from the Puerto Rico high school ranks in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, giving him an above-slot $597,500 bonus to sign him away from his Florida International commitment. He only hit during his pro debut in the Rookie-Level Arizona League, but the plan is to let him follow in Holmes’ footsteps. Rivera has some serious raw power to tap into from the left side of the plate, but there’s question about whether he’ll make enough contact to get to it consistently. There are some swing-and-miss issues -- he struck out in more than 37 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he’ll have to refine his approach. But Angels hitting instructors like his swing and think that will come with experience. On the mound, Rivera has been up to 95-96 mph with his fastball, sitting more in the low 90s, with plenty of room to add strength and consistent velocity. He’s shown both feel for spinning his breaking ball and for a changeup, but he’ll need to work on improving his secondary stuff along with his command of all his offerings. Like with his swing, Angels instructors like the biomechanics of Rivera’s delivery, leaving it a bit of a tossup which area he might have the better chance with if he had to choose one to pursue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Endersby was recruited as an infielder but moved to the mound at Cal State Fullerton, where he totaled 16 2/3 innings in three years before transferring to Concordia (Calif.). He made just five starts at the NCAA Division II level during the shortened 2020 season, yet impressed the Astros enough to sign for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Double-A and struck out 110 in 97 innings. Endersby employs the north-south attack pattern that Houston favors. He goes after hitters with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball with high spin rates and carry up in the zone and an upper-70s curveball with downer break. He also has a harder slider with sweeping action and a nascent changeup that lags behind the rest of his offerings. Endersby lacks physicality but he's athletic and has a quick arm. His control and command come and go, as does the consistency of his secondary pitches, so it's more likely that he winds up as a reliever than a starter. If he moves to the bullpen and concentrates on his fastball and curveball, he could reach the big leagues in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Rodriguez in July 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and the start of his pro career was bumpy because of the pandemic. It didn’t seem to slow him down, as he was named the DSL Royals Blue Player of the Year in 2021 and then brought his high energy to the States in 2022, slashing .306/.395/.514 between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A. Rodriguez’s best tool is hitting, with innate bat-to-ball skills, an efficient swing and a simple approach at the plate. He doesn’t fear velocity and has an excellent idea of the strike zone for someone who just finished his age-19 season -- his 10.8 percent walk rate and 16.2 percent strikeout rate were better in Columbia than Rookie ball. The switch-hitter has a good approach from both sides of the plate, but most of his pop -- which is below average right now -- comes from the left side. That could change with more reps on the right side and more strength. Rodriguez is an above-average defender at second base with quick hands and good footwork. Rodriguez has tools and youth on his side right now. The ingredients are there to make good on that upside as long as his contact skills and zone control continue. He seems to be limited to second base right now, but he could probably handle the left side of the infield if needed; certainly if he gets stronger and there’s emphasis on versatility. As a second baseman without a lot of thump, Rodriguez has a high floor as a utility infielder, but if the high average and on-base numbers continue against better pitching, perhaps there’s a leadoff candidate in his future.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Jarvis had been on the fringe of prospect lists at FanGraphs for years but his combination of below-average velocity and control (despite his fastball's other traits) kept him toward the bottom or off the list, entirely. In 2023 he had a two-tick velo spike and is now sitting 93-95 with plus-plus riding life. Jarvis' command is still not very good but his type of fastball gives him in-zone margin for error. His due north arm slot, which is largely where Jarvis' vertical ride comes from, also helps him impart depth on his breaking balls. His isn't overpowering but mixes in four average pitches and has thrown enough strikes to continue developing as a starter, especially while he has options left. Jarvis' extremely skinny build creates doubt about his ability to hold his new velo under a starter's workload and so he projects as a long-term long reliever here at FG.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: St Joseph’s most successful product has been left-hander Jamie Moyer, who spent a quarter century in the big leagues. There’s been one other catcher, Brian O’Keefe, who touched the Majors in 2022-23, but Cossetti is hoping to be the next. After four years at the Philadelphia-based school, Cossetti certainly didn’t hurt his stock with a strong showing in his second stint in MLB’s Draft League in 2022, helping him land in the 11th round of that year's Draft. He posted a .960 OPS across two levels of A ball in 2023, with a 163 RC+ that placed second among all catchers with more than 300 plate appearances, before finishing up with a defense-focused stint in the Arizona Fall League. Cossetti has the chance to be a productive right-handed hitter because he has a solid combination of strength and approach at the plate. He limits strikeouts and draws a ton of walks, getting him into better counts where he did fairly consistent damage. He registers high exit velocities, and there’s good power he should be able to continue to get to. Whether he can defend well enough to stay behind the plate is more of a question. He’s improved his arm strength to average, and he works very hard at his craft, but he’ll need to keep grinding to become an adequate receiver. The Twins don’t want to bet against his work ethic, but they’ll also keep getting him some reps at first base to get his bat in the lineup more regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers paid eight of the nine largest bonuses in their 2022 international class to Venezuelans, including $247,500 to Torres. He ranked third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 23 steals and fifth with seven homers in his U.S. debut last summer, the only player in the league to place in the top five in both categories. He was overmatched in a 10-game promotion to Single-A as an 18-year-old, going 4-for-37 (.108) with 18 strikeouts. Torres has one of the quickest bats among Rangers farmhands, and the loft in his left-handed stroke and his growing strength produce some of the best raw power. There are some questions about how much contact he'll make because his swing can get long and uphill, and he didn't do much damage against southpaws last year. He does display some characteristics of a good approach, mostly concentrating on balls from gap to gap and showing reasonable patience for a teenager. Torres flashes plus straight-line speed but projects to be more of an average runner once he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He steals more with savvy than quickness, so he likely won't be as much of a factor on the bases at higher levels. He's an average defender with similar arm strength in left and right field and at first base, the three positions he played (in order of frequency) in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers as a junior for South Carolina in 2021, apt timing considering he missed much of his sophomore campaign the previous year due to the pandemic. The Brewers selected him in the 10th round that summer and signed him below slot at $75,000. The right-handed slugger was a solid performer between High-A and Double-A his first full season, finishing with 14 homers and a 116 wRC+ in 99 games, but truly took off in a return to Biloxi this summer with a Southern League-best 26 homers and an .889 OPS that placed third on the circuit. A strong Arizona Fall League campaign solidified the breakout. Power, power, power -- that’s long been Clarke’s calling card and will continue to be the closer he gets to Milwaukee. His uphill swing enables the pop to play as 50.2 percent of his batted balls were flyballs in 2023, but it also can affect his overall contact rate as he struck out 29.2 percent of the time. Clarke balances the punchouts with a lot of walks, but even he’s admitted he needs to get to the power earlier in counts to keep the offensive profile balanced. A well-below-average runner, Clarke initially impressed Brewers officials with his improvements behind the plate, but he’s still viewed as a long-term first baseman, especially as he plays next to Jeferson Quero and bumps into William Contreras’ shadow. He has decent arm strength but lacks accuracy on throws, leading to a 10.3 percent caught-stealing rate in 2023. A full-time right-right first baseman has a high offensive bar to clear, but Clarke just might have the power to handle it. If he can serve as a third catcher on the roster too, all the better.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the 16 prospects who received six-figure bonuses from the Pirates at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Tsung-Che Cheng has jumped out as the best prospect to date. Castillo was close to the bottom of that list, getting $140,000 to sign in July 2019. He jumped on the map when he won the Florida Complex League batting title (.352), and while he wasn’t nearly as productive with a move to full-season Bradenton in 2023, he joined teammate Termarr Johnson as two of the eight players in the Minor Leagues to walk 100 or more times. Since signing, Castillo has shown off impressive bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate. He’s registered very low strikeout rates at each stop, carrying a 17.3 K rate into the 2024 season. He doesn’t give away at-bats and isn’t afraid to hit with two strikes. He couples that with excellent patience to be an on-base machine, when he can then use his speed to be a basestealing threat. What he lacks, however, is any impact at the plate, and he’s working to get more physical without taking away his all-fields approach, though he’s never going to have more than gap power. Castillo is so sound defensively, the sentiment is that he could handle playing in a Major League game at shortstop if need be. He’ll continue to get plenty of reps there, but he’s also proven to be a bit of a Swiss Army knife, one who did everything but catch for Bradenton in 2023. The Pirates love his aggressive style of play and his contact skills. If he can add just a little strength, he could carve out a future as a utility player in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took Beilenson as a money-saving senior sign in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, with his $25,000 under-slot bonus helping pay to sign Ryan Sloan. But Beilenson had success in college, especially once he moved to Duke after three years at Brown, saving 12 games for the Blue Devils while getting a pair of graduate degrees. While he was old for the High-A level where he began his first full season of pro ball, he pitched well enough to earn a promotion to Double-A after 20 appearances, putting him on the prospect map. Now 26, Beilenson is more a sum-of-his-parts kind of pitcher than a reliever who is going to blow hitters away. He has a foundation of three pitches but manipulates them into different shapes to give him a repertoire of as many as five. He’ll throw both a four- and a two-seam fastball, averaging around 93 mph. His best pitch is his kick-change that has splitter-like action to it. He’ll throw both a sweeper and a shorter, harder slider around 81 mph with cutter-like action. Beilenson can throw a ton of strikes with all his offerings, but it’s control over command, and he got hit more once he got to Double-A. If he can find a bit more consistency from one outing to the next, he could be knocking on the door to a big league bullpen job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long winding path for Mejia, who started his college career by redshirting at Arizona in 2019, then transferred to Pima Community College in 2020, but made just five starts there because of the pandemic. The right-hander went to New Mexico State after that, mostly relieving in 2021 then stepping into the rotation in 2022. He signed for $100,000 as an 11th-round pick that summer, spent all year with High-A Rome in 2023 and then had another solid, and durable, season with Double-A Mississippi in 2024. Mejia’s feel for pitching and the ability to mix his offerings to keep hitters off-balance stands out more than any of his pure stuff. His fastball averaged around 92 mph last year and maxed out at 94 mph. It doesn’t feature a ton of life, but he commands the pitch consistently. His low-80s slider is his go-to pitch, and he threw it almost as much as his heater in 2024, missing bats at a 42-percent clip. His 83-84 mph changeup is a decent third offering and he’s been working on a splitter as well. The 6-foot-3 Mejia does a nice job of repeating his delivery and has a history of throwing strikes, especially in 2022 with the Aggies and during his first pro season. His walk rate did jump a bit in 2024, but he’s posted consistently, topping 120 innings in each of his two full seasons. His ceiling is probably as a No. 5 type starter because of the lack of wow stuff, but he’s close to showing if it can work in the big leagues.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Cairone, who was signed away from a Coastal Carolina commitment for just over a million bucks, is a breakout candidate in this system. The smooth-operating southpaw has a gorgeous delivery and fairly projectable frame, and Cairone's fastball velocity has been climbing steadily throughout the last year and a half. During the summer after his junior year of high school, he was sitting about 86; post-2025 instructs (in a casual, short-outing setting), he was 91-93. Cairone (pronounced like "Tyrone", some Erykah Badu jokes were made during the completion of this prospect list) throws quality strikes with his fastball and showed similarly advanced feel for his 80-ish-mph slider.  That pitch is better in the zone than as a finisher right now. We're skeptical of the sustainability of new velocity like this when it's seen in well-rested, one- or two-inning spurts like Cairone's was in the fall, but we can't help but be excited by his overall stuff, feel, and athleticism ingredients, and are giving him fairly aggressive placement here.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Smooth-operating southpaw with upper-80s to low-90s heat. Feel for location, quality fastball strikes. Similarly advanced slider feel in the 78-81 mph range. Better in the zone than as a finisher right now. Late-arriving arm strength, spring breakout guy with starter mechanics and feel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The Brewers have set up a connection in New Jersey by taking four pitchers from the state in the past two Drafts, including top-70 picks Bryce Meccage and Chris Levonas in 2024 and Cairone and Sean Episcope in ’25. Cairone joined the organization from Delsea HS as the 68th pick last year -- the same selection Milwaukee picked up for not inking Levonas -- and signed him below slot for $1,097,500. The 6-foot-2 left-hander struck out 94 batters in 44 innings as a senior and helped his cause with a nice showing at the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. His fastball touches 95 mph but plays up with ride generated from a low release, and his extension close to 7 feet puts that heater right on top of batters. Holding the velocity will be a test on the pro side. Cairone’s low-80s slider sat between 2,900-3,000 rpms during the Combine, making it easy to dream on the breaking ball as a future plus pitch with good sweep. A solid cutter acts as a bridge pitch, and he can kill spin with a mid-80s changeup that still sits behind his other pitches in quality. Only 17 on Draft Day, Cairone fits a lot of the Milwaukee bill when it comes to Draft arms: young for the class, projectable and armed with pitches that plug nicely into models. Unfortunately, he was hospitalized after a serious car accident in the middle of the offseason, and while reports have been good about his initial recovery, he’ll likely need to be eased into his first full season. Once fully healthy and built up, Cairone will get plenty of runway to take off as a Brewer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seven years after the Tigers took a Draft flier on a college pitcher with mixed results a year removed from Tommy John surgery (Tarik Skubal), they went a similar route with Leys, who missed the 2024 season recovering from surgery before taking the mound for the University of Maine in 2025. Leys won America East Pitcher of the Year with a 2.69 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 67 innings, better than his first two seasons with the Black Bears. The Tigers drafted him in the fourth round, five rounds earlier than Skubal, and signed him for $574,900. While Leys isn’t big for a pitcher, he has a quick, fluid delivery with a big leg kick and a three-quarters arm angle. His fastball can touch 96 mph, setting up a slider and a changeup both in the low 80s. Leys greatly improved his strike throwing and command upon his return from surgery, cutting his walk rate in almost half from his first two seasons while ticking up his strikeout rate. The Tigers have been aggressive at times starting out college pitchers in full-season ball, and could do the same with Leys, who made an impression in Spring Training. If he can hold his command while adding more swing-and-miss, he could force his way up the system quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Draft picks taken after the 10th round are automatically assigned a slot value of $150,000. When a college senior gets taken in Round 11, as Clohisy was out of St. Louis in 2024, and signs for that exact slot amount, it tends to fly under the radar. But when that senior plays his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season and finishes third among all Minor Leaguers with 79 steals before stealing 22 more to lead the Arizona Fall League, as Clohisy did in 2025, folks tend to sit up and take notice. Clohisy’s future in the big leagues is directly connected to his legs. In 2025, regular season and AFL combined, he stole 101 bases in 120 attempts (84.2 percent success rate) in 152 games. Not only does he have great speed, he’s aggressive in using it, wreaking havoc at all times. His wheels also help him cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He can no doubt play center field, but has and will continue to get time in all three spots. That’s important because his future role would be as a fourth or fifth outfielder if it all clicks. And that will depend on how the left-handed hitter swings the bat. There is a little extra-base ability, but his job will always be to put the ball in play and get on base, and it will be interesting to see whether he can carry over the offensive success he had in Double-A and Arizona to lift him up to Atlanta.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Did you read the Junior Ciprian blurb and think “that sounds nice, but he’s a little too advanced for me?” Well, have I got the pitcher for you. Vasquez is another long and lean Dominican hurler. He generates some of the easiest 97s and 98s you’ll ever see, and both his raw ability to spin the ball and his feel for his change are good, particularly for the level. Complex-level bats were overwhelmed by both of them. 
Vasquez is very raw, though. While he’s made strides since his walk-the-world DSL days, he doesn't have much feel for where it’s going. He’s a hard lander, he gets off balance, and some scouts have said he’s got “darty” arm action, which you can think of as a guy who tends to aim the ball rather than really let it rip. Those issues are also limiting his ability to execute. He hasn't yet harnessed all that spin into anything more than a slurvy breaking ball, and while there’s a potential plus pitch in him, he’s a long way from finding it. The change is also inconsistent and will need reps to reach its projection. Inevitably, the range of outcomes for a teenager with a great arm is wide, and the top end of it here is a mid-rotation starter with three above average or better offerings. From my vantage, the athleticism and stroke is a little too concerning for that lofty of a projection. Arizona should keep starting Vasquez for the reps and maybe something clicks, but the overall package seems more like a reliever in the end, albeit one with upside in that role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Redona put up video game numbers in his first DSL season — 0.86 ERA, 0.67 WHIP, 36.8% K%, 2.6% BB% in 31.1 IP — thanks almost entirely to his mature command of a deceptive riding fastball. He doesn't throw all that hard, but the pitch averages 18 inches of vertical break and Redona commands it with machine-like precision to the top half of the zone. His fastball represented 70% of Redona's pitch deployment. His silky smooth arm action helps him sell a precocious changeup, and he will show you an average breaking ball anywhere in the 77-84 mph range, but this is more a prospect with a shot to have special command than one who'll grow into elite stuff. He's a priority name to know from rookie ball even though he's much more likely to be Tom Milone than Tom Glavine.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text: Bravo popped onto the radar because of his 2025 data (he posted an 88% contact rate during his debut season), and would have based on his visual scouting look in Florida this year, albeit for entirely different reasons. On paper, Bravo looks like a slappy contact hitter with special feel for the barrel but no power (16% hard-hit rate). In person, he has a bloodthirsty low-ball swing with an epic finish in the dirt behind him. He also looks like a prospect with strikeout risk, as his front foot is often bailing down the first base line when he swings, and his scoopy bat path leaves Bravo vulnerable to elevated fastballs away from him. When he gets a ball in his wheelhouse on the inner third of the dish, his swing looks like that of a baby Darryl Strawberry. Because the BoSox FCL roster is chock full of shortstops, Bravo’s reps there have been limited, but he’s looked competent on the opportunities he’s gotten. The incongruity between Bravo’s scouting look as a hitter versus his DSL data from last season is fascinating, but not deleterious. Most of what’s happening here is positive and exciting, giving the Red Sox yet another fun young infielder to monitor.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: There was a run on prep pitching just before the Phillies made their second selection in the 2016 draft, the year they took Mickey Moniak first overall. Gowdy was the last pitcher of that talent tier remaining and ended up eschewing a UCLA commit to go pro. A surgery and the pandemic combined to knock out three years of Gowdy's five-year pro career.
