His stuff was up in 2021, looking more like his peak amateur days (low-to-mid-90s, promising slider) while profiling on the middle relief/5th starter line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his four years at Princeton, Smith both relieved and started. He had his strongest year in the Tigers' rotation as a senior, enough for the Angels to take a low-risk flier on the left-hander in Round 18 of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just $3,000. After pitching out of the bullpen during his pro debut that summer, Smith took the opportunity to start in 2021 and ran with it, pitching across four levels to finish in Triple-A. Smith does have four pitches at his disposal, all coming from his strong, though undersized, 5-foot-11 frame. His fastball averaged around 92 mph in 2021, touching 94, but it plays up some because it has good ride up in the zone. His slider, a sweeper with a ton of horizontal movement, is his best secondary offering that can miss bats, a big reason why he struck out 10.6 per nine last season. His slower curve isn’t as good, but serves as a good get-me-over pitch for strike one and he uses his changeup effectively while starting to mix in a new cutter as well. Throughout his college career, Smith struggled with command, walking 4.4 per nine. He threw a ton more strikes in 2021, nearly cutting that walk rate in half. He’s on the map now, with the chance to serve as a No. 5 starter/long reliever type in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Munoz joined the Mariners during the 2019-20 international signing period for $195,000, then was among the many impacted by COVID interrupting the following season, which prevented him from pitching competitively until an assignment to the Dominican Summer League, where he spent 2021-22. The first year was inconsistent, but he rebounded in the second and made the midseason All-Star team. A projectable righty with room to keep adding strength, Munoz is another arm that Seattle’s player development staff has been banging the drum on. He’s up to the mid-90s on his fastball with decent arm-side run and above-average hop. He’s also shown flashes of a plus slider that generated a ton of whiffs and strikeouts with. It’ll probably need more depth as he progresses, but, so far, he commands it better than the heater. Now it’s a matter of if he can develop a third pitch and remain a starter, because there were a lot of positive signs with his strike throwing. It’s a changeup right now, but he doesn’t throw it often because of how good the other two have been. If he does go down a relief road, his path to the Majors could be accelerated.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene signed for just $17,500 as a South Alabama senior when the Yankees took him in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft. After missing out on his first full season due to the pandemic, he proved to be a steady performer as a reliever at the High-A, Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2021 and 2022. He spent all of last season with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, posting a 3.42 ERA, .199 average-against and 96 strikeouts in 68 1/3 innings, but he was still left off the Yankees' 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible due to a roster crunch. The Mets swooped in during the Rule 5 Draft, and in order to keep him, Greene must remain in their Major League bullpen for all of 2023. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches out of the stretch at the extreme first-base side of the rubber, and he fires in a low-90s fastball that can be deceptive with its apparent rise and cutting action. Despite the fastball being closer to average velo, that ride can make the heater extremely difficult to pick up, and hitters often hopelessly swung below the pitch at Triple-A. An upper-70s slider kept opposing batters from sitting on the fastball and played well into the Yankees’ pitching philosophy of prioritizing sweep on breaking pitches. An upper-80s changeup kept lefties honest but was a distant third pitch. If hitters can learn not to chase the high heat or the solid breaker, they can earn the occasional free pass from Greene, who walked 11.1 percent of the batters he faced in 2022. That control has been one reason why the righty has stayed in relief in the pros, but his two best pitches make him an MLB-ready bullpen option for the Mets.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scull’s father, Antonio, won three Olympic medals playing as a first baseman for Cuba. Anthony started his own path in baseball by signing with the Angels for $235,000 in September 2021. It took a while for the outfielder to show the Angels anything, getting into just 10 games in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then missing most of the 2022 season with a shoulder injury sustained when diving for a ball in the outfield. He did play a full slate of Arizona Complex League games in 2023, showing glimpses of some playable tools. Scull has a strong and athletic frame with the ability to do some damage from the left side of the plate. He makes a lot of hard contact, registering some of the better exit velocities in the lower levels of the Angels' system. He doesn’t strike out a ton, but he can be a bit too aggressive at the plate. It’s more of a line-drive swing right now, but there’s raw power to tap into with the potential to hit around 15 homers annually once he matures physically and with his approach. An above-average runner, Scull can play all three outfield spots with an average arm. He saw more time in center field than anywhere else in 2023 and he does have a chance to stay there should he develop into a regular at one position. A more likely outcome is for him to be a solid fourth outfielder type who moves around and provides a left-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited as a catcher by Boise State, Buxton moved to the mound with the Broncos, redshirted in 2019 and pitched in just four games during the shortened 2020 season. Boise State dropped baseball afterward, so he transferred to Lipscomb, where he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with seven wins in 2022 before getting drafted in the 15th round that July. He reached Double-A for one start at the end of his first full pro season and soaked up more experience in the Arizona Fall League afterward. Buxton relies heavily on his fastball, a power sinker that operates at 93-95 mph, reaches 97 and creates a ton of groundball contact -- his 2.06 groundout/airout ratio would have ranked fourth in the Minors last year if he had enough innings to qualify. He can flash a solid low-80s slider with nice sweep at times but he struggles to land it in the zone. He has made some strides with an 82-85 mph changeup with similar sink to his heater, and it could become an average offering if he uses it more often. To remain a starter, Buxton will need to throw more strikes. His control improved a bit during his six weeks in High-A last summer but remains fringy at best. He could wind up fitting toward the back of a big league rotation or wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers swiped Pacific Northwest prep pitchers away from Oregon State commitments in consecutive Drafts. The more recent, Swanson, was a two-sport star in Washington, the son of a high school basketball coach who was the top-ranked high school player in the state. The Tigers drafted Swanson in the ninth round and wooed him to pro ball with an above-slot $722,500 bonus. Swanson’s athleticism has allowed him to blossom as a pitcher at a later stage than others. His fastball ranged from the low-to-mid 90s in high school but is more of a power offering with carry since working with the Tigers’ pitching department to refine his delivery. His high-spin slider has a lot of movement and depth. His changeup needs work but could be the difference between starting and relieving. The Tigers drafted Swanson fully knowing he could take longer to develop but believing in the athlete and competitor. His introduction to pro ball will be delayed after he underwent Tommy John surgery ahead of the 2025 campaign, knocking him out for what would have been his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best sleeper in the Giants' 2024 international class, Tejada signed for $147,500 out of the Dominican Republic. Known most for his power when he turned pro, he turned in a nifty all-around offensive performance in his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He slashed .300/.405/.488 with 19 extra-base hits, 22 walks and 13 steals in 46 games. Tejada has plenty of strength in his stocky 5-foot-11 frame and generates impressive bat speed and high exit velocities with a simple right-handed stroke. In the DSL, he showed the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side and the possibility of 25-homer seasons in the future. Though he has a power mentality, he also displayed some feel for hitting and for managing the strike zone. Tejada makes the most of his average speed with an aggressive nature on the bases and good instincts in the outfield. He spent his pro debut in center field, yet his quickness is better suited for the corners in the long run. Though he has average to solid arm strength, he didn't record an assist in 42 games last summer.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: James signed for $2.5 million rather than head to Ole Miss and was assigned to Low-A Fredericksburg to start his pro career in 2026. Part of the crowded infield contingent there, he has played a mix of second base, third base and left field as of list publication. A terrific low-to-the-ground athlete, James can be slow to approach grounders and makes some plays unnecessarily close at first base. This is more an issue of polish and the speed of pro ball rather than talent, and he should still become a good infielder with time. While it was obvious that James had a power-over-hit skill set as a draft prospect, the degree to which that is true is coming into greater focus. He is pummeling pitches with power when he connects, but he's struggling to make adjustments to pro sliders. James can really run, he's strong, and he has power to both gaps. He's a fun, toolsy dev project who is probably going to take a while to mature on both sides of the ball.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Athletic shortstop with impressive power. Muscular, but loose and mobile. Terrific low-to-the-ground defender, has the arm strength for shortstop but needs to polish accuracy. Strikeout issues plagued him on the showcase circuit, where he ran a 69% contact rate. Swing is loose and explosive but isn't always well-connected or well-timed. Bottom-hand dominant swing that works best when James can get extended. Thunderous power in his wrists and hands. Defensive fit at shortstop should allow room for elevated strikeouts as long as James is getting to power. Right tail outcome is akin to a Trevor Story type of offensive performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: James had the look of a potential first-round pick after showing out as an underclassman on the showcase circuit and with Team USA’s 18-and-under team in 2023 but couldn’t replicate that same level of success in the summer before his senior year, including going 1-for-12 with six strikeouts at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He rebounded a bit in the spring at Davie County HS and won Gatorade’s Player of the Year honors in North Carolina as a result. Some scouts thought he was headed to Mississippi, but the Nationals selected him in the fifth round and signed him for $2.5 million, tied for the second-highest bonus in their 2025 class. A 6-foot infielder, James added weight going into his Draft year, trading off athleticism for strength in the process. With that additional impact, he profiles as a possible 20-homer hitter, especially if he can maintain his bat speed on the pro side. The focus on driving the ball also came with a regression in swing decisions, and he bit on a good number of non-fastballs outside the zone during his 2024 showcases. His right-handed swing has looked smoother in the past, and getting back to those mechanics would help his ability to hit for average in the pros. James has the actions, hands and above-average arm strength to handle shortstop, but his fringy speed limits his range on the dirt. With Eli Willits also in the organization, James is more likely to be a better fit at second or third base, and his arm could even work in a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Georgia's best prep pitching prospects in 2019, David slid to the Diamondbacks in the 35th round amid signability concerns and opted to attend Auburn instead. He never pitched for the Tigers during the pandemic-truncated 2020 season before bouncing from Gordon State (Ga.) JC to Northwest Florida State JC to NAIA program Southeastern (Fla.) before the Astros drafted him in 2024's 10th round as a fifth-year senior. He moved from Single-A to Double-A in his first full pro season, compiling a 3.47 ERA with 87 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings. David's fastball parks at 95-96 mph and peaks at 98, and he maintained that velocity throughout 2025. It features carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider doesn't get a lot of chases but does generate a lot of in-zone swings and misses, and he can turn it into an 89-91 mph cutter on occasion. After focusing primarily on his heater and slider in college, he has worked on incorporating a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with depth but has trouble landing both for strikes. There's effort in David's delivery that has prevented him from throwing consistent strikes, so he's more of multi-inning reliever than a starter in the long run. He spent the first two months of 2025 in the rotation at Single-A Fayetteville before shifting to the bullpen. He'll pitch at age 25 this season, and the less challenging role will accelerate his timetable to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abeldt was one of college baseball's best relievers in his first two years at Texas Christian, recording a 2.81 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and spending both summers with the U.S. collegiate national team. The Horned Frogs planned on turning him into a starter in 2025, but he blew out his elbow just before the beginning of the season and required Tommy John surgery in February. The Rangers still popped him in the fifth round and signed him for $450,000. Abeldt relies heavily on a 91-94 mph fastball that peaks at 96 and is much more effective than its ordinary velocity would indicate. His heater has riding action and plenty of deception coming out of a crossfire delivery, and it's nearly impossible to lift when he works down in the zone. He can't overpower hitters with a slider that sits around 80 mph, but it can baffle them with its sweeping action when it's on. While he doesn't use it much, Abeldt has the makings of an effective low-80s changeup with sink. He looks like a shorter, stronger version of Chris Sale with his slingy delivery, and it generates a lot of empty swings and groundballs. It remains to be seen if he can succeed as a starter, but he comes with a high floor as a quality lefty reliever once he returns to full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gourson spent three years starting for UCLA (mostly at second base), earning a reputation as a gamer who maximized what tools he had, even earning a spot on Team USA after his sophomore campaign in 2023. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular junior season, finishing with a .909 OPS, and the Pirates took a low-risk flyer on him in the ninth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for a touch under $190,000. After a nondescript pro debut after signing, he was one of the pleasant surprises of the Pirates' system in 2025, performing well in all facets of the game with High-A Greensboro and Double-A Altoona. Gourson earned a ticket to pro ball because of his approach at the plate, swing decisions and contact skills. There was enough bat-to-ball skill to think he had a chance, and that was apparent in 2025; he kept his strikeouts relatively low, despite a little more swing-and-miss once he got to Double-A, while also posting a walk rate north of 10 percent. What wasn’t expected was the increased impact from the left side of the plate. He gained a few miles per hour in bat speed and that resulted in a huge uptick in exit velocity, allowing for more quality contact. Gourson's instincts and aggressiveness make him an average runner or perhaps a slight tick above that as he stole 31 bags in 34 tries in 2025. He’s seen time at three infield positions -- all but shortstop -- and he should get some reps in the outfield corners as well. If he takes another step offensively, he has a utility role kind of future in the big leagues, and it’s hard to bet against him given his intangibles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tunink enticed scouts with his left-handed stroke and athleticism as an Illinois high schooler, his strong Notre Dame commitment clouded his signability in the 2024 Draft. The Dodgers floated him down to the eighth round and were able to land him for $412,500, the equivalent of fifth-round money. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his pro debut last summer after finishing fourth in the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (152), slugging (.550) and OPS (.967), but he also struck out at a 30 percent rate. Tunink's bat speed, growing strength and propensity for driving the ball in the air to his pull side generate high exit velocities and plus raw power. He's not overly aggressive in terms of chasing pitches, but he has holes in his swing that lead to too many in-zone misses. Viewed as more of a hit-over-power guy as an amateur, he flipped that projection in the ACL. Tunink features at least plus speed that makes him a basestealing threat and a solid center fielder. He has below-average arm strength and didn't record an assist in 35 outfield starts last year.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Sando thrived as a junior reliever at Santa Clara and then struggled as a senior starter and spent his first full pro season in the bullpen. After an early-2025 demotion to Low-A, he pitched so well that the Reds not only elevated him back to Dayton, but also moved him into the rotation there. Sando thrived, twirling some impressive six-inning outings late in the year, and was again promoted, this time to Double-A. 
Sando is a control-over-command southpaw with a low-three-quarters delivery that helps his fastball play up. He bullies the zone with uphill fastballs and can land both his slider and changeup for strikes, but neither of those pitches is especially nasty. You could consider Sando a swingman candidate for 2027, though it's more likely he winds up as a bullpen's second or third lefty.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Mariano is a switch-hitting middle infielder who draws Ozzie Albies starter kit comparisons from his most ardent proponents. He slashed .336/.466/.580 with more walks than strikeouts in his second DSL season after adding relevant physicality between years one and two. Mariano is built like a wiry defensive back. He's undersized but is definitely bigger than his listed 5-foot-7, 140 pounds, and his gorgeous swing is actualized to get to the modest power he currently has. This isn't a super projectable hitter likely to fit at a premium position (Mariano has experience at several positions, but our sources think second base is his best fit) and grow into big power, but Mariano is a special athlete who worked hard to add meaningful strength, and he's a skilled enough hitter that he might be able to punch above his weight. He's a high priority target on the 2026 Arizona Complex circuit.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Pacheco has had early-career success as a rookie ball starter, with 1.19 WHIP in 62.1 career innings. He throws hard, with his fastball residing in the 93-96 mph range through most of 2025 as he worked four to five innings per start. Pacheco's arm action is explosive, and he generates six-and-a-half feet of extension even though he's only six feet tall. He's been able to throw strikes despite his delivery featuring a good bit of effort, and he's walked just 6.5% of opposing hitters since signing. His arm action (and ability to kill spin) allows for lots of projection on his power changeup, which currently lives in the 86-90 mph range. His breaking ball is a blunt 80-mph curveball that might morph into a harder slider/cutter with time. It'd be easier to project Pacheco as a starter if he were a bigger athlete; it's rare for righties this size to wind up in a big league rotation. But he throws hard, throws strikes, and should have at least one viable secondary weapon at peak (the changeup), which would allow him to be a reliable middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Romero spent four seasons pitching in Cuba, mostly as a reliever, before he left in the hopes of landing a job in the United States. The A’s signed him for $350,000 in February 2017, and once they could get him to the United States that season, he pitched his way up to the California League. He closed for that Stockton team to start 2019 and earned a bump up to Double-A, then leapt to Triple-A in 2019, where he was considered for a callup to bolster the big league bullpen in September. The A’s opted not to recall Romero because they felt he was lacking in some of the intangibles, like holding runners on and fielding his position, that would get exposed at the highest level. Stuff-wise, there’s no question he’s just about ready to get big league hitters out. He can miss bats with both his fastball and his breaking ball. He’ll throw his heater up to 98 mph and is consistently in the 95-98 mph range. He complements it with a breaking ball he calls a slider, but is a bit more slurvy, thrown 86-89 mph with more tilt than a typical slider. Romero has the right mentality for the back end of a bullpen, going right after hitters without any fear. While he did improve his strike-throwing as 2019 went on, he can get out of whack with his delivery, leading to a spike in his walk rate. He’s worked on the little things that held him back and should contribute to the big league bullpen soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $350,000, Labrada made his debut among the Mariners’ Top 30 prospects for the first time in spring 2022 after wowing with his speed the season prior. Though the consensus is that Jonatan Clase might be the fastest player in Seattle’s system, Labrada led all Mariners Minor Leaguers with 32 stolen bases last year over 99 games. At 5-foot-9 and 165 pounds, he may be short in stature but he packs physicality. He possesses a good, compact swing from the left side, but is certainly more of a hit-over-power prospect. With his glove, Labrada profiles in center field given that he has advanced range, great jump, and again, elite speed. After graduating in 2021 from Low-A Modesto to High-A Everett, Labrada saw a dip in offensive production, but not an astronomical one. He still showed decent on-base skills and will continue to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019-20 international signing period might always be known for the addition of Francisco Álvarez for $2.7 million in July. One month later -- after New York added international bonus pool money in a deal that sent Jeurys Familia to Oakland -- the club also picked up Lugo for $475,000 as an infielder out of the Dominican Republic. After a mundane introduction to stateside ball, Lugo broke out offensively in 2022 with Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .261/.347/.427 with 10 homers in 84 games before moving up to High-A Brooklyn, where he was also an above-average hitter with a 115 wRC+ in 28 contests. Lugo’s power is better than his Florida State League numbers indicate as he regularly registered exit velocities above 95 mph. His 41.1 percent hard-hit rate on that circuit was on par with Major League sluggers like Ian Happ and C.J. Cron in 2022, and the 20-year-old -- who stands out for his strength more than bat speed -- may only get stronger from here. Batting from a slightly closed stance, Lugo can sometimes expand the zone, leading to strikeouts in about one-quarter of his plate appearances, and hitting for average likely won’t be a strong suit. At 6-foot-3, Lugo was large for shortstop, even by modern standards, and as a below-average runner, he’s a better fit at third base. He has the arm for that spot, and he has enough pop to provide offensive value away from a premium position. The 20-year-old was Rule 5-eligible this offseason but went unprotected and unpicked as he’s at least two years away from the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olson earned second-team all-Big Ten Conference honors and an invitation to try out for the U.S. national team as a Nebraska sophomore in 2022. He boosted his Draft stock with a strong performance against Michigan in front of a crowd of scouts last April and went in the fourth round, where he signed for a well below-slot $460,000. He made just one brief appearance after turning pro. A finesse left-hander, Olson has his most success when he's in command of his breaking pitches. His mid-70s curveball has a lot of downer break but lacks power and rarely lands in the zone, while his low-80s slider is more reliable in terms of strikes and chases. His fringy low-90s fastball peaks at 95 mph and doesn't miss many bats, and his mid-80s changeup has depth but gets too firm. Olson features a high-three-quarters arm slot and provides consistent strikes with all of his pitches except for his curve. He's physically maxed out at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, so he's unlikely to add significant velocity. He has a decent floor as an end-of-the-rotation starter with little margin for error with his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have a reputation of drafting college players who can get pushed to the big leagues in a hurry, but they broke away from that script when Day 3 of the 2023 Draft commenced. They had some bonus pool money left over to sign Wimmer -- a toolsy but raw high school shortstop from South Carolina -- away from his commitment to The Citadel as their 11th-round pick for close to $400,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games in the Arizona Complex League. It's likely going to require patience for Wimmer to grow into his raw tools. He’s a plus quick-twitch athlete and right-handed hitter who can use the whole field. His swing works and there might be some power to tap into in the future if he can add some strength to his lean frame. An above-average runner, he shows good instincts on the basepaths. While there’s work to be done on his footwork defensively, there’s some confidence he can stick at shortstop in the long run. It’s possible the Angels will move him around the diamond some, but don’t be surprised to see him stick up the middle -- at second or in center field -- if shortstop doesn’t work. He’s a bit like a piece of unmolded clay, one that the Angels can dream on becoming a Rodin.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Candiotti rode the knuckleball to a 16-year career in the Major Leagues. His son, Clark, utilizes a very different arsenal that took him on an interesting ride as a college player. Candiotti played for five schools in five years between St. Mary’s (2020), Vernon (Junior) College (2021), Grayson County Community College (2022), Wichita State (2023) and finally Arizona (2024). He was a Pac-12 All-Conference selection after posting a 3.39 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings with the Wildcats, and that helped push him to Padres with the 135th overall pick in the '24 Draft, where he signed for $80,000. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the look of a durable starter. He added fastball velocity between his time at Wichita State and Arizona, averaging around 93 mph with the latter while touching 96. The heater can feature good carry, eliciting chase above the zone. Candiotti, however, leaned even more heavily on his 83-85 mph slider, throwing it 45 percent of the time and using it against batters from both sides. It has sharp, short movement, allowing him to wear out the gloveside half of the plate. He mixed in a 78-82 mph curveball for a different breaking look and barely used his mid-80s changeup in ’24. Candiotti did a great job of throwing strikes in each of his last two collegiate seasons, but a significant portion of that was getting batters to expand the zone. That ability will be tested against pro bats. There is a certain temptation to throw Candiotti in the bullpen because of his age -- he'll be 24 entering his first full season -- but given his late college trajectory, he could have a fighting chance to stick in future rotations, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Etzel spent a semester at Texas A&M then played two seasons at Panola (Texas) JC, but it was actually a stint in the MLB Draft League that set him up for his professional future. He slashed .371/.463/.586 with 25 steals in 33 games there in 2022, putting himself on scouting radars a year before signing with the Orioles as a 10th-rounder out of Southern Mississippi. Baltimore sent him to the Rays as part of a three-prospect package for starter Zach Eflin in July 2024, then Tampa Bay shipped him to the Marlins for Nick Fortes a year later. Etzel’s performance dipped after a promotion to Double-A and fell off when he joined the Rays, as he batted .232 with a .692 OPS and a 35 percent strikeout rate in 36 games for Montgomery. The swing-and-miss jump was somewhat alarming, as Etzel typically makes a fair amount of contact (especially against fastballs) and already puts a lot of balls on the ground. Granted, he has the speed to make that work and added value by stealing 45 bases over 119 games last year, but it will require him to boost his slugging percentage with doubles and triples, not home runs. Despite his above-average speed, Etzel seems likely to settle in at a corner position. He played all three outfield spots at an almost exactly even rate last year and even saw time at first base in an effort to keep his bat in the lineup. He hasn't made much progress at Double-A this year, a telling sign that probably caps his ceiling as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 While Joswa Lugo received the highest bonus of any player from the Angels’ signing class at the start of the 2024 international signing period, De La Rosa received the most of any pitcher signed by the organization, getting $300,000 to get his pro career started. He did that in the Dominican Summer League and put his best foot forward out of the gate, finishing with a 2.79 ERA, .211 BAA and a 9.9 K/9 rate in a typically hitting-friendly environment. At 6-foot-4, the hope is De La Rosa can develop into an innings-eating workhorse-type starter. His fastball maxes out at 96 mph and typically sits 91-94, though the hope is more velocity will come as he matures. He has a solid 77-82 mph slider that flashes above average and could develop into an out pitch. There’s an upper-80s changeup in there, but it’s too firm and it’s behind the other two offerings. For his first time out, De La Rosa did a decent job of being in and around the strike zone. He’ll be just 18 as he comes stateside for the 2025 season and he’s a long way away, but with improved command and velocity to go along with a solid third pitch, he has a big league starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cohen spent five years at George Washington and was the Colonials' best starter in the final three before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2022. Since missing the first half of the 2024 season with a back strain, he has been one of the most unhittable relievers in the Minors during the past two years, logging a 1.62 ERA and .155 opponent average. Though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft and will compete for a big league bullpen job in 2026. Cohen's money pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that hitters can't lay off or catch up to when it ventures into the strike zone. His fastball is fairly ordinary, ranging from 92-94 mph and reaching 96 with nice carry at times but also below-average command that can make it vulnerable. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink can be a solid offering at it's best. Cohen hides the ball well with an up-tempo, upright delivery with a high leg kick. While his mechanics provide deception, they also hamper his control and have resulted in a 12 percent walk rate in pro ball. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grinsell made a big leap between his sophomore and junior seasons at Oregon, lowering his ERA by a full run and cutting his walk rate in half while becoming just the sixth pitcher in Ducks history to post 200 career strikeouts. While he wasn’t overpowering, his ability to miss bats and his athleticism -- he was a very good two-way player in high school -- led the Tigers to take a sixth-round pick on him in the 2025 Draft and sign him for $297,500. Deception is the name of the game for Grinsell, who doesn’t have a dominant pitch but has a good feel for sequencing and reading hitters. His fastball sits in the low 90s but plays up thanks in part to extension and location. It also sets up an 80 mph changeup that he hides well with a similar delivery. His slider was his third pitch in college. While he fits into the Tigers’ pitching philosophy of commanding the strike zone, he could also add velocity if the club can improve his delivery. Projection can be difficult with a college pitcher, but Grinsell’s athleticism provides some potential for upside if he can find another tick or two on his fastball, which could then make his changeup that much better. He’ll need an effective breaking pitch to make it as a starter, but a good fastball-changeup combination could be the foundation for a potential crafty lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round selection by the A’s in the 2024 MLB Draft out of Boston College, Leary underwhelmed a bit in his first taste of pro ball upon joining the organization. His first full season as a pro went much better, as he began the year at Single-A Stockton and earned a promotion to High-A Lansing, where he held his own over a 33-game stint. Between the two levels, Leary hit .269 with a .798 OPS in 126 games. Leary has above-average power potential which showed up in stints last season, with an ability to hit to all fields after working with the A’s to tighten up his swing. He can draw a decent amount of walks, but his 130 strikeouts last year highlight some swing-and-miss issues that will need to be corrected for him to fully take advantage of that power. Leary might be one of the better baserunners in the entire organization, evident by his 56 stolen bases in ‘25 while getting caught only eight times. Defensively, he can move around well, but his below-average arm likely limits him to left field, though the A’s plan to work with him on his quickening up his release to see if his positional versatility could expand to the other two outfield spots. The A’s are still trying to figure out just what type of player Leary might end up being, but there were some encouraging signs in his first full year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had a compensation pick after the fourth round of the 2025 Draft after losing Max Fried to free agency. They used it to pick up Williams, a middle infielder who was coming off a solid junior season at East Carolina, finishing with 14 homers and an OPS over 1.000 before going 8-for-20 and being named to the all-tournament team at the NCAA Greenville Regional. He signed for just under $500,000, a bit under slot, becoming the earliest-drafted hitter from the Pirates program since Connor Norby was a second-rounder in 2021. Williams brought his solid approach from the left side of the plate with him during his relatively brief 28-game pro debut last summer with Single-A Augusta. He could be an average hitter in the future with solid on-base skills and strike zone control. He drew more walks than strikeouts in his last year of college, part of what helped him get to his power more, with his over-the-fence pop coming mostly to his pull side. His debut with Augusta was solid, but the Braves think the underlying data points to even better contact rates to come. A plus runner who swiped 22 bases in 25 tries last year at East Carolina, Williams could have a potentially intriguing power-speed combination in the future. Where he ends up defensively is still up in the air. He played second and third in college, and his arm might be a tad short for the hot corner. His best bet long term to stick in one spot might be as an offensive-minded player at the keystone. But he’ll likely move around some, with center field one day not out of the question for a more likely utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were two Indiana natives on the World Cup-winning US 18-and-under national team in 2022: Max Clark and Tilly. While Clark went third overall to the Tigers in the 2023 Draft, Tilly was unselected as MLB Pipeline’s No. 208 prospect in the class and headed to Auburn instead. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in his two years in the SEC and sported a 5.48 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 46 innings as a Draft-eligible sophomore last year. The Mets took him in the seventh round and signed him for above slot at $397,500 to keep him from heading back to school. The Mets have early interest in developing Tilly as a starter because of his interesting pitch mix. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph, touching 97, and because of the average velocity, he was willing to go liberally to his secondaries in his final season on campus. Since his amateur days, Tilly has earned praise for the high spin rates on his low-80s slider, and he’s developed his mid-80s splitter into arguably an even better pitch, one with enough dip and movement to cause lefties fits. Tilly also worked in another high-spin curveball in the mid 70s with Auburn but saved it mostly for early counts. Tilly walked 13.4 percent of the batters he faced in his two years at Auburn -- a rate that would keep anyone in the bullpen early in their collegiate career -- but the Mets believe there’s untapped pitchability there, especially if they can tame some of his spinnier options. There’s a good chance Tilly would have gotten starting looks as junior anyways, and now that can happen under the eye of a New York organization that has specialized in pitching development in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a two-sport standout who didn't stop playing football until his senior year of high school. He was on scouts' radars in southern California but headed to pitch at UC Irvine. Although Injuries interrupted his progress over his two first years with the Anteaters, a chance to move into their rotation in March of his junior year allowed him to take off. He landed in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, and while he didn't pitch officially after signing, he got in some good work during instructs. An athletic 6-foot-5 right-hander, Kelly entered pro ball with three pitches and might now have four at his disposal. The Rockies are hoping there might be another tier of velocity to reach with his fastball, which currently sits in the 91-94 mph range, occasionally touching 96. It has some good metrics with some ride and finish to the pitch. But Kelly's really all about the spin. His upper-70s curve has 11-to-5 shape and regularly tops 3,000 rpm, and he can miss bats with his low-80s changeup as well. During instructs, he found a slider grip that works for him, giving him a fourth pitch that could be Major League average. Kelly started throwing better quality strikes when he became a starter during his junior year, and the hope is that trend continues. He has the pitch mix to start and will be given the opportunity to stick in a rotation if he can hold the zone consistently throughout his outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Rosa signed with the Yankees out of the Dominican Republic for $400,000 last April, receiving the third-highest bonus given to any left-hander on the 2025 international market. He quickly stood out with his stuff and strikes during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing immediate trade interest. Three months after he turned pro, the Giants acquired him in a four-prospect package in exchange for Camilo Doval. De la Rosa works with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96 with significant carry as well as armside run. Both of his secondary pitches also show promise. He throws both a tight slider and a sweepier version in the low 80s, and his fading changeup is a tick harder. While De La Rosa has three legitimate pitches and posted a 7 percent walk rate in his first taste of pro ball, there are questions about his ability to remain a starter in the long run. He's undersized and works uphill with some funk in his arm action, though his delivery provides deception without costing him control. If he does land in the bullpen, he has the upside to work in a late-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Pestka was one of a couple Reds' 2023 draft-and-follow prospects who played amateur ball in 2024 before agreeing to a deal with Cincy that May; Petska was committed to Tennessee and would have pitched there in 2025 had he not agreed to a deal. Instead he pitched in Daytona for a second summer and worked 54 innings in 31 relief outings. Petska has a great curveball and good feel for locating his pitches. He isn't a great athlete, but his delivery is easy and repeatable, and he located his fastball consistently in 2025 even though he was throwing two ticks harder than in pro ball the year before. Petska's pure breaking ball quality is the kind commonly seen in big league bullpens. His curveball freezes opposing hitters and is an effective strike-one offering, preceding elevated fastballs. A new cutter rounds out a deep mix of breaking balls that should eventually facilitate a middle relief role. Consider Petska a candidate for accelerated promotion in 2026, as his 40-man platform year is already upon us.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed two of the top infield prospects in the 2016-17 international class with seven-figure bonuses, signing Yasel Antuna ($3.9 million bonus) and Luis Garcia ($1.3 million) as part of a larger haul. They added another promising infielder the following year in Pena, inking the undersized switch-hitter for $150,000. The Dominican native has done nothing but hit since entering Washington’s system and batted .359/.455/.481 over 37 Rookie-level Gulf Coast League games in 2019, making his stateside debut at age 18. Pena’s ability to repeat his swing and barrel the ball from both sides of the plate already ranks among the best in the organization and could help him develop into an above-average hitter in the big leagues. He has a small frame and will never much in the way of home-run power, he does have the bat speed and strength needed to turn around good velocity and is comfortable hitting to all fields. A solid-to-plus runner, Pena’s quickness and speed help him on both sides of the ball. Though he’s seen time at shortstop, second and third base early in his career, Pena’s best long-term fit might be at the keystone based on his size and offensive profile. If it all clicks, he could develop into a scrappy, top-of-the-order catalyst type who wears out pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels drafted McIntosh in the 34th round after he swatted 16 homers as a Motlow State (Tenn.) CC freshman in 2018, but he chose to transfer to West Virginia rather than turn pro. He had modest success with the Mountaineers but performed well in the inaugural year of the MLB Draft League in 2021, landing him a $20,000 bonus from the Marlins as a nondrafted free agent. He quickly has become an organization favorite and spent his first full pro season in Double-A, where he helped Pensacola win the Southern League championship. A right-handed hitter, McIntosh produces some of the best exit velocities in the system and works deep counts in search of pitches he can drive to his pull side. Though he fits the power-over-hit profile, he draws plenty of walks and doesn't strike out excessively. He's surprisingly quick for a catcher, can flash solid run times and displays good instincts on the bases. It may be a stretch for McIntosh to remain behind the plate, however. He earns raves for his leadership and preparation skills, but he's a decent receiver at best, struggles to block balls and has below-average arm strength. He surrendered 97 steals (at an 85 percent success rate) in 67 games last year, and Miami plans on giving him time at first base to get him more at-bats in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCollum spent three seasons at Division II Wingate University, pitching almost entirely out of the bullpen and helping the team win a national championship in 2021. He went undrafted, but signed a free agent contract following the Draft and made his pro debut that summer with full-season Clearwater, recording inconsistent results over nine appearances. A return to the Single-A level in 2022 reaped much better results with a 1.45 ERA and a .111 average-against before a bad ankle sprain ended his season at the end of June. The 6-foot-5 right-hander might end up with three quality pitches. He throws his fastball in the 94-97 mph range with solid carry and offers a hard and short slider. His splitter is a developing third pitch, but there’s a chance it could become an out pitch in time. Command and control have held McCollum back, though. He walked more than seven per nine in college and really struggled during his pro debut. But he’s already improved his ability to find the zone since he signed, dropping that walk rate to 4.6 in 2022 while striking out 15.1 per nine. More strides in that direction could give him the chance to impact a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in May 2018, Rodriguez began his career in the bullpen because of major control issues (51 walks in 50 1/3 innings) during his first two years in the Dominican Summer League. After the lost pandemic season, he moved into the rotation at Single-A Palm Beach and had success with a 3.36 ERA and 88 strikeouts in 69 2/3 innings. His 2022 season in High-A Peoria (4.59 ERA, 119 strikeouts in 121 2/3 frames) was a bumpier ride, but it was notable that he nearly doubled his previous career-high workload. The Cardinals did not add him to the 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in the offseason, and he went unselected in that process. The 6-foot right-hander’s velocity has picked up in recent years as he’s matured and gotten stronger. He can sit 95-96 mph earlier in outings but typically settles in closer to 93-94 as he goes deeper, which makes sense for a pitcher still getting built up as a starter. He’ll showcase a quality mid-80s slider that he can work to either side of the plate while also mixing in an upper-70s curveball offering a slower breaking look. His mid-80s changeup still lacks consistency, and there are the makings of a cutter for another diversified offering. Rodriguez doesn’t have the same control issues he did earlier in his career, but his delivery lacks consistency and can make him to fly open, causing his command to waver. His career might go full circle with a return to the bullpen as a result, which could allow him to open the velo even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed with the Yankees for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022 and was one of several standouts on a prospect-laden team in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. The youngest batting qualifier in the circuit at age 17, he led the FCL with 47 RBI and ranked second with 10 homers. The Marlins acquired him in a three-team trade in March, sending Jon Berti to New York and also receiving outfield prospect Shane Sasaki from the Rays. After looking launch-happy and passive during his 2022 pro debut, Cruz displayed a better approach and more power last year. His quick left-handed stroke produces loud contact when he connects, and he could grow into plus pop if he fills out his projectable frame and adds more polish as a hitter. He controls the strike zone fine for a teenager, but his aggressiveness leads to less-than-ideal contact. Cruz presently has solid speed but is still learning to make the most of it on the bases and in the outfield. He's not an instinctive defender and spent most of his FCL time in right field, where he displays solid arm strength. To make it in center, he'd need to improve his reads and routes while retaining his quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara wasn’t a big-time prospect when the Marlins signed him for just $85,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of their international signing class in January 2023. But his performance as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League caught the Rays’ attention, and they landed him from Miami as part of a three-prospect return for infielder/outfielder Vidal Bruján and reliever Calvin Faucher. This could be the latest in a long line of moves in which the Rays have acquired a young Complex League prospect and watched him take off. Lara, hailing from Bani, has excellent bat speed and a loose, whippy swing from the left side of the plate that allows him to drive the ball well. He had enough skills and polish to perform in his professional debut in the DSL, slashing .305/.416/.445 with 23 walks and 37 strikeouts in 154 plate appearances. He’s skinny, at 6-foot-2 and 165 pounds, but he could develop above-average power as he fills out his frame. Where Lara lands defensively is another question. He started most of his games at shortstop last year, and he has the arm strength to handle the left side of the infield. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that he’ll stick at the six, but if he gets big enough, he might be a better fit at third base and could be athletic enough to handle a spot in the outfield. He’ll likely spend the season at the Rays’ Spring Training complex, first for extended spring camp then in the Florida Complex League. The Rays love his upside, but it’ll be years before his developmental path is totally clear.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2022 international signing class’ Top 50 list included two players from Panama: The first was catcher Adan Sanchez, who got $1.5 million to sign with the Cubs. Pineda stayed in the NL Central as well, as the No. 49 prospect received $800,000 to join the Reds organization. He had a solid, albeit brief, debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and then continued to show some hitterish tendencies in his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2023. A former standout in international youth competition, Pineda is a compact and strong right-handed hitter. He has a good feel to hit with the ability to find the barrel consistently while hitting the ball hard. He hasn’t started finding the seats yet, but he did start tapping into his extra-base authority in the ACL with a bunch of doubles. As he moves along, those could translate to long balls and he could eventually have average power. Pineda is a corner outfielder only because he’s a fringy runner and not overly athletic. His plus arm fits in right field and he’s a capable defender there. Now it’s a question of whether his run-producing capabilities manifest as he matures so he can profile as an everyday guy in that spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez has built a reputation for outstanding bat-to-ball skills ever since his high school days in Georgia. He brought them with him to Georgia Tech, where he hit .332 and had a .932 OPS the spring after finishing second in the Cape Cod League with a .331 average. The skillset intrigued the Pirates enough for them to take him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft and he continued to do his thing, hitting .325 during his pro debut in Bradenton. He quickly made his way from Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while he continued to build on his hit-over-power profile. The left-handed-hitting outfielder has a fairly high floor because of his knack for contact and lack of strikeouts, especially when combined with his plate discipline and willingness to draw walks. What’s lacking thus far has been impact; his exit velocities have been a little light and he’ll need to find a way to add more physicality and drive the ball more without sacrificing his contact skills. Gonzalez is a better baserunner than his average speed would indicate, and those instincts make him a thread on the basepaths. The lack of speed makes it seem unlikely that he can stick in center field, and he’s seen time in all three outfield spots. If he can’t play center, the offensive profile without more extra-base thump is a little tougher, but his feel for hitting gives the chance to perhaps be a fourth or fifth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 NCAA Division II player of the year after batting .408/.506/.901 with a school-record 28 homers at Point Loma Nazarene (Calif.), Christian transferred to San Diego for his Draft year. The Toreros' best power prospect since Kris Bryant, he slashed .364/.460/.828 with 26 homers to win West Coast Conference player of the year honors. He played briefly in Single-A after signing for $397,500 as a fifth-rounder. Christian's 6-foof-5, 225-pound frame gives him tremendous strength and leverage, and his right-handed stroke provides plenty of bat speed and loft. That combination results in well above-average raw power that allows him to smash balls out of any part of the ballpark. He does come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss concerns, especially against non-fastballs, and he struggled to produce with wood bats in college summer leagues. Christian moves well for his size, displaying fringy speed with decent instincts on the bases. After playing first base at Point Loma Nazarene, he moved to right field at San Diego and spent most of his short pro debut in left field. He has adequate range and average arm strength on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery ended Patteson’s 2022 college season early at Central Florida, but the Royals were convinced enough in their scouting of him and his makeup that they still drafted him in the fifth round that year. It took Patteson time to come back from the injury and start to make an impact, but his stuff shot up in 2025. He made 13 starts in High-A with a 1.99 ERA, while holding batters to a .199 average. He finished the year with 11 appearances (eight starts) in Double-A, where he had a 4.41 ERA. Patteson’s fastball hovered around 90-92 mph over the past few years, but once he got to Double-A in ‘25, he started running it up to the mid 90s and touching 97. The velo spike, which was more about a return to his pre-TJ form, also helped his main breaking ball become more firm as a mid-80s average slider that tries to be gyro but can get a little sweepy. Patteson also throws a curveball with good depth and feel to land it for strikes. His best weapon, though, is a mid-80s changeup with plus potential. Patteson throws strikes and has a clean delivery, hiding the ball well with short arm action. Lauded for his pitchability and being a student of the game, Patteson might be a late bloomer but is really coming into his own now that he’s reached the upper levels. He needs to show more consistency at Double-A and continue to refine his secondaries, but if the stuff continues to look like what it did there in ‘25, he has back-end rotation potential. The Royals might try him in the bullpen to see whether the stuff ticks up even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting himself on the Draft radar with three solid years at South Florida, Boser transferred to the University of Florida and boosted his stock as a senior with an impressive season. Entering the 2025 MLB Draft on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list, Boser landed with the A’s as an 11th-round pick. Ahead of his first full season as a pro, he got his feet wet with 32 games at Single-A Stockton. Boser has an intriguing profile as a hitter. He’s got some power to all fields and showed he can do some damage with the bat in college with good bat speed and balance at the plate. There’s also a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, which he’ll have to improve to tap into that power as a pro. Boser fits the mold of a versatile utility player who can provide strong defense at multiple positions that the A’s traditionally value highly, similar to past prospects such as Jeremy Eierman and Max Schueman. He has a good, accurate arm that should allow him to get plenty of reps at shortstop, third base and second base. He also worked to improve his athleticism in college, and that shows through on the bases as a decent runner. There is a solid floor here as a productive super-utility type, and the A’s liked what they saw from him at first glance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly bounced around a bit as an amateur, going from a two-way high school standout in Northern California to starting his college career at Texas A&M. After a redshirt year, he moved to McLennan Community College and played both ways, then was on the move again, this time to Arizona State as a pitcher only. He missed a bunch of bats as a reliever, helping him land in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, and he headed up to High-A to get his feet wet professionally. He capped things off by striking out the side to get the save that gave Everett a Northwest League championship. The 6-foot-4 Kelly is strong and physical and comes at hitters largely with a two-pitch mix and a funky delivery. His four-seam fastball topped out at 99 mph in college, and it misses bats thanks to its carry up in the zone. He backs it up with his 79-84 mph slider that can have good depth and bite to it at times, a breaking ball that could be at least above average if he can find the strike zone with it more. He had a changeup for lefties on occasion at ASU, but he might not need it, and there was some talk of him bringing a two-seamer he used to feature back into his repertoire. Kelly’s unusual mechanics come with a ton of effort and a low three-quarters arm slot and cross-body delivery. But he tends to get down the mound well and throw a decent amount of strikes. If he can be around the zone enough, especially with his slider, it’s not out of the question to see him in high-leverage relief situations in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Girton played three springs at Texas Tech but never found a regular spot in the rotation -- an injury-marred 2022 didn’t help -- and transferred to Oklahoma in '24. Ten of his 16 appearances with the Sooners were starts, but success was still limited with a 7.32 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 31 walks in 35 2/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the 10th round -- two rounds after taking OU teammate Ryan Lambert -- and signed him for below slot at $122,500. Girton dominated High-A Brooklyn in his first full season, posting a 2.59 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 76 1/3 innings, before slowing down in his final four starts with Double-A Binghamton. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches with bounce in his delivery and throws from a high three-quarters slot. His four-seam fastball can move in the mid 90s and acted like a downright weapon with cut-ride action at the top of the zone, getting whiffs on one-third of opponents’ swings against it across both levels in 2025. Girton works with two slider variations -- a mid-80s sweeper with a ton of horizontal break and a tighter upper-80s option that practically acts like a cutter. He has talked about adding a splitter but went to very little offspeed last season. Luckily for him, the sweeper can backfoot lefties well and helped fend off splits issues. Girton really struggled to deliver consistent strikes in school and looked to correct course midseason in ’25, only to struggle again after his move to the Eastern League. He’s already entering his age-24 season and might not have too long of a leash for starting, now that he’s seen the upper Minors, unless the control is ironed out or he finds a split/change. Even so, the fastball/sliders could put him on the fast track to Queens on their own.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing both ways but struggling on the mound as a North Carolina State freshman, Mendoza focused on his bat and his play at third and put together a strong sophomore campaign that he furthered with standout summer in the Cape Cod League. While an inconsistent junior campaign caused him to last until the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, he did rebound to win the New York-Penn League batting title (.370) in his pro debut and then spent most of his first full season in Double-A before reaching Triple-A in the next. Mendoza was a standout at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020. Mendoza has a knack for barreling the baseball from the right side of the plate with a line-drive swing that he controls well. He hits the ball to all fields, showing some extra-base pop but well-below-average over-the-fence power. Mendoza does have some strength, though, and he flashed sneaky power in his first full season. He’s a good athlete and fringy runner who earns high marks for his baserunning. Mendoza is an easy plus defender at third base and has the hands, footwork and arm strength needed to play anywhere on the infield. That includes shortstop, a position the Cardinals deployed him at more consistently with encouraging results in 2020. He also has seen time as a first baseman. Mendoza doesn’t have the power to fit the typical corner-infield offensive profile in the big leagues, but he does hit well enough to serve as a utility infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were certainly bigger names and bigger players than the 5-foot-9 Rivero in the Nationals’ 2018-19 international signing class, and in part because of the 2020 canceled season, it took the shortstop a little longer to prove himself within the system. That opportunity came last summer when Rivero hit .270/.409/.416 with three homers and more walks (19) than strikeouts (17) over 32 games in the Florida Complex League. Rivero was signed in the first place primarily because of his glovework at the premium position of shortstop. He shows exciting fluidity at the six and has looked like a smooth natural at that spot on the diamond ever since he entered pro ball. He gets rid of the ball quickly with a good arm too, giving him multiple ways to impact the game defensively. What earned Rivero his spot on this list, however, was his offensive improvements. He thrives on making a good amount of contact, and the Nationals have been enthused by how well he’s protected the plate at this early stage. The bat doesn’t come with much power, however, and for all Rivero’s defensive strengths, he isn’t much more than an average runner underway. Good, if light, hitters that are also no-doubt shortstops tend to find their ways onto Major League rosters. Rivero’s fit of that profile will be tested when he sees full-season ball for the first time in 2022, just before he becomes Rule 5-eligible in the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Ueckert logged a 6.17 ERA as a 23-year-old McNeese State senior in 2019, his arm strength intrigued the Cubs enough for them to sign him for $5,000 in the 27th round. He didn't get past Rookie ball in his pro debut and lost a year of development to the pandemic shutdown, so he began 2021 as an almost-25-year-old in High-A. He finished it in Double-A with a combined 1.45 ERA and 37 strikeouts in 31 innings between the two stops and turned himself into a legitimate prospect. Opponents batted just .129/.228/.238 against Ueckert, who took to some mechanical changes and came back from his layoff with dramatically improved stuff. His fastball gained 3-4 mph and now sits at 95-97 mph and reaches 99 with good carry in the zone. He backs it up with a short slider that often climbs into the low 90s and ties up both left-handers and right-handers. Ueckert has gotten stronger and has cleaned up his delivery since signing, which gave a boost to not only his stuff but also his control. He cut his walk rate from 5.7 per nine innings in two years at McNeese State to 4.6 in his debut to 3.5 last season. If he can build off his momentum from 2021, he could pitch in the big leagues this year and develop into a late-inning reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Blanco is a gigantic corner outfield/1B prospect with arguably the most present raw power in the January 2022 signing group. He absolutely towers over his father, who was twice a Baseball America Top 100 prospect but spent most of his pro career in Japan. The recent track record of hitters this size is not favorable, with only Franmil Reyes really panning out, but it's exciting to watch Blanco take BP and see how loose and athletic he is for his size. He signed for $900,000 and will be an unmistakable fixture on Pittsburgh's backfields for the next couple of years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trying to prove that a local kid can make good, Tolve went from the Georgia high school ranks to Kennesaw State for college. He parlayed a solid 2021 season (.319/.393/.498) to get drafted by his hometown Braves in Round 17 of the 2021 Draft. He showed off some interesting tools during a solid first full season with High-A Rome in 2022, but his climb to Double-A in 2023 was interrupted by a quad strain that limited him to just 50 games. He made up for some lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s healthy, Tolve has been an athletic left-handed hitting catcher, a demographic that’s often in high demand. He is capable of making loud contact, though there’s too much swing-and-miss in his game. He did improve his strikeout rate a bit in 2023 (27.2 percent, compared to 32 percent in 2022), and he will draw some walks. There’s raw extra-base pop there if he can be a bit more consistent in finding the barrel at the plate Tolve runs very well, especially for a catcher, and he’s been athletic enough to play other positions in the past. His agility is an asset as a backstop; he’s a solid receiver with good arm strength. If he can continue to refine his approach at the upper levels, he could be a solid big league backup in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of inconsistent work at the University of Maryland, Staine transferred to Central Florida for the chance to have a more certain role. While a minor back issue and a blister slowed him down some, his ability to pitch well -- mostly as the Knights’ Friday night starter -- allowed him to land in the fifth round with the Rockies. While he didn’t pitch competitively after signing, he did make a good impression with the club's player development staff during instructs. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a loose arm and some athleticism on the mound, Staine has four pitches that give him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 93 mph and touches 96 and it features good ride to it, which plays well at the top of the zone when he needs it to. His low-80s slider should be an average breaking ball, and he has a slower curve he can land early in counts. He’ll flash a decent changeup, but will need to commit to it more after not throwing it much in college. More than anything, the Rockies love how Staine goes right after hitters with a repeatable up-tempo delivery. He’ll need to refine his command to remain a starter long term, but the organization feels like he has the mentality to develop into a guy who can navigate through a lineup multiple times and be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brailer Guerrero was the big name in the Rays’ 2023 international signing class, but they may have landed another player to watch in Monzon. The infielder from La Guaira, Venezuela, was signed for $300,000 by Rays scouts Marlon Roche and William Bergolla. Initially viewed as a defensive-oriented shortstop who could also make contact at the plate, he immediately performed well in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old and jumped onto the prospect radar. Monzon is one of the Rays’ best young players coming out of the DSL, and his .281/.395/.421 batting line reflects some of the things he does well. His hit tool stands out ahead of his power, which is more gap to gap at this point, but he controls the strike zone well from the left side of the plate and he ultimately had more walks (35) than strikeouts (30) in 205 plate appearances during his 46-game professional debut. Considering he was signed as a glove-first prospect, it’s an especially interesting offensive profile for someone his age -- but he’s obviously yet to be tested by even Florida Complex League pitching. Monzon played 25 games at shortstop, 10 at third base and nine at second last season. He’s a shortstop for at least the short term, with above-average actions, solid instincts in the field and enough arm to hold down the spot. The question is more about how he grows physically, as he bulked up quickly to 6-foot and 160 pounds with some projection remaining on his frame. If he gets bigger, it’s more an issue of lateral quickness and whether he’s better suited for one of the other infield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez reached a deal with the A’s for $800,000 during the 2022 international signing period, a figure that was only topped among the club’s agreements that year by outfielder Carlos Pacheco, who signed for $1.2 million. After playing 44 games in the Dominican Summer League last year, his second summer there, he should make his United States debut in 2024. Gonzalez has outstanding bat-to-ball skills and an overall advanced approach at the plate. He has been described as hitterish in the box with an ability to drive the ball to all fields, and his power should show up more as he grows into his 6-foot-2 frame. Though young, he does seem to already be drawing his fair share of walks while also limiting the strikeout totals. While Gonzalez is considered more of a bat-first catcher, the A’s have been pleased with his defensive skills thus far, though there is certainly room for improvement behind the plate. He has an above-average arm and should stick as a backstop, but the A’s also will get him some time at first base this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia, a cousin of Wilmer Flores (both the Giants infielder and the Tigers pitching prospect), joined the Mets system out of Venezuela in June 2021 and made it to full-season ball last year with mixed results. His 5.04 ERA in 80 1/3 innings between Single-A St. Lucie and High-A Brooklyn didn’t quite pop, but he did strike out 106 batters in that span. His 31.9 percent K rate in the Florida State League ranked third among the 46 pitchers on the circuit with at least 60 frames. The 6-foot right-hander throws a 92-94 mph two-seam fastball (topping out at 96.7) out of a low slot that lower-level batters just found difficult to pick up, leading to a strong whiff rate and some weak contact. He primarily paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that gave him an option with good gloveside break as compared to the armside movement of the two-seamer. He showed the occasional low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup too, but he understands which pitch is his bread and butter. Garcia walked 14.6 percent of batters faced between those two levels. That’s a slight improvement from 15.6 percent in 2022 but an example of why many believe he’ll remain in a relief role. He’ll still only be 21 years old as he heads back to the High-A level, and there are some in the organization who believe he’s on the precipice of a breakout as he continues to rack up K’s and finetune his command with more stateside experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed a then 17-year-old Aquino for only $16,000 out of the Dominican Republic on the first day of the 2021 international period and have seen him steadily climb the ranks one level a year since. After stints on the Dominican and Arizona Complex circuits, the right-hander posted a 2.75 ERA and 1.26 WHIP with 86 strikeouts over 88 1/3 frames for Single-A Carolina this summer. That inning output more than doubled his total from 2021 and '22 combined (78 1/3), so Milwaukee officials found it particularly promising that Aquino was still growing into himself toward the end of his age-20 campaign. Aquino shows largely average fastball velocity around 92-94 mph but can crank it up as high as 96 at times. His low-80s slider is his best pitch with impressive two-plane movement that can drive his whiff rate. Despite averaging less than a K per inning, his 14.5 swinging-strike percentage was ninth-best among 29 Carolina Leaguers with at least 80 innings in 2023. The vertical drop, in particular, can make the breaker look closer to a curveball at times, but it’s still effective. Aquino’s mid-80s changeup remains behind the other two offerings, and without a quality third pitch, lefties batted .288 with a .381 OBP off the hurler in 2023. The 6-foot righty found the zone with better regularity as the season wore on, walking only five batters in his final six outings (27 IP). More disciplined upper-level hitters could hold off chasing the diving sliders out of the zone, pushing that walk rate back up in years to come, but the improvements at least help Aquino’s odds of starting for now. Even so, his best chance of being an impact Major Leaguer might be as a two-pitch reliever who leans into his best tools in shorter appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merejo was born in Florida and grew up there before moving to the Dominican Republic late in his high school career and signing for $340,000 in 2023. He followed up a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League by coming to the United States at age 18 last year. After beginning the season in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he concluded it by batting .282/.372/.466 in the final month Single-A as one of the Carolina League's youngest players. Unlike most of the Guardians' international signings, Merejo stands out more for his power than his hitting ability. His physicality and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke produce plus raw pop, and he taps into most of it by concentrating on driving balls in the air to his pull side too. He has some feel to hit and is willing to take walks, though he'll have to tone down his approach because it leaves him vulnerable to non-fastballs. Most of Merejo's value will come from his bat. Though he stole 11 bases in 77 games last year, he's a below-average runner who's probably limited to first base. He committed 10 errors in 53 starts there in 2024 while also getting time on the outfield corners, where he displayed solid arm strength but substandard range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barnett headed to Division II Wingate as a two-way player before exploding offensively as a junior in 2024. His 26 homers were second-most for that level of collegiate baseball, while his .739 slugging percentage placed 32nd among qualifiers. He posted a .349 average and 1.138 OPS over his 59 games with the Bulldogs while also making six appearances out of the bullpen, striking out seven and walking six over five frames. The Padres took him in the 11th round in the '24 Draft and signed him for $175,000 ($25,000 of which counted toward their bonus pool). Barnett only hit and played corner outfield with Single-A Lake Elsinore after joining the organization, but he pitched in late workouts and turned more than a few heads on the mound. He ran his fastball up to 97 and averaged closer to the mid-90s. His slider sat in the upper-80s with a hard cutter-like break, and that pitch could easily be a weapon, too. The ball comes out of his 6-foot-2 frame easily, and his delivery isn’t overcomplicated. With his position-player background and athleticism, he could get to average control with the right professional instruction. As much as many in the organization prefer Barnett’s work on the mound, the Padres will still give him a chance to DH part-time to begin his first full season. His power is undeniable from the right side, but he really struggled against non-fastballs in the California League last year. Had Barnett shown this level of stuff more consistently, some believe he would have gone several rounds earlier as a pitcher alone, and that’s likely where his future lies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hipwell played just 76 games in three seasons at Santa Clara and had little experience with wood bats in summer ball, so he was tougher to evaluate than most collegians in the 2024 Draft. He lost the final three weeks of his sophomore year and the first two months of his junior season to a suspension for performance-enhancing drugs, which he attributed to an over-the-counter supplement. Signed for $345,700 as a sixth-rounder, he batted .196/.360/.402 with five homers and 40 strikeouts in his 29-game pro debut in Single-A. Hipwell is built to hit for a power with a quick left-handed stroke with loft, a strong 6-foot-3 frame and a pull-focused mindset.
