He broke the hamate bone in his left hand during his first full season and hurt his right shoulder diving for a flyball in his second, but he finally stayed healthy in 2021 before joining the Cubs along with righty pitching prospect Daniel Palencia in a July trade for Andrew Chafin. Deichmann's best attribute is his considerable raw power from the left side of the plate, which he generates with bat speed and strength. After batting .232 in his first three years as a pro and leading the Arizona Fall League with nine homers in 23 games after the 2019 season, he has employed a more selective approach in Triple-A this year. He's making more contact and drawing more walks but also homered just four times in 60 games before the deal, and he's no longer clearly a power-over-hit guy. Though he possesses fringy speed, Deichmann has good instincts on the bases and will swipe bags if the defense forgets about him. An infielder in his first two college seasons, he has developed into an average defender on the outfield corners. His solid arm strength plays well in right field.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: It’s easy to draw unflattering conclusions from Deichmann’s age, but it’s important to take into account the fluky bad luck that muddied the first several years of his development. He was hit in the face by a pitch in 2017 and required surgery, endured a broken hamate in ’18 and a shoulder injury in ’19, and then there was the pandemic. Now, at 26, Deichmann’s primary draw is still his raw power, which is undeniable, but the only real in-game glimpse of it came when he hit nine home runs in 23 games during the 2019 Arizona Fall League. He started 2021 with the A’s Triple-A affiliate, and while his on base percentage ballooned thanks to his patience at the plate — he walked 19.2% of the time during his Vegas stint — he only sent four home runs out of the notoriously hitter-friendly ballpark over the course of 60 games. He was traded to the Cubs near the deadline as part of the Andrew Chafin deal, and shortly thereafter was called upon to fill in for an injured Jason Heyward on the big-league roster. He spent the rest of season up and down between Triple-A and the majors, with his numbers just shy of league average in his games in Iowa, and nothing short of atrocious in the big leagues, though the sample was tiny. He'll need to reharness the OBP he flashed in early 2021, or finally tap into his power, before he can be considered a viable everyday corner outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's a rift between Deichmann's obvious raw power and his in-game power production. He hit nearly as many home runs during his six-week 2019 Fall League stint as he did during his entire season that year at Double-A Midland, where his statline may have been compromised by an injured shoulder. It was the latest of several weird injuries that have limited Deichmann's playing time. He was hit in the face by a pitch in 2017 and required surgery, then broke a hamate in '18, the shoulder in '19, and then there was the pandemic. We're still talking about a 26-year-old corner outfielder who has struck out in excess of 30% of the time at his last couple stops, and that's scary, but Deichmann crushes righties and is pretty likely to play some sort of part-time role, at least. His walk rates exploded early in 2021 and it only took him a couple of weeks to accumulate nearly as many walks as he did in all of '19. This may be a small sample blip or an indication of a change that could enable Deichmann to fit in as more than just a corner platoon bat, but he's most likely that.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Peacock has a heavy, low-90s sinker (he was 92-94 for me in the Fall) that enabled him to generate a 68% groundball rate in 2019. His slider has a 2800 rpm spin rate and is hard at 86-89, but visual evaluations of that pitch put it closer to average. His changeup moves and tails; at times it's plus, at others it's easy to identify out of his hand due to altered release/arm speed. On one level, Peacock is a one-pitch 25-year-old, but on another, he has a dominant, grounder-inducing fastball and his secondaries have some characteristics that may just need to be refined for one or both of them to be effective. He projects as an middle reliever. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A native of Newcastle, Australia, Wells has a chance to become the third Orioles player to hail from Down Under after signing for $300,000 in August 2015. He’s risen steadily through their system since, his only hiccup coming due to no fault of his own in 2020, which he spent almost entirely in Australia due to the coronavirus pandemic. Wells was the organization’s Minor League Pitcher of the Year in 2017, a SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game selection in 2018, and went 8-6 with a 2.95 ERA and 1.07 WHIP at Double-A Bowie in 2019 before turning heads with a stellar showing in the Arizona Fall League. The Orioles added Wells to the 40-man roster in November, hinting at a potential 2021 debut. With three quality pitches and plus control, Wells succeeds despite a fastball that used to live in the upper 80s, though it consistently clocked in at 90-91 mph late in ’19. His above-average changeup is an equalizer and he pairs it with an improving 12-to-6 curveball that helps keep hitters off balance. Both play up due to Wells’ ability to throw them for strikes to both sides of the plate, and he’s added a serviceable slider to use predominatly against right-handed hitters. Plus-command allows Wells to limit free passes and keep the ball in the ballpark; he’s averaged 1.4 walks-per-nine in over 475 career innings and allowed just 10 homers across 153 innings in 2019. While he will never miss many bats, Wells’ ability to spot three distinct pitches gives him a high floor that should translate to a back-end starter or swingman at the very least. Some believe he has a chance to exceed those projections and potentially become a mid-rotation starter in the Majors.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: How good does a pitcher's secondary stuff and command need to be to succeed in today's game with an upper-80s fastball? We may be about to find out. Baltimore's rebuild should give Wells an opportunity to perform six innings' worth of surgery every fifth day. His fastball only sits 87-89 mph but it has plus-plus vertical movement and Wells locates it up and to his glove side with remarkable consistency. His most-used secondary pitch is a cartoonish, low-70s curveball, which wreaks havoc on hitters' timing and balance, often making them look like basketball players trying not to commit a lane violation. His slider is more typical-looking (in the 78-80 mph area), while Wells' changeup is entirely reliant on his command. All of these pitches live in areas where they're either tough to hit or not hittable at all, allowing for fifth starter projection despite below-average stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: How good does one's secondary stuff and command need to be to succeed in today's game with an upper-80s fastball? We may be about to find out. Baltimore's rebuild should give Wells an opportunity to perform six innings' worth of surgery every fifth day. His fastball only sits 87-89 but it has plus-plus vertical movement. This is also a lefty with a good changeup, and those tend to outperform projections. If Wells can find a breaking ball (his slow curveball has some utility, and he has a newly-developed slider), then he'll pitch toward the back of a rotation for a long time. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player as a Virginia high schooler, Lee went to the Royals in the third round in 2016 and became strictly a position player. Pre-pandemic, he was moved aggressively up the system due to his speed (stealing as many as 53 bags at Double-A in 2019) and strong on-base skills. After Lee was added to the 40-man roster in November 2020, Kansas City traded him three months later to the Mets as part of a three-team deal that brought in Andrew Benintendi from the Red Sox. Lee was a statistical Triple-A standout in Syracuse, leading full-season qualifiers with a .451 OBP while finishing with 14 homers and a .951 OPS in 23 games. He was used for an 11-game Major League cameo in May but went 1-for-18 with 13 strikeouts. As his 18.3 percent walk rate indicated in 2021, Lee can be patient at the plate, but that borders too much on passivity. He did get more aggressive as the season wore on and will need that to continue to make the most of his offensive potential. The left-handed slugger has always shown above-average raw power. A high ground-ball rate blunts that slugging potential, and while some gains were made in that department last year, he still hit the ball on the ground 51.5 percent of the time. Lee’s above-average speed and plus arm (dating back to his pitching days) give him defensive assets, and he profiles best in right field, where he spent most of last season. The 5-foot-10 prospect isn’t far from his floor as a bench outfield bat, and he’ll need to continue his improvements on aggression and launch angle to have a chance at being a Major League fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee was a third-round pick by the Royals in 2016 after a stellar two-way showing out of a Virginia high school. Kansas City kept him as a position player only and moved Lee aggressively up the chain, including an assignment to Double-A in 2019 when he opened the season at just 20 years old. Lee held his own with a 112 wRC+ in that campaign but stood out most for his 53 stolen bases, which ranked second in the entire Minors behind only then-fellow Royal Nick Heath’s 60. Lee was added to the 40-man last November and was traded to the Mets three months later in a three-team involving the Red Sox and Andrew Benintendi. Lee is no stranger to two of three true outcomes, having struck out in 28.2 percent and walked in 11.9 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A. That balances out the offensive profile. He loses a few points as well for hitting the ball primarily on the ground with a 59.3 percent ground-ball rate that led the Texas League in 2019. That keeps him from playing into what could be above-average power. As such, elevation was a key focus during his time at the Royals’ alternate training site last year, and it deserves watching whether he can reverse that trend when he returns to play. The other tools are the standouts of the profile right now. Lee showed in 2019 that he can steal bags by the dozens, and that speed gives him a good shot at sticking in center. The arm is even better than the glove and is a true plus tool, so if some route-running issues push him to a corner, he can still help any club defensively. The Mets inserted themselves into the Kansas City-Boston trade in order to pick up Lee, so they were obvious admirers of the outfielder’s skill set. However after a few games with the Major League club in the first half of 2021, Lee has been overlooked while positing an impressive on-base percentage and overall OPS at Triple-A Syracuse. This remains his age-23 season, and after establishing a little more consistency at Triple-A, he could still very well carve out a role as a fourth outfielder in the Majors down the line.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Lee was a two-way high schooler with more of a leadoff skill set until he got yoked as a senior and showed up to pro ball with surprising power. He had four years of statistical success while with Kansas City, but his in-game power output has come down as he's climbed the minors. He was part of the Andrew Benintendi three-team deal, ended up with the Mets, and has had spare big league reps over the last two years amid continued strikeout struggles. He is still a power-over-hit type of prospect who takes giant hacks, often falling to one knee as he finishes. His big, long, uppercut swing and huge bat speed generate considerable raw power but also lead to lots of strikeouts, and he can really only impact pitches in the bottom of the strike zone. He has the tools of a Three True Outcomes platoon right fielder, one who potentially plays above-average corner outfield defense thanks to his speed, but there's K-related bust risk here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Lee was a two-way high schooler with more of a leadoff skillset until he got yoked as a senior and showed up to the AZL with surprising power. He had four years of statistical success while with Kansas City but his in-game power output has come down as he's climbed. During Lee's 2019 season at Double-A, he hit .264/.363/.372 with a 12% walk rate and a whopping 53 steals. Then Lee spent 2020 at the Royals' alternate site and went to play winter ball in Puerto Rico for the second consecutive offseason. He didn't hit well there but did look pretty good in center field. In February, Lee was part of the Andrew Benintendi three-team deal and ended up with the Mets. He wasn't as good during his few defensive opportunities this spring and, as he always has, Lee continues to strike out a lot. He is a power-over-hit type of prospect who takes giant hacks, often falling to one knee as he finishes. His big, long, uppercut swing and huge bat speed generate considerable raw power but also lead to lots of strikeouts, and he can really only lift pitches in the bottom of the strike zone. He has the tools of a three true outcomes right fielder, one who potentially plays above-average corner outfield defense. Maybe some of this is due to how intense his swings are, but I get 40-grade run times on Lee from home to first, and I don't see him stealing a ton of bases or playing center field in the big leagues. The quality of his at-bats against elite competition has been mixed, at best. It's likely going to take a swing adjustment to get Lee hitting for relevant power in games. I think he could be the larger half of a corner platoon if either more of that pop shows up in games or Lee's approach eventually enables him to make more contact. (Alternate site, Puerto Rican Winter League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida, Welker was a fourth-round pick back in 2016 and the Rockies went about $300,000 over slot to sign the infielder. He didn’t hit below .329 over his first three summers of pro ball, establishing self as one of the better pure hitters in the Minors. A shoulder injury didn’t help him with a move to Double-A in 2019, though he did earn a spot on the 40-man roster following the shortened 2020 season. He served an 80-game suspension in 2021 for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, returning late and making his big league debut last September. At his best, Welker still shows off the skills of a very gifted hitter. Even when he’s struggled, he’s shown a willingness to work counts and draw walks, keeping his strikeout rate relatively low. He has a knack for contact and can drive the ball to all fields, showing an aptitude for making adjustments during an at-bat. There is raw power to tap into, but he’s struggled when he’s tried to sell out for power and would be better suited just letting it come naturally from his right-handed swing. While Welker has solid hands and a strong arm that work at third, his lack of speed might mean first base is a better home long-term. Either corner puts pressure on his bat and he’ll have to be more consistently productive to profile well as a regular at either corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The best player to come out of Stoneman Douglas High School to date has been Anthony Rizzo, who was a sixth-round pick in the 2007 Draft. Thirteen years later, Jesus Luzardo was a third-round pick and the most recent alum to make the big leagues. Welker was part of that same 2016 Draft, going a round later than his lefty teammate. For much of his Minor League career, he lived up to his offensive potential, hitting .337 over his first two-plus years of pro ball. He hit a wall, and dealt with a shoulder injury, after a hot start in Double-A in 2019, then struggled in the Arizona Fall League. Still believing in his bat, the Rockies added him to the 40-man roster following the 2020 season, though Walker was given an 80-game suspension after testing positive for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone (DHCMT), a performance-enhancing substance, in May. Still just 23 years old for the 2021 season, there’s plenty of time for Welker to rediscover the swing and approach that made him look like a future plus hitter from the right side of the plate. When he’s in sync, he combines his knowledge of the strike zone with his ability to drive the ball to all fields. He’s willing to draw walks and doesn’t strike out a ton, even when he struggled in 2019. He gets into trouble when he gets out of his game plan and tries to hit for power, rather than let it come naturally. While Welker doesn’t run well, he has the tools to play a solid third base, with good hands and enough arm for the hot corner. He started seeing more time at first base in 2019 because of his lack of speed and, of course, Nolan Arenado. The latter is gone, but Welker should still get reps at both infield corners, once he returns from his suspension.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Welker served an 80-game suspension for Dehydrochlormethyltestosterone at the start of the season, returning in July for about a month of Triple-A reps and an eventual September call-up. He's another prospect with a water-carrying hit tool in this system, as Welker has beautiful feel for all-fields contact and covers the whole strike zone. He has a well-balanced, long, slow leg kick and is great at diving and hitting pitches away from him the other way. He stays inside the baseball and works center and right/center field most of the time, only really turning on hanging breaking balls with pull power. Welker also lacks anything even approaching the typical raw power for a corner infield prospect, and he's highly unlikely to be an average everyday player because of this. He can, however, play an integral corner role because of the amount of contact he makes. From a hands and actions standpoint, Welker is actually fine at third base, it's his lateral quickness and range that's at issue. There are teams that care more about that than others, but Welker's size at his age puts him in an area at risk of earlier athletic decline, so he might only be a viable third baseman early on in his big league career. Elehuris Montero is a version of this fringe 3B/1B part time profile with more power.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: From a hands and actions standpoint, Welker is actually fine at third base. It's his lateral quickness that's an issue, and why he's generally considered a first base prospect. But same as we've seen Travis Shaw and Max Muncy play elsewhere, it stands to reason someone out there thinks Welker can stay at third, or handle duties around the second base bag in certain situations. Those are the teams most likely to think he can play something resembling an everyday role, because while he has excellent feel to hit, he lacks the raw power typical of first base. Though he's not especially athletic, Welker's swing is. He's a loose rotator with a well-balanced, long, slow leg kick and he's really great at diving and hitting pitches away from him the other way. He stays inside the baseball and works center and right/center field most of the time, only really turning on hanging breaking balls with pull power. I like his bat enough to consider him a role-playing corner bat but the power/defensive spectrum shortcomings leave him short of a more regular role. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jones both started and relieved at Washington State, with very mixed results, but the Phillies felt his size, raw stuff and left-handedness was worth a flier in the 18th round of the 2017 Draft. After pitching out of the pen during his pro debut that summer, Jones had two fairly successful seasons starting, touching Triple-A in 2019. After being added to the 40-man roster in 2020, he moved back to a relief role in 2021 and made his big league debut before a very strong turn in the Arizona Fall League. The 6-foot-5 lefty has the stuff to get big league hitters out; it’s just a question of landing that stuff in the strike zone enough to do so. His fastball easily touches 95-96 mph and averaged around 94 in 2021 and it often has cutting action to it, leading to solid groundball ratios throughout his career. He’s thrown both a curve and slider in the past, but he focused on the slider especially in the AFL with good results, with the chance for it to be a true out pitch. He’s also had a changeup in his repertoire, but he may not need it as a reliever. That’s the role he’s going to have from now on as his walk rate spiked in 2021. He threw better strikes in the AFL, though he still walked 6.1 per nine in a small sample. With his swing-and-miss stuff (11.3 K/9 in his career in the Minors), he doesn’t need pinpoint command to play a role in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2021 The 2017 Draft has already produced some late-round big leaguers, like Cardinals’ 27th-rounder Kodi Whitley and Angels 30th-rounder Jeremy Beasley, a list that also includes Phillies’ 10th-rounder Connor Brogdon. Jones, a Phillies flier taken in the 18th round that June, is about ready to join them after a 2019 season that saw him pitch his way to Triple-A and a 2020 that included time at the Phillies’ alternate training site and a spot on the 40-man roster. Jones typically uses three pitches, all of which can get outs. It starts with a fastball that’s up to 96 mph with natural cut to it, a pitch that has gotten a groundball percentage well over 50 percent. He misses bats, 12 of them per nine innings in 2019, with a plus curve and a slider that’s above-average. He does have a below-average changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much at this point. That, combined with command issues, he’s walked 4.6 per nine innings, means the 6-foot-5 lefty’s future is very likely in a bullpen. The good news is the combination of that lively fastball and his array of breaking stuff could allow him to play a significant role if he can find the strike zone a bit more consistently.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Jones is a lumbering lefty who creates a unique angle with his delivery that allows his fastball to play above its mid-90s velocity. Given his troubling command and limited repertoire, it was no surprise when he was moved to a bullpen role in 2021. He was up and down several times during the season without appearing, and finally had a brief major-league debut in August, facing three batters and recording an out, a hit, and a walk before exiting the game. If he can locate his slider to his glove side consistently (he did in 2019), he'll be a middle-inning bullpen piece, but his current control puts him more in the up/down bucket. Of the many wild upper-level relievers the Phillies have had over the last few years, Jones is the only homegrown one to make the 40-man roster.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Jones found a better slider in 2019 and went from a lefty with average stuff to one with an out pitch. His fastball command is not good and not only relegates him to the bullpen, but might make him volatile in that role. He sat 91-94 and touched 96 as a starter in 2019 and his velocity remained the same at last year's alt site, though the heater plays above its velocity because of its angle and carry. He only worked with two pitches at the alt site so expect him to be put in a bullpen role in 2021. If he can locate his slider to his glove side consistently (he did in 2019), then he'll be a bullpen weapon. He's one of several lefties competing for a 2021 spot, though he's likely to be up and down this year. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his college days, Dohy lived up to the “have left arm, will travel” adage, attending three schools in three years. The Phillies took Dohy, a starter at Division II Cal Poly in 2017, in the 16th round in that June’s Draft and immediately put him in the bullpen with good results. The lefty reliever made it to Double-A in his first full season and up to Triple-A in 2019, though he didn’t pitch particularly well there. Though he didn’t pitch at the alternate training site or in instructional league play, the Phillies still decided to protect his left arm on the 40-man roster this past offseason. The 6-foot-2 lefty brings an intriguing combination of deception and stuff to a future big league bullpen. There’s funk in his delivery, making it hard for hitters to pick the ball up, contributing to his 13.8 strikeout per nine rate in his career heading into 2021. He’s typically topped out in the mid-90s, but was up to 98-99 mph on Rapsodo during offseason workouts. It remains to be seen if those are real velocity gains. He has one of the best changeups in the system, with good separation from his fastball and thrown with excellent deception. At times, his slider is a wipeout pitch, though it’s less consistent. Dohy has shown the ability to miss bats with all three pitches. What he hasn’t been able to do is find the strike zone consistently enough. He’s walked 7.0 batters per nine innings, which will keep him from having any lasting impact in the big leagues. If he can find the strike zone a bit more frequently, his stuff is more than good enough to be a reliever at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A plus changeup and mid-90s velo spearhead an option years trial relief profile for Dohy, whose excellent stuff is undercut by his poor control. This sort of stuff is still somewhat new for the lefty, who experienced a velo bump upon his move to the bullpen and has had his breaking ball overhauled (it's still not great). He's on the 40-man and part of a crowded group of southpaws fighting for a spot in a magmatic bullpen. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers selected the Puerto Rican backstop out of Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy with the 75th overall pick in 2016. His breakout campaign came in 2019, when he was named Carolina League MVP after hitting .270/.323/.473 with 19 homers for High-A Carolina. He followed that up with a strong showing at the alternate training site a year later. Milwaukee added Feliciano to its 40-man roster in November 2020, but 2021 was a rough season for him. Feliciano, who appeared in one Major League game in May, missed nearly two months with a right shoulder impingement and hit just .210/.246/.314 (46 wRC+) over 114 plate appearances with Triple-A Nashville. A trip to the Arizona Fall League (.318/.348/.432) helped end the year on a brighter note. Ever since he was drafted, Feliciano has used his bat to raise his prospect profile. He utilizes a compact right-handed swing to drive the ball with authority, and he has the above-average raw power to threaten for 15-20 homers over a full Major League season. Among reasons for optimism in 2021, his strikeout rate did drop a touch at Triple-A, but he isn’t the most cautious swinger with just a 3.5 percent walk rate. Feliciano’s shoulder troubles weren’t a first last season -- he also needed arthroscopic surgery in the 2018-19 offseason -- and it’s becoming a concern whether his injury history will affect his ability to stay behind the plate. At his best, he’s an agile catcher with above-average arm strength, and the Brewers are optimistic he can get back to that level. He needs consistent reps to find that form, and those should come in his second 40-man season in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have not hit big drafting and developing catchers. The last home-grown catcher to represent them at an All-Star Game was Jonathan Lucroy in 2014 and ‘16. Before that, it was Dave Nilsson in 1999, but Nilsson was already an established pro in Australia before he signed with the Brewers. But now the Brewers have a relatively deep crop of backstops led by Feliciano, the No. 75 overall pick in the 2016 Draft. After nagging injuries ruined his 2018, including a shoulder flare-up in the Arizona Fall League that required arthroscopic surgery in the offseason, Feliciano got back on track during a breakout 2019 at the advanced Class A level; he was Carolina League MVP after leading the circuit in home runs (19), RBIs (81), slugging (.477) and total bases (210) at age 20, and he was added to the 40-man roster this past offseason. Feliciano’s strength is his bat. His clean and compact right-handed swing yields consistently hard contact as well as above-average game power that plays from the left-center gap to the right-field line. There is great potential for more if Feliciano can bring down his 28.8 percent strikeout rate from 2019 and cut down one of the Minors’ highest swinging-strike rates (19.7 percent). Defensively, Feliciano has enough tools to be a catcher long-term, particularly his arm. He’ll be a bat-first guy, but should be able to stick behind the plate at the highest level. A shoulder impingement has limited both his production and game experience in 2021, but the Brewers are still believers that Feliciano can be a productive catcher when fully healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: While we're sympathetic to the notion that catching in the Fall League is one of the more difficult jobs in the sport (since you're at the end of a long season and suddenly have to learn a huge, totally new staff), Feliciano looked unplayable back there during the 2021 AFL season and we think it's time to move on from him as a catching prospect. His combination of bat-to-ball skills and power once made Feliciano an enticing, high-ceiling prospect, but he's not likely to play any sort of role unless he can catch since his approach and resulting OBP output have him short of profiling at 1B/DH. Having made little to no progress as a defender, and after having put very little performance on paper due to persistent injury, Feliciano is a change-of-scenery flier at this point.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text:
Feliciano is one of the more talented offensive catching prospects in the minors thanks to a potent combination of power and barrel feel. When he puts balls in play, they're very often scorched -- just under 50% of the balls he hit in 2019 entered play at 95 mph or above, which is a 65 on the 20-80 scale if you curve out big leaguers' hard hit rates. All of that seems likely to be hampered by Feliciano's hedonistic approach. The dude likes to swing, and has only walked at a 6% clip as a pro. 
Feliciano is the sort of catcher who will benefit from an automated strike zone turning the position into a pass/fail endeavor, as he is a well below-average receiver and framer, but does pass back there. Ball-blocking is an issue here, though Feliciano currently spends most of his time on one knee, and does so even in some situations with runners on base, which might leave him more vulnerable to pitches in the dirt now than it will if one-knee catching goes away as soon as pitch framing stops being a thing. Feliciano has also missed two seasons due to some combination of injury (most recently a lingering shoulder issue to start 2021) and the pandemic, so maybe pieces of this will still develop. His arm (I have him popping in the 1.96 to 2.05 range with mixed accuracy) is fine. In many ways Feliciano's profile is similar to Francisco Mejía's, without that incredible hit streak and elite arm. Mejía has an amazing hit/power combination that's undercut by a poor approach, and if he can't catch (he's still not very good), then he's a low-OBP LF/DH and that's a very tough profile. There's risk that Feliciano's defensive profile bottoms out entirely and I expect he'll have some big league misadventures on defense for a while even if it doesn't. But Feliciano is so talented a hitter that his right tail outcome includes making an All-Star team or two, and he's likely to get myriad opportunities to seize a sizable role. Players like this tend to have some fat years and some lean ones; some of that is inherent with the catcher position. This is where I value a near-ready player of this ilk.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bettinger was more of a reliever than a starter during his four years at the University of Virginia, and he worked exclusively out of the bullpen as a senior in 2017. The Brewers still liked this strike-throwing ability enough to select him in the 10th round and transition him into a starting role. Early results were inconsistent until Bettinger’s breakout season for Double-A Biloxi in 2019, when he finished second in the Southern League with 1.07 WHIP and 157 strikeouts in 146 1/3 innings. The Brewers added the former Cavalier to the 40-man roster in November 2020, and he was solid at Triple-A Nashville last year with a 4.75 ERA, 98 strikeouts and 26 walks in 96 2/3 innings. He made four appearances (one start) for the Brewers in the first half of the 2021 season but is still seeking consistent Major League success. The Virginia native doesn’t boast a true plus pitch as part of his arsenal, but he makes the most of a deep pitch mix. His heater averaged 91.5 mph in the Majors last season, and he’s typically right around that 89-92 mph velocity range. The pitch plays up with some deception out of Bettinger’s 6-foot-2 frame, aided by decent extension toward home plate. He adds in a mid-70s curveball with good break and an upper-80s cutter that works well off the fastball and can be effective against either hitters on either side of the plate. A low-80s changeup remains below average. Bettinger, who turns 27 in July, is yet to walk more than 7 percent of his batters faced at any full-season level, including Triple-A and the Majors, where his BB rates were below 6.3 percent. He will still get starting looks because of that control, but he might be most effective soon as a long reliever for Milwaukee.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round pick in 2017 who signed for $10,000 after a strong senior season as a long reliever at Virginia, Bettinger was moved into a starting role upon entering pro ball and has surged to the brink of the big leagues thanks to his penchant for throwing strikes. He struggled in his first full season in ‘18, recording a 5.45 ERA between the two Class A levels, but the Brewers still decided to push the right-hander up to Double-A Biloxi in 2019. After Bettinger got off to another shaky start, he pitched increasingly well and showed more velocity as the season unfolded, putting him on the organization’s prospect map. He finished among Southern League leaders in starts (T1st, 26), strikeouts (2nd, 157), WHIP (2nd, 1.07), innings (2nd, 146 1/3), opponent average (4th, .223) and ERA (6th, 3.44). The Brewers added Bettinger to the 40-man roster in November 2020 and president of baseball operations David Stearns predicted he would contribute at the big league level in 2021. That proved prescient when Bettinger made his Major League debut back in May. Though Bettinger has always featured some deception with crossfire action in his delivery, he found a new level of effectiveness in Double-A thanks an uptick in velocity. With Biloxi, the right-hander was touching 94-95 mph with his fastball early in games and sitting in the low 90s consistently, and that continued in 2020 at the Brewers’ alternate training site. He throws two different breaking balls -- a curveball that flashes above average and a slider with cutter-like action that plays nicely off his fastball. A changeup gives Bettinger a usable fourth pitch. He knows how to mix his pitches and throws a lot of strikes, showing above-average control and solid command. Bettinger could become a back-end starter, though most evaluators believe he will end up pitching as a multi-inning long reliever. That’s a valuable role for a Brewers team known for using the full 40-man roster and blending the lines between starters and relievers.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A 2017 senior sign reliever coming out of Virginia, Bettinger experienced a velo bump in his second pro season and also developed better movement separation between his curveball and slider, which has enabled both of them to play better. He still only sits 89-92 and experienced a significant drop in his fastball spin rate compared to 2019 per our sourced data, but Bettinger still managed a 24% strikeout rate and 6% walk rate against Triple-A hitters in 2021. He had a rough couple of big league outings amid an otherwise fine season in the minors. Bettinger's heater plays because he gets way, way down the mound and generates about seven feet of extension, helping to create a flatter approach angle, which causes his heater to jump on hitters. He also has a power pitcher's style of curveball, with power downward movement generating swings and misses even though it's a 74 mph pitch. We consider him a high-probability spot starter type.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A senior sign reliever coming out of Virginia, Bettinger experienced a velo bump in his second pro season and also developed better movement separation between his curveball and slider, which has enabled both of them to play better. He still only sits 89-92 but he gets way, way down the mound and generates about seven feet of extension, causing his heater to jump on hitters and create flatter approach angle. His fastball is also spin-efficient and has plus vertical movement. Bettinger is older and he's struggled in his one spot start and two relief appearances in 2021. In those outings, his fastball spin rates are roughly 300 rpm below the data I sourced from the 2019 minor leagues. I still think he finds a way to settle in as a fifth/sixth starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondón signed for only $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016 and needed two-and-a-half seasons before jumping to full-season ball. His breakout came in 2019 when he was named Cardinals Minor League Pitcher of the Year, having posted a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts in 160 innings between High-A and Double-A. He moved to Triple-A for his age-23 season and put up more pedestrian numbers (4.58 ERA, 68 strikeouts in 76 2/3 innings), but he did make his Major League debut with a pair of relief outings in June. The 6-foot-1 right-hander averaged 93.1 mph on his heater in those brief MLB looks, and that’s around where his fastball was in the Minors as well. He can touch the mid-90s when needed, and the fastball plays up because of some natural deception and late movement. Rondón pitches a bit backward with much better splits against lefties than righties (.223 average-against vs. .329, respectively, at Triple-A) in part because of a low-80s fading changeup. His slider and curveball can flash average with the former looking slightly better than the latter at this stage, but both have suboptimal spin rates and can hang a bit too much, leading to the punishment from fellow righties. To Rondón’s credit, he did improve his control rates in 2021, dropping it from 8.9 percent in 2019 to 6.5 percent. He also deserves plaudits for working with a four-pitch mix that he can sequence well, keeping hitters off even when the raw stuff doesn’t stand out. His pitchability makes him a potential No. 5 starter, and entering his age-24 season, he isn’t far from reaching that role. A focus on just one breaking ball to go with the fastball-changeup could also work in a bullpen setting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rondon’s career got off to a bit of a slow start after he signed with the Cardinals as an 18-year-old for $25,000 in 2016. The native of the Dominican Republic spent two seasons in Rookie ball before he started to rise up the ranks. Rondon reached full-season ball in the second half of the 2018 campaign and followed up the strong showing with an award-winning 2019. He began the year with Class A Advanced Palm Beach, where he was named a midseason All-Star before being promoted to Double-A Springfield and ultimately named the Cardinals’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year after posting a 2.93 ERA with 159 strikeouts over 160 innings split between the two levels. The 2021 season got off to a rough start as Rondon was hit hard and struggled in his first Triple-A experience, though he did make a couple of scoreless appearances in the Majors. Rondon impressed at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020, facing advanced hitters and showing a good understanding of how to sequence pitches. His delivery creates natural deception, which often helps his fastball play above its velocity. The fastball features late movement and sits in the mid 90s, but can also touch 97 mph on occasion. Rondon can vary the shape of his curveball, a pitch with heavy downward action that reminds some of a slider. He’s also shown an ability to keep hitters off-balance with an average changeup. The right-hander needs to improve his command and control, but he has shown he’s capable of handling a starter’s workload. The 2021 numbers have been a bit of a disappointment, but it’s important to remember he’s still just 23-years-old. Rondon’s ceiling seems to be at the back end of a rotation, though his fastball/curveball combo, paired with his pitchability, could also play well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McClanahan spurned the Mets as a 26th-rounder in 2015 and honored his commitment to South Florida, only to have his freshman year wiped out by Tommy John surgery. He emerged as one of more interesting pitching prospects in the 2018 Draft as a junior by ranking second in the nation in strikeouts per nine innings (14.2), though a regression in command cost him some traction late in the spring. He still became a first-round pick in June, going to the Rays with the No. 31 overall pick, and received a slightly above-slot bonus of $2,230,100. McClanahan impressed during his brief pro debut, making four scoreless starts during which he fanned 13 and allowed three hits across seven innings. McClanahan's Draft stock took off early last spring with reports of the left-hander's fastball reaching 100 mph. It set an unfair standard for his future outings, and some teams were turned off when he failed to achieve the same elite velocity in subsequent starts. That being said, McClanahan does throw exceptionally hard, as he'll sit 92-95 mph and reach back for a few extra ticks. McClanahan's slider, though inconsistent, is an above-average pitch and complements his heater nicely, and scouts believe that his upper-80s changeup will be at least average once he develops better feel. McClanahan's high strikeout rate in college came with a high walk rate. That, plus a delivery that features a fairly big recoil, has led some evaluators to project him as a future reliever -- albeit one who could get to the big leagues in a hurry. But with a loose and very athletic frame, McClanahan might be able to get away with those mechanics, and the Rays are committed to developing him as a starter.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Throughout his late high school and early college careers (the latter of which was paused by a Tommy John), McClanahan's stuff climbed from the mid-80s to the mid-90s. In the first start of his draft year, he hit 100 mph and flashed above average secondary stuff, which put him among the draft's top prospects right out of the gate. But things started to unravel from there. A finger injury, bad weather, fluctuating stuff, frustrating control, and questions about his maturity all contributed to a draft-day tumble to pick No. 31 and the hometown Rays. A year later, those concerns seemed trite. A more consistent, balanced delivery enabled McClanahan to throw more strikes and he absolutely carved A-ball. He got especially hot over a nine-game stretch at Hi-A, where he walked just eight over 49 innings. He ended up with 154 K in 120.2 innings, and reached Double-A. Then, after he had pitched at the alternate site all year, the Rays decided to foist McClanahan onto their playoff roster, and he made his big league debut in the playoffs. It did not go well, with McClanahan giving up a lot of really hard contact, but everyone got to see how hard he throws and how nasty his breaking stuff can be. I still have McClanahan evaluated as a power reliever. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Top 100
mlb_pipeline.text: Crochet rated as Mississippi's best prep pitching prospect in 2017 but wasn't quite ready for pro ball or particularly signable, so he fell to the Brewers in the 34th round. He bounced between Tennessee's rotation and bullpen in his first two college seasons, earning the Volunteers' first NCAA tournament victory since 2005 last June -- just two weeks after a line drive fractured and dislocated his jaw. He was sensational in fall practice, vaulting him into top-10-pick consideration, but missed three weeks as a precaution with soreness in his shoulder and made just one appearance during the truncated 2020 season. After working with a 91-95 mph fastball and topping out at 97 during the spring, Crochet dealt at 96-100 for most of the fall, and his heater already played better than its velocity because it has high spin rates. His 82-85 mph slider features above-average spin rates as well and his long arms create difficult angle on his breaking ball. He flashes a well above-average changeup at times, throwing it around 90 mph with deceptive arm speed. For a 6-foot-6 pitcher, Crochet does a nice job of keeping his long levers in sync and providing strikes. Scouts like his delivery and arm action, though he still needs to refine his command to make the most of his overpowering stuff. His short track record with his improved arsenal is a concern, but he still could surpass R.A. Dickey (18th overall, 1996) as the highest-drafted Volunteers pitcher ever.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Crochet spent most of his college career in the bullpen, making just one pre-draft start in 2020 after missing the first few weeks of the college season with what the Volunteers claimed was shoulder soreness. (Major league teams were skeptical of that explanation and thought his absence had to do with an off-the-field matter.) In that lone appearance this spring, Crochet threw 3.1 innings and was absolutely electric, touching 99 with his fastball while flashing a 70-grade slider. How teams valued him leading up to the draft (the relief risk, the injury or makeup issues) was highly variable. Their confidence seemed to be determined by who in the org had seen him and when (many teams weren't able to get a decision-maker to see him in person in 2020), but those that focused on his pitch data, which was shared among all the teams, thought he had among the best raw stuff in the entire draft class and was one of the few pitchers available who might pitch at the top of a rotation or in the back of a bullpen. Crochet was also among the high-octane college pitchers thought capable of going straight to the big leagues in a relief role, something more broadly considered by clubs due to the structure of the 2020 player pool. Out of Burl Carraway, Clayton Beeter, etc., only Crochet actually did. After he tuned up at the alternate site for about two months, Crochet was added to the 40-man and sent to the big leagues in mid-September. He pitched six innings in five relief appearances, walked no one (though he was pretty wild if you put on the tape), allowed just three hits and no runs, and struck out eight big leaguers. He made the White Sox playoff roster but left his first career postseason outing with a flexor strain, which ended his season. He's healthy now, training and throwing at the team's complex in Arizona. Because he barely threw in 2020, he's likely to be on a strict innings limit in 2021. The club is going to try to thread the needle here and use Crochet in a relief role while still trying to develop him as a long-term starter. Players in this situation tend to wind up in the bullpen, and that's where I have Crochet projected based on his strike-throwing limitations, independent of his shortened developmental timeline. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Murphy, now 25, endured myriad severe injuries dating back to high school and missed large swaths of time during his minor league career. Then in 2019, he was forced to remake his delivery when, as he was on the precipice of the big leagues, the Umpire's Association ruled it to be illegal. His front leg would kick up, then come all the way back down and briefly make contact with the mound again before he'd stride toward home. Murphy's performance fell apart as he tried to make an adjustment that would satisfy the somewhat officious ruling, and he had some really rough starts in the middle of 2019 before getting hurt again toward the end of the year. Then there was a pandemic, which you may know. Healthy and working with a legal delivery during the summer of 2020, Murphy finally made his big league debut. He threw six innings across four relief appearances, and worked 94-98 and touched 99 with his fastball (which has sinker movement). His curveball is average, and Murphy throws lots of strikes. Of the group of major league-ready up/down relief types in this system, Murphy is the most consistent strike-thrower, and the least-likely to have a nuclear outing. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: After the Red Sox asked him to take a mechanical detour early in 2018, Houck's arm slot migrated south again, back to where it lived when he was an electric college starter. He finally made his big league debut in 2020 and worked with a two-seamer, four-seamer and slider across three starts, with his fastballs sitting in the 90-96 mph range. Some folks in baseball think he'll be a Justin Masterson-style starter, and perhaps he'll be put in that role as the Sox rebuild, but on a competitive team, I have Houck projected in a multi-inning relief role, and think his velo could climb to the top of that 90-96 band and touch above it in shorter outings. He started working with a splitter last year, and it showed glimpses of bat-missing bottom at the alternate site (he barely used it in major league games). If that pitches develops, then he'll just be able to start, long-term. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third-round pick by Minnesota in 2015, Blankenhorn didn't progress as quickly as hoped but did make his big league debut last September and doubled in his lone start. He had trouble finding a defensive home with the Twins, who designated him for assignment this May soon after he made a critical error in an extra-innings loss to the Athletics. He made brief stops with the Dodgers and Mariners as part of the waiver-wire merry-go-round before landing with the Mets on June 1. Blankenhorn has a chance to hit for average and power from the left side of the plate, and he set a career high with 19 homers in his last full season in 2019 after he started turning on more pitches. While his bat-to-ball skills allow him to make enough contact, his aggressive approach limits his ability to draw walks and get the most out of his solid raw pop. He has the upside of a .270 hitter with 20 homers per year if he receives regular at-bats. The biggest question is where Blankenhorn fits on the diamond with his fringy speed and hands and average arm strength. The Twins used him primarily at second and third base, but those positions seem to be a stretch at the big league level. They started giving him more time in left field in 2019 and that ultimately may be his best option, though he really profiles best as an offensive-minded utilityman.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Blankenhorn played in one big league game in 2020 but otherwise spent the year at the alternate site, so his report is the same. He's a situational bat-first piece who might need a change of scenery to carve out the sort of bench role I think he's capable of playing. He's had some injury stuff and isn't very mobile, but Blankenhorn now has a track record of hitting up through Double-A. He makes consistent, hard contact but without a lot of lift. You want to hide this guy at second base or left field and let him mash. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 The seventh overall pick in the 2016 Draft, Garrett signed for $4,145,900, but blew out his elbow in his fourth pro start and required Tommy John surgery in June 2017. He returned to the mound 22 months later and has spent parts of the past two seasons with the Marlins, logging a 5.18 ERA while winning two of his nine starts. He once had the ceiling of a mid-rotation starter, but his stuff has backed up as he has shuttled between Triple-A and Miami. Scouts rated Garrett's curveball as one of the best in the 2016 high school class, but it wasn't as powerful or sharp as usual in 2021, when it sat around 75-79 mph. He had more success last year with his recently added slider, which operates at 83-85 mph with sweep and drop, and he shows feel for backfooting it against right-handers. He utilizes two- and four-seam fastballs, which usually range from 88-91 mph and feature ordinary life, while his mid-80s changeup has some fade but not enough velocity separation from his heaters. Garrett has a history of throwing strikes but has nibbled around the zone in the Majors, where hitters have teed off on his diminished stuff. The hope is that he can find a better rhythm if he stops bouncing back and forth from Triple-A and reclaim the solid fastball and plus curveball he featured in the past. If not, he's probably looking at a future as a reliever who relies on his breaking pitches to survive.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The third-highest drafted Alabama high schooler ever, Garrett went seventh overall in 2016 and signed for $4,145,900. He blew out his elbow in his fourth pro start and had Tommy John surgery in June 2017, costing him all of the following season. He made a strong return to the mound in 2019 and debuted in the big leagues last September with two brief starts. Garrett has regained what scouts considered one of the best curveballs in the 2016 prep class, a low-80s bender with quality depth that's effective against both lefties and righties. His fastball is more notable for his command and downhill angle than velocity or life, and it parked around 89 mph during his brief stint in the Majors after sitting at 90-93 and topping out at 96 the year before. His fading changeup projects as a solid third offering as he continues to use it more often. Garrett has nice feel for locating his pitches and sequencing them to set up hitters. After big leaguers teed off on his diminished fastball, he'll need to find more consistent velocity in order to reach his ceiling of a mid-rotation starter. The hope is that his heater will bounce back with more regular work in 2021.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Garrett, who recently exhausted rookie eligibility, still looks like a generic fifth starter (89-92 mph, touching 93, plus slider, command-reliant changeup), but his velocity has slowly been climbing, year after year, since he returned from Tommy John. He's throwing harder for the second straight season, and Garrett has had to sharpen his command to deal with the reduced velocity he experienced coming off TJ (he was in the mid-90s as a high schooler). If he can somehow continue to throw harder, then he'll come close to hitting his pre-draft projections, or at least peaking there. It's not likely, but it is plausible. Until then, he's a crafty, fun-to-watch backend lefty.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Garrett made his big league debut last year and now projects as a fifth starter. He has a short, repeatable arm action and wields four vanilla pitches; his fastball has settled into the 91-93 range over the last couple of years. His slider and changeup are both pretty hard for a guy who only throws about 92, with each routinely sitting in the 83-86 mph range. His best chance of missing bats comes via a well-located curveball, and Garrett does a great job of living just beneath the zone to his glove side with it. He's a lower-variance fifth starter prospect likely to play a depth role in the big leagues this year. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Nelson had been a strike-throwing lefty relief prospect with Cleveland but struggled uncharacteristically with walks in 2021 amid a drastic reduction in his workload (he threw just 25 innings) and spin rates. The Diamondbacks claimed him off of waivers from the Guardians after the season, and he figures to get an up/down relief opportunity with the Snakes in 2022; he could stick in Phoenix with a bounce back. Nelson hides the ball really well, typically goes right at hitters, his fastball once had very high spin for a pitch at its velocity, and he has a nasty, downward-breaking slider that he throws about half the time. He also developed an upper-80s cutter that, at least as far as our looks are concerned, is relatively new.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros made a haul early in the 2015 Draft, taking future big leaguers Alex Bregman and Kyle Tucker within the top five picks before selecting Cameron at No. 37 overall and signing him for $4 million. Viewed as someone who might need extra time to develop in the Minors, Cameron was overmatched in his first taste of full-season ball in 2016, and he also struggled at the outset of 2017 before things started to click. He was finishing off a fantastic second half in the Midwest League when the Astros packaged him with Franklin Perez and Jake Rogers to the Tigers for Justin Verlander. He began to put it all together in 2018, ascending from high Class A to Triple-A at age 21 before a standout turn in the Arizona Fall League. The son of former big league center fielder Mike Cameron, Daz has the chance to be an impactful up-the-middle big leaguer as well. Mechanical changes that put him in a better position to hit made a huge difference and contributed directly to his turnaround at the plate. Perhaps more importantly, Cameron has developed a real approach at the plate, showing selective aggressiveness with a hit-to-all fields mentality early in the count. He's started to tap into some power, too, and some scouts believe he'll be a 15-20-homer guy in the big leagues. A plus runner and overall graceful athlete, Cameron can steal a base but will have to learn to be more efficient in the future. That speed to go along with plus defensive instincts will allow him to stay in center for the long haul, and he has the arm strength needed for an outfield corner. Cameron's ceiling is still coming into focus, but all the pieces are there for him to develop into an everyday center fielder at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Coming off his worst statistical season as a pro, Cameron needed a bounce-back campaign, but instead we had the bizarre cadence of 2020. Cameron was at the alternate site, at one point hit the COVID IL, and had a tough 59 plate appearances in the big leagues during a September look. His above-average speed (Daz covers ground in center and runs well underway, but he takes a while getting out of the box and ran a lot of 4.4s home to first in 2020) plays better in center thanks to excellent reads and jumps, and his arm is average if not a tick above. He can flash average power at times, but his best offensive trait as a pro has been an advanced knowledge of the strike zone. While he draws his fair share of walks, he has also accumulated disturbingly high strikeout totals, with some pointing to a hitch-driven, scoopy swing. Because of his skillbase (fine in center, strike zone feel, some power) Daz still has a shot to end up producing like a 45 or 50 if he can simply outhit where we currently have him projected. If not, then he's more like a traditional fourth outfielder. (Alternate site, MLB, Puerto Rican Winter League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Schmidt had Tommy John surgery a month before the 2017 Draft, the Yankees believed in his talent enough to select him 16th overall, allowing them to sign him for a below-slot $2,184,300 bonus and invest more in later picks. He arrived in New York in September 2020 with just 114 innings of pro experience but has battled his command in brief big league trials the last two years. Expected to contend for a rotation spot last spring, he instead strained his elbow and didn't return until late July. Schmidt's velocity was down a bit in 2021, but when at his best he'll range from 92-97 mph with his two- and four-seam fastballs, creating heavy sink on the former and cut and carry on the latter. His secondary pitches did a much better job of dodging bats than his fastball did last season, led by a low-80s curveball with power and depth. He also dusted off an upper-80s slider/cutter that he had shelved for a while, and both it and a tumbling changeup with similar velocity can be plus offerings when they're on. Schmidt has the quality arsenal to help the Yankees as a starter, but he'll have to refine his command to make an impact. He has a history of throwing strikes, but his command has never been as sharp as his control, and he has struggled to keep big leaguers from pounding his fastball. He doesn't have an especially athletic delivery and must prove he can handle a full workload after elbow issues cropped up in 2019 and 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Schmidt had Tommy John surgery a month before the 2017 Draft but still went in the first round, signing for a below-slot $2,184,300 as the 16th overall pick. The Yankees didn't really turn him loose until 2019, when he looked better than ever down the stretch while leading Trenton to the Double-A Eastern League championship. He continued to shine in Spring Training, Summer Camp and at New York's alternate training site last year, and he made his big league debut in September with just 114 innings of pro experience. Schmidt employs both two- and four-seam fastballs that range from 92-97 mph with heavy sink on the former and cut and carry on the latter. His curveball took a step forward after he scrapped a promising slider to focus on one breaking ball, and it's now his best pitch, a power bender that sits at 82-85 mph with high spin rates and quality depth. He also has a tumbling changeup that grades as plus at its best. Though Schmidt has a history of throwing strikes, his command isn't as strong as his control and he got knocked around in his brief introduction to the Majors when he fell behind in the count too often. His delivery isn't the smoothest but does provide some deception. His lack of size and his mechanics led to concerns about his durability prior to his Tommy John surgery, and he missed a month in 2019 with minor elbow inflammation before getting sidelined again this spring with an elbow strain.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Schmidt looked primed for a big role on the major league squad in 2021, but a spring training elbow strain lingered well into the summer, delaying his return to the mound until late July and limiting his time in the big leagues to just a couple of appearances at the end of the season. It’s hard to know if Schmidt was ever fully healthy last season, as his stuff was below what he had shown in previous years. His two- and four-seam fastballs sat between 92-94 mph and were generally two ticks under the range he had normally shown in the past. His best pitch remains a low-80s curveball with strong, late bite, but he’s also brought an upper-80s slider back into his arsenal and it’s nearly as effective an offering. His changeup is firm but moves well. Schmidt’s injury history (he had Tommy John surgery in 2017) and lunging, unathletic delivery have many wondering if he’d just be better off as a reliever, despite his deep repertoire. The Yankees, meanwhile, are just hoping his stuff can rebound to its previous level before they spend too much time considering his future role.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Schmidt's breaking ball spin rates in 2020 were about 300 rpm higher than what I had on record from him in 2019 and he also threw substantially harder, though that might be because he was deployed in a couple of relief outings and a short start. He works with what amounts to four different pitches: a high-spin two-seamer that he works to his arm side, a four-seamer that he locates up and to his glove side, a nasty two-plane breaking ball, and a changeup. It's a slam dunk starter's repertoire in a vacuum, but Schmidt has one of the longer, gnarlier arm actions in baseball and already has one surgery under his belt. He also shows pretty significant release variation depending on pitch type, with his breaking balls coming from a lower, wider point while his fastballs, especially the four-seamer, comes from a vertical one. All of his release points viewed at once look more like a crescent rather than one tight, circular cluster. It's possible hitters will be able to pick up on this, but it's also possible Schmidt hides the ball so well that they won't. It's something we'll just have to learn by watching big leaguers face him.  The confluence of arm action length, release variance and injury history all create substantial relief risk here, but even if Schmidt ends up in a role of that sort, I think his repertoire depth will enable him to either close or work in a valuable multi-inning role. (Update: Schmidt has an elbow injury that will keep him out almost all of 2021, with a September return hopeful)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2017-18 international signing class, García got $2.5 million to sign with the Phillies and almost immediately set out to prove he was worth it, making his pro debut stateside and winning the Gulf Coast League batting title in 2018. His move to full-season ball in 2019 was a disaster offensively and then he missed out on a year of at-bats due to the shutdown. He did use 2020 to add strength and that started showing when he repeated Low-A, putting up better numbers all around and earning a late bump up to High-A and a 40-man roster addition in the offseason. His offensive struggles returned in 2022, however, and the Tigers claimed him on waivers from the Phils in September. A switch-hitting shortstop, García really started to find his swing in 2021, especially in the power department, more than doubling his career total with 13 homers for the season. That added strength has led to better bat speed and increased exit velocities from both sides and his improved approach -- his walk rate increased significantly and his strikeout rate dropped compared to 2019 -- allowed him to get to his raw power more consistently. Even with the increased physicality, García still looks every bit like an everyday shortstop defensively. He’ll need to continue to watch his conditioning, but he has excellent actions and a plus arm from the premium position. He’s continued to get reps at second and with there being enough confidence in his future as a middle infielder, he still has time to turn himself into a bench option in the Detroit system. García only turns 22 in October.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2017-18 international signing period opened, Garcia was the third highest-ranked shortstop, behind only current No. 1 overall prospect Wander Franco and Jelfry Marte, who joined Franco with the Rays. Garcia’s $2.5-million bonus was actually higher than the top prospect in that period, Shohei Ohtani, and early on, he looked ready to provide plenty of return that investment when he won the Gulf Coast League batting title during his pro debut in 2018. He wasn’t ready for the push to full-season ball in 2019, but used the shutdown time to increase strength and he performed very well at instructs last fall. After focusing on strength and conditioning to go along with footwork and agility, Garcia showed up to instructs looking a lot different than the player who posted a .516 OPS in Low A in 2019. The at-bats from both sides of the plate were much improved, with increased bat speed and better exit velocity as he continues to refine his overall approach and recognize spin better. Garcia has shown the ability to play a solid shortstop with a strong arm and enough range to stay there long-term. He continued to get reps at second to increase his versatility and took strides toward making the pivot from that side of the infield. The Phillies are still very bullish on him as a future starting middle infielder, one who will be just 20 for all of the 2021 season.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: It was hard to know what to expect from García heading into the 2021 campaign. His impressive small sample of Rookie Ball production (he won the GCL batting title in 2018 at age 17) was followed up by a horrendous 2019 at Low-A, during which he posted a wRC+ of just 55. After the lost 2020 season, a 20-year-old García returned to Low-A and his on-paper production resurged, with his walk rate showing especially marked improvement (caveats related to automated balls and strikes apply). It was enough for the Phillies to put García on their 40-man, a move almost certainly made solely to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft, as García is still too green to project for 2022 big league impact. While he has gotten strong enough to handle full-season pitching, he needs to continue if he's going to hit big leaguers. At barely 21, that's feasible for García, who lacks typical projection but looks stocky and strong everywhere but in his arms. The main feature here is still García's terrific defensive actions, which are a middle infield lock. His build allows his swing to be practically compact even though it's long, which enables him to check a lot of boxes we like: switch-hitting, short-levered, above-average rate of contact, middle infield profile. Those things alone allow for lots of on-roster utility. As García goes from big-bonus teenager to upper-level college-aged player, his ultimate ceiling is coming into greater focus, and increasingly it's looking like that of a good utility guy.

fangraphs.label: 2021graduates
fangraphs.text: Of the many hard-throwing young 20-somethings who occupied the thick middle of this list a few years ago, Garcia is the one whose touch-and-feel command really emerged. He's now a lock to remain a starter and will likely play an integral role in Houston's rotation going forward. During the course of a start, he'll typically sit in the 90-94 range and touch as high as 96 while working an awful lot to his glove side with the heater and his two very distinct breaking balls. Both Garcia's slider/cutter and curveball are average, though his slider has a little more lateral movement than it did in 2020, so maybe that pitch is above now. It's his tailing mid-80s changeup that has the nastiest action, and the best chance to finish big league hitters. Garcia was a 32% strikeout, 11% walk rate guy in the minors, including his most recent full season in 2019, the only time in his pro career he's exceeded 100 innings. He no longer looks like the sort of pitcher who'll produce peripherals like that over a full season and I'd expect both of those rate stats to fall. The lack of a short- and long-term workload track record and the leap Garcia might be asked to make in a rotation coming off a short 2020 create some extra volatility here, but Garcia's arm action is so loose and his lower half is so robust and strong that it might be less of an issue for him than it would be for others. He projects as a big-league ready No. 4/5 starter who'll produce in the 1.5 to 2 WAR range. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Garcia went from 2018 stat-stuffer to 2019 full-season flop, albeit as an 18-year-old who the org just pushed too fast (though guys like Andres Gimenez and Washington's Luis Garcia recently handled their aggressive promotions). Then we had no 2020 Low-A sequel season by which to evaluate Garcia's progress; instead, all we have is his Instructional League look, which was very glove-centric. Indeed, Garcia is an excellent young defensive shortstop but doesn't have clear everyday offensive ability. He may still grow into requisite strength but we're not talking about a traditionally projectable 6-foot-2 frame here, as Garcia's a shorter, stockier guy. He's starting to track more like a high-probability utility infielder. If he ends up a regular, it'll be because his feel for contact drives his offensive profile, and as a young switch-hitter with some barrel variability, I think that's possible. We'll just need to see some on-field production to project that sort of outcome. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Weigel bounced around to three different colleges as an amateur and after a solid junior season pitching in relief at the University of Houston, the Braves made him their seventh-round pick in 2015. Given a chance to start, the big right-hander had reached Triple-A and was just about knocking on the big league door when he needed Tommy John surgery. He did return at the very end of the summer in 2018 and participated in instructional league play, then shook off the rust to pitch his way back to Triple-A in 2019 and got called up to Atlanta for the first time in July, though he didn't appear in a game during his first stint in the big leagues. Weigel pitches at 93-94 mph as a starter but showed the ability to get 97-98 mph on occasion, and could pitch there consistently in shorter stints should the Braves ever put him back in the bullpen. He does have two distinct breaking balls, and he'll go back and forth depending on which one he has a better feel for. It might behoove him to focus on one, with the slider the leading candidate, if he returns to relieving. His changeup does give him an option against left-handed hitters. Now healthy, Weigel is once again ready to impact the big league staff. He could serve as a back end starter, but it might be exciting to see how his already-good stuff plays up as a short reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Weigel has been on the Braves 40-man for a couple of seasons but hasn't made much of an impact with the big league club because he's struggled to rein in his command. Weigel has big stuff. Though his fastball's spin axis causes it to play down, it's hard enough (92-95 early this spring, harder in the past) to be a viable offering, and his two breaking balls have elite spin. His feel for release and location was all over the place during his 2020 debut. If that doesn't improve, Weigel should just be in the 35+ tier as an up/down type of reliever, though two of his option years have already passed and at some point soon it'll be sink or swim. Though he still has four pitches, Weigel's days of maybe projecting as a starter are likely over. Expect him to lean on his breaking stuff (his slider has incredible horizontal movement) in relief. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most of the international signings that make a splash involve six or seven figures and a 16-year-old with a ridiculous ceiling. Hernandez has the ceiling right, but he signed at age 19 and received just $15,000 to sign in July 2016 out of Venezuela. His 2017 pro debut in the Appalachian League was up-and-down, but he started showing why the Royals are excited about him with a move to full-season ball in 2018, though his season was delayed by a death in the family early and cut short by some fatigue at the end of the summer. He wasn't able to make much progress in 2019, as a fractured rib suffered in Spring Training kept him off the mound until June. Projectable at 6-foot-4, Hernandez is still growing into his body and his fastball. He easily sits around 94 mph and touches 97 mph regularly, with many feeling he could be sitting in the 96- to 97-mph range at some point in the future. At its best, the right-hander's curve is better than his changeup, though the latter is more consistent. With his long levers, it's hard for him to repeat his mechanics on his breaking ball, but it has the potential to be a plus pitch. He's showing an increasing ability to land all three pitches for strikes. Hernandez's fatigue at the end of the year led to some minor arm issues, but those mostly stemmed from him not being physically prepared for a long season. The hope is to get him through a full season healthy, with a full slate of starts, as he continues to mature both physically and mentally to the rigors of being a starting pitcher.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: When Hernandez first really began generating buzz during instructs a couple of years ago, he was "only" sitting 94-98. He's throwing even harder now, sitting 96-99 and getting up to 100. Hernandez brings premium arm strength from a relief-only look. He's a below-average athlete with a long arm swing and is a good example of pitcher with good fastball control (lots of strikes) but not command (not in precise locations). His secondaries (a low-80s curveball and upper-80s changeup) are more reliant on location to miss bats. I think the changeup is the better pure offering but Hernandez has more consistent feel for the curve. Something with his secondaries needs to improve if he's going to be a late-inning, impact relief piece, so I have him projected in a foundational middle-inning role, the kind of reliever who just lives on your roster rather than one the club is willing to option for a fresh, similar option. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021graduates
fangraphs.text: Bickford, who has finally seized hold of a big league role after a very long and eventful prospectdom. Bickford had a velo spike as a high school senior but teams were late to identify and vet him. The Blue Jays took him tent overall but failed to sign him and Bickford went to Fullerton where he struggled as a freshman. On the Cape after his freshman year, he was so electric that, in order to take advantage of the spike in his stock, Bickford transferred to the College of Southern Nevada to be draft eligibile as soon as possible.
