After the 2022 season, Kay hopped around affiliated ball (the Cubs, back to the Mets, the A's), then went abroad and has worked as a starter in NPB for the past two seasons. 
His arsenal has gone through many iterations, including his signature cambio disappearing entirely at times. The changeup has been back in the fold in Japan, but Kay’s path to 291.2 IP of 2.53 ERA-ball in two years with the BayStars has been forged through mucking things up in the zone with three different fastball shapes (four-seamer, cutter, sinker), with a sweeping slider on hand to give lefties a hard time. His contact-heavy, groundball-oriented attack (55.8% GB rate in 2025) could pay a hefty tax upon returning to a more damage-oriented league. But there’s a small paradox in that the pre-arb, optionable arms that teams like to use for multi-inning relief/spot starter swingman roles often have their workloads monitored, while Kay is fresh off throwing a ton of strikes (6.8% walk rate) in a 155 frames and is well-suited to soak up the innings that slip through the cracks of a 162-game season.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Zeuch doesn't have dominant stuff but he's a keen sequencer with a firm grasp on how best to deploy his pitches to efficiently tally outs. He mostly pitches to contact with a low-90s sinker that has very steep downhill plane thanks to his height and fairly upright delivery. It has helped him generate groundball rates near 60% as a pro. He seems to have ditched his curveball in favor of a new cutter he deployed with great frequency during his best 2020 outing against Baltimore. His walk rates have slipped the last couple of years and his stuff doesn't afford him much margin for error in the zone, so now he looks like more of a spot starter than a consistent backend piece, but if his cutter turns out to be a real weapon then he's back in that backend starter bucket. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A converted shortstop, Guerra had premium velocity almost immediately upon taking the mound; he mostly sits 97-99 and will touch 100. His fastball featured natural cut initially, but it has quickly morphed into a pitch with sink and tail. It can miss bats when it's located to his glove side but isn't a dominant, in-zone offering; instead it generates groundballs. Guerra's slider is similarly dependent on precise command, which he doesn't have just yet. The best converted pitchers tend to ascend pretty quickly, and Guerra's now a couple years into his transition, beyond the usual two-year timeline of Jansen, Motte, and other late-inning types. Maybe I should be allowing for a longer timeline for him to really pop because Guerra's fastball shape was overhauled, and this version of him is still relatively new. The Padres are also walking a roster tightrope here. Guerra is out of options. When he comes off the 60-day IL this year, he'll need to rehab and be ready to help a pennant-chasing big league club right away, without the security blanket of an option if things aren't going well. He might be a better fit with an org that can give him low-stakes big league reps in the short-term with the hopes of enjoying fully-formed upside later. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Even though he's performed in the upper-levels of the minors for years, Wong has bounced around waivers. First a 40-man casualty of Tampa Bay and the Angels before landing in San Francisco, and now back with Los Angeles, Wong's versatility, speed, and contact ability from the left side fit like a glove in a low-impact bench role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Davis homered off Carlos Rodon on the first pitch he saw in college and took him deep again as a sophomore, positioning himself as a potential top-five-rounds pick as an Appalachian State junior in 2015. But he tore the labrum in his right (throwing) shoulder early that spring, ending his season and dropping him all the way to the 24th round and the Twins, who signed him for $50,000. He didn't make his pro debut until 2016 and didn't break out until 2019, when he slammed 36 homers -- 10 in 27 Triple-A games and his first big league blast after the Giants acquired him as part of the Sam Dyson trade in July. Davis' tool profile and his statistical profile are somewhat at odds. He's very strong and generates at least plus raw power and impressive exit velocities from the right side of the plate, but he doesn't drive the ball in the air consistently and had the fourth-highest ground-ball rate (51 percent) of any Minor Leaguer with 20 or more homers in 2019. He displayed elite sprint speed during his September callup, but he plays closer to average on the bases and in the field, stealing just 34 bases in his first 452 pro games. That dichotomy won't matter if Davis' power continues to play like it did a year ago. To establish himself in the Majors, he'll need to continue to build on the progress he made with his plate discipline last season. He plays all three outfield positions but has spent the vast majority of his time in right field, where his pop and solid arm fit the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals are still learning about Bolaños, who they acquired with Franchy Cordero from the Padres for Tim Hill in July 2020. San Diego signed Bolaños for $2 million in the 2016-17 international class at age 19 after defecting from Cuba, and it took some time for Bolaños to adjust to professional ball in the United States. He made a serious leap in 2019, posting a 3.66 ERA between Class A Advanced and Double-A, earning a September callup to the Padres’ big league roster. He’s an intriguing prospect for the Royals and was able to flash some stuff for them at the alternate training site and in two abbreviated starts in Kansas City. A right flexor strain has kept him from building on that impact in 2021, though he was on the mend in August. Bolaños has a strong starter’s build at 6-foot-2 and could still grow into his frame. He has a four-pitch mix highlighted by his fastball, which sits around 94-95 mph and has cut, sink or rise to it depending on how he throws it. Both breaking pitches are high-spin, with a biting slider that sits in the mid-to-high 80s and an 80-mph curve that drops tightly. He doesn’t use his high-80s changeup often, but it does have some cut action to it. Bolaños' delivery has quirks, and he will likely need to smooth it out to gain better control. Bolaños’ pitch-mix, velocity and athletic build project him as a starter, and that’s what he’ll continue to develop as in the Royals system when healthy, ultimately projecting as a back-of-the-rotation arm. He could do well in a middle-relief role with an intriguing pitch mix, too.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bolaños was up with the big league squad last June for three solid relief appearances, then returned to Triple-A for the remainder of the 2021 season. He started the 2022 season there as well, making three starts in April before being called up once again to fill out the Royals bullpen. His walks were up and strikeouts down in his first few appearances, which is of particular concern given the fact that his fastball isn't much of a swing-and-miss generator, but he’s regained the command of his four-pitch mix in his more recent appearances. Bolaños only ever started as a minor leaguer, but the innings he’s accrued as a major leaguer thus far have all been out of the ‘pen. This may keep the door open to the back end of the rotation, and that potential outcome boosts his profile as a whole.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: It's not often that "hard-throwing" and "kitchen sink" end up in the same player report but here is Bolaños, who will touch 99 (sit 94) and work with both four- and two-seamers, plus a slider, curveball, changeup, and even a mythically-rare eephus curveball in the upper-60s. None of his secondary stuff is very good and Bolaños has a long arm action that impacts his command, so I have him in a lower-leverage relief role. His starter's pedigree means he's rotation depth for now, and there's a chance he ends up pitching in the back of someone's rotation via more coherent command if, like so many others, his arm action shortens up and enables better command. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way talent throughout his amateur career, Neuse was Oklahoma's shortstop and a reliever for three years. He parlayed a big junior season with the bat into being ranked No. 50 on MLB Pipeline's Top 200 Draft prospects list and landed with the Nationals as their second-round pick. He was having a solid first full season in A ball when he was sent to the A's along with lefty Jesus Luzardo and reliever Blake Treinin in return for Sean Doolittle and Ryan Madson. Neuse made it to Double-A before that 2017 season was over and performed very well in the Arizona Fall League. He stumbled when he moved to Triple-A in 2018, but after hitting .224 in the first half, he righted the ship with a .321 second half. When at his best, Neuse utilizes a compact and simple right-handed swing while also showing an ability to drive the ball to all fields. He came out of his gameplan in Triple-A at the start of the year, not seeing as many pitches and swinging and missing at an alarming rate. When he got back on track, his strikeout rate plummeted and he drew more walks. The power he showed in 2017 didn't completely return, but he was driving the ball a bit more. A below-average runner, Neuse still has plenty of range to play third to go with a plus arm that fires mid-90s fastball from the mound, allowing him to stay at the hot corner long-term. There's a Matt Chapman-sized roadblock for Neuse in Oakland, so he might need to find work around the field and has seen time at his college position as well as a little time at second base in 2018.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Neuse is a power-over-hit infielder with a pretty long performance track record, save for a 2018 Triple-A hiccup. His peripherals have always been a little scary, but he's hit for power pretty consistently. Neuse's broad strokes profile is like J.D. Davis': a two-way college guy who's a third base fit thanks to his arm strength and whose big righty power comes with Ks. I have Neuse in as a four corners bat with uncommon power for that profile. He's an interesting roster compliment to Edwin Ríos, though the A's weren't inclined to give Neuse reps last year even as Matt Chapman was hurt and their second basemen were struggling. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays landed Diaz at the outset of the 2014-15 international period, signing him for $1.6 million one day after they had inked phenom Vladimir Guerrero Jr. The Dominican right-hander flashed promise early in his career but also produced uneven results as he struggled to throw strikes. While he still has gains to make with regards to his control, Diaz's stuff has steadily ticked up each year as he's added strength and logged experience. It all started to click for him in 2018, as Diaz pitched his way up to the Florida State League as part of a breakout campaign. Diaz's athleticism and quick arm help him generate easy velocity. He sits in the mid-90s with a lively fastball that he pairs with an above-average breaking ball. He misses bats with both pitches, while the crossfire in Diaz's delivery gives him natural deception and makes him especially tough on right-handed hitters. His changeup remains a work in progress, though Diaz has made strides in developing in the past year to the point where it's at least usable against left-handed hitters. His control, though still below-average, was markedly better last season as he trimmed his walk rate to 3.2 BB/9 from 4.8 in 2017. After wearing down physically early in his career, Diaz has worked hard to add strength and improve his durability. His efforts showed in 2018 in the form of 147 1/3 innings, nearly double his workload from the previous year. Diaz's all-around progress continues to give him life as a starter, though many scouts believe he's ticketed for the bullpen, where his fastball-curveball combo could play up in short bursts. Diaz could very well debut in that role in 2019 after the Blue Jays added him to their 40-man roster during the offseason.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Diaz has projected as a single-inning middle reliever for quite some time, even though he had been developed as a starter throughout his entire minor league career. He held mid-90s velocity deep into games as a minor league starter and sat 94-98 during a horrendous single-game debut in 2019, seemingly unable to time his arm swing and find a consistent release point during a disastrous inning against the Orioles. That wasn't sufficient justification to slide Diaz's FV down on its own, but then he missed all of 2020 with a severe lat strain and only began pitching in games again for Estrellas Orientales in the Dominican Winter League, where he again sat in the mid-90s (94-97 according to a source). The Mets acquired him from Toronto in January for Steven Matz. The development of Diaz in the rotation improved his changeup enough that it became a sinking/tailing low-90s weapon and his best secondary pitch. He's going to bully hitters with velocity and that changeup, and command consistency will dictate whether it's in an up/down capacity or whether Diaz stays on the Mets big league roster consistently. (Injury rehab)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Signed way back in 2010, Daza didn't get to the United States until the 2014 season. Since then, however, all he's done is hit, posting averages of over .300 in every season. That earned him a spot on the 40-man roster following the 2017 season and he probably would have contributed in Colorado last year if not for a hamstring injury that limited him to just 54 games and shut him down in late July. He did make up for lost time by hitting well in the Venezuelan Winter League. Daza has a knack for barreling up the baseball and picks up hits in bunches, and while he's perfectly happy to shoot line drives the other way, he did start turning on pitches and driving them to his pull side more effectively in 2018, though over-the-fence power is never going to be a big part of his game. He's not a burner, but he runs well enough to be an effective baserunner and uses his speed well in center field. Considered the best center field prospect in the system, he has plus instincts, reads and routes to go along with excellent first-step quickness. He makes it look easy out there as a true ball hawk. How he continues to impact the baseball might determine his ultimate ceiling, but at the very least, he's a very valuable fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKay won the prestigious John Olerud Two-Way Player of the Year Award in each of his three seasons at Louisville and was considered by many to be the best two-way Draft prospect since Dave Winfield (1973). He became the No. 4 overall pick in the 2017 Draft and signed for $7,005,000 after garnering both the Golden Spikes and Dick Howser Awards as a junior. He reached the Majors as a two-way player in 2019, debuting in June and then pitching well enough to earn a spot on the Rays' postseason roster, and he was expected to take on a more significant role with the club in 2020. Instead, McKay started the season late due to a positive coronavirus test during the summer before requiring season-ending surgery to repair a torn labrum in August. He went under the knife again in November 2021, this time for thoracic outlet syndrome decompression surgery. When healthy, McKay operates with plus command of four average-or-better pitches when he’s healthy. He confidently pitches to both sides of the plate with both his 92-95 mph fastball and cutter in the upper 80s, and he knows how to disrupt hitters’ timing by working in an average curveball with top-to-bottom shape. His least-used pitch in 2019 was an average mid-80s changeup that he will need to develop to combat right-handed hitters. A quality athlete, McKay typically repeats his delivery well and has been a consistent strike-thrower at every stage of his career. While it’s difficult to predict what type of impact the multiple surgeries will have on McKay’s stuff and performance in the future, the nature of the injuries alone is enough to raise valid concerns about the left-hander's future role. His best path forward toward contributing in 2022 and beyond is likely on the mound. That's on hold until he can show a full recovery.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A lengthy parade of injuries has not only derailed McKay's career, but kept him about one inning shy of graduating off of prospect lists for nearly three years. He pitched in a handful of rehab outings last July and August, with his fastball averaging just 90 mph during that time. McKay was once a 1.1 draft candidate, arguably a top five talent both as a pitcher and a hitter while at Louisville. After toying with both in pro ball, he rose to the upper levels of the minors and into our 60 FV tier as a pitcher by developing plus command of a deep repertoire of quality (but not dominant) offerings, and looked like a major league ready mid-rotation starter just before the injuries began piling up. He spent the start of 2022 camp in the COVID protocols and only threw one bullpen session prior to publication.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Nobody knows exactly how to adjust where McKay falls on the overall prospect continuum after his August 2020 shoulder surgery. He was just 1.1 innings shy of graduating off prospect lists entirely in 2019, and would have graduated in 2020 had he stepped on a mound even once, but a bout with COVID delayed his activity at the alternate site, and then shoulder discomfort, which had plagued him the year before, resurfaced once he began to throw bullpens. The situation is similar to Cardinals righty Alex Reyes', who accrued 46 big league innings before he needed Tommy John, which derailed his ability to pitch out of the rotation early in his career due to the rehab timeline. This injury is especially scary for McKay since part of the reason he peaked as a 60 FV was because he projected to throw a ton of innings and generate 3-plus annual WAR on the strength of his durability. Now it sounds like he won't be ready for the start of camp. His fastball only sits 90-94 and touches 96, which is pretty average, but McKay keeps it away from the middle of the zone where it can really be hammered and often ties hitters up with it because he locates so well; his swinging strike rate on the heater was close to 17% in the minors, so I think it'll play. His cutter command is arguably even better, and he peppers the glove side of the plate with it at will. Changeup usage was scarce in his 49-inning big league sample but I think it will be one of the focal points of his repertoire, perhaps usurping the curveball, which has a stronger visual evaluation than it does if you look at the spin data. It's a repertoire/command profile similar to that of a lot of good lefties (Hyun Jin Ryu, Mike Minor, Cole Hamels), though most of them are more reliant on the cambio than McKay has been to this point. He now fits in with other major league-ready, strike-throwing 2 WAR starters toward the back of the top 100, though he needs to slide behind the ones who will be ready for the start of the season, and the ones who are coming off an elbow injury rather than a shoulder. (Alternate site, Injured)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Signed for an over-slot $912,500 as a third-round pick out of a Mississippi high school in 2014, Bradley won the Rookie-level Arizona League triple crown (.361, eight homers, 50 RBIs) in his pro debut and home-run titles in two Class A leagues in his first two full seasons. He has continued to mash in the upper Minors, slamming 50 homers between Double-A and Triple-A in 2017-18. He's a classic three-true-outcomes player, posting 162-game averages of 34 homers, 78 walks and 188 strikeouts through his first five years as a pro. Bradley's bat speed and strength create massive left-handed power to all fields, and he tries to make the most of it every time he takes a swing. He does have some natural hitting ability but his ultra-aggressive approach has resulted in a 27-percent strikeout rate in pro ball, including a career-worst 34 percent during his first month in Triple-A last August. Though he's not going to hit for average, he gets pitched around and takes enough walks to fuel healthy on-base percentages. While almost all of Bradley's value comes from his offense, he made a concerted effort to get into better shape and dropped 25 pounds during the 2017-18 offseason. He's still a bottom-of-the-scale runner, but he showed some improvement at first base, where he has a chance to become an average defender with an arm to match. He doesn't cover enough ground to play the outfield, so DH is his only other option.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bradley was at the alt site all year, so his report stays the same. He's a three true outcomes DH prospect who I think will have a front-loaded career in terms of production based on his build and athleticism. There's a non-zero chance the strikeouts cause the power production to bottom out against big league pitching, in which case Bradley could take the Roberto Ramos route to Asia. He'll compete with Josh Naylor, Franmil Reyes and the other Cleveland DH types next spring. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Palumbo weighed 160 pounds and threw in the mid-80s as a New York high school senior in 2013, area scout Takeshi Sakurayama liked his loose arm and signed him for $32,000 as a 30th-rounder. He didn't reach full-season ball until the end of his third pro season but began blossoming into one of the Rangers' best pitching prospects in 2016, only to succumb to Tommy John surgery in April 2017. He returned to the mound in June 2018, reclaimed his stuff and made his big league debut a year later. Palumbo's best pitch is his 78-82 mph curveball, a plus offering with high spin rates, good depth and 11-5 break. He also features high spin on his four-seam fastball, which sits at 91-94 mph, tops out at 96 and gets on hitters quicker than they expect. He's making progress with his changeup, which he needs to do a better job of keeping right-handers in check. Though he has a smaller frame than desired in a starter, Palumbo helps his cause with athleticism and arm speed. While he throws strikes and doesn't have much effort in his delivery, there's still concern about his long-term durability because his 97 1/3 innings last year represented a career high in seven pro seasons. A potential mid-rotation starter, he should resurface in Texas at some point in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If adversity on the field is a great teacher, Bolt might have a master's degree by now. After a huge freshman season at North Carolina, the outfielder struggled as a sophomore and junior, but the A's rolled the dice on his raw tools and took him in the fourth round of the 2015 Draft. He struggled to hit for much of his first two-plus years as a pro and really scuffled with a move to Double-A to start the 2018 season. Bolt went back down to the California League, righted himself, then played his way on to the 40-man roster with a huge finish to the year, back in Double-A and a stint in the Arizona Fall League. The A's always felt Bolt had the ability to succeed, but just hadn't been able to find the level of consistency to tap into his tools. He can hit for average and power from both sides of the plate, though the power really shows up left-handed (17 of his 19 homers in 2018 came from that side). He has enough speed to steal a base, and he finished just one home run and one steal shy of a 20-20 campaign last year. Bolt has the speed and instincts to play center field and the strong arm to play right. He has the acumen to play all three outfield positions and he's likely to be a fourth outfielder in the big leagues. Now that he's starting to put it together on a daily basis, though, don't rule out Bolt finding a regular spot in the lineup.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: It's possible Gutierrez will get a 2021 shot to supplant Hunter Dozier, who has only had one good season, but Dozier had a good spring and Guti was beaten out for an opening day bench spot by Hanser Alberto. Though he has some clear tools, Gutierrez lacks an obvious role. A no-doubt plus defender at third base (he has great range, feet, hands, arm strength, and an internal clock), Gutierrez also had some of the best TrackMan data in this system in 2019 but doesn't elicit great visual evaluations as a hitter. His swing is a little long, he fouls off a lot of hittable pitches, and he's a bit of a free-swinger. He may be a nice multi-positional infield role player but he'll need to start seeing consistent time at other positions to do that. He may end up being squeezed off the roster and getting a shot on a rebuilding club with a more obvious path to playing time. (Alternate site, MLB, LIDOM)

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: After eight seasons of weathering the minor league wilderness, the former top 100 prospect looked the part over 15 awesome starts with Hanshin in 2025, striking out 113 in 90  2/3 innings of 1.39 ERA-ball with the Central League team. Duplantier’s delivery has gained an extra degree of counter rotation since heading out east, and he relatedly threw more strikes (5.7% walk rate) than his last tour of affiliated ball. When he comes out of the gate pumping high-90s gas with big-time extension and a bevy of playable secondaries, he looks like a viable leverage arm. And since Duplantier already is dogged by a lengthy injury history and tended to see his velocity back all the way into the low-90s by the middle innings even while dominating in Japan, airing out in short bursts looks like the most reasonable path to the 31-year-old contributing to a winning team.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Duplantier had been injury-free since college (where he dealt with shoulder problems) until 2018, when he had hamstring issues in the spring, and biceps tendinitis later in the summer. The lost innings resulted in an Arizona Fall League stint, during which Duplantier was one of the better pitching prospects in the league. Despite the biceps issue, his velocity was fine in the Fall, when he sat 93-96 and showed three good, clearly demarcated secondary pitches. Then 2019 came. Dup's stuff was not as crisp during the spring, and he was shuttled back and forth between Triple-A and the big leagues several times; he had a shoulder issue in the middle of the summer and his stuff was down again later in the year. I have nothing on him from Arizona's alt site and I'm not even sure if he pitched there. He sat 91 in his first 2021 spring start. With that kind of velo, he's more likely a fifth starter. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick by Arizona in the 2013 Draft, Williams spent parts of two seasons in the D-backs' system before they dealt him to Tampa Bay in the November 2014 Jeremy Hellickson trade. Things started to click for Williams in 2017 at Double-A, as the then 21-year-old impressed with his feel to hit and power potential, but he was unable to build upon that success last year in Triple-A. He did, however, make his big league debut in July, logging one at-bat with the Rays, who traded him to the Cardinals 10 days later in the Tommy Pham deal. He opened 2019 behind schedule as a result of a fractured right hand suffered while punching a television during the offseason. A lower body injury in May then sidelined him for nearly a month. Williams has always intrigued scouts with his natural hitting ability and projectable power, but it hasn't come together for him as quickly as it seemed it might earlier in his career. He has an aggressive approach and good bat-to-ball skills from the left side of the plate, and there's plenty of raw power for him to tap into. Right now, though, Williams makes way too much ground-ball contact -- he's posted ground-ball rates north of 50 percent in every pro season -- so a mechanical adjustment may be necessary to unlock his potential at the plate. The D-backs moved Williams from shortstop, his high school position, to the outfield at the start of his career. He's become an average defender out there, spending most of his time in left, with average arm strength that enabled him to record 17 outfield assists in 2018.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Williams has made an appearance in three seperate big league seasons dating back to 2018, but has still only played seven total games as he's been toward the back of the Cardinals' recent outfield logjam at the upper levels. Williams does a lot of good stuff in the box. He has plus raw power and has feel for the zone. I've seen him pull his hands in and get the barrel on pitches up and in, and I've seen him make mid-flight adjustments to breaking balls and hit them hard the other way. Williams' problem has been that he struggles to lift the ball. He had the second-highest 2019 average exit velo in this system but also had lowest average launch angle. With a couple of different swings across three different orgs (he was drafted as a high school shortstop by Arizona, traded to Tampa Bay for Jeremy Hellickson, then sent to St. Louis for Tommy Pham), it's probably too late for a relevant change. But Williams still has enough offensive utility to play a corner platoon role. John Nogowski arguably outhit him during the spring (in my opinion, Williams' at-bat quality was better than his raw numbers indicate) but Williams is the better roster fit with the other big league Cardinals due to his handedness. An extra option year was imposed on Williams before the season and retaining that option by rostering him increases his short-term trade value a little bit. He should end up making an occasional start against a righty and come off the bench to face them later in games. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text:
One of the flashier amateur shortstop defenders of the last couple decades, Cholowsky was a late-first round prospect as an Arizona high schooler who wanted top-of-the-draft money to sign. Enough teams were worried about how much he'd hit that they had him more toward the back of the first round, and though the White Sox are rumored to have made a run at him, he ended up at UCLA. There, Cholowsky took a big enough leap as a sophomore hitter to make himself the odds on favorite to go first in the draft. He cut his strikeout rate to 9.3% and hit 23 homers. When you combine everything Cholowsky participated in in 2025 (the college season, Team USA trials and international play, and fall ball at UCLA), he had an 1.127 OPS. 
Cholowsky's highlight reel defensive ability is the bedrock of his game. His hands, actions and body control are incredible, and make him a potential Gold Glove shortstop despite middling range. For such a great shortstop, Roch is a thicker-in-the-middle athlete, and it's possible his range will depreciate as he ages and make him merely a 55 or 60-grade shortstop in his late 20s. On offense, Cholowsky's ability to tuck his hands inside the baseball and barrel stuff on the inner third has improved a lot since high school, but he's still a little long to some parts of the zone. He identifies and adjusts to breaking stuff and moves the barrel around pretty well, but middling plate discipline and Cholowsky's lever length combine to keep his hit tool projection a little south of average. He should still be able to access pull-side power with regularity because of his style of swing and good (for a shortstop) power. Though Roch is a different physical package, his tools are very similar to what Dansby Swanson's were coming out of Vanderbilt. He'll probably strike out more than most of his shortstop peers, but get to pull power and play awesome defense en route to some seasons with 3-plus WAR.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: Cholowsky is a broad-shouldered, projectable shortstop with a multi-sport pedigree (he also played quarterback) and a baseball industry family (his dad played pro ball for nearly a decade in the minors and is now the Reds' Four Corners area scout, while his mom worked for the A's). He is the best defensive infielder in the 2023 draft class, with some of the slickest and flashiest defensive actions of any draft prospect since Francisco Lindor. He also posted surprisingly good bat-to-ball data on the showcase circuit (per Synergy, a 2-to-1 BIP-to-Whiff ratio across 362 pitches on film in 2022), but to the eye, his swing has a hole up around his hands. Most of Roch's contact is concentrated down-and-away from him, and he has impressive oppo power but he tends to inside out a lot of pitches he should pull. There are scouts who don't consider it a totally functional swing and there's risk Cholowsky's hit tool will prevent him from being a regular. But his defense is going to play at the big league level. He has a realistic utility infield floor with an everyday shortstop ceiling if he can get on top of pro fastballs.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Ford was a draft-eligible sophomore in 2025 who crushed during his two years at UVA and is then committed to Tennessee via the transfer portal for his junior year. He's a well-built 6-foot-5, 200 pound guy with corner infield experience who moved from first base to right field in 2025 and then played center field on Cape Cod. Lever length and late-triggering hands create an inside-out nature to Ford's ball-in-play profile; he is much more apt to pull breaking balls with authority than fastballs. He has explosive hands and bat speed, some feel to hit, and power that's already shown up in game action. Below-average plate discipline, but the tools and projection foundation here is exciting and features a lot of power now, and probably more in the future. This is a late first round prospect entering 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Draft-eligible sophomore who crushed during his two years at UVA and is now committed to Tennessee via the transfer portal and not expected to sign. Well-built 6-foot-5, 200 pound guy with corner infield experience. Moved from first base to right field in 2025 and is currently playing center field on Cape Cod. Lever length and late-triggering hands create an inside-out nature to ball-in-play profile; much more apt to pull breaking balls with authority than fastballs. Has explosive hands and bat speed, some feel to hit, and power that's already shown up in game action. Has below-average plate discipline, but the tools and projection foundation here is exciting and features a lot of power now, and probably more in the future. A first round prospect entering 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text:
Gracia is a strapping, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 center fielder with big league physicality and a great two-year track record of hitting at Duke prior to his draft year transfer to Virginia. A gorgeous low-ball lefty swing produces nearly average all-fields power for Gracia, who likely isn't done growing into raw thump. He will hit the baseball where it's pitched and do damage to all fields. Gracia's selectivity and hand-eye coordination allow him to move the bat around the hitting zone with uncommon feel for such a big, long-levered hitter, and he posted a comfortably plus contact rate in 2025. 
Gracia isn't a burner, but his feel for center field is good. He's comfortable going back on balls hit over his head and looks smooth at the catch point. There's a chance he outgrows center field, but for now, his skills out there are suitable for continued development. He's one of the most well-rounded hitters in the 2026 draft class and has a shot to go first overall if he's added sufficient strength without sacrificing the speed that would allow him to continue developing in center field.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Flora has an ideal pitcher's build and movement patterns at a loose-armed 6-foot-5. He was able to sustain upper-90s velocity for 75 innings in 2025, 30 more than the prior year. Flora sits 97 and regularly touches 100 with plus extension. His arm speed makes the baseball very difficult to pick up out of his hand and gives Flora's seldom-used changeup huge long-term projection. Right now his fastball and a couple of different sliders make up 95% of his pitch usage. Flora has great feel for locating lateral-action sliders to both sides of the plate, some slower, some as hard as 87-89 mph. His mechanical and athletic foundation are very exciting, as is his arm strength and breaking ball feel, but he has a little more pitch development ahead of him than most top-of-the-class arms.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Emerson is a well-rounded prospect who is a virtual lock to remain at shortstop for the long haul thanks to plus range, actions, and arm strength. He's a grinder in the box who takes a ton of pitches and spoils borderline offerings until opposing hurlers give in and either give him something to hit or walk him. A twitchy, bottom-hand dominant swing results in all-fields doubles contact. Emerson is of medium build — he's not the second coming of Corey Seager or Bobby Witt Jr. — but skilled high school shortstops like this tend to come off the board within the top 10 picks and eventually become everyday players at the position.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Lackey is a well-rounded, rapidly-improving catcher prospect who went from having no Division I offers as an underclassman to being a potential top five pick. The best college catcher in any draft class tends to come off the board in the top 10, and Lackey is a good bet to do just that. His game has no obvious holes on either side of the ball. His footwork coming out of his crouch can have inconsistent direction, but when he has a smooth exchange, he'll pop around 1.90, which is plus. He's a skinny 20-year-old (he turns 21 the week before the draft) who still has room for mass and strength on his frame, but already Lackey is a strong pitcher framer and ball-blocker. He's also a good contact hitter with a gorgeous swing. Again, Lackey has no obvious weak point as a hitter, and he's especially good at buttoning fastballs, which he had a 91% contact rate against in 2025. His all-fields approach yields a lot of gap doubles right now but those might turn into home runs as Lackey fills out. This is a good primary catching prospect and an instantaneous Top 100 guy upon entry into pro ball, a potential future All-Star.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Reese posted a .901 OPS as a freshman outfielder at Houston, then transferred to Mississippi State (where he mostly played third base) and ripped 40 extra-base hits in 57 games with the Bulldogs despite a bone fragment floating in one of his toes, which was surgered in the autumn. Reese has plus lefty power and bat speed generated by a low-ball swing. He can drop the bat head and drive pitches in the lower third to all fields, with enough power to threaten both foul poles. Reese is rather chase-prone but is otherwise a stable hitting prospect who covers a good bit of the zone. Though he's not a lock to remain at third base, he looked good enough toward the end of 2025 to merit a good long look there in pro ball. If he can remain at third, he'll have a shot to profile as an everyday player even with lesser OBP skills. If he needs to move to first base or an outfield corner, his lack of plate discipline will be more of a problem. Reese is talented enough to be drafted inside the top 10.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text:
Lebron is an incredible athlete with ideal athletic projection, and the two traits give him a shot to grow into impact power while remaining an excellent shortstop defender. He's a slender, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 or so, built like an athlete who could play any sport well. Right now that serves to make Lebron a great shortstop defender. He has great range, he bends well, and his hands, actions and arm strength are all plus or better. To be built like he is and move like he does at his size makes it easy to project Lebron at shortstop in perpetuity while also forecasting added strength as he matures. 
Whether Lebron will actually be able to hit enough to get to his power is the big question. His pitch recognition and feel to hit are both incredibly raw, and Lebron struck out at an alarming rate in 2025 (24%, worse than his freshman season) and has concerning chase and miss splits against secondary pitches. College players with such a wide range of outcomes are pretty rare, and Lebron's possible ceiling (if his feel to hit improves) makes him a likely high pick even though he's at risk of hitting too little to matter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Flukey is a lanky 6-foot-6 righty who held mid-90s velocity across 101 innings in 2025, culminating in a great start against LSU in the College World Series. His 12-to-6 curveball has nearly 20 mph of velocity separation from his fastball, and even though that pitch looks easy to spot out of hand, it has enough depth that it generated a plus-plus miss rate in 2025. Flukey's fastball and curveball represented 83% of his pitch usage as a sophomore, but his slider (which averaged 83 mph) and changeup were both effective when he threw them. Flukey's slider acts as a strike-garnering pitch (he threw both it and his fastball for strikes more than 70% of the time), while his changeup was flashing bat-missing tail late in the season. He has a longer, fairly violent arm action, and there were games when Flukey struggled to get any miss on his fastball because his size imparts hittable downward angle on that pitch. He has mid-rotation ceiling if it turns out this slow curveball can keep playing like an impact pitch.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Rojas is a prototypical prep lefty who looks an awful lot like Marlins southpaw Thomas White looked just a few years ago. He is built like a star power pitcher at a fluid 6-foot-4, and Rojas' full-body flexibility and whippy arm are on full display as he pedals home and unwinds. He'll deliver a rise/tail fastball from a low-three-quarters slot, a low enough angle that Rojas can elevate his heater for whiffs. And he does; both Rojas' fastball and frisbee slider generated an elite miss rate on the showcase circuit. His slider is a seamed sickle with ridiculous length, starting from the lefty batter's box and darting all the way across the plate. Though he doesn't have a fully formed changeup right now, Rojas is so limber that it's likely he'll develop one in time. This looks like a potential Andrew Miller sequel.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text:
Becker, whose father played A-ball with Cleveland, is a lefty-hitting shortstop with rare body projection for a college infielder. He has oppo gap power and enough juice to threaten the wall just left of center field and, at a wiry-framed 6-foot-3, he has room to add strength and do even more damage. Becker swings with a naturally vertical bat path; his hands hang over the strike zone as they load and then loop through the zone in a way that evokes Freddie Freeman. Becker doesn't have that kind of bat control, but it does help him lift the ball even when he's making contact at the top of the zone. Because he swings with a stiff, high front side, he can struggle to dip and connect with lower, softer pitches, especially changeups. 
He needs technical refinement on defense (he needs to stay on top of the baseball on deeper throws), but Becker has the range and athleticism to develop at shortstop and hopefully stay lithe enough to remain there for the long haul. There are scouts who think he'll outgrow short, but they're fine with it as long as it comes with more power. If Becker has another season like both of his underclass years (.366/.459/.637 career line entering his draft year), his floor is probably in the middle of the first round.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Spangler is a very projectable 6-foot-3, lefty-hitting infielder from Northern California. His swing is bottom-hand dominant and has some length, but he still managed an 85% contact rate on the showcase circuit across a multi-year sample. His size makes it possible that, over time, he'll need to move off of shortstop to third base, but if that happens, he'll probably have enough power to profile there. There are scouts who think he'll be tough to sign.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Peterson was one of the best unsigned high school pitchers from the 2023 class, and had two walk-prone underclass seasons at Florida. He has the stuff of a top 10 pick, with a riding fastball in the mid-to-upper 90s, a power breaking ball in the mid-80s, and a plus-flashing changeup in the 84-87 mph range. His delivery is stiff, especially Peterson's landing leg, and he has some head and shoulder violence through release. Florida hasn't always developed their pitchers in the best way, and it's possible a pro team will be able to polish Peterson's mechanics and command quickly after drafting him. He'll be an impact starter if someone can.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: You can make the argument that Peterson checks more scouting boxes than any other high school pitcher in this draft class except maybe a fully-operational Thomas White, and he entered the 2023 spring with a shot to emerge as a surefire first round prospect, but he wasn't throwing especially hard at NHSI and has had issues with breaking ball consistency this spring. He's young for the class, has a well-composed, high-waisted frame (that's closer to maxed than ideal, but still good), and his arm speed is sensational. He's parallel to the ground at layback, then creates vertical ride on his fastball by virtue of his hand position on release. His delivery already looks a lot like what teams like the Red Sox and Tigers try to get their pitching prospects to do, with a curt arm action, allowing for consistent release. Peterson's shapely mid-70s breaking ball has depth but sometimes lacks power and bite. He sells his changeup with his arm speed and, when things are clicking for him, his pitch mix is as advanced as any high schooler in this class. He was up to 97 mph toward the end of the high school season and is a high-upside prospect who should go in the comp or early second round, though that may not be high enough to keep him from heading to Florida.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text:
Helfrick was a highly-regarded high school prospect in Northern California who ventured all the way to the SEC for college. After struggling as a freshman, he had a power-hitting breakout as a sophomore and clubbed 15 homers in 61 games, then struggled with Team USA. Overt physicality, power, and steady catching defense (both receiving and ball blocking) give Helfrick a floor of sorts. It's common for big league catchers to hit around .200, and that's what's likely in the cards for Helfrick, who swings over the top of a lot of soft stuff in the bottom of the zone. He should crush quite a few high fastballs to his pull side and slug even though he will probably strike out 30% of the time in pro ball. 
On defense, his size and strength help make Helfrick a quiet, subtle receiver around the edges of the zone, and he's a skilled, mobile ball-blocker. He has an above-average arm that plays down because his exchange takes too long, and this needs some polish. Luke Stevenson went 35th overall in 2025 after striking out more often than Helfrick did as a sophomore, and Helfrick is a better defender, so his draft stock is just ahead of that area as he enters his junior season.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: A power-hitting catching prospect who has hit in games on the showcase circuit, Helfrick has a shot to be a primary catcher because of his offense. He certainly looks the part of a pro athlete in the uniform at a sturdy 6-foot-2, and Helfrick is already capable of hitting for power to the right/center gap as well as to his pull side. Despite some breaking ball chase, Helfrick performed pretty well from a contact rate standpoint against his showcase peers. Most of his extra-base damage comes on pitches in a pretty narrow portion of the strike zone, mainly ones out away from him that he can get extended on. Helfrick's receiving is still pretty crude for his age, and his footwork and exchange need cleaning up, but these are common issues for a teenage catcher and Helfrick has above-average raw arm strength. The ingredients are here, they just need a lot of seasoning.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Teel hit .321/.442/.577 in two years at Virginia and was a draft-eligible sophomore in 2025 who transferred to Mississippi State for 2026 rather than humor the draft process. He doesn't have huge top-end speed but did some incredible stuff on defense toward the end of the 2025 season, diving in the gaps with no regard for his own well being. Teel could be passable in center on grit and instincts, but is more likely to rove all over the outfield. He posted a 95% zone contact rate in 2025. Teel swings bent at the waist, which helps facilitate excellent plate coverage. Style can look slash-and-dash-y on the surface, but Teel has consistent feel for elevation. Makes well-struck contact to all fields. Would be a doubles machine if he had half a grade more power. Well-rounded fourth outfield prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Doesn't have huge top-end speed but did some incredible stuff on defense toward the end of the season, diving in the gaps with no regard for his own well being. Could be passable in center on grit and instincts, more likely to rove all over the outfield. Posted a 95% zone contact rate in 2025. Swings bent at the waist, which helps facilitate excellent plate coverage. Style can look slash-and-dash-y on the surface, but Teel has consistent feel for elevation. Makes well-struck contact to all fields. Would be a doubles machine if he had half a grade more power. Well-rounded fourth outfield prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: A physical lefty with a great curveball, Bolemon didn't allow an earned run during his junior year of high school and struck out two batters per inning during varsity play. In 12 showcase outings during the summer, all over the world, Bolemon dominated his elite peers and allowed just an .085 opponent average in 144 batters faced. This is despite not throwing all that hard. Bolemon's fastball averaged just 92 mph on the showcase circuit and touched 96. His arm action is incredibly deceptive and loose; hitters don't seem to pick up the baseball out of Bolemon's hand, it just appears out from behind his head and sneaks past hem. Both his fastball and breaking ball have generated plus-plus swing and miss in an environment with good hitters. Bolemon's quick arm action might eventually yield a good offspeed pitch, but it's tough to turn over a straight changeup from his slot. He might end up adding a splitter or modified cambio down the road. Right now, he's a sturdy-looking strike-thrower who looks like he's going to have at least two 60-grade pitches.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Brunson was drafted by the Blue Jays out of San Clemente High School in California but ended up at TCU, where he's been the everyday center fielder for two years. He is as well-rounded a college prospect as there is in the 2026 draft. Brunson is a plus runner and center field defender who has great gap-to-gap range and tracks balls hit over his head with ease and comfort. His all-fields contact approach yields mostly singles and doubles, but Brunson has big league physicality at 6-foot-3, 200 pounds, and his exit velocities are comfortably above the college average. His in-zone contact rate, across all of 2025 and during conference play, was above 90%. He has a good fourth outfielder's floor and might yet develop the strength to hit for enough power to be a first division regular out there, as Brunson will be barely 21 on draft day and is still filling out.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Strosnider was a multi-sport high schooler (baseball, hoops, track) who struggled during the early portion of his freshman year at TCU before getting hot in the middle of the season. The toolshed outfielder slashed .350/.420/.650 and had 34 extra base hits (including 10 triples) in 56 games as a freshman. Strosnider's swing is similar to that of a young Cody Bellinger, featuring a blend of athleticism and effort that leads to big all-fields power, but also a good number of strikeouts. Though his surface stats improved throughout his freshman campaign, his contact rate was actually worse once TCU got into Big 12 play, and was comfortably below the college average. Strosnider runs well but played only right field as a freshman. If it turns out he can develop into a good center field defender, then the strikeouts will be easier to swallow. Strosnider is risky but has big ceiling as a power-hitting center fielder. His more likely outcome is as a strong side corner platoon option.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Sorrell enters his draft spring as one of the higher variance college hitters in the entire class. He might swing and miss as much as he did in 2025 (his contact rate was only 70%) and slide out of the first round, or he might looks good in center field, make slightly more contact, and go inside the top 10. Sorrell certainly has the power to be a top pick, and he showed it in 2025 even though he was dealing with a hamate injury for a stretch of that season. He has big lefty bat speed and power that makes him capable of leaving the yard to all fields. He's a shorter-levered guy who can flatten his bat path to cover fastballs at the belt, which isn't true of many of the other whiff-risk college hitters in the 2026 draft. Sorrell also dealt with a hamstring issue in 2025 and fellow outfielder Jac LaViolette took center field reps from him when Sorrell was healthy. How he looks on defense in 2026 will be important. If his contact ability improves and Sorrell also looks playable in center field, he could be this draft's Colton Cowser.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Maniscalco is a very athletic young shortstop who was originally going to be part of the 2027 class, but reclassified to 2026. He'll be just a shade over 17 years old on draft day. Maniscalco is a switch-hitter with a sweet lefty swing and acrobatic actions on defense. He's very skinny, but he's also 17. He's got a chance to go very high in the draft depending on how his body develops between now and the summer. If he has become meaningfully stronger, he could be this draft's Jordan Yost or Steele Hall.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Bell is an athletic, switch-hitting shortstop who the Rays drafted 66th overall in 2024 but failed to sign. He had a good freshman season at Kentucky — .296/.385/.522, 10 homers — and is an age-eligible sophomore entering 2026, as he turns 21 at the very end of June. Bell is a competent and pretty dangerous hitter from both sides of the dish. His lefty swing has big natural loft, while his righty swing is well-connected from the ground up and lets him generate good bat speed. Though some of Bell's swings are imbalanced, that's not unusual for a switch-hitter this age, and it's impressive that he was able to maintain a 77% contact rate once conference play began in his first season. Bell is very athletic but needs polish on defense, especially his throwing stroke and accuracy. He throws from a lower slot and some of them sail on him. The athletic components to play shortstop (and probably all over the diamond) are here, and Bell's big league projection probably resides in a multi-positional utility role. He's a mid-first round prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: High school pitchers participating in the grueling pre-draft circuit often have velo swoons at some point during the showcase process as they pitch all summer and get worn out travelling all over the place. It was the opposite for Schmidt, who added a tick-and-a-half throughout the summer and ended it throwing harder than when it began. Schmidt's delivery looks a lot like Yusei Kikuchi's and Gage Jump's, except on a more sizeable individual, creating rise/run life on his fastball and two-plane break (from Schmidt's POV, the 4 o'clock face of a clock) on his nasty breaking ball. He'll occasionally bury a firm changeup, as hard as 89 mph, but that pitch is a distant third offering right now. Schmidt's a little thicker than most high school pitchers, but he throws strikes with two pitches that are easily plus. In Schmidt's case, his fastball and slider are playing like elite pitches, not merely plus ones. We'd like to see him add a pitch that can more obviously help him navigate righty batters.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Waechter has a rise/run fastball that consistently finishes toward the up/arm side quadrant of the zone, where it plays best. He was able to miss a plus-plus rate of bats on the showcase circuit even tough his heater sits just 93. Waechter's slider, which averages 86 mph, is more often used as an in-zone offering tunneling off of his fastball rather than a chase pitch off the edge of the plate. It still has a plus miss and chase rate even though it's not used for that most of the time. Waechter's arm action is beautiful and fluid, allowing for changeup projection into his mid-20s. He might end up with multiple different breaking balls when all is said and done, and has a chance to be a mid-rotation starter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Condon is an explosive athlete whose skill set is like a lot of recent undersized speedsters (like Slater de Brun and Slade Caldwell) except that it comes in a more traditional 5-foot-11 package. Condon's front side often bails toward first base when he swings, which leaves him vulnerable to sliders away from him, but his ability to swing really hard and generate some power at his size is remarkable. Plus-plus speed allows for comfortable center field projection. This is one of the twitchier, more athletic players in the 2026 draft and a classic late first or comp round prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Peterson is a hard-swinging third base prospect who has short levers for a 6-foot-3 hitter. There are times when his swing is out of control, but he still managed an 80% contact rate on the showcase circuit and he has enough power to threaten fences in all directions. A slick third base defender with a well-rounded, lefty-hitting skill set, Peterson has a shot to go toward the back of the first round.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Johnson has incredible hand speed and managed an 84% contact rate during two years on the showcase circuit even though his swing often has bad footwork and balance. There are times when Johnson totally cuts his stride, robs himself of athleticism, and yet still stings the baseball because of how much power he's able to generate with his hands and wrists. Pro instruction might coax out a better, more stable offensive player. Even though Johnson's hands on the infield are bad enough that he's projected to the outfield here, his potential hit/power combo gives him the ceiling of a heart-of-the-order hitter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Ruiz is one of the better high school shortstop defenders of the last several years and projects as a plus-plus glove at the position. He's also a smaller athlete who will be 19 on draft day. With the cement relatively dry on his 5-foot-10 frame, he is unlikely to grow into meaningful power and is more likely to be a second-division regular or excellent utilityman.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: An Arkansas righty and the brother of Cubs prospect Jaxon Wiggins, Carson touched 102 last year, but then blew out and had elbow surgery in May. A typical return timeline puts him in play for pre-draft bullpens and hopefully an air-it-out session at the Draft Combine. He could be a quick-moving, late-inning reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Brother of Cubs pitching prospect Jaxon Wiggins. Among the most exciting combinations of present velocity and long-term frame projection in the draft. Gawky 6-foot-5 with mid-to-upper-90s fastball velocity already on board. Plays down a tad due to downhill plane and ineffectual shape, may need to lean into sink as a pro. Erratic command, which isn't uncommon for high school pitchers this size and age, and with this kind of arm strength. Slider is a banger when it's released well. Has powerful downward movement in the 83-87 mph range. Big time raw talent with relief risk.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Sdao is a skinny 6-foot-2 lefty who spent most of 2024 as a long reliever, posting a 55-to-9 K-to-BB ratio in 48.2 innings. He needed TJ in the fall and missed all of 2025. Sdao has a great arm action, and sat 92-94 with riding life in 2024; his slider performed like a plus pitch and has big lateral movement in the 79-83 mph range, while his changeup has big projection thanks to his arm action. Starter's stuff is in range for Sdao's dev, but he's much less proven than most college starters.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Skinny 6-foot-2 lefty who spent most of 2024 as a long reliever, posted 55-to-9 K-to-BB ratio in 48.2 innings. Needed TJ in the fall and missed all of 2025. Great arm action, sat 92-94 with riding life in 2024; slider performed like a plus pitch, has big lateral movement in the 79-83 mph range. Changeup has big projection thanks to arm action. Starter's stuff in range for Sdao's dev, but he's much less proven than most college starters.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Burress has had two absurd seasons at Georgia Tech and entered his draft year as a career .357/.490/.756 hitter, like a 5-foot-9 Barry Bonds. For an outfielder this size to be a great big leaguer would be mold-breaking. Short of Kirby Puckett (pun intended), righty-hitting outfielders like this don't tend to turn into impact players. While Burress is definitely a good athlete and more explosive than a lot of hitters his size, nothing but his surface-level stats indicate he's an elite player. His contact, chase, and measured power are all closer to the college average, it's just that Burress' ultra-short levers allow him to be on time to pull balls in play straight down the left field line a lot of the time. Burress runs well enough to try and develop in center field, but he's not a lock to stay there. Here he's projected to center not because of enthusiasm that he'll be great there, but because it's the position at which his offense has the best chance of profiling. Burress' performance has been an outlier, but he doesn't pass the visual scouting smell test to that degree, and here he's assessed more as a comp round prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: A .334/.407/.483 hitter in two years at Cal (and a .380/.442/.439 hitter across two seasons on Cape Cod), Advincula transferred to Georgia Tech for his draft year. He's got one of the better pure hit tools in the 2026 draft, tracking pitches like a hawk and moving his barrel all over the zone to spoil tough pitches and slice singles and doubles into play. He's a chase-prone hitter who offers at too many secondary pitches below the zone, but Advincula finds a way to put the barrel on them anyway. Though he has a slasher's approach to hitting, Advincula isn't a little guy, he's an even six feet tall with below-average raw power. It's no big juice, but it's enough not to drag down the way his hit tool plays. Advincula has only played second base in college, but is athletic and rangy and might be able to run around in the outfield, if not play a second infield position. He has a shot to be an Adam Frazier type of everyday second baseman.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Broussard is a plus-plus runner and plus contact hitter who tracks pitches well and hits with a style that takes advantage of his speed. He's a good center field defender and should at least be a good fourth outfielder, but he's also one of the younger college hitters in the entire 2026 draft class and might yet grow into a sneaky amount of power.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Curiel was a high-profile high school underclassman in Southern California because of his tapered, projectable build, speed, and feel for contact. He didn't develop much bat speed or power by the time his senior year arrived and, slated to be a draft eligible sophomore in two years anyway, he matriculated to LSU. In his freshman year, Curiel slashed .345/.470/.519 and posted an incredible 95% in-zone contact rate. That mark is way, way better than anything Curiel was able to muster in high school and, because of the length of his swing, isn't something he projects to do in pro ball. Curiel's swing is mechanically similar to Roman Anthony's, but with just a fraction of Anthony's bat speed. He's late to the contact point against a lot of fastballs and tends to slice them the other way. This is a warning sign that a hitter lacks the bat speed to handle big league velocity, and this risk applies to Curiel. Though he played left field as a freshman, Curiel can really run and should be developed in center field as a pro. He's built like a premium athlete but doesn't have the strength to hit for power right now, and adding muscle will be a priority for him after he signs. If you're willing to take Curiel's freshman year contact performance at face value, then he should be a top 10 prospect in this draft. More likely, he's a speedy extra outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: A physical, mistake-crushing second baseman, Rembert slashed .344/.467/.555 with more walks than strikeouts during his freshman season at Auburn and .370/.414/.648 combined between Cape Cod and Team USA activity during the summer. He's a draft-eligible sophomore in 2026. Rembert's power is his best tool. He's a short-levered hitter but strong enough to have hit some big pull-side blasts in 2025, and though his swing is fairly flat, he seems to have feel for impacting the bottom of the baseball and generating loft. An outsized portion of his contact is both hard and in the air; his barrel rate was a little more than two standard deviations above he NCAA average last year. Because Rembert is a second base-only defender, he needs to get to that power in games as a pro. Some of his underlying data (his in-zone contact rate was a little worse than the NCAA average, more starkly after conference play began) suggests that his hit tool might not be able to sustain the 14% K% he managed in 2025. He's an early second round prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Lombard is an imposing physical presence, built like a young tight end and wielding some of the best power in the 2026 high school class, especially among the prospects who can play a valuable defensive position. But his contact rate on the showcase circuit (61% across 824 pitches in 2024 and 2025) is a ruby red flag because there aren't big leaguers with contact rates that low. One would need to project significant improvement in this area for him to be considered a viable big leaguer in any capacity, let alone the sort of star you'd expect a $4 million player to be. If by some miracle he turns into a decent hitter, the ceiling on Lombard is a 35-homer shortstop or third baseman.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Comeau is a very projectable 6-foot-4 lefty-hitting infielder whose slower twitch actions will likely make him a better long-term fit at third base. He showed good plate coverage during his showcase summer, especially for one of the younger, longer-levered hitters in the class. He's a graceful rotator who could grow into meaningful power if he gets stronger as he matures. He's an "Eye of the Beholder" over-slot candidate for the second or third round of the draft.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Brick reclassified from the 2027 group after he hit well with Team USA at the U19 World Cup in Japan. Though we have more limited and less reliable showcase data for Brick because he was facing a lot of 2027s during the last two years, the data we do have is very positive; an 83% contact rate on a projectable 6-foot-2 catcher. Brick moves the barrel around the zone well and his top hand drives his swing, giving him a shot to grow into a blend of contact and power. Brick has a ton of developing to do on defense. His crouch is high, and his footwork is erratic. Those don't add risk to his profile so much as they'll likely add time to his developmental journey.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Sims looks like an NBA wing player on the mound at an ultra-long 6-foot-8. He doesn't yet have total control of his body and scatters his upper-90s fastball all over the place. Even though Sims' body isn't often well-connected throughout his delivery, he's still touching 100 pretty regularly and will likely throw even harder as he continues to fill out, especially if he eventually shifts into relief. Sims' slider has big depth and finish in the dirt to his glove side; it's a future plus pitch and will probably be his best one at peak. It will be a challenge for a pro dev group to take the raw material here (freaky size, arm speed, and a great slider) and see if it can be polished ito a late-inning diamond.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Lord is a XXL righty with a good (albeit slightly slow) slider that features plus depth in the 77-79 mph range. For how big Lord is, he is very coordinated and balanced throughout his delivery and is likely to throw starter-quality strikes with his fastball and slider. His changeup flashes bat-missing sink, but only once every 10 or so attempts. His size creates downhill plane on his fastball that might make it vulnerable to damage if Lord only ever sits 93, but he's a good athlete for his size and should grow into better velocity as he matures. He looks like an innings-eating no. 4/5 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Wisener has one of the better breaking balls among the high school pitchers in the 2026 class, a two-planed sweeper in the 81-86 mph range. Wisener was sitting 94-96 for one inning at Area Codes in 2025 and then was sitting there again at the start of 2026. His fastball runs downhill and is going to play down unless he leans into sink. Wisener is usually very balanced and under control as he lands and finishes his delivery, which helps him locate the baseball consistently. Sharp command might help his breaking ball play like a premium weapon. He's an older seven-figure prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Volchko was an electric, hard-throwing high school righty from Northern California who struggled in two seasons at Stanford (he had an ERA over 6.00 as a soph) and transferred to Georgia. At his best, Volchko has a hairy mid-90s fastball, plus cutter/slider, and a firm, low-90s changeup with sink and tail. His fastball's movement does not allow that pitch to miss bats. The possibility that a change of scenery will help his stuff play better is why Volchko is speculatively ranked here.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: A 6-foot-4 human trebuchet, Volchko has an extreme overhand slot that helps his fastball carry and his curveball dive. He is lanky and long and might yet throw harder as he matures. And more velocity has already started to arrive, as Volchko was 91-94 last summer but was peaking in the 97-98 mph range during the spring of 2023. His delivery is violent about the head and shoulders, and his hat often flies off his head during his release. His mechanics and inefficient style of pitching are bullpen indicators, but he might end up with two plus or better pitches and be a late-inning weapon even if that's true. He's committed to Stanford.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Rose is a former catcher who has become a contact-oriented corner outfielder in college. Advanced bat control drives an offensive skill set that it diluted by Rose's tendency to chase. He could be a Harold Ramírez type of role player as a part-time corner outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: If Rose can clean up his defensive shortcomings (mostly his arm — per Synergy, he only caught three of 24 would-be basestealers in 2022), he has a shot to be an everyday catcher thanks to his precocious feel to hit. Lauded for his makeup, it's fair to bet he will. Rose is a willing and mobile ball-blocker whose framing and receiving are fair, while his throws to the bag tend to be in the 2.00 to 2.05 range with mixed accuracy. His downward bat path enables him to get on top of high fastballs but it also causes him to drive the ball into the ground a ton. He has the frame and in-the-box athleticism to do more damage as he reaches physical maturity, but it might take a swing change to actualize. Even a one-dimensional offensive catcher is a boon at the big league level, and while you have to project heavily on several aspects of Rose's game for him to get there, based on this young man's attitude and athleticism, it's not all that out of reach.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Malony is a viable defensive shortstop who has posted two practically identical underclass years at Oregon, with a .968 OPS in both campaigns. He's a strapping 6-foot-1, has authoritative hitting hands, and is often on time to pull. But Malony's style has him pulling off a lot of sliders, and he doesn't always track the baseball well, so his hit tool projection here is a good bit south of what it'd be if one were to take his 2025 data at face value. A viable shortstop fit, Malony projects as a utilityman in the Zack Short mold.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: A .347/.465/.614 career hitter in two years at Maryland before transferring to Texas A&M for his draft spring, Hacopian has a ridiculous TrackMan readout (95% contact rate versus fastballs in 2025, including on Cape Cod, 57% hard-hit rate during his sophomore season with the Terps). He is less toolsy to the eye, however, as his kind of odd, high-effort swing, medium frame, and realistic 2B/3B fit on defense make him look more like a contact-oriented utilityman. Hacopian didn't really hit for power with wood on Cape Cod (he slugged .364), which is more in line with the expectations set by his look as a hitter (middling size, strength and a lot of effort needed to swing hard). He has more of a late-second or third round feel from a visual scouting standpoint, but might be someone's data darling.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Bogenpohl is a massive 6-foot-6 outfielder with all-fields power and surprising feel for center field. A former two-way player, he broke Ryan Howard's freshman home run record at Missouri State back in 2024 before his numbers took a bit of a dip in 2025. Bogenpohl's lever length makes his swing a tenuous bet to hit pro velocity. He's already hitting a lot of middle-middle fastballs to the opposite field because he's not on time to pull them, and Bogenpohl's 70% contact rate is in a danger zone for a college hitter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Tinney is a monstrous 6-foot-4 catcher who had a power-hitting breakout as a sophomore at Notre Dame, where he slugged .753 before entering the transfer portal and heading to Austin. Tinney has plus pull power and, especially after conference play began in 2025, he was among the college baseball leaders in hard-hit rate. He struggled to stay with sliders on Cape Cod and struck out nearly as much as he did during the regular season in half as many games. Tinney has big hit tool risk and needs refinement on defense, especially his framing.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Grahovac is a physical 3B/OF who hit 23 homers as a freshman despite whiffing a ton. As a sophomore, he played just six games before tearing the labrum in his left shoulder, which required surgery. He's a high-variance 2026 prospect who had strikeout risk prior to the injury.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Bowen is a muscular, physically mature corner outfield prospect who is already generating plus bat speed. His swing is a little too awkward looking to accept that his showcase contact performance (76%, average) will hold in pro ball.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Hirschkorn's coordination for an athlete his size is remarkable, and the 6-foot-7 righty is able to locate his plus-flashing slider with mature precision and consistency. These gyro sliders enjoy a little extra depth thanks to his remarkable size, as well as his feel for spotting it. The rest of Hirschkorn's repertoire is below average, and his fastball was only sitting 93 with downhill angle last summer. There may eventually be an offspeed pitch here because Hirschkorn's feel for pitching is very special for a high schooler his size. Right now, he looks more like a Jonathan Bowlan starter kit than a righty CC Sabathia or anything like that.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Borthwick is a gigantic righty who drives way down the mound and misses bats with a plus slider. His build and delivery are very similar to Alek Manoah's, except Borthwick isn't quite that big yet. His slider falls off the table and he locates it well, just off the corner of the plate. It will be important for him to develop a third pitch in pro ball. His build, lack of current repertoire depth, and the effort in his delivery combine to create a good bit of relief risk here.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text:
An NPB first round pick out of Fukodai Ohori high school in 2020, the strapping 6-foot-2 Yamashita took an enormous leap as a "prospect" in 2023, his age-21 season and his first in Japan's top league after two years with Orix's farm club. He sustained a five-tick (!) fastball velo bump despite a huge increase in his season-long workload and posted a 1.99 ERA across 95 innings, though his breakout year was punctuated by a stress reaction in his back. His 2024 got off to a very rocky start, and Yamashita was demoted to the Buffaloes bullpen and then the minors, before he rebounded in a profound way down the stretch and struck out 56 guys in his final 40 innings. In 2025, Yamashita again felt back discomfort, this time during spring training, and missed all but the final few weeks of the season with another stress reaction. He looked sensational in September and October, working with three plus-flashing pitches and something approaching starter-quality command.
Yamashita's fastball is parked in the 95-97 mph range, and throughout the last three years has tended to peak in the 98-100 band depending on the start.
