mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Slider: 65 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 The July 2, 2017 international window famously brought Julio Rodríguez to the Seattle organization from the Dominican Republic. Signing from the same country for just $45,000, Hernandez did not enter pro ball with nearly the same notoriety, nor does he have Rodríguez’s sky-high ceiling, but he has the opportunity to give the class another notable name. The 5-foot-11 right-hander broke out at Single-A Modesto in 2022 and won California League Pitcher of the Year honors after leading the circuit in ERA (3.39), WHIP (1.14), batting average against (.193) and strikeouts (143) over 116 2/3 frames. The Brewers acquired Hernandez for reliever Justin Topa in early January, bolstering their pitching ranks. If there’s one thing to know about Hernandez, it’s that he throws a wicked 78-80 mph slider and he throws it more than half the time. The breaking ball sweeps well across the zone and led to him leading the Cal League with a 14.7 percent swinging-strike rate. The reason why Hernandez leans on his slider so heavily is likely obvious; his other stuff isn’t nearly as good. A low-90s fastball that touches 94 is average at best, and his lack of projectable size should keep more velo from coming. His below-average changeup makes him a rough matchup against lefties too. Hernandez walked 11.1 percent of his batters faced with Modesto, though Milwaukee officials came away pleasantly surprised by his ability to spot his pitches during early offseason bullpens. It’s still more likely Hernandez is headed toward a future righty-heavy role in a Major League bullpen, where his slider could be an even more devastating pitch.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An undrafted free agent out of tiny San Joaquin Delta junior college, Denoyer was more or less unknown when the Orioles signed him out of the Northwoods League in 2019. Thanks to the pandemic, he didn’t really burst onto the scene until two years later, when he opened enough eyes to reach High-A Aberdeen as a 23-year-old in 2021. Then, Denoyer was one of the organization's surprise breakouts in 2022, reaching Double-A in May and pitching to a 2.79 ERA with a 69-11 strikeout-to-walk ratio for Bowie. He made up some reps lost to injury with a solid showing in the Arizona Fall League before the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster prior to the Rule 5 Draft in December. The 6-foot-5, 225-pound Denoyer has a starter’s build and a three-pitch mix: a fastball that touches 95 mph and averages 93, a low-80s sweeping breaking ball and a splitter in the mid-to-upper-80s. That combination has allowed him to generate whiffs wherever he’s pitched, including 12.0 strikeouts-per-nine at Bowie and more punchouts (21) than innings (20) in the AFL. He did so while not issuing a ton of walks (2.1 per nine in ’22). So far most of Denoyer's work has come out of the bullpen, but he started in the AFL and pitched at least four innings in eight of his final 10 starts at Bowie. The solid control he’s shown would also seem to bode well for a future multi-inning role. While Denoyer’s ascension may have caught some off guard, his age, frame and repertoire suggest a potential big league swingman with a bulk reliever floor.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Denoyer signed as an undrafted free agent after the Orioles were impressed with his stuff in the 2019 Northwoods League. He spent most of his first full pro season (2021) as a starter before transitioning to a three- or four-inning piggyback relief role in 2022. He thrived, reached Double-A, and was impressive enough in the Arizona Fall League to warrant a 40-man add after the season. Denoyer's four-pitch mix features a fastball that has enjoyed a two-tick bump from 2021 and now sits 93-94 mph and will touch 96. The angle of his heater makes it vulnerable in the strike zone, so Denoyer often pitches backwards off his breaking balls to get ahead, then finishes hitters with a combination of high fastballs and diving splitters. It's not an efficient means of accruing outs but it works, enough that Denoyer has gone from "undrafted sleeper" to "high-probability big league contributor" in a span of three years. He's likely to debut at some point in 2023 and be an innings-eating mid-game option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he committed to the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Vela decided to go pro as a 28th-round pick in 2017, signing with the Padres for $125,000 -- the max they could give him without dipping into their bonus pool. After being stuck at the Arizona complex for three straight seasons, the southpaw showed signs of a breakout with 21 Single-A and High-A starts in 2021. He was just as good in his return to Fort Wayne a year later, posting a 3.83 ERA with 101 K’s in 87 innings. He made nine late-season appearances at Double-A San Antonio, where walks (20 in 22 2/3 innings) caught up to him in a big way. Vela’s improvements over the previous two seasons coincided with a jump in velocity, and he’s now touching the mid-90s and usually sitting around 92-94 mph. His low-80s curve comes with enough vertical break to make it an above-average pitch and a definite weapon against fellow left-handers, who can look foolish swinging over it. A mid-80s changeup gives him three solid options and helps fend off splits issues. Vela’s delivery can look too stiff, and he’ll often fly open as he releases, leading to several missed locations. He walked 12.5 percent of his batters faced in High-A last season, and that number exploded to 18.5 percent against the more patient Double-A hitters. Barring any significant changes in his age-24 season, those control woes are going to force him into a relief role, and it was notable that the Padres made five of his nine San Antonio appearances come out of the bullpen already.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: I'm not exactly sure what's going on with Vela health-wise. He was on the IL due to bone spurs in his elbow until a late-June rehab outing that lasted less than an inning, and he hasn't pitched again since. When I saw him during the spring, he was sitting 92, with all of his curveballs average or better, and several of them plus. When I went back to check his 2022 pitch data (there's nothing else from this season to go on yet), I was surprised to see his changeup missed bats at a plus rate last year. His changeup feel has outpaced its quality in my looks, but it performed in a big way against High-A hitters in 2022. There's a backend starter foundation here, Vela is just seemingly still dinged up.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Acevedo was the 23rd-ranked international prospect from the 2023 class and signed for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic. One thread running through this system is the advanced lefty outfield stick with middling physical projection, and that describes Acevedo. His polished hit tool drives an otherwise vanilla corner outfield profile. Acevedo's pretty swing has some natural loft without taking away from his ability to make lots of contact, and he's loose in the hips and shoulders. He might hit enough to be a good everyday player despite the other tools being middling. He'll begin his pro career as the DSL team's leadoff man.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: One of the more polished all-around players in the 2023 international signing class, Ereu has plus infield footwork and actions, and is physical enough to threaten the gaps on offense. He looks like a third round West Coast college infielder in his skills and build, and is perceived to have a high floor.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Pitchers who throw a ton of strikes and have plus changeups tend to find their way into the back of a big league rotation, even if it's just in the Tommy Milone Taxi Squad role. That describes Melean, who has a ridiculous downward drop and tail. Melean uses it to garner whiffs from hitters of both handednesses and it's easily a plus offering, and maybe better than that. His fastball and slider are more average, but his fastball command (he threw strikes at a 70% clip with his heater in 2022) enables Melean to set his slider up on the outer edge. He's a high-probability backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Rodríguez is the oldest player to ever appear on a FanGraphs prospect list at age 33, and he'll be on again next year because he had an arthroscopic shoulder surgery in early May and will likely miss the rest of the 2023 season. He's old enough to have signed with the Devil Rays (puts a dollar in the swear jar) back when they were still called that, a time so distant that Rodríguez's MiLB player page transactions don't go back far enough to include his signing date. Before this season with the Cardinals, Rodríguez had last pitched in affiliated ball in 2015 with the Yankees, who still controlled his rights (which is why the Cardinals Rule 5'd him from the Yanks over the winter). He spent the last several years pitching in Mexico and Venezuela, where his arm strength exploded. He was working 97-100 mph at times last August for Mexico’s Dos Laredos, up from the 90-92 range he showed during the 2022 Caribbean Series less than a year before. Rodríguez has a rock-and-fire delivery that was generating a 97-99 mph fastballs before the injury. He was mixing in a 93-96 mph cutter and the occasional low-80s curveball, bullying hitters with velo without a modicum of precision. It was a middle relief look and remains a really fun story, provided he can come back from the shoulder injury.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Of all the Rays pitching prospects on the complex in 2023, Hernandez has the best combination of present starter traits and physical projection at a lanky 6-foot-2 or so. He sits 91-94 with riding life and will peak in the 95-96 range while incorporating a slider with uncommon velocity for his age, a cuttery pitch that peaks around 89 mph. His feel for the breaking ball and a changeup are both advanced for such a young pitcher, and unlike fellow young righty Santiago Suarez, it's easy to envision Hernandez adding more velocity as his frame fills out. Upping the quality of his secondary pitches, which are currently succeeding more because of his command than pure stuff, is the developmental key here. We're talking about a teenage pitcher with medium physical projection, so we don't want go too crazy and stuff him in the 40+ FV tier or above just yet, but if there's a player in the Rays' complex group with a chance to really break out over time, it's probably Hernandez.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text:
Peguero has performed from a contact and on-base standpoint across two rookie ball seasons and has now added 15 pounds of muscle since signing. Yes, he's short, but Peguero's broad shoulders give him the foundation for yet more strength. There may be sneaky ceiling here if you're willing to project more power than you might otherwise forecast for a 5-foot-8 guy because of his athleticism and body composition, and in Peguero's case there's an argument you can. His lefty swing still presents barriers to actual power because it's such a downward-cutting, grounder-oriented swing. The short-levered Peguero tracks pitches deep into the zone and can make in-flight adjustments to breaking stuff, the sorts of hitting skills often present in Rays prospects. 
An athletic fit anywhere on the infield, Peguero's current lack of arm strength makes it tough to project him as a viable left-side infielder. That makes it much more important that his power develops (arm strength improvements for position players are very difficult to project) since we may ultimately be talking about a second base-only defender.  With two very important offensive pieces (contact and plate discipline) already in place for Peguero, there are pathways for him to be to become a 45-grade player or better (add game power in spite of his size, or add at least a grade of arm strength), but they are relatively narrow, low-probability paths.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: A torn meniscus kept Barete from playing during the 2022 regular season, but his extended spring training and instructs look were both very promising. The twitchy 21-year-old has an old school leadoff man's skill set, searing liners and hard-hit grounders to all fields, then digging for first with all-out effort. As intense an on-field competitor as there is in this system, Barete's on-field makeup fortifies scout confidence that he will find a way to max out his abilities and play a complementary big league role.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Carico has a lot of strong heuristic qualities (he's young for the 2023 draft class, plays a premium position, and until a March 2023 injury he was one of the best statistical performers in the draft class) but isn't as well-regarded from a visual scouting standpoint. While he showed a plus arm as a sophomore, Carico's receiving needed a lot of work, and he mostly DH'd as a junior. He isn't a lock to stick behind the plate but is definitely good enough for the Cubs to give things the old college try, because his ceiling is biggest if he becomes a viable defender. On offense Carico shows good plate coverage and power to both gaps. He picked up reps on Cape Cod after the season and before the draft and wasn't especially great there, but his statistical track record is incredible. He hit .354/.514/.690 during his college career. Carico lasted way longer than I had him projected before the draft (I had him 53rd overall, in the 40+ FV tier) which caused a bit of a re-evaluation here. He was still a good value pick where the Cubs got him and hopefully with good health he can return to catching.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: While still a work-in-progress as a receiver, Carico is a lefty-hitting catcher with an athletic swing and plus arm. He covers most of the plate, has power to both gaps, and if his offensive performance holds water against better pitching than Carico will see in the Atlantic 10, he might do enough on offense to be a primary catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: Looked meaningfully stronger during the spring of 2023, with fastball velos more often in the 93-95 mph range than the summer before. Upshot angle of heater gives it a shot to play at basically any velo in the 90s. Breaking ball quality is only okay, tends not to have nasty bite and depth but does have long break at times. Changeup is identifiable out of the hand right now, but he has feel for creating action on it. Relatively advanced fastball command and three-pitch foundation gives him a shot to start, breaking ball is more a potential big league weapon than a present one, and the cement is closer to dry on his frame than last summer.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Unknown to FanGraphs until he showed up at the 2023 MLB Draft Combine, Gonzalez had one of the better high school BPs at the event and arguably the prettiest swing. He's a loose rotator with lovely natural loft, though his swing does have some length to it. His swing path and length leads to a lot of oppo gap contact and a general inability to turn on the ball as of the 2023 draft. This creates some hit tool risk, as Gonzalez may not be able to get around on pro fastballs, but there's rare catcher bat speed here. His receiving is predictably raw, but the twitch and explosion from his crouch and Gonzalez's raw arm strength are both exciting. He's a young-for-the-class dev project with extreme risk/variance and uncommon ceiling for a third rounder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene starred at the 2019 Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad, propelling him to the Mets in the supplemental second round a year later. New York traded him to the Guardians along with Andrés Giménez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January 2021, so his pro debut came with his second organization. He has one of the higher ceilings among the system's outfielders but will require time to develop. Greene has some natural feel for hitting and makes consistent line-drive contact from the left side of the plate. He employed an extremely patient approach in his debut, drawing 35 walks in 43 games while repeatedly using the opposite field. He has enough bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he looks to turn on more pitches and launch them in the air. While Greene has plus speed, he's still learning how to get the most out of it as a basestealer and center fielder. He's smoothing out his reads and routes in center, where his quickness helps him recover from some of his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center field but precludes him from right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene's athleticism stood out on the prep showcase circuit in 2019, when he starred at the Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad. The Mets made him a supplemental second-round pick last June and signed him away from a Missouri commitment for $850,000. His only experience with the Mets came in instructional league before they traded him to the Indians along with Andrés Gimenez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January. Greene has the hand-eye coordination and line-drive-oriented left-handed stroke to hit for average. Scouts believe he relied more on natural ability than swing mechanics or approach as an amateur, giving him the opportunity to improve quickly as he gets more instruction in pro ball. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop 15-20 home run power, especially if he adds some more loft. With speed that earns plus and even some well-above-average grades from some evaluators, Greene is aggressive on the bases. His quickness helps him outrun some of his mistakes, but he needs to improve his reads and routes in center field. If he doesn't, his fringy arm strength will relegate him to left field.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Greene came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal and has an interesting blend of soft skills and frame projection. He's an extremely patient (arguably passive) hitter with below-average bat speed and power right now, but he is super lanky and loose and should grow into more strength and power as he matures. Greene's feel to hit is not as advanced as his idea of the strike zone, and because he's so skinny and young, he needs to use his whole body to swing hard and tends to take big rips right through the center of the zone without real feel for the barrel. Scouts don't think he can play center field, which makes it imperative that he start to get stronger and make more authoritative contact. Because he's treaded water in these areas for the last year, Greene is more in a late-projection flier category now than he is a high-ceiling, high-variance prospect. Were he a college hitter, he'd be set to go late in Day Two of the draft.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Greene came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal and has an interesting blend of soft skills and power projection. He's an extremely patient hitter with below-average bat speed and power right now, but he is super lanky and loose and should grow into more strength and power as he matures. Greene's feel to hit is not as advanced as his idea of the strike zone and because he's so skinny and young, he needs to use his whole body to swing hard and tends to take big rips right through the center of the zone without real feel for the barrel. He glides from gap-to-gap and is a viable center field candidate for now, though at his age and with his frame there's a chance he fills out in a way that pushes him to a corner, but of course that might come with lots of power. Still in very nascent stages of development, Greene is a slow-burning prospect who needs to get stronger to be a big leaguer at all, but he could break out in a big way if that physicality arrives.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Greene was a 2020 draftee out of a SoCal high school, and he's a frame-based projection prospect who may have had a bigger breakout senior year had the pandemic not squashed his pre-draft season. Teams and scouts who liked him best as an amateur thought he had pretty good feel for contact and were projecting on both his broad-shouldered, He's an average athlete who struggled to get over his front side on throws from the outfield during my looks at him in 2019. That's one of a few developmental things to watch as Greene traverses the minors. The big one, though, is his swing. As an amateur (again, going off my 2019 summer looks here) his swing was really long and needed pretty significant polish to be playable, but he wasn't loading his hands quite as deep during his first pro instructs, and he had a better Fall than expected. It's likely that Cleveland's amateur report drove their desire to acquire Greene since he was a recent draftee who only saw instructs action. And in this regard Greene isn't your typical Cleveland prospect in that he was a little older than the typical high school prospect and is already 19 and a half. However, since you're reading this list, you know they have a penchant for SoCal hitters. Some scouts do not agree with me about the swing. They like Greene's cut and had him in the late-first, early-second round mix. I had him in the third round as a higher variance sort, with the speed for center field (for now), considerable body projection (which might impact the range in center), and the need for a swing overhaul. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers general manager Al Avila and LSU head coach Paul Mainieri worked together three decades ago at St. Thomas University in Miami. When Hess had an up-and-down junior season, bouncing between the rotation and bullpen, Detroit saw him fall down draft boards and selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 MLB Draft, believing he could be a solid reliever. After dominating NY-Penn League hitters, his midsummer jump to Class A West Michigan flashed the potential the Tigers believed they could tap, including 22 strikeouts over 21 innings. The combination of Hess’ 6-foot-6 frame and a projectable power fastball tantalized scouts, even if the statistics didn’t back it up. Though Hess started for most of his collegiate career, he was more effective out of bullpen, including a dominant freshman season. His fastball plays more solidly into the mid-90s in shorter stints, pairing with a slider that works in the low to mid-80s with darting movement. He has a changeup but neither needs nor uses it much in relief stints. While his tall frame creates leverage, command has been a challenge throughout his career, including 11 walks at West Michigan. Like former University of Miami closer Bryan Garcia a few years earlier, the Tigers drafted Hess hoping his college experience would allow him to move quickly through the system and reach Detroit sooner than expected. Garcia moved from West Michigan to Triple-A Toledo in his first full pro season; the Tigers would love to see Hess do the same, giving them a middle relief or setup option in 2021.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The Braves tried to use the pool space they would have saved by signing Carter Stewart to an under-slot deal to land Hess in 2018, but he went back to school and got about a quarter million the following year. He has projected as a reliever for pretty much his entire life as a prospect, at times looking like a late-inning weapon. After reaching Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in 2022, Hess seemed tee'd up to reach Detroit in 2022, but instead he blew out during the spring and had TJ before spring training had even begun. Hess was back in time to break camp with West Michigan on rehab assignment, but he was shut down after just five appearances. Other teams' internal systems list his reason as returning to the IL as "right elbow surgery," but it's unclear if Hess has simply had a setback during recovery from the 2022 TJ or if he's gone under the knife again. A Tigers contact did not want to confirm injury specifics for this list. Healthy Hess can touch 97 mph, and his low-80s slider has good sweep to it and is frequently his out pitch. Hess also has a solid low-80s changeup, but he barely threw it in 2021. If it turns out he's had another season-ending injury, then he should probably just be in the honorable mention section of the list since a big part of the optimism around Hess was that he'd race to Detroit once he showed he was healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Hess reached Double-A at the end of 2021 and while he showed a continued propensity for missing bats, his combination of plus stuff and fringy command still indicates a future in middle relief rather than as someone who can be trusted in the later innings. With a long frame and violent delivery, it’s unlikely Hess will ever have anything resembling precision to his game, but he has the weapons to get hitters out simply by keeping the ball in the zone. His lively fastball sits in the mid-90s and can touch 97, while his low-80s slider has good sweep to it and is frequently his out pitch. A part-time starter in college, Hess has a solid low-80s changeup he’s confident using against right-handed hitters, but he barely threw it in 2021. His ability to throw strikes waivers from at-bat to at-bat, and declined overall in 2021, and he has a tendency to aim the ball when he needs a strike, leading to grooved pitches and hard contract. Hess will likely return to Double-A Erie to begin the year, and his future as either a legitimate bullpen piece or run-of-the-mill Quad-A arm-strength reliever will depend on just how much he can harness his arsenal.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Hess always had the stuff to start for LSU, but troubles with command and pitch efficiency led to an inability to maintain a rotation slot while there. Drafted in the seventh round in 2019, the Tigers liked what they saw in him during shorter stings and have developed him as a pure reliever. There’s nothing complicated about what Hess does. He’s a long-levered righty who comes in and tries to miss bats with a traditional fastball/slider combination. While he lacks true smoke, he still can sit in the 94-96 range with his fastball, which features good life, and his velocity-driven low 80s slider has missed bats in the minors. It’s an arm-heavy delivery with little load or lower-half incorporation and a tick of violence, and it’s hard to see him ever being in possession of anything resembling above-average command. Hess has had a velocity dip early this spring, but still could move quickly as a potential bullpen piece whose overall game falls a bit short of late-inning leverage situations. (Alternate site)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Solis moved faster than expected after signing for $450,000 out of Venezuela in 2016, reaching the Rookie-level Appalachian League during his pro debut the following summer. He overcame some early-season control issues to pitch well in Class A in 2018 until he blew out his elbow in August. He had Tommy John surgery and may not return to game action until 2020. Solis went from working with an 89-91 mph fastball when he signed to sitting at 93-95 mph and touching 97 with late hop and cutting action when he got hurt. He could add more velocity because he still has physical projection remaining and Tommy John rehab often leaves pitchers stronger than ever. His hard slider has the potential to become a plus pitch and he also shows promising feel for his changeup. His long arms allow Solis to create good extension and downhill plane on his pitches. He repeats his delivery well and had a history of throwing strikes until his elbow began to give out. If he can regain his health and upgrade his secondary pitches, he has a chance to become a No. 3 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Solis has been in the Astros system since 2017, but due to two Tommy John surgeries (one before and one right after missing the 2020 season due to the pandemic), 2023 marked his first taste of affiliated ball since 2018. Once on a starter track, the prolonged delay to his development over the past several years has caused him to veer into a relief-only outlook, and even that one is rather murky. He still features a four-pitch mix, but his slider usage is more than triple that of either his curveball or changeup, and he’s exclusively fastball/slider against right-handed hitters. In his return to the mound this season, he’s thus far walking more batters than he’s striking out, and with his runway shorter than ever, it’s becoming a question of whether he'll ever come close to actualizing the potential that once earned him Picks to Click recognition. If you think his walk issues are being caused by literally a half decade of rust, perhaps he's got some bounce back left in him.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Solis hasn't pitched in affiliated ball since 2018 due to multiple Tommy John surgeries and the pandemic sandwiched in between. When he has thrown, he has been exciting, if quite wild. He came out during 2021 spring training sitting 93-97 mph, and over the course of four total innings against big leaguers, garnered at least one swing-and-miss with each of his pitches. He also struggled badly with his mechanical consistency and command, and the big league varsity lineups shelled him. It feels like he's been a prospect forever, and the track record of players who go this long without actually playing is not very good, but Solis is still just 22 as of list publication and has big stuff when healthy. 
In addition to the mid-90s heat with vertical action, he has a power pitcher's overhand curveball to go with a firm, upper-80s slider and changeup. The movement he creates on the slider and changeup is mediocre-looking (note also that his 2021 spring spin rates, per Savant, were below my sourced numbers from '18, either because he was hurt or in anticipation of sticky stuff enforcement), but their shapes deviate enough from his fastball/curveball combo that they play well when located, though that doesn't happen regularly. The fastball/curveball, meanwhile, have more margin for error due to sheer nastiness. While Solis has filled out during the last couple of years, his lower half is still weak, which impacts his delivery's consistency and his command. At this stage, he is much more likely to return as a reliever than a starter, perhaps with a pared-down repertoire. He is a little over a year removed from the second TJ and theoretically on track for a late-season rehab, but the Astros don't really have any incentive to show the industry how he looks. If he comes back and looks great, they'll have to use a 40-man space on him or risk losing him in the Rule 5 to a club that likes what they saw, whereas if they slow-play his rehab and he doesn't throw, they get to keep him in the org anyway.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text:
Solis had Tommy John late in the summer of 2018, so he didn't pitch at all in 2019. He was a Pick to Click after the 2019 season in anticipation of him exploding when he returned from rehab, but because of COVID, he didn't pitch until the fall, only returning for 2020 instructs. Scouts who have covered Houston the last couple of years count Solis among the most talented pitchers in the org and think he has as much upside as guys like Forrest Whitley and Bryan Abreu, if not more. He came out during 2021 spring training sitting 93-97 and during the course of four total innings against big leaguers, garnered at least one swing-and-miss with each of his pitches. He also struggled badly with his mechanical consistency and command, and the Mets varsity lineup shelled him. But remember that Solis is still just a 21-year-old who has barely pitched the last two years. If you line up his broad strokes age/stuff quality/relief-risk profile, it lines up pretty closely to LSU prospect Jaden Hill, who entered the 2021 season as a likely top 10 draft pick (he recently blew out). Solis should be close to a healthy Hill on the FV continuum. 
In addition to the mid-90s heat with vertical action, Solis has a power pitcher's overhand curveball to go with a firm, upper-80s slider and changeup. The movement he creates on the slider and changeup is mediocre-looking (note also that his 2021 spring spin rates, per Savant, were below my sourced numbers from 2018) but their shapes deviate enough from his fastball/curveball combo that they play well when located, which doesn't happen regularly yet. The fastball/curveball, meanwhile, have more margin for error due to sheer nastiness. While Solis has filled out during the last couple of years, his lower half is still weak, which impacts his delivery's consistency and his command. If the command piece can be ironed out, Solis has a mid-rotation future. If not, it lies in high-leverage relief. (Update: Solis had TJ in late June. It's the second of his career.)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Daniels' loud tools stood out much more than his performance in his first two years in college, when he batted .176 with a 38-percent strikeout rate at Tennessee and .168 with a 44-percent whiff rate in the wood-bat Cape Cod League. He did an about-face to hit .357/.478/.750 with 13 extra-base hits in 17 games as a junior in 2020, though scouts still weren't completely sure what to make of him because the shortened season ended before he could prove himself in Southeastern Conference play. He became one of the highest-ceilinged players in the Houston system after signing for $400,000 as a fourth-rounder. Daniels wowed the Astros during instructional league, where he generated impressive exit velocities and displayed the best speed among position players in camp. The ball makes a different sound coming off his bat and he has well above-average raw power, but he still has to show he can erase a history of swinging through hittable fastballs and struggling against breaking balls and changeups. He spent the fall trying to simplify his right-handed swing, starting his hands higher to shorten his first move and elevate more balls. With speed that draws well above-average grades from some evaluators, Daniels could be at least at 20-20 player if he figures things out at the plate. Though he spent much of his final season in college at DH, he has the quickness to stick in center field as a pro if he improves his reads and routes. He has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: It's not as if hitting prospects with huge power and severe strikeout issues are rare, but what is rare is that Daniels barely performed in college but is still seen as a guy with huge power potential. In part due to injuries and then the pandemic, Daniels never played more than 35 games in a college season and never homered more than five times in a single campaign. He struck out roughly 40% of the time combined between his underclass seasons at Tennessee and the wood bat summer ball he played amid them, then exploded during non-conference play in 2020, walking as much as he struck out while slashing .357/.478/.750 for four short weeks. He draws some Giancarlo Stanton swing comps because of his closed stance/stride and tucked hands, and Daniels' raw power is only a grade shy of Stanton's. Daniels can also really run and has the Michael Vick, sportscar forward tilt and posture as he does. He'll run some plus times straight through the bag and some 70-grade times with the turn on his way to second base. The bust probability here is high because the track record for college hitters striking out this much and succeeding is very sparse, but guys with this kind of power/speed combo don't exactly grow on trees.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unsigned during the 2018-19 international period, Dominguez moved from Venezuela to the Dominican Republic to focus on improving his velocity. The venue change paid dividends when the Mets inked the right-hander just before his 18th birthday in November 2019. The 2020 shutdown kept Dominguez from seeing the Minors in his first season, though he did stay stateside that summer and work out with other Venezuelans at the Mets’ Spring Training facility. Dominguez remained in Florida in 2021 but was highly limited, making only 10 appearances (12 innings) in the Florida Complex League while the Mets had him focus on developing routines and getting in better shape to handle the rigors of a starting role. Dominguez underwent Tommy John surgery in March and is in line to return for 2023. There remains ample stuff on which to dream here. Dominguez stands 6-foot-5 and uses every bit of that size to throw in the mid-90s, touching as high as 99. The heater works well up in the zone too, when Dominguez is at his best with his command. A low-80s slider -- previously deemed a curve -- shows promising spin and break, but it lacks consistency compared to the fastball. He technically possesses a changeup with some movement, but it has a long way to go to become an average offering. Between last year’s and this year's surgery, Dominguez’s inexperience could mean there’s still room for ample growth, especially when it comes to his secondary pitches. But early results make the 20-year-old look more and more like a future reliever who relies on his velocity to blow by hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It isn’t often a great sign when an international player (outside of Cuba) signs a year after he is first eligible, but the plan has worked out well for Dominguez so far. Originally eligible for the 2018-19 signing period, the Venezuela native finally inked a deal with the Mets in November 2019 following a move to the Dominican Republic, where he focused on improving his velocity. Dominguez has yet to appear in a Minor League game but has some experience stateside after the coronavirus pandemic forced him and other Venezuelans to work out of New York’s Spring Training facility in Port St. Lucie last summer. The 6-foot-5 right-hander uses his size to his advantage to sit in the mid-90s and has touched as high as 99 in the past. The Mets have been pleased with the way his breaking ball – previously classified as a curveball but now looking more like a slider – has progressed because of the way he can spin it. It shows above-average potential with late break. The changeup made strides in 2020 and now shows promising movement of its own. The command needs to be the next thing to come for the tall righty, and New York hopes improvements with his release point will aide in that category once he is able to get in games more consistently. Dominguez has the pieces and physicality in place to be a starter. He just needs the game action to put all of those into place against actual opponents. If the command doesn’t quite come around, the velocity gives him a good shot at seeing Major League time in a bullpen setting, but as a pitcher still only entering his age-19 season, that conversation remains far off.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Dominguez was a known and not all that highly regarded pitching prospect at the beginning of 2019, when he was a 17-year-old Venezuelan righty with some effort who sat 90-93 mph. Then he was 94-97 at an event in the summer, which caused teams to reconsider him, though some clubs wanted to see it another time or two to make sure it wasn't an anomaly. The Mets moved quickly, but Dominguez's $95,000 bonus reflected some level of uncertainty. Between when Dominguez was waiting for his contract to be approved and the end of Dominican instructs, he continued to sit in the mid-90s and hit 99, flashing a plus breaking ball at times. He was then deployed with extreme caution in 2021, working in two-inning relief stints with significant rest between outings, sitting 94-95 with sink. He had Tommy John not long before the 2022 season and was still rehabbing as of list publication. Given how he was deployed before the surgery, it's fair to project Dominguez as a reliever at this point, but he's still a high-priority backfield target in case things have somehow taken a leap coming out of rehab.

He's only thrown a handful of times since the velo spike and not even all of the Mets upper level decision makers have seen him yet, but the talent level is on par with a compensation or second-round pick. There's just significantly more uncertainty and less track record than even later-developing players taken in that range, like Josh Wolf. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen battled the strike zone for two seasons at Fresno State before winning the Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he had one of the best fastballs in that year's Draft, he wasn't a consensus first-round talent, but the Cubs selected him 27th overall and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has had only sporadic success as a pro starter and spent six weeks in the middle of the 2022 season changing his mechanics at the club's training base in Arizona. Jensen owns one of the harder two-seam fastballs in the Minors, operating at 94-96 mph and reaching 98 with power sink, and he trusts it more than a four-seamer with more velocity and less life that gets rocked when he doesn't keep it up in the zone. He has yet to find a reliable complement to his heater, with his low-80s curveball serving as his second-best pitch last year. He also has an upper-80s slider and changeup, but the latter lacks movement, and he doesn't throw either for strikes. After shortening his arm action and stride and reworking how he uses his lower half in his delivery, Jensen gained a tick more velocity, but his secondary pitches still weren't effective, and he still struggled with his control and command. Chicago still believed in him enough to add him to the 40-man roster last November, but it may be time to move him to the bullpen. His path to the big leagues is as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen struggled to throw strikes in his first two seasons at Fresno State before dominating in his third, winning the Mountain West Conference's pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he was not a consensus first-round talent, the Cubs selected him 27th overall that June and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has continued to showcase power stuff and inconsistent control and command in pro ball while reaching Double-A at the end of his first full pro season in 2021. Jensen throws his two-seam fastball with atypical velocity, working at 94-96 mph and topping out at 98 with quality sink, and he trusts it more than a harder four-seamer that lacks life and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it up in the zone. His slider has gotten harder and sharper in pro ball, sitting in the mid-80s and touching 90 mph, and he has added a low-80s curveball to give him a softer option with more downer break. He's still refining a mid-80s changeup with fairly ordinary life. The Cubs still believe Jensen can translate his athleticism into enough control and command to be an effective starter. But he also has a funky delivery with a lot of moving parts that he struggles to keep in sync, preventing him from locating his pitches where he wants on a consistent basis. Most scouts outside of the organization believe he's destined for the bullpen, where he could focus on his fastball and slider and perhaps become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After recording a 5.84 ERA while battling the strike zone in his first two seasons at Fresno State, Jensen dominated in 2019, winning his final nine starts en route to Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards. He wasn't a consensus first-round talent but the Cubs made him the first Bulldogs arm selected that high since Matt Garza in 2005, signing him for a below-slot $2 million as the 27th overall pick. He comes with a good deal of upside but also a hefty amount of reliever risk. Jensen had the best fastball in the 2019 college class, working with sinking two-seamers and riding four-seamers while sitting in the mid-90s deep into games and peaking in the upper 90s. At Fresno State, he relied heavily on his heaters and his slider, an 82-85 mph offering that got sharper when he altered his grip midway through his junior season. The Cubs have had him develop a curveball with more depth to play off his four-seamer and also have encouraged him to use his changeup more often. Jensen's long-term role and success will come down to his ability to throw strikes. Chicago believes his quality athleticism will translate into control and command and enable him to remain a starter, though he averaged 4.2 walks per nine innings in college (2.4 as a junior) and issued 14 free passes in his 12-inning pro debut. Scouts outside the organization believe his long arm action and the effort in his delivery eventually will land him in the bullpen, where he could become a closer.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Jensen’s raw athleticism and arm strength have been the crux of his profile since he was an amateur, and they still are, though he hasn't really developed in a meaningful way. While he now has a five-pitch mix — including two distinct mid-90s fastballs — none of Jensen’s secondaries are especially good, and his command of them is poor; not one of his trio of secondaries (curveball, slider, changeup) garnered a strike percentage over the 50% mark in 2022. At the time of our last update on Jensen earlier this season, the Cubs were still using him as a starter. Since then, he has only been used in a relief role, first moving to the bullpen at Double-A. There, he improved his strikeout rate by more than 7% and cut his walk rate in half, but his command backslid upon a promotion to Triple-A Iowa. Lackluster command of his secondaries and a violently effortful delivery that features a long arm action were perhaps always likely to push him to the ‘pen. Even though none of those pitches are very good, it’s possible Jensen’s repertoire depth will enable him to work in a multi-inning relief role. He certainly has the stamina to sustain plus velocity for multiple innings, but most big league relievers have at least two plus pitches, and he has been searching for a second one for a while now.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Jensen is a plus-plus on-mound athlete with incredible arm speed for someone his size. His high-octane delivery features a huge, open stride and one of the longer arm actions in the minors, a violent visual look that pushes him toward the bullpen even though Jensen fills the zone enough to start, holds his velocity deep in games, and generates lots of groundballs, which are all starter traits. He's still searching for the consistent secondary offerings that would help enable him to navigate a big league lineup several times over, and a new curveball joined Jensen's hard, upper-80s slider and changeup this year. He misses bats at an average rate, each offering doing a little bit of damage in the Fall League, where Jensen sat 94-97 and touched 98. The second breaking ball has increased his chances of starting, but we still think Jensen will end up as an impact reliever whose repertoire depth lets him work with more than just single-inning length.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Jensen had one of the best arms in the 2019 Draft. Strong and athletic despite being quite small, he holds 94-97 deep into games and has touched 100. He can make his fastball ride or tail, and he uses it very frequently. His secondaries are not as nasty, but they're workable and flash average right now. There's a lot pointing to a relief role here because of the size, delivery (Jensen's arm action is very long), and the reality that two pitches need to develop for him to start, but the fastball gives him a chance to be a high-leverage or multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thomas was an infielder who only pitched a little bit when he signed with Cleveland for $200,000 out of the Bahamas in the middle of the 2016-17 international signing period. His elite arm strength landed him on the mound after he signed and was what the Pirates were interested in when they acquired him in November 2018 in the Jordan Luplow deal. He took a big step forward in rookie ball in 2019, but the 2020 shutdown seemed to impact him adversely as a move to High-A in 2021 did not go so well. Even though Thomas didn’t throw quite as hard in 2021 as he has previously, there’s still plenty of fastball to work with. He’ll easily sit in the mid-90s and regularly touch the upper-90s and has hit triple digits in the past, with his four-seamer showing very good life up in the zone. He has not made much progress with his secondary stuff. He does show a solid slider that can miss bats, but it can lose its shape, and while he has a changeup, it hasn’t developed much. While he’s an athletic 6-foot-4 presence on the mound, Thomas has struggled to repeat his delivery and his walk rate jumped in 2021. He’s still more thrower than pitcher and was deemed so far away that he wasn’t protected on the 40-man roster last offseason. His best track at this point is probably as a reliever, though the Pirates might let him keep going out as a starter so he can work on his complete repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: What seemed like a minor trade at the time has provided the Pirates with one of their most exciting pitching prospects. An infielder in the Bahamas who was put on the mound because of his arm strength by the Indians after signing him for $200,000 in December 2016, Thomas spent the summers of 2017 and 2018 in the Dominican Summer League and Rookie-level Arizona Leagues before being sent to the Pirates, along with infielder Erik Gonzalez, in return for Jordan Luplow and Max Moroff. He dominated the Rookie-level Appalachian League in his first year with the Pirates. It’s hard not to like Thomas’ combination of size, arm strength and athleticism on the mound. Thomas has continued to add velocity as he’s filled out his 6-foot-4 frame, and he averaged 96 mph with his fastball in 2019 and reached triple digits, showing good life up in the zone. He will need to rely less on that fastball and trust his slider, which flashes above average and misses bats, but can get slurvy at times, and he will have to commit to throwing his changeup. Thomas took a nice step forward in terms of his command the last time he faced real competition, cutting his walk rate tremendously. He needs more time working on his craft to become a complete pitcher, one who has the chance to be a dynamic starter if his secondary pitches continue to improve.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Thomas’ 2022 was a tale of two seasons. In April and May, he posted a strikeout rate of 15.9% and a walk rate of 14.5%; from June to September, he improved those marks to 28.5% and 6.9%, respectively. His fastball remains in the mid-90s but continues to underperform in terms of its bat-missing ability due to its hittable line. His low-80s slider, which has late, two-plane bite, has improved considerably and is now an above-average big league pitch. He also threw a smattering of changeups in 2022, though it amounted to fewer than a dozen across his 50.2 innings of work at Double-A, and the changeup didn't show up at all when the Bahamian took the mound for Great Britain’s WBC squad. But the improvement on his slider means he could solidify a role as a middle reliever, especially if the converted infielder is able to re-establish the fastball velos he flirted with a few years ago.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Cleveland for Jordan Luplow, Thomas is a converted infielder with the Vitruvian Pitcher's build at a strapping 6-foot-4. He quickly developed elite arm strength and we had high hopes for the eventual development of Thomas' secondary stuff, but as he approaches age 23, it hasn't gotten much better. He also lost a little bit of velocity in 2021 and was only sitting 95 mph. Thomas' fastball relies on arm strength to play. At this point, if he can develop one good secondary weapon and become a bullpen piece, that will be a good outcome. His slider, which isn't all that hard (it sits about 82) for a guy who throws in the mid-90s, is furthest ahead right now.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Cleveland for Jordan Luplow, Thomas is a converted infielder with the Vitruvian Pitcher's build at a strapping 6-foot-4. His arm action is very similar to Shane Bieber's, and it's very short for a pitcher with Thomas' shooting guard build. While his frame, athleticism and arm strength all remain elite, Thomas' breaking stuff remains inconsistent and unremarkable, and he still lacks any modicum of changeup feel. I'm still confident Thomas will end up with a good breaking ball, even if it only gets there because of either his ability to command it so consistently or through sheer velocity if he ends up in the bullpen, which will happen if he can't find a third pitch. He may need to experiment with a split if there's going to be one since the action changeup grip and release didn't seem to suit him in the Fall. A bullpen projection means Thomas would need to slide south on this list closer to Brailyn Marquez, who's closer to the big leagues. There remains huge upside here, in part because Thomas still hasn't pitched all that much, and the pandemic prevented him from doing so. At one point Jacob deGrom was also nothing but arm strength and an elite pitcher's frame, but Tahnaj has been hovering in that area for a little over a year now. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston in the 2021 Kyle Schwarber trade, Ramirez didn't pitch in 2022 and hasn't yet in 2023 as he recovers from a TJ. Recall that Ramirez also had arm issues throughout 2021, so it has been a few years since we've seen him totally healthy. Fully-operational Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he wasn't working up there as often as he could. His slider has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, Ramirez experienced an unexpected velo bump that began at 2020 instructs, where he was 92-94 mph and topping out at 96 without having lost any command. He was viewed as a changeup/command backend type before the velo bump. Still just 22, Ramirez's injury history is long enough to throttle him down into this FV tier and re-evaluate him when he's finally healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston in the 2021 Kyle Schwarber trade, Ramirez won't pitch in 2022 as he deals with an elbow issue that has plagued him for huge chunks of the last two years. Healthy Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he doesn't work up there as often as he could. His slider has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, Ramirez experienced an unexpected velo bump that began at 2020 instructs, where he was 92-94 mph and topping out at 96 without having lost any command, or having begun to overthrow his breaking ball or anything of that nature. He was viewed as a changeup/command backend type before the velo bump, which moved him into the 40+ tier entering 2021 and through the time of the Schwarber trade. In the little bit of 2021 that Ramirez did pitch, he was again sitting 93-94 mph. His injury creates a somewhat awkward 40-man situation, as Ramirez was a possible post-2022 addition, and his injury arguably makes him easier for opposing teams to Rule 5 stash on their 60-day IL. He's a candidate to be one of the prospects teams request medicals for ahead of the Rule 5.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Here's what I wrote about Ramirez last year when he was coming off a very successful 13-start stretch in the New York-Penn League (61 innings, 63 punch outs, 16 walks): "Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he doesn't work up there as often as he could. His slider is average but has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, there's no overt physical projection that allows us to get excited about Ramirez growing into a monster fastball, so instead we think he's a developmental fifth starter." Well, Ramirez started throwing harder. He was sitting 92-94 at Instructional League and was topping out at 96 without having lost any command, or having begun to overthrow his breaking ball, or anything of that nature. Changeup/command guys tend to outpace traditional projections and though the developmental setting could have allowed for a short-term velo bump that won't hold over a long season (I have Aldo sitting 90-94 in 2019), Ramirez is still on track to be a pitcher similar to Seabold by the time his 40-man deadline arrives. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez signed with the Red Sox for $550,000 in April 2018 -- a few weeks before his 17th birthday -- after getting some pro experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League. He dominated out of the gate, allowing just one earned run in 23 innings in the Dominican Summer League that year, and he was showing signs of a full-season breakout at Single-A Salem in 2021 (2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts in 31 innings) when he was dealt to the Nationals in a July deal straight up for Kyle Schwarber. He had been limited by elbow tendinitis at the time of the trade, and after doing some rehab work in the Florida Complex League, he underwent Tommy John surgery in spring 2022, meaning he still hasn’t pitched for a full-season Washington affiliate. Before the elbow issues, the 6-foot right-hander was showing improved velocity to the 92-95 mph range and was touching the high 90s from a high slot. He also sported a mid-80s changeup with good fade, and while lefties still hit him better than righties at Single-A, it should help fend off the splits from getting too extreme. An upper-70s curveball with depth rounded out his arsenal and gave him the three quality pitches needed to start. Command was rarely an issue for Ramirez pre-Tommy John, though that ability to spot the ball well all over the zone will be tested in his return. He has gotten back to playing catch this offseason, and evaluators will be paying attention to how well his repertoire returns when he retakes the mound throughout the summer of his age-22 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez had some pro ball experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League when the Red Sox purchased his contract for $550,000 in April 2018, just a month shy of his 17th birthday. He dominated the Dominican Summer League that season, giving up just one earned run in 23 innings, and proceeded to strike out 24 percent of the batters he faced at Class A Short Season Lowell a year later. The pandemic delayed a further breakout, but Ramirez showed promise upon his return in 2021 with a 2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts and eight walks in 31 innings at Low-A. Elbow tendinitis limited his first-half contributions, and he was traded to the Nationals straight-up for Kyle Schwarber at the Deadline in July. He rehabbed in the Florida Complex League late in 2021 and then unfortunately needed Tommy John surgery in the spring of 2022, forcing him out for the entire season. The 6-foot right-hander throws from a high slot and has seen his velocity pick up since entering the Minors to the point where he sits in the 92-95 mph range, touching the high-90s on occasion. The mid-80s changeup is his best secondary with promising fade, and it should help him fight rough lefty-righty splits. He isn’t afraid of going to an upper-70s curve that could be a solid third offering with its downward break. Ramirez’s best asset remains his command and ability to spot the ball both up and down in the zone. On paper, he has all the pieces to be a solid back-end starter, even if nothing is a true plus pitch yet. But the elbow concerns lower that floor.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Marceaux is still only sitting about 90 mph, but his secondaries are all pretty good and he commands them well enough to profile as a spot starter. Breaking ball shape and depth are Marceaux's most impressive traits, and even though they don't have especially different shapes, the gap in speed between his curveball and slider gives hitters different looks. His changeup has also taken a step forward in pro ball. He is currently in the Double-A rotation and is near-ready injury depth.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Marceaux has four pitches and, when you consider how much better he was at limiting walks as a junior, has a pretty good chance to remain a starter in pro ball. Both of his breaking balls flash plus, he has plus raw breaking ball spin, and his slider's angle has back-foot utility against lefty hitters. He needs to polish his breaking balls' shapes so those pitches are more distinct, as Marceaux will likely need to lean heavily on them as a pro, since his fastball and changeup are both below average. He's a high-probability depth starter or bulk middle innings reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marceaux jumped on the national stage as a Louisiana prepster who pitched for Team USA’s 18U squad in 2017, then stayed home to play for Louisiana State. He spent three years in the Tigers rotation and saved the best for last, topping 100 innings and finishing with a 2.54 ERA to help him land in the third round of the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. He hurled his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season, though he was only able to make two starts for Rocket City because of back issues. He returned to Double-A in 2023 and was traded to the Mets in June in a package for Eduardo Escobar. Marceaux uses a combination of feel for pitching and a huge competitive streak to succeed. His fastball plays up a bit because it has good run and he can command it to both sides of the plate even though it averages around 91-92 mph. He has two distinct breaking pitches, manipulating the shape of his slider and curve and keeping hitters off balance with both. His low-80s changeup has very good fade and is often his best secondary pitch. As evidenced by his 1.72 groundout-to-flyout ratio and just a 7.2 per nine strikeout rate, Marceaux is much more about generating weak contact than missing bats. The Angels feel he might have the best pitch execution in the system, which he’s going to need to continue to have success with his average stuff at the upper levels and reach the big leagues as a No. 5-type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler, Marceaux was one of many standout pitchers on USA Baseball’s 18-and-under team in 2017, a Louisiana area prepster who had an advanced feel for pitching with stuff that didn’t wow anyone. He came out of Louisiana State three years later very much the same pitcher, but with a much better resume. After adding a strong 2021 season to it, he landed in the third round in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft, but barely pitched after signing due to his heavy college workload. He jumped on the fast track in his first full season, however, pitching his way to Double-A in 2022. The six-foot Marceaux uses pitchability, command and competitiveness to get the most out of his four-pitch mix. His fastball averaged just a tick over 91 mph in 2021, topping out at 94, but it’s a successful pitch because it has good run to it and he commands it well. He throws both a slider and a curve in the low-80s, and both are above-average offerings. He has a fading changeup, also thrown in the low-80s like his breaking stuff, missing bats with all three and generating a lot of groundballs. Marceaux’s command coming from a simple and repeatable delivery, along with his makeup, are going to help him maximize his potential. The ceiling isn’t high, but his floor is, and he could move quickly and make it up to the big leagues as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A defensive standout during his days at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Meyer was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 167 Draft prospect in the 2018 Draft and went right around that spot in the sixth round (170th overall). He struggled offensively in his first two trips to the Minors but started to show some offensive improvements in 2021, finishing with a .251/.337/.324 line and three homers in 62 games between Double-A and Triple-A. He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster when he first became Rule 5-eligible last November. It’s defense, defense and more defense when it comes to Meyer’s profile. He regularly shows good hands in his receiving behind the plate and moves well back there as well, which comes in handy with blocking. His arm strength is at least above-average, and it plays up even more because of his ability to record impressive pop times. It’s a strong defensive base for a catching prospect. Unfortunately, Meyer’s bat hurts his case to play a more prominent role. He makes contact at a decent rate (striking out 17.9 percent of the time in 2021) and takes his walks (9.3 percent), but that’s about where the positives end. Meyer has a history of putting the ball on the ground more than half the time and isn’t a threat to post a slugging percentage much above .350. That said, backstops with Meyer’s glovework will always get jobs as backups at the top level, and as he heads into his age-24 season, the former Mustang isn’t far off from helping the Mets in that way. They can’t allow him to carry a roster spot, however, until he can be slightly better offensively.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The undersized Meyer is a solid defensive catcher with a plus arm, and he has long performed above the average of whatever minor league level he's been assigned to, mostly due to contact skills rather than any kind of power. Even though he's off to a slow start at Syracuse in 2023, Meyer still looks like he has average bat-to-ball skills and 30-grade power. It isn't sexy, but it's enough to hop around as the third catcher on someone's 40-man for a half decade.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Meyer is a fantastic defensive catcher with a plus arm, and he has long performed above the average of whatever minor league level he's been assigned to, mostly due to contact skills rather than any kind of power. The catching situation in crowded, but Meyer is ready to be the third catcher on someone's 40-man and should have a very long career as a backup/third catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Peguero is a lanky, relatively projectable corner outfield prospect with precocious bat-to-ball skills even though he clearly hasn't totally grown into his body. His hitting hands are quick, he moves the barrel around the zone, and Peguero cuts his leg kick with two strikes and lets his hands do the work, an advanced approach for such a young player. He is likely to move to a corner as he fills out since he's only an average runner right now, but he's initially being developed in center field. He hit .286/.355/.423 in the 2022 DSL with just 16% strikeouts and 6% walks. Keep an eye on the walk rate going forward, because that's a pretty low mark for that level of play. Peguero might progress more quickly than the other hitters in his class since his feel to hit is relatively advanced. He doesn't have gigantic tools, but he's a well-rounded youngster and among the most promising recent signees in the org.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A prototypical corner outfield prospect, Peguero is lanky, projectable and has fair feel to hit right now even though he clearly hasn't totally grown into his body. Peguero cuts his leg kick with two strikes and lets his hitting hands do the work, an advanced approach for such a young player. He is likely to move to a corner as he fills out since he's only an average runner right now, but he's initially being developed in center field.
