When he hit his way from High-A Greensboro to Double-A Altoona in 2021, finishing with a .939 OPS, the Bucs thought they perhaps had a steal on their hands. But his first full season at the upper levels in 2022 -- back with Altoona -- did not go nearly as well. The left-handed-hitting Fraizer still has the ability to hit the ball hard, recording high exit velocities when things are clicking. He really lost his approach in 2022 and it snowballed as he struggled, with the outfielder often trying to do too much. His swing mechanics also went significantly sideways and his tendency to cut himself off on the front part of his swing -- which didn’t hurt him in 2021 -- really caused him trouble against better pitching in 2022. Fraizer’s speed still plays well and he can steal a base, as well as play a very solid center field. He needs to simplify things and just let his natural ability and tools take over. The Pirates didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster last offseason and he wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 Draft. At age 25, the clock is ticking. He may have overperformed in 2021 and underperformed last year; the key will be in finding a middle ground somewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer didn’t have much success in his first two years at the University of Arizona, despite obvious size and athleticism. He was at the start of a breakout season as a junior in 2019 when he broke a hamate, leaving most teams unsure of who he was as a player. The Pirates liked his tools enough to take a flyer on him in the third round of that June’s Draft and he had an understandably rusty return from injury during his pro debut. Unseen by most during the pandemic, Fraizer took off in 2021, going from High-A to Double-A and earning a spot on the second team of MLB Pipeline’s Prospect Team of the Year. Even during his up-and-down days at Arizona, Fraizer has shown an advanced knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to work counts and draw walks. That continued in 2021 as he walked in over 11 percent of his plate appearances while limiting strikeouts, making consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. He changed his setup in 2021 with obviously positive effects, spreading out a bit more and staying more balanced, which helped him drive the ball and tap into his raw power. Fraizer’s plus speed is an asset on both sides of the ball, as he continues to learn the craft of stealing bases and covers a lot of ground in center field, where the Pirates believe he can stay long term, though he’s continued to get reps in all three spots. The Pirates saw Fraizer’s confidence soar in 2021 and now that he believes in his own ability to produce, he has the chance to continue developing into a big league regular.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Fraizer only really played consistently as a sophomore at Arizona, pencilled into the starting lineup just 23 times combined between his freshman and junior years. The latter was shortened by a broken hamate, but after posting a vanilla sophomore line, Fraizer went bonkers during his shortened 2019 and had an OPS over 1.000 in about five weeks of play. Several teams had him stuffed based on the pre-injury look, and he ended up going in the third round even though his career line was commensurate with that of a traditional fourth outfielder. His post-draft performance (.221/.287/.266 in the Penn League) was in that vein, too, though remember Fraizer was dealing with the backend of a hamate break, which can sap power output for months. Further obscured from evaluation by the pandemic and the loss of the 2020 season, Fraizer made his full-season debut as a 23-year-old at High-A Greensboro in 2021 and obliterated the level, slashing .314/.401/.578 with 20 homers before a month-long promotion to Altoona to finish the year. There's been a swing change here, too. Fraizer's stance has opened up, and his top hand seems to be more involved with a swing that now has more consistent lift and intent to do damage than before. Twenty pumps from a potential center fielder will get your attention, especially when they're climbing the minor league ladder as fast as Fraizer. His numbers against lefties are troubling, as is Fraizer's rather expansive, chase-prone approach, which is at least in danger of diluting his quality of contact. Staying in center field (it's going to be close — he's tightly-wound and has above-average speed but isn't a true burner and he's rapidly filling out) gives Fraizer a shot to be a regular, while settling into a corner gives him more of a platoon projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies gave Ortiz $4 million to sign at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period, the fifth-highest bonus given to an international amateur player during that period. Since then, he’s tantalized with his offensive potential, though not consistently. He wasn’t added to the 40-man roster in 2020, but then had a turn-around season with High-A Jersey City in 2021, got bumped up to Double-A and earned that roster spot. A return to Reading in 2022 saw some regression and he didn’t perform well in the Arizona Fall League. In 2021, Ortiz’s pitch recognition improved, as did his walk and strikeout rates, but in 2022, he struggled in those departments, whiffing in 32.7 percent of his plate appearances and walking in 8.5 percent of them. His high chase and overall swing-and miss rates kept him from tapping into his plus plus raw power. When he does make contact, it’s loud, and he still managed to hit 17 homers in 2022, mostly to the pull side, but the right-handed hitter is going to have to rediscover a better overall approach to use his best tool more consistently. Ortiz has proven to be a better athlete than many had expected and he’s a capable enough defender in the outfield corners, with the offensive power profile and strong arm to fit in right field in the big leagues. Whether he gets the chance to do that as a big league regular will be determined by his ability to make more contact at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz, who signed with the Phillies in July 2015 for $4 million, was not added to the 40-man roster in the fall of 2020 after a rough 2019 season and getting time in instructional league play in 2020, but he also wasn’t selected in the Rule 5 Draft that December. After really improving his conditioning, he had a big 2021 in a return to High-A, slugging .521 there to earn his first trip to Double-A. The Phillies saw enough this time around to add him to the 40-man following the season. While there’s still work to be done in terms of his overall approach, Ortiz’s pitch recognition improved in 2021, with better walk and strikeout rates. That allowed the right-handed hitter to get to his easily plus power more consistently, though there will always be a good amount of swing-and-miss to his game. Ortiz’s cleaned up body also led to better defensive play, including considerable time in center field. Long-term, Ortiz is destined to play a corner spot, with the kind of arm that works well in right. If the 23-year-old’s approach gains are for real, he could have the power profile for the spot as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz was No. 10 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list at the start of the 2015-16 signing period and received one of the year’s highest bonuses, getting a $4 million bonus to sign with the Phillies. Since then, he’s shown off his power, to go along with approach issues, while being young for his level. He participated in instructional league play in 2020, but wasn’t added to the 40-man roster in the offseason. There’s absolutely no question about Ortiz’s raw power from the right side of the plate, which is close to top of the scale. It helped him finish second in the Florida State League in home runs in 2019 as a 20-year-old, but worries about the swing-and-miss in his game abound. He’s struck out in nearly 32 percent of his plate appearances in his two years of full-season ball. He’s had a tendency to chase breaking stuff out of the zone in particular and he has worked on shortening his swing a bit, with the Phillies preaching that he’s strong enough with above-average bat speed that the power will come naturally with more contact. The 6-foot-3 Ortiz is a much better athlete than anyone anticipated and moves very well in the outfield, seeing some time in center field in 2019. With a plus arm and that power, he still could develop into a run-producing right fielder type, but he’s going to have to prove he can cut down on the K’s first.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Ortiz repeated High-A to start 2021, the same level where he hit about 20 bombs but reached base at a sub-.300 clip in '19. Now 22, he dominated there (.262/.358/.521, though with a 28% K% and .378 BABIP) while continuing to play defense in the outfield, including part-time in center field. He still hasn't played first base in an affiliated game, so while we've had Ortiz projected there since the day he signed, now that he's on the 40-man roster it's time to change course and project him to the outfield. While staying there lowers the offensive bar Ortiz would need to clear to profile as a big leaguer, his hit tool is still below what we think fits in an everyday capacity in the outfield. We liken Ortiz to the Kyle Blanks/Christian Walker-type hitters in the Quad-A/low-end corner area, the sorts of bats who tend to find roster equilibrium in an org that has a playing time opportunity rather than forcing their way into their parent club's plans.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Ortiz's report: 1B/DH profiles like this need to perform on paper. Ortiz was passed over in the 2020 Rule 5 and needs to hit from the minor league starting gun this year to stay alive. He finished second in the Florida State League in homers but still managed to end the year with an overall batting line below the league's average. He's more svelte than he was as an amateur, and while he's still big-bodied, he's stronger than he is soft. He even got a little bit of run in center field last year, but at age 22, Ortiz is built like José Abreu is right now and is probably destined for first base. I once thought a DH/1B future was a lock, but Ortiz has stayed in the outfield to this point, so I have no idea what kind of infield hands he has. The power gives him a real shot to be a regular, and while the peripherals make him very scary, Ortiz gets some grace for being 20 in the Florida State League in 2019 even though he had a sub-.300 OBP. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The vast majority of players to make it to the big leagues from New Hampshire have been pitchers, though Ryan McKenna has spent time in the Orioles' outfield after being a 2015 fourth-round pick out of high school. Lavigne would like to be the next Granite State prep bat to make it. The Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million as a Competitive Balance Round A pick in 2018, then saw him have a tremendous pro debut that summer. It’s taken him a while to find his footing since then, though he started figuring some things out in 2021 and hit his way to Double-A for the first time in 2022, finishing things off with a solid Arizona Fall League showing. Lavigne entered pro ball with a definite hit-over-power profile, but he got into trouble when he started to try to sell out for power too much. He got back to a better overall approach in 2022, drawing more walks and showing the ability to make more consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. The power is going to come thanks to his natural strength and bat speed and the Rockies were pleased with how he adjusted to the Eastern League after his promotion. It’s possible Lavigne will never be more than a fringy defender at first base, one with a below-average arm, but this part of his game improved as well in 2022. He’s a tireless worker, one who will be at the upper levels of the Rockies' system at age 23 for most of the 2023 season and who still has the potential to develop into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavigne was a bit of a pop-up prospect from the New Hampshire high school ranks, not exactly a hotbed for professional talent, as the 2018 Draft approached. He landed in the Competitive Balance Round A and the Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million. It seemed like a very shrewd investment based on his pro debut in the Pioneer League (.996 OPS), but he really seemed lost for most of his first full season of pro ball in 2019. A return to Low-A in 2021 was a good move as he righted the ship and earned a bump up a level for the final two months of the season. When he was struggling, Lavigne was getting caught between the hitter he’d always been, one focused on contact with excellent plate discipline, and the one he thought he had to be, a power-hitting first baseman. He sold out for power too much in 2019 and got out of his approach. He’s still learning to catch the ball out front and let his natural strength do its thing. In 2021, he started getting much more comfortable with his swing and was adjusting to velocity more consistently. Lavigne is going to have to hit to keep moving up, as he’s a fringy defender at first base with a below-average arm. He’s grown into more of a leadership role, and the Rockies noticed that after he helped Fresno win a ton of games in Low-A, he led Spokane to the High-A West playoffs as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-handed pitcher Chris Carpenter is the highest-drafted high school player ever from New Hampshire, taken No. 15 overall back in 1993. After popping up to land in the Competitive Balance Round A in 2018, Lavigne became just the second prep player since Carpenter (Jeff Locke, 2006) to get taken in the top two rounds from the Granite State. He made a very strong first impression when he posted a .996 OPS in his pro debut, but struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2019, though the Rockies were pleased with his adjustments in instructional league play in 2020. At his best, Lavigne’s strengths as a left-handed hitter are his knowledge of the strike zone and his ability to drive the ball to all fields. While he drew a lot of walks in 2019, he was too passive at the plate and missed too many good pitches to hit. He also got pull-happy and tried to sell out for power, leading to a spike in strikeouts, instead of just letting his natural strength and bat speed do the work. At instructs, he looked more like the 2018 version than the lost ’19 edition, making more hard contact and using the entire field more consistently. It will be Lavigne’s bat that will carry him to the big leagues, as he’s definitely a first baseman only with a below-average arm. The Rockies are optimistic he righted the ship last fall and hope the reps of a full season will fully get him back on track.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Lavigne still has a sound approach, a big, strong frame, and a good-looking uppercut swing, but his bat path is grooved and the scouts who saw him at instructs have concerns about how much contact he's capable of making. His swing enables him to turn on fastballs left up and in, which is atypical for a hitter this size, but he struggles to connect with stuff up and away from him and that's where a lot of fastballs live nowadays. His age, approach, present power, and frame have me holding over his FV from last year but this is a prospect whose 2021 on-paper performance feels pretty important. We still don't have a big leaguer born in New Hampshire. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Valerio has a .302/.399/.443 career line with more walks than strikeouts up through High-A, and he plays an up-the-middle position. Yes, Valerio is small, listed at just 5-foot-7, 165 pounds, but his swing is balanced, and he maintains barrel accuracy despite a high level of effort. Plus, his short levers enable him to get on top of fastballs that many hitters cannot. Based on Valerio's level of in-the-box athleticism, I have big belief in his hit tool, and don't think he is going to bottom out due to a lack of physicality. Landlocked at second base, it's possible Valerio ends up with a trajectory similar to César Hernández's, where at times his lack of versatility puts pressure on other elements of a team's roster.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Valerio (acquired from the Mets in the Keon Broxton deal) is a compact infielder with excellent feel for contact. He has a big, slow leg kick and takes a lot of high-effort swings but it doesn't undermine his ability to put the bat on the ball, and he's currently among the minor league leaders in swinging strike rate. Valerio is neither especially strong nor especially projectable, and he's a better long-term fit at either second or third base. Ideally a player falling in that range of the defensive spectrum would have a better shot to grow into power, and so Valerio projects as a versatile, 1-ish WAR multi-positional infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things were looking up for Valerio when he went from a $10,000 signing with the Mets in March 2018 to a piece in the Keon Broxton trade with the Brewers in January 2019 to an impressive full-season performer in 2021. Last season, however, changed that narrative when Valerio found himself challenged in the upper Minors for the first time. The Dominican Republic native slashed just .228/.313/.357 with 12 homers in 113 games at Double-A Biloxi. Even with that down year, Valerio still exhibits signs of controlling the zone well. His 16.7 percent K rate may have been a career high, but it was still well above-average by Southern League standards. A 10 percent walk rate was solid too and roughly in line with Valerio’s career marks. He’s added some lift to his swing in the last two years, and while that’s increased his homer output to 23 in that span, a relative lack of overall strength led to some weak fly balls and a .249 BABIP that dulled his whole offensive performance. Valerio needs to hit because he’s yet to lock in as an average defender anywhere. His below-average arm has made second base his primary position, and the Brewers started mixing in more left field last year. Average speed doesn’t help matters at either spot, though he is more aggressive on the basepaths than his raw wheels would indicate with 61 steals on his resume since 2021. Finding the perfect marriage between keeping his K/BB ratio in check and perhaps getting back to what he’s best at with spraying line drives could put Valerio back on track in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valerio signed with the Mets at 17 years old in March 2018 and immediately took to the pro game with a .319 average and 6.9 percent K rate in that year’s Dominican Summer League. The 5-foot-7 infielder caught the attention of Brewers scouts, and Milwaukee acquired the then-teen in a January 2019 trade for Keon Broxton. After a solid stateside debut in 2019, Valerio’s true breakout came at Low-A Carolina last season as he hit .314/.430/.469 with more walks (54) than strikeouts (49) in 85 games. A late-season promotion to High-A Wisconsin saw more power from the 20-year-old. One thing is abundantly clear in Valerio’s career -- he can hit. His career .302 average entering 2022 speaks to that, and his career 113/120 K/BB ratio highlights his plate discipline and bat-to-ball skills. It’s decent power for a player sized at just 5-foot-7, 165 pounds, given how much hard contact he already makes, but his 11 homers in 2021 likely will be his ceiling at higher levels. Valerio isn’t a burner, but he was an active baserunner in the lower levels (where rule changes encouraged action on the basepaths) with 31 steals in 40 attempts. The Brewers want to find Valerio a defensive home, and that’s their next challenge in his development. He has second, third and short on his Minor League resume, but his below-average arm should keep him at the keystone. Milwaukee hasn’t ruled out trying him in center either to see if that can stick. The Dominican Republic native has gone from a low-level trade pickup to a bat his organization wants in the lineup at every level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sequera, a $750,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2019, was one of the surprises of the Tigers' international crop in 2021, when he posted an .823 OPS and 23 extra-base hits in just 46 games to win MVP honors in the Florida Complex League. His promotion to Single-A Lakeland for 2022 left him a bit more exposed, but he still produced 28 doubles and 19 homers in 116 games and had a solid late-season run before fading in the final week. Sequera steps to the plate looking for hard contact to the pull side, an approach that leads to high chase rates and strikeout totals -- though he dropped his strikeout rate 7 percent from 2021 to 2022. He homered on 20 percent of his fly balls in 2021, an unsustainable performance, but answered in 2022 with more line drives and better pitch recognition, if not results. His athleticism has not translated into speed on the basepaths. He moves well at shortstop and has a knack for highlight plays but could eventually shift over to third if he continues to grow. While Sequera has slugged his way alongside Cristian Santana and Roberto Campos to give the Tigers a trio of intriguing international prospects on their way up the system, Sequera is the least heralded of the group. He might never be a high-average hitter, but if he can maintain power numbers, he could work his way into the Tigers’ infield picture. Advanced pitching at High-A West Michigan could temper his aggressiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Roberto Campos was the headline signing of the Tigers’ 2019 international class, Sequera was rather overlooked as a Venezuelan shortstop who received a $750,000 bonus. Despite missing the Dominican Summer League when it was canceled due to the pandemic, Sequera enjoyed an eye-opening pro debut by winning MVP honors in a Rookie-level Florida Complex League well stocked with prospects. He got extra bases on more than half his 42 hits for the season, including 11 home runs, and finished with a flourish, including four long balls, four doubles and 17 RBIs over his final 12 games. Sequera takes an aggressive pull approach at the plate that leads to high strikeout totals but consistently hard contact when he connects. He has enough bat speed to turn on fastballs with authority on different parts of the plate. He shows some pitch recognition, but like many hitters his age looking for power, will also chase breaking balls out of the zone. He moves well at shortstop for his size, especially on balls up the middle, and has worked to improve his range. He could shift to third as his body fills out. The Tigers once had a pipeline of talent coming out of Venezuela, including Avisail Garcia and Eugenio Suarez, but Sequera has the potential to be the best Tigers prospect from the country since those days. He got his first taste of full-season ball with Single-A Lakeland this summer and has shown pop, but little patience at the plate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Sequera is a barrel-chested teenage infielder who hit for impressive power on the complex in 2021. What he has in present power he lacks in long-term projection, though, as it's likely the muscular Sequera ends up as a shift-aided second baseman, or a third baseman during the bulk of his career. So long as he can keep the strikeouts in check, he has the pop to play a meaningful role at either of those positions at the very least.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Willis is an XXL high school prospect with a much more consistent delivery than most 6-foot-7 prepsters. He sits in the low-90s and has solid curveball feel, projecting as an innings-eating fourth starter. There was a point when Willis was sitting 82-85 mph as an amateur, then came back from ulnar nerve decompression surgery peaking in the mid-90s. He's currently dealing with an arm issue and hasn't pitched in 2022, making him a deep projection prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Willis is an XXL high school prospect with a much more consistent delivery than most 6-foot-7 prepsters. He sits in the low-90s and has solid curveball feel. He projects as an inning-eating fourth starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis hasn’t been seen a ton in recent years, both at the amateur and pro levels. He underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery in July 2020, which knocked him out for many showcase events that summer. The Cardinals still liked enough of what they saw to select the Colorado high-school product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft and sign him away from a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus. Another arm issue limited him to six appearances (four starts) in the Florida Complex League last season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander has plenty of size on the bump, so while he touches the mid-90s but sits more in the 89-92 mph range these days, there’s still hope he can add a few ticks of velo as he continues to age and mature. (He’ll just turn 20 before Opening Day this spring.) His curveball has long been his preferred secondary, and while he’ll flash an occasional good-looking changeup, it’s still lagging behind the other two offerings. One of the promising signs of Willis’ 2022 was that he walked only two of the 46 batters he faced in the FCL, notable for someone with so much missed time. The Cardinals took it easy with Tink Hence out of the gate too, then watched him blossom into a Top 100 prospect. Willis lacks Hence’s premium stuff and ceiling, but like the other right-hander, he has ample time to blossom into a quality starting prospect, especially if his pitches take a step forward the more he throws them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery on his right elbow in the middle of July 2020, knocking him out of many showcase events. Almost exactly one year to the day later, he was a Draft pick in his home state of Colorado. The Regis Jesuit High School product showed enough health and stuff in his senior spring to get the Cardinals to select him in the seventh round, and St. Louis coaxed him out of a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus, well above the $211,500 assigned to the slot. The right-hander, who made one appearance in the Florida Complex League, stands out for his size at 6-foot-5, and with some projection remaining, there is hope that he can add even more velocity. As it stands, he’s around 90-94 mph, occasionally touching a smidge or two higher. His curveball looks like a solid secondary already, and he sells a sinking changeup well with his arm speed, though it remains behind the curve. Willis remains a work in progress with his command, perhaps no surprise for such a young pitcher his size. Interestingly, he was the only high school pitcher selected by the Cardinals over last year’s 20-round Draft, so it’s clear they see enough moldable parts in him as he begins his pro career. It wouldn’t be a shock if St. Louis took a conservative approach with him early on, just as they did with Tink Hence in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rojas was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 prospect on the 2022 International Top 50, and he received a $1.3 million bonus to sign with the Padres on Jan. 15, becoming San Diego’s second-highest signee of the class behind only Jarlin Susana ($1.7 million). The Cuba native moved to the Dominican Summer League and quickly caught some eyes by walking more times (26) than he struck out (23) while hitting .279/.373/.357 over 46 games. To put that in further context, Rojas’ 1.13 K/BB ratio ranked 16th among 255 qualifiers in the DSL, and he has the advanced knowledge of the strike zone and short left-handed swing to back up those numbers. He also wasn’t afraid of using the whole field, going the opposite way roughly a third of the time, as he tried to protect the plate. Rojas’ performance came with zero homers, but there’s always been a belief that something close to average pop could come as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-1 frame. An average runner, the teenager wasn’t afraid to press the issue on the basepaths with 14 steals, though that will be tested as he gets off the complex. He played only shortstop -- and the Padres believe he can stick there -- but he has the arm strength to handle third, where he might be a better fit long-term. San Diego officials think they might be able to get aggressive with Rojas in year two because of his approach, and he could see full-season ball at some point before 2023 is up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An intriguing combination of power and speed, Rojas signed with the Padres for $1.3 million on January 15, 2022. The 17-year-old, ranked as the No. 24 prospect on MLB Pipeline’s International Top 50, reminds some of a young Yoán Moncada with his projectable 6-foot-1, 190-pound frame. Rojas, a Cuban native, already flashes some power and has a chance to develop into an above-average hitter with his advanced approach and plate discipline. Described as a pure hitter, Rojas has a quick, compact swing and uses the whole field better than most hitters in his age group. An average runner with a strong arm, Rojas will start his career at shortstop, but some feel he may eventually shift to second or third. He has an enticing skill set and there’s a lot to dream on, but he’s still a ways away.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A physical lefty stick who just signed in January and hasn't yet come stateside, Rojas' carrying tool is his bat. Though he's worked out at shortstop in the past, he may end up trending way down the defensive spectrum due to his size and lack of arm strength. On his way there, he'll likely become a versatile defender, with a combination of second, third, and left field looking most likely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon could have been a pretty high Draft pick out of high school in 2017, but he ended up being just a late-round flier by the Braves because of his commitment to Miami. After missing most of his freshman year with a knee injury, he pitched in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation over the next two years, with his feel enough for the Rockies to take him in the second round of the shortened 2020 Draft. He had a solid first full season in High-A but wasn’t able to build on it in 2022 as a lat strain kept him off the mound for much of the year. There’s confidence that McMahon will bounce back healthy and return to his right-handed pitchability ways. He can get swings-and-misses with all of his offerings, starting with a low-90s fastball that has solid action down in the zone. His changeup is his best secondary offering, with good arm speed and deception, and his slider was tightening up from the slurve he featured in college. While he doesn’t have a true plus out pitch, he doesn’t hunt strikeouts and focuses more on executing pitches. He is willing to throw any of his pitches with two strikes to put hitters away. McMahon’s ability to fill up the zone can hurt him at times because hitters know strikes are coming and he has been too predictable with his pitch usage. Using his changeup more against right-handed hitters, pitching backward occasionally and setting up hitters better in general will help him reach his high floor as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon went from the Philadelphia high school ranks into the University of Miami rotation, though a knee injury kept him out for the bulk of his freshman year in 2018. He pitched pretty well in the weekend rotation as a sophomore and showed his solid feel for pitching in the shortened 2020 season enough to generate some first-round looks. He landed in the second round to the Rockies, threw well at instructs that fall and had a solid first full season in High-A in 2021. His progress was delayed in 2022 as a lat strain kept him from throwing a competitive pitch until late July. The right-hander has a solid three-pitch mix with a very good idea of how to use his entire repertoire. He pitches to both sides of the plate very well, starting with a fastball that sits low-90s and touches a bit higher, thrown with good late action down in the zone. His changeup is an above-average pitch that he throws with good deception and arm speed, missing bats and getting ground-ball contact with it. His breaking ball can be a bit of a hybrid/slurve type of a pitch, but it’s trending in the right direction towards more of a tight slider. While McMahon can throw strikes and can keep hitters off-balance by mixing his pitches and tunneling his secondary stuff off his fastball well, he still needs to work on his command within the zone. His fastball can flatten out at times, causing him to get hit, but he has the pitching IQ to reach his ceiling as a No. 4-type tarter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A multi-sport standout in high school out of Philadelphia, McMahon was a solid pitching prospect in 2017, but slid deep into Day 3 of the Draft because of his commitment to the University of Miami. After missing a large chunk of his freshman year with a knee injury and serving as the Saturday starter as a sophomore, McMahon pitched very well for Team USA and continued to throw well during the shortened 2020 season. While he did get some first-round buzz, he landed near the top of the second round, where the Rockies went a bit over slot to sign him before watching him throw very well at instructs. During his time in instructional league play, McMahon really stood out with his pitchability, especially his fastball command. He can run it up to the mid-90s with late action when he keeps it down and he’s shown the ability to reach back for a bit more when needed. While he has good feel for spin, his breaking ball can be a bit of a slurvy hybrid, but should be tight slider with good late three-quarters tilt to it, a potential plus pitch. His changeup gets swings and misses as well as generates weak contact. In addition to the breaking ball consistency, he’ll have to continue to work on shortening his deeper arm action to help keep his stuff from flattening out. Thanks to his athleticism and feel for pitching, he has a very good chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: McMahon was a notable prospect in high school following his pre-draft summer, when he was sitting in the low-90s with a good slider. His stuff didn't spike during his senior year, so he ended up at Miami, where it did. He was consistently touching 96 or 97 mph during his 2019 and '20 outings with the Hurricanes, and averaged 92.5 mph both years. He sat about a tick below that on average during his 2021 pro debut, while throwing many more innings than ever before across about 20 starts. McMahon's fastball has tail and sink, and its movement mimics a still-improving changeup, while his slider remains his go-to finishing pitch. For how violent his delivery is, McMahon fills the zone with his fastball and is pretty good at locating his slider consistently to his glove side, although not always in a precise, enticing location. He often appears to be "underneath" his changeup and creates lateral action on it but inconsistent dive, though sometimes he actually gets impact dive on the change when he releases it late and it ends up glove-side. He's had some injury issues (knee tendinitis in 2018, shoulder soreness in '19) but McMahon has No. 4/5 starter stuff with a chance for more if the changeup keeps coming.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: McMahon was a notable prospect following his pre-draft summer in high school, when he was sitting in the low-90s with a good slider. His stuff didn't spike during his senior year, so he ended up at Miami, where it did. Now McMahon consistently touches 96 or 97 during his outings and sits in the 91-95 range, his fastball has tail and sink, and its movement mimics a still-improving changeup, while McMahon's slider remains his go-to finishing pitch. For how violent his delivery is, McMahon fills the zone with his fastball and is pretty good at locating his slider consistently to his glove side, although not always in a precise, enticing location. He often appears to be "underneath" his changeup, and creates lateral action on it but inconsistent dive; sometimes he actually gets impact dive on the change when he releases it late and it ends up glove-side. Yes, he's had some injury issues (knee tendinitis in 2018, shoulder soreness in '19) but McMahon has No. 4/5 starter stuff with a chance for more if the change keeps coming. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top pitching prospects in the 2020-21 international class -- and also one of the youngest -- Pinto didn’t debut until ‘22 due to pandemic-impacted issues in his first year and minor injuries in his second. The Mariners instead instilled a conditioning-heavy plan for the Venezuela native, which he ate up. And now that he’s better built up his body, the focus transitions to the Mariners’ mantra of 'Dominate The Zone.' Pinto’s numbers weren’t stellar in his first pro year, but much of that was marred by Jekyll and Hyde performances -- he would dominate for 1-2 innings, then lose it. Yet everything from the naked eye to the under-the-hood numbers suggest that he possesses above-average fastball velocity that can continue to grow. The true out pitch is his curveball, which generates comical swings and takes from his three-quarters arm slot. There’s good bend and depth, suggesting it can be a big league offering. He does a solid job of repeating his delivery, which also bodes well. For all these reasons, the lean and loose Pinto will probably require more patience because the delivery isn’t quite there yet. But if he can transform the dominant flashes into consistency, there could be big upside -- because the pure stuff is certainly there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitching prospect signed in the 2020-21 international signing period and basically the youngest, Pinto has yet to pitch in a professional game, mostly due to the limited baseball and physical resources where he was stationed during the peak of the pandemic shutdown. So Seattle instead had the 17-year-old focus exclusively on conditioning and getting in better shape last season. Scouts estimate Pinto is up to 6-foot-4 and really lean and projectable, with an incredibly loose delivery. He’s now hitting the low 90s with plenty of opportunity to keep growing into velocity. His best pitch is a curveball, a tight breaking ball with good depth that has a chance to be at least a plus pitch in the future. He already has solid feel for a changeup. Pinto is long and loose and does a nice job of repeating his delivery, which could eventually lead to better-than-average control and command. There’s a long way to go here, but with patience could come a very exciting left-handed starting pitching prospect -- especially since he’ll pitch a full season in 2022.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Mezquita has close to average big league raw power at age 20 and has gotten to it in games throughout the early stages of his domestic career despite some swing-and-miss tendencies. He's of medium build (and that may be generous), but not of medium bat speed and explosion, as his pull-heavy uppercut swing is built to do damage. Mezquita's breaking ball recognition is only fair. If you hang it, he will bang it, but he's also apt to chase ones off the plate. Though he's not built like a prototypical right field prospect, Mezquita's power over hit skill set fits in that mold.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mezquita decided to stick with the Braves and re-sign after his original $300,000 bonus in 2017 was nullified as part of the penalty for international signing infractions. His first two summers in the organization -- the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Gulf Coast League in 2019 -- were fairly nondescript, but his tools showed up a bit more consistently after the shutdown in Complex League play during the summer of 2021. He performed decently in his full-season debut in Augusta in 2022, but he scuffled with a promotion to High-A Rome. There are some raw tools for Mezquita to work with, though he’s still learning how to use them on a regular basis. He has good bat speed from the right side of the plate and raw power to tap into, but it’s yet to show up in games. He’s capable of hitting the ball hard but is often too aggressive at the plate, and while he’s willing to draw some walks, his penchant for swinging and missing continues to be a concern. Mezquita runs well and is capable of stealing a base, but he’s not electric when it comes to his speed and athleticism. That could mean that he won’t stick in center field long term, and while he has a strong enough arm for a corner spot, that would put much more pressure on a bat that has yet to come around.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Watters has a power pitcher's mid-90s fastball/curveball combination, and his curve has unusually high velocity for a pitch with vertical shape. He struggled badly with walks during his draft year in Morgantown, but it was his first season as a starter, and he had only thrown about 34 innings prior to 2022. He's likely a relief-only prospect, but he has two plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watters transitioned from pitching in the bullpen his first two years at West Virginia to starting in 2022. The stuff he showed in the Mountaineers' weekend rotation was tantalizing, highlighted by a 15-strikeout performance against Texas, and it was enough for the A’s to take him in the fourth round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Getting his feet wet with a couple of outings at High-A Lansing, he’ll look to begin his ascent as a starter through the system in his first full season as a pro. Watters is a strong presence on the mound at 6-foot-4. His fastball was up to 99 mph during his junior year and touched triple digits in his time as a reliever. He also possesses a plus pitch in his power curve, missing plenty of bats as a true 12-to-6 that sits in the mid-80s. There’s also a mid-80s changeup in there, though it’s less polished compared to his other two offerings. Command will need to improve for Watters to have a chance to start at the next level. While the stuff was high-octane in college, he usually had little idea of how to locate it. Given his track record as a reliever, there’s a strong chance he ends up back in the bullpen, where he can rear back and overpower hitters with two plus pitches.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Gold has plus bat speed and pull power but he may not have a position due to issues with throwing accuracy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers spent much of the 2022 Draft stocking up on college bats. Gold was among the most polished, a three-year performer at Boston College who posted a .940 OPS as a sophomore and .958 as a junior. The Tigers’ front office has changed since drafting Gold, but his combination of hitting ability and zone control fit the mold of hitter that new president of baseball operations Scott Harris has touted as the model for the organization. Though Gold struggled in a late-season stint at Single-A Lakeland last summer, his quick swing and line-drive approach to all fields is expected to translate well once he gets acclimated to pro ball and develops a routine. The bigger question might be power. He never reached double digits in home runs at BC, and just two of his 13 pro hits last summer went for extra bases, both doubles. He doesn’t tend to chase much. Gold alternated between second and third base in Lakeland, but his strong arm and body frame could work better at third. Gold turned 22 last fall, and the Tigers could aim to push him if he can handle pitching in Lakeland early in the season. He’ll have to fight his way through a crowded group of infielders in the Tigers farm system, but for an organization that badly needs offense, Gold’s hit-first resume should get a fair shot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners coveted Polcovich enough out of Oklahoma State that they used one of their five picks in the shortened 2020 Draft on him. The immediate transition to pro ball, however, was not seamless, especially after he climbed in the second half of ‘21 to Double-A Arkansas, where he slashed .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) and struggled to establish any confidence. But his ‘22 at the affiliate was a big turnaround. He raised his OPS by nearly 300 points and did so with a healthy sample size of 524 plate appearances. He also continued to flash his speed and has drawn praise as one of the best baserunners in the system. He also can play all over the infield and outfield, making him that much more valuable in the eyes of a club that puts a huge premium on defensive versatility all the way up to the Majors. Based on his trajectory, with a few hiccups followed by promise, Polcovich has drawn comparisons to Sam Haggerty. The big thing with him to continue climbing will be showing that his turnaround in ‘22 was legitimate and that he can produce consistently with the bat. The switch-hitter bats more naturally righty, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. And even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promotion to Double-A Arkansas in 2021 was an eye-opening one for the middle infielder, as Polcovich hit .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) in 149 plate appearances. The Mariners believe their third-round pick from ‘20 still had a solid process, approach and good pitch recognition, but wasn’t seeing results. As such, it took a mental toll that led him to pressing more. The club has chalked up those Double-A struggles to bad luck. He was much better at High A Everett earlier last season with a .980 OPS. Polcovich has a shorter stature at 5-foot-10, and while his tools aren’t incredibly loud, he profiles with solid on-base potential and he’s a switch-hitter. Though he bats more naturally from the right side, he’s been able to make enough contact from the left to stick with both moving forward. The power profile isn’t exactly strong, but he does have some extra-base potential within the gaps rather than over the wall. He’s also described as a solid runner and smart base runner. Defensively, Polcovich came up as a second baseman at Oklahoma State, but the Mariners have used him all over, including shortstop and center field. He’s dependable with an average arm yet doesn’t necessarily stand out at one spot over the others. The Mariners covet that kind of versatility, which could make him a valued commodity if his bat catches up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a former 10-year pro ball player, Polcovich spent one year at the University of Kentucky then moved on to Northwest Florida State College for two seasons and Oklahoma State after that. He began to catch scouts’ eyes after hitting .305 in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, and he was batting .344/.494/.578 with 19 walks and eight steals in 18 games for the Cowboys last spring before the shutdown, which was enough for the Mariners to nab him in the third round and sign him for a below-slot bonus of $575,000. The switch-hitting Polcovich bats more naturally from the right side, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. Overall, he has a solid approach, and even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential, though his power is more gap-to-gap than over-the-wall at this point. He runs well and is a smart baserunner. At various stops, Polcovich has played a number of positions defensively, including second and third at OSU and center field on the Cape. He’s dependable at a number of spots with an average arm, but he doesn’t necessarily profile at one defensive home. That could lead to a future similar to his dad’s, albeit with a bit more thump in his bat. He made a strong first impression on the Mariners during his time at the alternate training site last summer.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Polcovich checks a lot of the boxes we like here at FanGraphs. He's a short-levered, switch-hitting, up-the-middle player with above-average bat speed. He does not have great tactile feel to hit and just sort of rips the bat through the zone as hard as he can, so his likely ceiling had been as a versatile power-over-hit sort who could hopefully play a passable second base and a good center field based on his speed and athleticism. Polcovich has really bulked up, and now has a lower half that looks like it was designed by an Instagram algorithm, in Anthony Recker territory. His mobility has regressed and he's been limited to 2B/DH duty this year, and there isn't really a path to profiling if he isn't bringing defensive versatility to the party.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There is a difference between being short and being small. Kaden Polcovich is about 5-foot-8, but he's also pound-for-pound the strongest prospect I saw during minor league spring training in Arizona. Polcovich generates big power with a max-effort style of hitting and is a threat to do damage from both sides of the plate. He's also a plus runner with experience at many different positions, including second base and center field. So why was he undrafted for two consecutive years while he was at Northwest Florida State? The max-effort swings have driven swing-and-miss concerns, and while Polcovich has the range for the middle of the diamond, his defensive hands and actions are below-average. So on the one hand, he's a switch-hitting up-the-middle player with power, while on the other, he's a positionless player with strikeout issues. After two years at Northwest Florida, Polcovich was seen on the 2019 Cape, and at Oklahoma State early in 2020. He raked during a non-conference play (the Cowboys had a bold non-conference slate) and buoyed his draft stock into the Day Two mix. He's raw for a player his age, but Polcovich has impact tools. Even with a 30 bat, he projects to play a role similar to the one Sam Haggerty is playing now, expect with more meaningful power. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Shoemaker, a Canadian lefty, experienced a huge velo spike and was into the 93-95 mph range during his draft spring after sitting about 87 during the 2020 summer. He's been back in the low-90s early on during Complex League play in 2022 and remains an physical projection sleeper in the extreme. His delivery is pretty violent, and he struggled to get on top of his upper-70s slider during 2020 showcase play, which caused it to flatten out, but Shoemaker also has a ton of room on his frame for strength and, hopefully, velocity.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Canadian lefty Adam Shoemaker (11th) experienced a huge velo spike and was into the 93-95 range this spring after sitting about 87 during the 2020 summer. His delivery is pretty violent but Shoemaker also has a ton of room on his frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the first 10 rounds of the 2021 Draft, the Braves had a little extra bonus pool money to go after some talent on Day 3. That’s how they were able to sign Shoemaker, a native of Ontario, away from his commitment to St. John’s University, with an over-slot bonus of $477,500 in the 11th round. It’s been slow going for the projectable lefty, not surprising given how little he got to pitch in high school, both because of the weather and COVID protocols in Canada, spending the last two summers in the Florida Complex League. At 6-foot-6, Shoemaker is very much a \"baby giraffe\" type on the mound, one who’s thrown just 43 1/3 innings over his first two summers, missing time in 2022 with some minor shoulder issues. There’s plenty of ceiling to reach, with a fastball that touches 94-95 mph but doesn’t live in that range, a mid-80s slider that has the chance to become a solid offering and some feel for a changeup that he needs to throw more. Shoemaker is definitely still growing into his body, and the Braves are hopeful that added strength will lead an uptick of stuff. It will also help him repeat his delivery and command the baseball more consistently. He needs reps more than anything, as Atlanta was very cautious with this project, with the hopes that he can be a late-blooming left-handed starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big projectable left-handers are often a hot commodity in the Draft, but not as much when they can’t be seen. A native of Ontario, Shoemaker couldn’t pitch much and couldn’t be seen much because of strict pandemic protocols in Canada. He was able to get to the States a bit to show what he could do and the Braves thought his size and potential were enough to go over slot in the 11th round of the 2021 Draft for $477,500 to sign him away from his commitment to St. John’s. While there’s a lot of unknown about Shoemaker, one thing is certain: there is definite upside potential. The 6-foot-6 southpaw can throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range, shows a pretty solid mid-80s slider and does have some feel for a changeup, but hasn’t thrown it much to date. He attended Braves strength camps during the offseason and if he can keep becoming more physical, those strength gains could translate into more velocity. Shoemaker is a solid athlete with the chance to repeat his delivery and throw a decent amount of strikes. He’s pitched so little over the last couple of years that the Braves are sure to proceed cautiously, with a huge variance of potential outcomes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $195,000 out of Mexico in 2019, Melendez made a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League later that year and opened eyes by coming back from the pandemic layoff to strike out 38 in 18 1/3 Single-A innings to open 2021. He finished that season as a 19-year-old in Double-A, making him the youngest pitcher in the Texas League, and he retained that status when he returned to Corpus Christi for all of 2022. He battled his control and command throughout last season and has missed most of 2023 with elbow issues. Melendez has gained about 5 mph in fastball velocity since turning pro, now dealing at 92-95 mph and touching 98. His 5-foot-8 build and over-the-top delivery created an unusual look for hitters, and the shape and carry on his heater resulted in a 31 percent swing-and-miss rate on his heater in 2022. His 77-80 mph curveball and tight 82-85 mph slider had shown signs of becoming solid pitches in the past, but he didn't throw them for strikes or miss bats with them last year. Melendez's fading low-80s changeup was actually his second-most effective offering in 2022, though he doesn't trust it much. While his delivery provides a lot of deception, he also struggles to keep it in sync and doesn't have a track record of throwing strikes. With his size and control issues, he's more multi-inning reliever than starter, but his fastball is a true weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico for $195,000 in 2019, Melendez made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After his development was limited to instructional league in 2020, he opened last season by dominating Low-A hitters with a 0.84 ERA and 38 strikeouts in 18 1/3 innings. Just 19 years old, he earned a promotion to High-A in June and another to Double-A in September. Melendez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now operates at 92-95, though the shape and carry on his heater are more notable than its velocity. He backs it up with a pair of solid breaking pitches, with his 78-80 mph curveball slightly more effective than his 83-85 mph slider. His sinking changeup is still a work in progress but he shows some encouraging feel for it. Melendez has an advanced ability to sequence his four-pitch mix and the deception in his delivery helps his stuff play up. He might be more of a multi-inning reliever than a starter, however. He's shorter than desired at 5-foot-8, he doesn't have a track record of filling the strike zone and he has to prove his stuff will hold up over a full pro season.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Melendez, who looks like he'd fit into a child's XL t-shirt, has already reached Double-A as a 20-year-old starter and is punching out over 30% of opposing hitters while struggling with walks. He powers a mid-90s fastball right past hitters at the letters, aided by his lack of height and due north arm slot, which creates enough ride on the pitch for him to miss bats in the strike zone. While his other pitches flash bat-missing movement on occasion, especially his 12-to-6 curveball and his changeup, they are more consistently below average, though Melendez is still only 20, and only one of them needs to become more consistent for him to profile in middle relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s too early for the 2018-19 international signing class to have made a big league impact in Colorado, the Rockies' efforts during that period are showing up on the prospect landscape. Warming Bernabel is in the organization’s top 10 and Juan Brito was dealt to bring in Nolan Jones. Guerrero, who signed for $650,000 in July of 2018, is perhaps a step behind Bernabel, but has pretty much hit everywhere he’s been, from his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019 to his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021 and his step up to full-season ball in 2022. Since signing, Guerrero has displayed a knack for finding the barrel. It’s kind of a controlled aggression at the plate as he’s not one to see a ton of pitches, but he rarely strikes out, with a 15.6 percent K rate heading into the 2023 season. He’s slight and wiry, but he started tapping into some raw power more consistently in 2022, though it still remains to be seen how much strength he can add to maintain that extra-base authority. Though he’s just an average runner, Guerrero is an aggressive baserunner and can steal a base. He’s played all three outfield positions since moving from the infield in 2021, but is mostly likely a corner guy long term and his defense has improved markedly. That puts more pressure on his bat, but the Rockies like his confidence and his response to things like late-game pressure to make them a bit more bullish about his offensive upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies handed out nine bonuses of six figures or higher during the 2018-19 international signing period. Guerrero was closer to the top of the list when he received $650,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the period. Since then, he’s done nothing but hit, with a .319 average in the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut in 2019 and then a .318 average in his United States debut in 2021 in the Arizona Complex League. Guerrero has already shown a very good feel at the plate and even though it’s more of a “see the ball, hit the ball” approach, he’s limited his strikeouts and even drawn some walks. How much he can add muscle to his ultra-lean frame will help determine how much impact he has at the plate, with the Rockies expressing confidence he’s going to grow into more extra-base thump. Signed as a shortstop, Guerrero mostly played third during his DSL debut and shifted to the outfield in 2021 where he used his athleticism more than he exhbited any idea of how to actually play the position. He’s an aggressive baserunner who plays with super-high energy but has average speed, so a corner spot makes the most sense. He might just be scratching the surface, with the ceiling to eventually grow into a big league regular with an exceptional bat.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The spindly Guerrero has very precocious feel for contact and a swing that is much more elegant and precise than it is explosive. He can hit and has done nothing but since entering pro ball, slashing .319 with an OBP just south of .400 in both of his first two pro seasons. Narrowly built, it's not obvious that Guerrero will develop typical big league strength and power, especially not for a left field, which is where he's trending on the defensive spectrum. He's another very young 2022 40-man eval in this org, so he might move quickly if the Rockies want to stress test his bat to better inform their decision about whether to 40 him or not. He's a very interesting sleeper who could blow up if he comes to camp with more physicality.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The 19-year-old Batista doesn’t have dominant stuff, but he is a projectable youngster keeping his head above water in full-season ball, and has a chance to carve out a backend rotation spot down the line. His low-90s fastball touches 94 mph and plays best at the letters, living more off of angle than explosive movement. Batista also has an average, low-80s slider and a fringe curveball, both of which could add power as he continues to physically mature. His delivery is balanced and consistent enough to project Batista as a starter, though he hasn't shown any early indicators that he’s going to have special, role-cementing command. For now, he’s a well-rounded developmental starter, probably a lower-variance one likely to mature into a fifth to seventh starter type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players the Astros signed in their 2018-19 international class, Batista signed for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His career started slowly, with a pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League followed by the pandemic shutdown and then a 7.46 ERA in a brief stint in the United States in 2021. He took a huge step forward last year, posting a 2.67 ERA with a .178 opponents' average against and 127 strikeouts in 107 2/3 innings while earning a late promotion to High-A at age 20. Batista works at 91-94 mph and tops out at 96 with the projectability to add more velocity, and his fastball also features the flat approach angle with carry and armside run that's in vogue. His best pitch is a plus low-80s slider with two-plane break and he also throws an upper-70s curveball with similar shape. He shows some feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade but it's still a work in progress. More polished than most of Houston's younger pitching prospects, Batista has a sound delivery and generally repeats it well. He could have average control and at least decent command once he's fully developed. He has the ingredients to become a four-pitch starter and also could be a bullpen asset who concentrates on his fastball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bradley’s senior year at the University of Georgia got off to a fast start when he had a .397/.513/.730 line through 18 games, only to come to a screeching halt because of the pandemic. The five-round 2020 Draft left him unselected, but he was part of the Royals’ undrafted free agent class that summer. Bradley’s contact rates have fueled his rise, and he slashed .293/.382/.455 with 12 homers at Double-A in 2022. Bradley has a good eye and reacts well to where the ball is thrown, spraying the ball all over the field rather than pulling everything. He uses a slightly open stance and has a smooth left-handed swing, but he doesn’t garner a lot of power, even for an older guy with a bigger frame. He makes up for that with his situational hitting and awareness of the strike zone, lowering his strikeout rate to 18.3 percent in Double-A last year. Bradley has a high baseball IQ, leading to more stolen bases (19 last year) than his average speed originally accounted for. He’s likely limited to left field because of his below-average arm. Bradley has been a solid all-around contributor in his first two years as a Royal. If that continues, he could find a role as a fourth outfielder. Evaluators would like to see a little more power to give him a higher ceiling, but the hit tool could carry him far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates shortstop Oneil Cruz, Rafael Cruz signed with the Twins for $500,000 when the 2020-21 international signing period opened up in January 2021. He struggled out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League that year but righted the ship with a return to the DSL in 2022, hitting well enough to earn a trip stateside to finish the year in the Florida Complex League. Most facets of Cruz’s game are still pretty raw. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate and showed he could get to it with a .558 slugging percentage in the DSL last year. He had a tendency to try to hit every pitch hard, which worked in the Dominican, but he scuffled and pressed a bit when he got to the FCL and had to start refining his approach. There’s some swing-and-miss to his game, but more reps against better pitching should help him learn to make better swing decisions. It's a little unclear where Cruz will play defensively long term. He was a shortstop when he first signed, but the Twins moved him to third base before he even played a game. He has a very strong arm that fits the hot corner and he’s continued to work on his throwing and fielding accuracy. He’s played a good amount of first as well, and while it’s way too early to pigeonhole him, some see a future as a first-base/DH type. Wherever he plays, his offensive potential will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Consuegra for $500,000 in July 2017, and it took nearly five years for the outfielder to reach somewhere above the Dominican or Florida Complex Leagues due to various injuries and the 2020 pandemic-canceled season. Finally able to hit triple-digit games played for the first time, the Dominican Republic native broke out at Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .251/.324/.431 with eight homers and eight steals in 66 games before coming back to earth at High-A Brooklyn (90 wRC+), where the pitcher-friendly confines of Coney Island may have played a part. He got an 11-game look in the Arizona Fall League ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility but remained unprotected and unpicked in the early winter. What makes Consuegra such a promising talent is that he’s loaded up with tools. His raw power ranks among the best in the Mets system, and it was certainly notable that he finished with eight balls struck at 110-plus mph during his time in the Florida State League (per Statcast). He’s also an above-average runner who can cover good ground from any of the three outfield spots. His plus arm strength, capable of firing 95+ mph missiles from the grass, helped him pick up 13 outfield assists last season (with two more in the AFL). The separator will be Consuegra’s overall performance with the bat. His swing can get too long, and a 25.9 percent K rate in ’22 is likely only to get worse as he dives into the upper Minors. He’ll get much-needed reps to improve the bat in what is still technically his second full season in 2023, and the rest of the profile gives him a shot at being a fourth outfielder down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Atencio joined the Mets in July 2018 at the same time as top New York prospect Francisco Álvarez, but it’s been a much slower road through the system for the southpaw. The Venezuela native pitched in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and 2021, showing signs of a breakout coming out of the pandemic with 76 strikeouts in 48 innings during the latter season. He jumped to Single-A St. Lucie in 2022 and handled the assignment fairly well with a 2.27 ERA and 48 strikeouts in 39 2/3 innings, though he did walk 23 over that span. The 6-foot left-hander sat in the average velocity range with a 91-93 mph fastball, which did touch 95 at times. He worked hard to establish the four-seamer in his first trip to a full-season affiliate, throwing it 58 percent of the time. His 82-85 mph changeup could get fairly firm but still was average with an ability to get whiffs against righties, while his upper-70s sweeper has enough depth to be a putaway pitch too. Atencio’s 13.6 percent walk rate with St. Lucie marked a career high as he fought wildness. That’s a tough pill to swallow for a hurler without a true plus pitch at present. That said, the three-pitch mix he’s flashed over the past two seasons keeps his starting dreams alive. Despite being passed over for Rule 5 protection in 2022, Atencio enters his age-21 season with a limited workload on his arm, so the potential for further growth certainly exists.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At nearly 22, Jimenez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Blue Jays out of the Dominican Republic in 2015. He didn't do much to distinguish himself until the second half of 2019, when he logged a 1.87 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 33 2/3 innings in his first taste of Double-A. When Toronto opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, the Giants nabbed him in the Rule 5 Draft a month later. He was sent back to the Blue Jays last August and was once again left unprotected, leading to the A’s taking him in the 2020 edtion of the Rule 5. Jimenez can overpower hitters with his fastball, which parks at 94-96 mph, peaks at 98 and features above-average spin rates and riding life. He also misses bats with a low-80s slider with two-plane break. He uses a changeup with similar velocity to keep left-handers in check. Jimenez uses his 6-foot-3 frame and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill angle on his pitches. Though he has three effective pitches and throws strikes, he has been a full-time reliever since 2018 and he should remain in that role. The A’s must keep him on their active big league roster throughout 2021 and can't send him to the Minors without placing him on waivers and offering him back to the Jays for half of his $100,000 draft price.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Jiménez was picked by San Francisco in the 2019 Rule 5 Draft and by Oakland in 2020, and in both instances he was returned to the Jays, signing again with Oakland on a minor league deal this offseason. He tends to pitch backwards off his inconsistent, plus-flashing curveball. He's a likely up/down reliever with plus arm strength.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Jimenez was picked by San Francisco in the 2019 Rule 5 Draft and by Oakland in 2020, and in both instances he was returned to the Jays. Jimenez also signed late, agreeing to his first pro contract just before he turned 22. He also missed most of 2017 due to injury, and those sorts of factors combined to limit him to just 33 innings above A-ball even though he is about to turn 26. He sits 93-95, touches 97, the heater spins at about 2450 rpm, and Jimenez’s vertical arm slot makes it hard for hitters to discern the fastball and his power breaking ball from one another. He's in the up.down relief bucket.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf opened eyes when he hit 97 mph in his first appearance as a senior at St. Thomas High (Houston) in 2019, and he parlayed a strong spring into an above-slot $2.15 million bonus from the Mets as a second-rounder. He dazzled during his abbreviated pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he struck out 12 of the 33 batters he faced, and again in instructional league following the canceled 2020 Minor League season. The Indians acquired him as part of a four-player package in the January trade that sent Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco to New York. Adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and lowering his arm slot has helped Wolf’s stuff take off. Those changes increased the velocity and movement on his fastball, which ranged from 90-97 mph with armside run during the spring and averaged 94 mph during his pro debut. He has a second future plus pitch in a curveball that registers in the low 80s with 12-to-6 break when he stays on top of it. Wolf's changeup isn't as effective as his other two pitches, though he can flash some solid ones with fade and tumble that point toward it becoming at least average. Wolf’s athleticism, quick arm and clean delivery enable him to pitch to both sides of the plate and all four quadrants of the strike zone, and he earns high marks for his aptitude with regards to making adjustments. He has plenty of room still to add strength to his projectable frame and should continue to get better with those physical gains as well as his development on the mound.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Wolf came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal looking like a pretty typical seven-figure teenage pitching prospect in terms of size and arm strength, with slightly nastier secondary stuff. After he was dominant on the Mets backfields in 2019, he had just a fair '21 with Cleveland, struggling somewhat with walks and posting a 5.35 ERA. He was inducing a lot of groundballs, though, and is still a pretty projectable 21-year-old pitcher who already sits 92-95 mph, has a great slider (which he used a whopping 40% of the time in 2021) and natural arm-side action on his changeup. Wolf's delivery and rail-thin frame have long put him in a relief risk area, and the early-career walks and a "minor" injury that kept him from breaking camp to start 2022 (Cleveland did not reveal the specifics to FanGraphs) add to that likelihood. Based on the depth of his repertoire, that could be in a multi-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Wolf was a 2019 high school draftee from Texas who had a velo bump between his showcase summer and senior spring, when he was suddenly 94-97 with a plus breaking ball at times. He does not have your typical starter's build even though his on-paper measurables are pretty standard for a starter. He's very narrow and spindly rather than strapping and broad. Plus, Wolf's arm action is much longer than a starting pitcher's typically is, but that's something that Cleveland has been good at altering. That might aid Wolf's changeup growth. He has nascent feel for locating the change, but not for creating action on it. I think a path to starting more likely means a developmental course that ends with Wolf having two distinct breaking balls. Based on his frame composition, atypical delivery, and style of pitching, I have Wolf projected in relief, but he has high-leverage stuff. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carraway first piqued Dallas Baptist's interest as a center fielder and threw in the mid-80s as a Texas high school senior in 2017, so he wasn't a high-priority recruit and didn't attract interest from pro clubs. His velocity began to climb as a freshman but he was so raw that he made just two appearances and retired only one of the seven batters he faced. He made a huge leap forward as a sophomore, averaging 15.6 strikeouts per nine innings as the Patriots' closer and becoming the first player in school history to make the U.S. collegiate national team. The favorite to be the first reliever drafted in 2020, Carraway has a pair of overpowering pitches in his fastball and curveball. His heater sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with riding action, while his downer curve usually parks in the upper 70s. His pitches play up because they have high spin rates and he gets good extension in his delivery, and both can grade as well above average when at their best. As a 6-footer who lacks physicality and features a lot of effort in his high three-quarters delivery, Carraway is strictly a reliever. His control and command have improved in college but still need to get better if he's going to hold down a high-leverage role in the big leagues. He should be one of the first players from the 2020 Draft to reach the Majors.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Carraway is a prototypical lefty power pitcher, working up in the zone with his mid-90s fastball and creating vertical action with his sharp curveball. With his high arm slot, Carraway produces some of the best TrackMan/Hawk-Eye data on the planet, and one source compared his stuff to a left-handed version of James Karinchak. During instructs, his fastball sat 94-96 with a ton of ride to it, and his breaking ball is wickedly deep and pairs with that heater to keep batters confused. He pitches exclusively from the stretch and sets up with his back almost completely turned to the plate, which helps him hide the ball despite his arm action being on the longer side. He spent most of the season working out of the High-A bullpen before a promotion that saw him finish the year at Double-A. His strikeout rate was a stellar 34.7% at High-A but was bundled with a high walk rate almost as high (28.6%). In his small sample at Double-A (4.2 IP), he doled out more free passes than fans. As it stands now, his command is still the most significant hurdle to him leveraging his impressive two-pitch mix, and it's so rough at this point that it needs another full grade of development for Carraway to be usable at all. There is a rumor that some area scouts were intentionally tanking their reports on Carraway because they wanted to counterbalance what they thought would be overzealous analytical evaluations of his stuff. The eyeball scouts were skeptical Carraway would ever throw strikes, and they may still be correct.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Carraway is a prototypical lefty power pitcher with some of the best TrackMan/Hawk-Eye data on the planet. His 94-96 mph fastball has an exceptionally vertical attack with a massively rising fastball and ultra-deep breaking ball. It's high-leverage stuff. Carraway needs to polish his control a little bit to fully actualize it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
