Standing in at a listed 6-foot-4, Torres shows the most promise as a potential power bat with good raw pop, bat speed and natural strength out of his large frame. Those same long levers have caused him some issues in trying to sync up an approach at the plate, and he struggled with chasing pitches outside of the zone in 2021, causing even lackluster power numbers. The Cardinals maintain that Torres’ discipline could improve with more exposure to full-season pitching, and the lost pandemic year could have interrupted that necessary experience. Torres has been primarily a right fielder for much of his pro career because of just average speed, and he has the arm to play out there. He picked up six outfield assists from right in 2021 and nine in total across all three spots on the grass. While Torres will still only be 22 for the entire 2022 season, his position as a corner outfielder raises the need for him to start hitting more regularly and turning that raw power into in-game performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres impressed with Colombia’s 15-and-under national team in the Pan-American Championships and signed with the Indians for $150,000 in 2016. However, his prospect stock started to elevate in 2018 with a strong performance in the Rookie-level Arizona League. The Cardinals noticed the impressive stateside debut and acquired Torres and Conner Capel that July in exchange for Oscar Mercado. Torres raked during a short stint in the Gulf Coast League to finish 2018 and was rewarded with an aggressive assignment to begin 2019, though he didn’t fare well initially and was bumped down a level, where he got back on track. Torres got off to a fast start with High-A Peoria in 2021 and showed impressive strides in several areas of his offensive game. Torres, listed at 6-foot-4, has a projectable frame and enticing tools across the board. Bat speed and natural strength help generate power to all fields, though he sometimes has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone. He does show the ability to manage an at-bat and there is confidence that better plate discipline will come with time. While he has played all three outfield positions in his career, he profiles best in right field long term. There’s still plenty of room for growth, but he has the look of a future right fielder. The outfielder has limited experience in full-season ball and will need time to develop on both offense and defense, but the potential is there for Torres to become a regular contributor.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Torres' blurb as he was not at the alternate site: After Torres, who was acquired from Cleveland for Oscar Mercado during the summer of 2018, paved over rookie ball, the Cardinals skipped him over two levels, sending him right from 2019 extended spring training to Low-A in early-May. He struggled, striking out nearly 40% of the time, and after a couple of weeks the Cards hit the breaks and sent him down to Johnson City for the remainder of the summer. Torres bounced back in a huge way, hitting .286/.391/.527 in the Tennessee humidity. This is a traditional corner outfield projection prospect. Torres is an immense teenager built much like Franmil Reyes was at the same age. Torres has a chance to grow into similar power as he fills out, though hopefully he stays a little more agile than Reyes has and is able to play better outfield defense. Some of the swing elements (how long the barrel is in the zone, the stride length) may need to change to max out the game power, but there's middle-of-the-order thump here. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowles signed with the Angels for $850,000 back in July 2017 out of the Bahamas and it looked like a strong investment when he hit .311 with a .391 on-base percentage in his pro debut across two levels of Rookie ball in 2018. He didn’t perform as well in 2019 and really struggled offensively with a move to full-season ball for the first time in 2021. The fact that Knowles is a super high-energy player is a plus, but it’s also an obstacle. While he’s capable of making hard contact from both sides of the plate, he needs to learn to slow things down and rediscover his approach. Early on, he would draw walks and work counts, but that regressed in 2021, with his strikeout rate ticking up as he chased out of the zone too frequently. There isn’t much power in his profile, so he needs to get back to putting the ball in play and letting his plus speed wreak havoc. On the plus side, the Angels had encouraged Knowles to use that speed more aggressively on the basepaths and he responded by going 31-for-32 in stolen-base attempts last year. He’s a capable defender in center field, but showed that not only can he handle all three outfield spots, but he started getting reps at shortstop as well. If he can get back to more regular contact, he could be an athletic super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels handed out bonuses of six figures or more during the 2017-18 international signing period, led, of course, by the signing of Shohei Ohtani. Knowles, a toolsy outfielder from the Bahamas, got the third-highest bonus from the organization that period, $850,000, then made a strong debut in the United States in 2018. His 2019 wasn’t as solid, but he appeared to make some very good strides on both sides of the ball in instructional league play in 2020. While Knowles’ numbers dipped in 2019, he still did show off a good amount of tools to work with. He can make hard contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, and even in 2019, showed an ability to work counts and draw walks. Strong, but not big, he’s not likely ever to have more than fringy power, but should have the ability to drive the ball to the gaps and use his speed to his advantage. The Angels continue to encourage Knowles to use that plus speed more on the basepaths to become a threat to steal, something that improved at instructs. Knowles has the chance to be a very good defensive center fielder, one who could stay there long-term, and he’s shown the ability to play all three outfield spots well. He’s also gotten some time at second base, but it’ll be how much his bat advances that will determine if he can reach his ceiling as an everyday big leaguer.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Knowles has electric tools -- a plus arm, plus-plus speed, sneaky power for a guy his size -- and until 2021 has been very young for the levels at which he's played (2.5 years younger than average, per BRef), which puts his statline in better context. That's not to say Knowles' bat doesn't need polish. His left-handed swing (this system has a lot of switch-hitters) is pretty grooved and long, leaving him vulnerable on the inner third. I think he's likely to be strikeout prone from that side for good. From the right side, he might be able to do real damage. He has great feel for the zone, his swing is just limited from the left side in an important way. I have him projected as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a big senior season at Missouri, where he finished with a .930 OPS, Harris still didn’t get a ton of attention from teams. The Braves took a low-risk chance by drafting him in the 32nd round, signing him for just $10,000. He initially took the opportunity and ran with it, hitting his way to Double-A in his first full season of pro ball and performing well in the Arizona Fall League. The shutdown hurt his momentum and he didn’t replicate his success in a full season in Double-A, posting a .671 OPS in 2021. Harris’ calling card during that first full season was his knack for barreling up the baseball. He employs a simple right-handed swing when he’s in sync that leads to hard, line drive contact to all fields. He has some extra-base authority, with a little home run pop to his pull side, but he’s definitely a hit-over-power kind of guy. An average runner with an average arm, Harris has played both outfield corners as a pro, with left being a better fit. It’s more likely he can carve out a career as a fourth or fifth outfielder if he can get back to the offensive consistency that was his hallmark in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris didn’t have much to show for his first three years at Missouri except an uptick in power production as a junior. When he posted a .930 OPS as a senior, the Braves took a flier on him in the 32nd round and gave him $10,000. He hit his way across three levels, reaching Double-A, in his first full season of pro ball, and then performed well in the Arizona Fall League. He wasn’t able to build on that momentum when the 2020 season was shut down and he wasn’t a part of the action at the Braves’ alternate camp. More than anything, Harris’ feel for the barrel is what stands out. He has a simple right-handed swing that allows him to make consistent hard contact and send line drives to all fields. There’s extra-base thump in his bat as well, with home run power more to his pull side, and there could be more raw pop for him to tap into to all fields. Harris is an average runner and is probably best suited to be a left fielder if he’s going to be a regular at one position. He worked on his conditioning and his defense during the shutdown, which should help him maximize opportunities to get his bat into a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the fastest and most athletic high schoolers in the 2020 Draft, he also came with concerns about his physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), swing and strong commitment to UCLA. That enabled the Dodgers to take the local Southern California product with the 100th overall choice and sign him for a well-over-slot $1,622,500. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Low-A, where he hit .231/.323/.339 with a 30 percent strikeout rate and 12 steals in 76 games. Vogel's best tool is his plus-plus speed and he ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase. He's a potentially dynamic basestealer and could become a plus defender in center field once he refines his reads and routes. His plus arm is stronger than most in center. Vogel had an awkward load in his right-handed stroke when he turned pro, and Los Angeles is trying to help him smooth it out with some mechanical changes. He has good hand-eye coordination and can display electric bat speed at times, but he must get stronger so he can impact the ball more regularly. He did add 15 pounds this offseason, though he'll also need to develop a more patient approach to get going at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the better athletes in the 2020 Draft, he lasted until the third round because he lacked physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), missed a lot of the summer showcase circuit with a back injury and had a strong commitment to UCLA. The Dodgers pounced on the Southern California prep product with the 100th overall pick and signed him for a well over-slot $1,622,500. He was the youngest player (age 18) at their alternate site during the summer and performed well in instructional league. Vogel ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase and consistently displays plus-plus speed. He uses his quickness to create chaos on the bases and cover a lot of ground in center field, where his instincts could make him a plus defender. He also has a plus arm, stronger than most in center, and can play anywhere in the outfield. Vogel has both offensive upside and work to do at the plate. In addition to his quickness, which should help him get on base, he also can flash some electric bat speed and shows feel for recognizing pitches. He has an awkward load in his right-handed swing that can lead to swings and misses, however, so Los Angeles will try to smooth out his stroke and get him to drive the ball more consistently.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: My pre-draft report on Vogel was light compared to the kind of bonus he got from the Dodgers and what he looked like during Instructional League, so he's moved up a FV tier into the 40s. I initially had him in as a one-tool speedster with some crude bat control, but he hit the ball pretty consistently during the Fall, and against advanced pitching. I'm still skeptical about his power projection but with his speed and the defensive fit it enables in center field, all he needs is a vanilla blend of contact and power to be a useful big leaguer. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Intrigued with his upside, the Padres took Lawson 71st overall in the 2016 Draft and signed him for $1.9 million, more than double the slot value. The right-hander struggled to find consistency in 2017 and 2018, but flashed plus stuff and gave glimpses of his high ceiling. Lawson impressed late in the 2019 season and then dominated in the Arizona Fall League, but underwent Tommy John surgery in March 2020 and was limited to just 6 2/3 innings in 2021. Lawson sits in the mid 90s with his fastball and complements it with a mid-70s curveball that can be a hammer at its peak. Scouts believe the curve will continue to improve, but he's yet to show great command of the offering. Lawson also features a promising changeup that has quickly become a third weapon for him. An excellent athlete, Lawson has grown into his muscular 6-foot-4 frame. He's made strides with the consistency of his delivery, too, but he needs to cut down the walks. Lawson has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency, but the Padres feel he's only scratching the surface of his potential. Once he harnesses his talents and logs some consistent innings, he could develop into a back-end starter or a dominant bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres gambled on Lawson’s upside, giving him $1.9 million (more than twice slot value) after selecting him with the 71st overall pick in the 2016 Draft. In his two full Minor League seasons, Lawson never found any measure of consistency, with an ERA hovering around 5, but he continued to flash promising stuff and a high ceiling. His overall numbers are hardly indicative of his potential, and he showed signs of a breakout late in 2019 -- only to have his ‘20 campaign wiped out by Tommy John surgery. Lawson operates in the mid 90s with a mid-70s curveball that can be a hammer when thrown right. Scouts believe the curve will continue to improve, but he's yet to show great command of the pitch. Lawson also features a promising changeup that quickly has become a third weapon for him. An excellent athlete, Lawson has grown into his muscular 6-foot-4 frame. He's made strides with the consistency of his delivery, too, but he needs to cut down on his walk totals. No question, Lawson has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency, but the Padres feel he's only scratching the surface of his potential. Once he harnesses his talents, he could develop into a back-end starter or a dominant bullpen option.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change here as Lawson has been rehabbing from TJ: Some teams moved off of Lawson when he had some injury issues as a high school senior, but the Padres found themselves flush with pool money after taking underslot prospects late in the first round (Hudson Potts and Eric Lauer), which enabled them to give Lawson $1.9 million in the second, $1 million above slot. He filled out, began throwing harder, added power to a curveball that has ticked up nearly 10 mph since he was an amateur, and stayed healthy until May of 2019 when he was shut down and given a PRP injection in his elbow. He made a few Fall League appearances during which he looked fine, sitting 93-96 with the usual above-average curveball and sinking, mid-80s changeup. Then last spring, after a big league camp outing against the Cubs, Lawson was shut down again and eventually opted for Tommy John surgery in late-March. He had No. 4/5 starter projection before the surgery, which now increases the odds that he eventually works out of the bullpen. (TJ Rehab)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: He's been held behind his fellow 2016 class members because Barley's on-field decision-making and consistency are taking longer to cook. He still makes the occasional highlight reel defensive play, runs 4.10, or hits a 420-foot bomb and as long as he's doing that stuff, he'll have a home on these lists. For now, that Barley both went to an affiliate in 2019 and performed there was a big step. He needs to keep doing that. His physical ability is not in question; he needs to level up from a baseball procedure and consistency standpoint. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barley was known primarily for plus run tool when he signed with the Padres for $1 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2016. He was raw in every other aspect of the game, and that remains true nearly seven years later. The 6-foot infielder has yet to crack above Low-A ball, and it’s at that level that he spent the entire 2021 season. San Diego dealt Barley to Washington at the 2021 Trade Deadline in a move for Daniel Hudson, and while he managed only a .205/.312/.303 line in 33 games with Low-A Fredericksburg, he was still named the Nationals’ Minor League Baserunner of the Year with 12 steals in that timeframe. Barley uses a twitchy, uppercut swing designed to get the most of his above-average raw power. Sometimes, it leads to some impressive drives to left field. All too often, it leads to an unhealthy amount of strikeouts, specifically a K rate of 29.8 percent last season. The right-handed slugger did start to walk more in 2021, but it’s still going to take some significant improvements in his overall approach for him to become an average hitter. The speed continues to be dynamic; Barley ranked fifth in Low-A with 45 stolen bases in 2021. After their early looks, the Nationals believe their still relatively new prospect can stick at shortstop because of his range and strong arm, but developing defensive consistency will be key after Barley was error-prone in 2021. Perhaps the change of scenery is what will do Barley best, and Washington is ready to make him part of its rebuild movement. Considering Barley has been Rule 5-eligible and unprotected in each of the last two years, the clock is ticking for the 22-year-old.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There were no instructs for Rodriguez, so his report from the fall of 2019 remains the same: Scouts who saw Rodriguez during 2019 instructs really like his long-term physical projection and consider him one of the toolsier low-level hitting prospects in this system, but he did strike out a concerning amount in the DSL prior to their looks at him. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top infielder in Miami's 2018 international class, Rodriguez signed for $300,000 out of Venezuela. Though he batted just .229/.321/.346 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons sandwiched around the pandemic shutdown, those numbers belie his offensive upside. Rodriguez still is figuring out his left-handed swing but generates plenty of bat speed and could produce 20 or more homers on an annual basis. To do so, he must improve his ability to recognize pitches and control the strike zone. He uses the opposite field almost too much and puts the ball in play on the ground too often. Signed as a shortstop, Rodriguez split time between there and third base in his pro debut and played mostly at the hot corner in 2021. He has nice infield actions, soft hands and solid arm strength, but his fringy speed and quickness limit his range at shortstop and he could slow down further as he matures physically. He makes some youthful mistakes at third base, just like he does at the plate, but time is still on his side because he'll be just 20 throughout the 2022 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hajjar was a solid pitching prospect while in high school in Massachusetts, but opted not to sign with the Brewers as a late-round choice in 2018 to honor his commitment to Michigan. He missed his freshman year after tearing his ACL playing pickup basketball, but came back and led the Wolverines rotation the next two years. While his stuff wasn’t super-sharp, he led the Big Ten in strikeouts in 2021 and landed in the second round of the Draft, where the Twins signed him to full slot. He was missing a lot of bats, albeit with a surprisingly high walk rate, in Single-A when he was part of the crop of prospects the Reds got from the Twins in return for Tyler Mahle at the Trade Deadline. The big lefty didn’t throw an official pitch for the Twins after a full workload at Michigan, but they were thrilled to see his stuff tick up in the short time they worked with Hajjar after he signed. While his fastball averaged around 90 mph in college in 2021, he was more around 93 mph, touching a bit higher, in bullpen sessions with the Twins, though he was averaging around 92 mph in the Florida State League this year. He can miss bats with all of his secondary offerings and he used his plus low-80s changeup with good tumble and his upper-70s curveball effectively last year. He’s been working to add velocity to his low-80s slider and to focus on adding lateral movement to it so it can be a better weapon against left-handed hitters. Hajjar’s overhand delivery creates deception, making him a tougher at-bat. He generally has a good feel for pitching, though he’s struggled with walks during his full-season debut, with a good chance to improve improve his command as he progresses, with perhaps more in the tank as he keeps adding strength to that 6-foot-5 frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick in 2018 after he won Big West Conference player of the year accolades at Cal Poly, McKenna slugged a feeble .303 in his full-season debut the following year. He used his pandemic layoff to add strength, hit the ball with more authority than ever in instructional league in 2020 and then got off to a .305/.390/.616 start. He injured his shoulder a week after his promotion to Double-A, missed a month and didn't hit nearly as well once he returned. More of a disciplined hitter who peppered the gaps in college, McKenna now is pulling the ball in the air with more authority. His bat speed and strength give him solid raw pop from the right side of the plate and he's doing a better job of tapping into it. His 34 percent strikeout rate last year leads to question about whether his power-seeking approach will work against more advanced pitchers, and Houston did leave him off its 40-man roster last November. A solid runner, McKenna can steal an occasional base and cover ground in the outfield. While he's not a burner, his quickness and instincts allow him to get the job done in center field. He has solid arm strength and threw out eight runners in 74 games last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most colleges recruited Barefoot as a pitcher, so he chose Campbell because it was the lone school that offered him a chance to hit. He missed his first season recovering from ankle surgery before starring as a redshirt sophomore in 2018, winning batting title in the Big South Conference (.364) and Cape Cod League (.379) as well as the Cape MVP award. He had an injury-marred pro debut after signing as a sixth-rounder in 2019, then saw his OPS decline from 1.017 in Low-A to .895 in High-A to .525 in Double-A during his first full pro season last year. A rare bats-right/throws-left player, Barefoot has a busy swing but makes it work thanks to his hand-eye coordination. Predominantly a contact hitter in college, he's now looking to launch balls in the air, which has resulted in inconsistent production and a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first two years as a pro. He was overmatched in his first taste of Double-A and will have to make better swing decisions in order to realize his 20-homer potential. Barefoot is deceptively athletic and can flash plus speed and arm strength. He's an aggressive baserunner who used his quickness to steal 21 bases in 25 attempts in 2021. He can play an average center field but fits better in right, where he's a solid defender and shows off an arm that was clocked up to 94 mph during his brief stints on the mound at Campbell.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berryhill's college career took him from Georgia Southern to Walters State (Tenn.) CC to South Carolina before he signed with the Reds for $149,500 as a redshirt sophomore in 2019. After the Astros acquired him in exchange for Cionel Perez in January 2021, he won the organization's Minor League Player of the Year award by batting .295/.413/.562 with 15 homers in 73 games at three levels. An aspiring country singer, he performed the national anthem before games at Low-A Fayetteville and High-A Asheville last season. Berryhill started seeing the ball better last year once he started wearing contacts. His best tools is his plus raw power from the right side of the plate, and he started getting to it more consistently once he started making adjustments to close a hole at the top of his strike zone. He concentrates on launching balls to his pull side, which led to a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first full pro season, but he also draws a healthy number of walks. Surprisingly athletic for a 6-foot-1, 227-pound catcher, Berryhill has below-average speed and runs the bases well. Though he's relatively inexperienced behind the plate, he has soft hands and decent receiving skills, while his arm is fringy. He profiles as an offensive-minded backup who also can handle first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Collins starred at McKinney Boyd High School in Texas and looked like he might be headed to Oklahoma State for college ball. The Braves loved his speed and feel to hit enough to nab him in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft, signing him for an above-slot $447,500 and making him the first ever draftee from his school. Collins returned their faith in him by hitting .347/.424/.453 with 12 steals in 23 Florida Complex League games. The left-handed hitting outfielder’s calling card is his speed, which is nearly close to top of the scale. He’s a legitimate basestealing threat who registers very low times from home to first and uses his legs well to stretch singles to doubles and doubles to triples. He can make a lot of contact, but is content to spray the ball around the field. He’s not likely to ever be a big power guy, but added strength will help him impact the ball more consistently. Collins’ speed is also an asset in the outfield and while he’ll need to sharpen his reads and routes, he does have the chance to stick in center field. If he can keep getting on base and get strong enough to drive the ball a little, he could profile as an intriguing table-setting type in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon joined the Dodgers organization for $350,000 as part of a 2015-16 international classic that included Yordan Alvarez, Yadier Alvarez and Yusniel Diaz. He put himself on the map with 13 homers and a 1.044 OPS over 52 games in the Dominican Summer League the following year but trailed off some due to low averages and high K rates in the seasons that followed. At age 23, Rincon looked like he was righting the ship in his second trip to Double-A in 2021 and was moved to the Mets last July in a trade for Billy McKinney. He finished with a .265/.334/.496 line and 22 homers between the two organizations, marking his third Minor League campaign with 20-plus dingers. As you might expect, power is what makes the 6-foot-3 right-handed slugger a notable prospect. Mets officials were quickly impressed by both his raw and in-game pop, and the latter plays so well because of Rincon’s ability to lift the ball, especially to his pull side. His 81 homers since 2017 (his first full season) are 16th-most in the Minor Leagues. Unfortunately, the power comes with whiff concerns; Rincon’s swinging strike rate of 17 percent was 17th-highest among 142 Double-A qualifiers, and it will only get worse at Triple-A or the Majors, barring changes. A below-average runner, Rincon is limited to the corner outfield spots. He has enough arm to play in right, and it was notable that the Mets moved him there after the trade, whereas the Dodgers featured him more in left. He doesn’t add much value defensively beyond the arm, and that places even more emphasis on the slugging ability. The 24-year-old will get to prove he can power his way to Queens with his first assignment to Triple-A in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peroza played out of Carlos Guillen’s academy in Venezuela before signing with the Mets for $280,000 on July 2, 2016. He moved stateside in his first Minor League season after a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, but it was a slow climb from there. Because of late development and the 2020 canceled season, the right-handed slugger didn’t see full-season ball until last year. It was at Low-A St. Lucie that he put up his best numbers yet -- .274/.404/.442, seven homers in 64 games. His numbers after a promotion to High-A Brooklyn were slightly stifled by an extreme pitchers' environment at Coney Island. It’s a classic power-first, corner-infielder profile. Peroza’s top exit velocity at Low-A was 110.6 mph, and he had two of the six hardest hit balls by a St. Lucie batter, despite his limited experience there. He shows natural strength from his 6-foot-1, 221-pound frame, and he plays into it with good lift at the plate. (Of his batted balls in St. Lucie, 42.3 percent were fly balls.) He showed promising patience with a 12.6 percent walk rate between the two levels, but that also led to him striking out in about a quarter of his plate appearances. That K rate could go up as he climbs toward Queens. Peroza’s above-average arm makes him a good fit for third base, though a lack of speed and range may move him to first, especially considering the Mets’ Minor League depth at the hot corner. His trajectory when it comes to getting the raw power to play in games will get him a chance to fight for a place in the New York infield hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies signed Azuaje out of Venezuela for $400,000 as part of an aggressive 2018-19 international signing period for the organization that saw them hand out bonuses of six figures or more to 15 players. He had a solid, if unspectacular, debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, missed 2020 because of the shutdown, then came to the United States and the Florida Complex League in 2021, where he swung the bat well, albeit in a 19-game sample. Small and stocky, Azuaje reminds some of former big league infielder Placido Polanco in terms of body type. He makes a ton of contact with a hit-over-power approach from the right side of the plate, showing the ability to send line drives to all fields. He’s had some home run pop show up, with five homers in 45 at-bats in the FCL, but he can get too overly aggressive at the plate and will have to keep refining his approach. When the Phillies first signed Azuaje, he was a plus runner with 6.5 speed. He’s physically matured and slowed down to be more of an average runner, though he’s worked to get in better shape. While he’s played three infield positions in his brief career, his best spot is second, the position he has the greatest chance to become an offensive-minded regular at.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Casey was a two-way player at Boston College but told teams he preferred hitting, despite posting better numbers on the mound. He fell to the Dodgers in the 20th round in 2017 as a result. Inconsistent success marked his first two seasons in pro ball before he managed 23 homers at High-A and Double-A in 2019. He was hitting .296/.362/.462 over 73 games as a 25-year-old back in Tulsa last season when Los Angeles sent him to Washington in the six-player deal involving Trea Turner and Max Scherzer. Shortly after, Casey ran into a roadblock at Triple-A, hitting .179 with a 38.8 percent K rate over 38 games. Eligible for the Rule 5 Draft for a second time, he was added to the 40-man in November after strengthening his case in the Arizona Fall League. Casey still possesses a strong arm from his days as a BC pitcher, and he uses it to great effect from the outfield grass. He also boasts plus speed that makes him an annual candidate to swipe 15-plus bags in a full season. While he played a lot of right field in the Dodgers system, it was notable that Casey played primarily in center for the Nationals following the trade. He could likely step right into the Washington outfield mix without the MLB club missing a beat defensively. There are legit questions about Casey’s bat, however. He has shown K rates right around 30 percent for much of his time in the upper Minors. That hinders his ability to tap into his solid raw power, as does his history of putting the ball primarily on the ground. Casey isn’t far from being a fourth-outfield type in the Majors because of his wheels and defense. But his age at 26 and performance in the box might keep him from ever being more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals signed Luis García, Yasel Antuna and Israel Pineda -- one prospect graduate and two Top 30 stalwarts -- as part of their 2016-17 international class. Méndez, a $600,000 signing out of Venezuela, did not quite make the same noise on the professional scene during the early years of his career. That changed in 2021. The 5-foot-10 outfielder hit .287/.343/.440 with five homers, 36 total extra-base hits and 11 steals in 85 games at Low-A and High-A. His 111 wRC+ was third-best among Nats Minor League qualifiers. It’s the hit tool that drives Méndez’s rise to prospect prominence these days. He exhibits a repeatable swing from the left side, allowing him to display strong bat-to-ball skills. While he did strike out roughly a quarter of the time in 2021, Méndez does make decently hard contact when he strikes the ball, leading to an average hit projection. Double-digit homers might be a stretch with the power and launch angle playing more to gaps than over the fence. With above-average speed, Méndez is a threat to steal and can cover ground in the outfield. He played all three spots last year, but his below-average arm plays better in left or center. Nationals officials have drawn comparisons to Grégor Blanco, the 10-year Major Leaguer who was light on power but added speed and defensive value. That would be a positive outcome at its most extreme for Méndez, but it paints a picture of what type of player he could be if the 2021 gains continue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A .333 hitter over his two seasons as a leadoff man at Texas Tech, Holt inspired something in Brewers scouts because -- despite not being ranked among MLB Pipeline’s Top 200 in the 2019 Draft class -- he signed for $450,000 (the third-highest bonus given out by Milwaukee that year) as a seventh-rounder. After not being an instructional league standout in 2020, Holt certainly played to his strengths in his first full season last year, hitting .283/.403/.341 with 17 steals and a 52/68 K/BB ratio in 97 games at High-A and Double-A. In case that last stat didn’t make it clear, Holt hates to strike out. With two strikes, he will get wide in his left-handed hitting stance and choke up to spray the ball anywhere in play, bucking modern trends. As a result, he fanned only 11.8 percent of the time between Wisconsin and Biloxi last season for the best K rate among Milwaukee full-season qualifiers. Of course, Holt needs to be a big-time contact hitter because he showcases little raw power; only 18 of his 102 hits last season went for extra bases. A part-time outfielder in college, Holt split his time between second and third base in 2021. Despite good speed to help with range, he doesn’t quite have the hands to stick up the middle, meaning he might have to spend more time at the hot corner. He has the arm for the position, if not the traditional offensive profile associated with it. Whether it’s his speed or contact rate, Holt finds little ways to put his stamp on games, and it’s in those margins that he might carve out a Major League infield role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pérez might still be remembered best as a candidate for the first overall spot in the 2016 Draft. He tested positive for a performance-enhancing substance days before the process began, and MLB Pipeline’s No. 9 Draft prospect fell to the Cardinals at No. 23 overall instead. The Puerto Rico native hasn’t exactly enjoyed a strong offensive start to his career. A broken hand limited him in 2017, and he didn’t see his first full-season action until 2019 with Class A Peoria, where he hit just .269 with a .654 OPS in 118 games. Pérez added strength ahead of 2021 and enjoyed arguably his best offensive season yet at Double-A Springfield with a .265/.322/.339 line and a career-best four homers in 98 games. Pérez’s prospect stock remains in place because of his non-offensive tools. A near-plus-plus runner, he shows excellent range at the demanding position of shortstop and has the hands to handle most anything hit his way. A plus arm makes the defensive profile even better. Pérez has used his speed to swipe 20-plus bags each of his past two seasons, and his performance on the basepaths may be his best offensive asset. Otherwise, he can get too aggressive at the plate. So while his 14.9 percent swinging-strike rate isn’t overly high, he doesn’t quite drive balls adequately when he does make contact. Only 17 of his 86 hits went for extra bases in 2021, and his career full-season high for slugging percentage is a meager .339. Pérez hasn’t been added to the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible the past two years, but the glove and speed could get the 23-year-old a Major League look on their own merits, if only as a light-hitting bench option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A teammate of fellow Cardinal Lars Nootbaar at USC, Lunn didn’t become a starter until his junior year in 2019, and he posted a 3.69 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 83 innings that spring. The Cardinals selected him in the 11th round and signed him for $125,000 -- the max they could without dipping into their bonus pool. Lunn’s full-season debut had to wait until 2021, and he spent it entirely with High-A Peoria, where he was a strike-throwing machine, especially late. He walked only five batters over his final 10 starts with the Chiefs and finished with a 3.96 ERA with 121 strikeouts and 20 walks over 120 1/3 frames. His 4.1 percent walk rate led Cardinals full-season qualifiers and was second among High-A starters. The 6-foot-3 right-hander won’t necessarily bowl anyone over with stuff. He throws around 90-92 mph with the fastball, though it features good ride at the top of the zone and he spots it well. A mid-70s, loopier curveball tunnels well off the heater, leaving some High-A hitters shaking their heads heading back to the dugout. He’ll throw the occasional low-80s slider as well to give another breaking-ball look, though it doesn’t pop the same way as the curve, and a mid-80s, though occasionally firm, changeup helped him keep pretty solid splits against righties and lefties. The strike-throwing ability is what makes Lunn pop, and it was certainly encouraging the way he grew into that skill as 2021 went on. It’s control over command, though, and he can get occasionally rocked if the stuff is too much in the zone, especially the fastball. The control will keep him in a starting role as he enters the upper Minors, but if the stuff is to truly tick up, a move back to the bullpen for the first time since 2018 might be in the cards down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Yurchak led NCAA Division I with a 41/12 BB/K ratio in 2017, his lone season at Binghamton after transferring from Wake Forest, prompting the White Sox to sign the redshirt sophomore for an over-slot $150,000 in the 12th round. The Dodgers acquired him in a November 2018 trade for Manny Banuelos that didn't appear to be very significant -- until last year. After going 4-for-42 in May, he batted .403 the rest of the way to lead the Minors in hitting (.365) and finish second in on-base percentage (.443). Thanks to his sweet left-handed swing, uncanny hand-eye coordination and fine command of the strike zone, Yurchak has posted a .321/.421/.466 line while advancing to Double-A in four pro seasons. While he's strong, he doesn't have much loft in his stroke and he doesn't produce high exit velocities. His hit-over-power approach might have him max out at 12-15 homers per season, which would make it difficult for him to profile as a regular at first base. First base and DH are the only realistic lineup options for Yurchak, who has well-below-average speed and athleticism. He's an adequate defender at best at first base, though he does have average arm strength. He has seen brief action at third base and left field as a pro but lacks the range for either position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $80,000 out of Mexico in the 2016-17 international period, Ruiz flew under the radar in a Padres class that also included Adrian Morejon, Michel Baez, Gabriel Arias and Tucupita Marcano. Ruiz put together a few average years in his introduction to pro ball, but broke out early in 2021 with a career-high 15 homers over 72 games for High-A Fort Wayne. He was promoted to Double-A, where he hit another six homers, but struggled over 35 games to end the season. Ruiz has a sound swing from the left side, though he’s yet to hit above .253 for a full-season club. He certainly takes his free passes with walk rates around 10 percent at every Minor League stop, and that helps the hit tool some. A slight leg kick and an improved fly-ball rate helped the pull-side power tick up in 2021, though he has a tendency to lose his approach and increase his strikeout rate when he starts trying to hit for too much power. Ruiz has played all three outfield positions, but profiles best in either center or right as he runs well and has an above-average arm. A lack of a true plus tool could limit Ruiz from being an everyday starting outfielder in the Majors, though his ability to play all three outfield spots could earn him a roster spot as a fourth outfielder, especially if he continues to make strides with the bat.

fangraphs.label: 2021graduates
fangraphs.text: Merryweather is in his 30s, throws four pitches, and has multiple big-league saves under his belt, all of which makes him an atypical prospect even before considering the factors that complicate his projection. His average heater topped 97 mph last season and his three secondaries afford him many plans of attack. When he's at his best, righties have no chance against his high-80s slider and lefties must guess whether he's going high with the fastball or down and out with the change with two strikes. There's a late-inning ceiling here, but two concerns loom large. First up, injuries: Merryweather has battled them constantly throughout his career, including 2021 when he missed most of the year with an oblique strain. His spin rate was also down a couple hundred rpms when he returned from the shelf, and his slider didn't have quite the same bite as we saw in April and in 2020. If that's a new normal, he's still a good arm to have, but it tilts his projection toward more of a seventh-inning role than that of a true setup man.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Merryweather was once one of those anonymous, strike-throwing Cleveland prospects who had a dramatic uptick in stuff a little later in pro ball. For Merryweather that meant mid-90s heat, a good changeup and curveball, and a breakout 2017 during which he nearly reached the majors. Then he needed surgery before the 2018 season began, was traded that year as part of the Josh Donaldson rental deal, and wasn't back until late in 2019 as a reliever, when he looked ready to make an immediate bullpen impact, sitting 95-97 (up from 93-96) with his fastball in the Arizona Fall League. He threw harder still when the 2020 season finally rolled around, parked at 96-99 and touching 100. Toward the very end of the season he was once again shut down with elbow tendinitis. It's concerning that over the last several years, Merryweather has been healthy and pitching in games for just a few weeks. But he has knockout backend bullpen stuff right now, and for a lot of prospects in this and other systems, that would be a great outcome. He's prominently represented here, despite his age, because of that. It's also worth noting a fourth option year has been imposed upon Merryweather due to his injury history, which isn't great for him but certainly buoys his trade value a little bit because teams value roster flexibility. (Alternate site, MLB)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text:
Once upon a time, García, still rookie eligible at age 28, was a 50 FV prospect and my favorite of the many Cardinals outfielders from that era, including Randy Arozarena. Then he spent an extended period of time at the upper levels and his over-aggressive approach at the plate was exposed. Even though he hit more than 50 home runs combined in 2018 and '19, and slugged about .560 during that span, García's peripherals were so horrendous that he still managed to post batting lines below league average because he was only reaching base at a .290 clip, and everyone in the PCL was hitting for big power at that time. During that stretch, he was passed on the org depth chart by several players, including Tyler O'Neill, Arozarena, Oscar Mercado, and Lane Thomas, and fell into the "toolsy older lottery ticket" prospect bucket. The Cardinals eventually ran out of space and time and unceremoniously DFA'd Garcia, then traded him to Texas for cash. He spent 2020 at the alt site and got a three-game shot of espresso, then was foisted into the 2021 lineup and has been on a most epic heater. 
He already has 16 homers (he hit his 16th literally as I was typing this sentence on Wednesday), tied for the major league lead, and has come through in huge late-game moments. I do not expect it to continue because García's approach is still terrifying. He's near the bottom of the league in O-swing%, and he's in the bottom 25 of qualified hitters by Contact and Swinging Strike%. He's been beaten by velocity at the top of the zone and I think it's only a matter of time before opposing pitchers adjust to him, though García's 16th bomb was a 94 mph heater at the letters so maybe he's the one who's going to adjust. I don't want to throw water on the situation because García is a lot of fun and part of me wants to be vindicated for stuffing this guy on the top 100 a couple of years ago, but we see shooting star performances like this every so often and García has several of the approach-related traits that indicate it will end and that he'll be a streaky bench outfielder deep into his 30s.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: It felt as though the Dodgers had moved on from Sborz because they had several other relievers like him around, except those other relievers had more option years left. Since dealing Sborz for Jhan Zambrano, components of Sborz's delivery are now timed differently, and his delivery has more pace. He's also added a curveball, and his fastball has more carry now than it did while he was with the Dodgers. Amid all these changes, Sborz is also throwing harder. He looked like a solid middle relief piece for the longest time but has clearly leveled up out of nowhere.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The effervescent Mercedes' long, circuitous path to the big leagues culminated in just one 2020 plate appearance, but he remains in the White Sox mix to play a situational, bat-only bench or part-time role in the immediate future. I wrote last year that Mercedes is built such that he looks ripped and fat at the same time, and if you've been watching him catch for Licey in the Dominican Winter League, you can see he's begun to trend toward the latter. It doesn't matter all that much though because, anticipated rule changes or not, he can't catch, nor can he really play first base. Instead, his is a DH-only profile with serious strength, bat speed, and hand-eye coordination that might enable him to play a valuable situational role if he can overcome a propensity to chase. It's not as if the Yermínator lacks any kind of approach. With two strikes, he ditches his huge leg kick and focuses on putting the ball in play with just his hands and wrists, and he often still hits the ball hard like this because he's so strong. Perhaps he'll have some trade value once baseball moves to a universal designated hitter but I tend to think Mercedes' epicurean sensibilities at the plate would undermine his ability to play every day. Instead, I think if he's deployed in situations where the opposing pitcher can't pitch around him and has to throw strikes, he'll be a very, very dangerous late-game hitter. How the org decides to prioritize his opportunities versus Adolfo's, Zack Collins' and others might be up to the new manager. (Alternate site, MLB (barely), LIDOM)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Seby spent the year at the alternate site and his report in unchanged, though it's worth noting that the departure of James McCann and the defensive abilities of those left behind (aside from Yasmani Grandal) make it more likely that he sees big league time in 2021. He's going to strike out a lot, so much that it will be detrimental to his offensive output relative to the average big leaguer, but that's true of a lot of backup catchers. Zavala is a viable defensive catcher with above-average raw power, and I think he'd run into as many as 10 homers as a full-season backup. Where he sits amidst a crowded catching situation in Chicago depends on how the org views Mercedes and Collins defensively. He's likely the third catcher during his option years and someone's backup once those expire. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2021graduates
fangraphs.text: Rodríguez pitched one shutout inning during the 2021 Futures Game, allowing one walk and striking out Oakland’s Tyler Soderstrom. In that inning of work, his fastball topped out at 99, and he showcased a ton of movement across his arsenal. That performance, along with improved control in his time in Double- and Triple-A, was enough to convince Chicago to add him to the big league roster, with Rodríguez claiming one of the spots vacated during the Cubs’ busy trade deadline. His velocity and movement followed him to the majors, most notably his two-seamer, which can hit triple digits with a lot of run, and his slider, which he routinely throws around 90 mph with 40 inches of vertical break. In his major league debut, Rodríguez's strike throwing regressed across a small, 20-game sample and we think it's likely to keep him from late-inning work despite the quality of his stuff, while concerns about frame/athletic longevity are also at play here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Rodriguez will be one of the Cubs' Futures Game reps. He sits 96-98 and will touch 99 while mixing in a power curveball in the mid-80s. He's a 30-grade athlete with relief-only control and projects in middle relief.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text:
Like Max Bain, Nance is another Indy Ball signee who had a velo spike during the off year, but unlike Bain, whose affiliated career just began this year, Nance has had a longer runway. He signed out of the independent Frontier League early in 2016 and pitched in the middle levels of the Cubs’ system for nearly half a decade before showing way bigger velocity this year. He was 91–94 in 2019 but got up to 97–98 during his single-inning big league debut. 
Nance had three strong relief outings at Triple-A Iowa (combined: 6 IP, 1 H, 1 BB, 10 K) before the call-up. There he was more 94–96 and topping out at 97, really only throwing his mid-80s power slurve apart from the fastball. His heater has big tailing action and is capable of running off the hips of lefty batters and back over the plate. As I wrote regarding Julian Merryweather on the Blue Jays list, just because this guy is 30 doesn't mean he’s not a prospect. He’s rookie-eligible, has roster flexibility, and is under team control the same as any young player. He’s also a pitcher who clearly has immediate big league bullpen utility. The likelihood of age-related decline during his years of team control does complicate where he falls on the FV scale since I care about all six or seven of those years, but teams need to decide how they value a guy like this versus a more traditional prospect, so I will, too. Would you rather have Nance or Anderson Espinoza right now? How about Jay Groome? If either of those younger arms were to end up sitting 97-plus with an upper-80s hammer breaking ball out of the bullpen, we'd think it was a great outcome given what they have dealt with on the way there. Well, Nance is that right now.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: If you recall, De León was once a top 100 prospect, working 93-96 at that time, but his career was sidetracked by an incessant slew of injuries. His velocity began to climb in 2019, as he was 89-93 as a starter and then more 92-95 as a reliever late that year. Prior to the shutdown, the Reds had planned to start De León in the Triple-A rotation and use him as a spot starter in his final option year. Instead he came up from the alt site in a bullpen role and his velocity continued to climb. He was parked at 95, touching 98. Deployed as a starter in the Clemente League (Puerto Rican Winter League), De León has been sitting 94-98 with his usual plus changeup. His command will probably continue to relegate him to the bullpen, but since he's out of option years, he'll likely stay on the roster in a middle-inning role, perhaps replacing Michael Lorenzen in a medium-leverage role. (Alternate site, MLB, Puerto Rican Winter League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bergen was the Giants 2018 Rule 5 pick and spent the early part of 2019 with them, intil he was put on the 60-day IL with a shoulder injury in the middle of that season. He was returned to the Blue Jays in late August and finished 2019 with them, then has bounced back and forth from TOR and ARI (Robbie Ray, DFA). Both before and immediately after his shoulder injury, Bergen was pitching with below-average velocity, sitting 89-92. In 2020, he had a spike, now sitting 93-95 and touching 96. He also has a big-breaking curveball averaging nearly 2900rpms. All of this has come in concert with a delivery that looks more fluid and explosive. He's a big league-ready lefty middle relief piece with three options remaining, and I expect he'll live on the active roster membrane for a while. (Alternate site, MLB)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lora offered the best raw power in the 2019 international class and the Rangers pulled off a trade to make sure they had the money to sign him. They shipped a pair of depth right-handers to the White Sox for injured Nate Jones last July, assuming $2.5 million in salary obligations while obtaining $1 million in bonus pool cash. They agreed to terms with Lora on a $3.9 million bonus in August and officially finalized the deal in September. More massive than his listed 6-foot-3 and 190 pounds, Lora is built like Joey Gallo and has the potential to do similar damage at the plate. He has uncanny bat speed and strength for a 17-year-old, producing elite exit velocities and huge right-handed power to all fields. His aggressive mentality does create some swing-and-miss concerns. Though he's huge for his age, Lora moves surprisingly well for his size. He has been clocked as fast as 6.7 seconds in the 60-yard dash and could have fringy to average speed once he's physically mature. He projects as an average defender on the outfield corners and may have enough arm strength to handle right field.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Lora's report as he was in a severe car accident in March and has yet to report to camp: Lora is a traditional corner outfield power bat with big present raw power and a somewhat mature build. There are some long-term questions about that build because Lora is so huge for a prospect his age and reports about his conditioning while he was an amateur were mixed, but he looked svelte during the fall of 2019, and his relative physical maturity also gives him a better chance of moving quickly through the minors. He often has clumsy in-the-box footwork but deft hitting hands. Last fall, he took several ugly-looking, unbalanced swings but still found a way to get the barrel there, and even when he miss-hits balls they're still put in play hard because of how strong Lora is. His future depends entirely on his hit tool as it's pretty clear the power to hit in the middle of an order is going to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roederer drew Andrew Bentinendi comparisons as a California high school senior in 2018, but also injured his non-throwing shoulder and had a UCLA commitment, so he was available to Chicago at the 77th overall pick. Signed for an over-slot $1.2 million, he endured a rough first full pro season because low Class A pitchers quickly exploited his aggressiveness by throwing him changeups. He made some progress in the final six weeks but has barely played since then, because the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the 2020 Minor League season and he injured his throwing elbow this May, requiring Tommy John surgery. The key for Roederer will be to understand who he is as a hitter. With a smooth left-handed swing, bat speed and the ability to work counts, he could hit .280-.300 with 20-25 homers on an annual basis. He won't reach that potential, however, unless he stops worrying about launching balls to his pull side, develops a gap-to-gap approach and does a better job recognizing offspeed pitches. Roederer is an asset on the bases with solid speed, good instincts and an aggressive nature. The Cubs believe his high baseball IQ gives him the chance to remain in center field, though he'll have to shift to a corner if he loses any quickness as he adds muscle. His arm strength graded as fringy before his elbow reconstruction and is better suited for left field than right.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: As a high school underclassman, Roederer looked like a hit-first tweener outfielder. He added a bunch of good weight and strength and had significantly more raw power when he arrived in the AZL after signing, having already begun to trade a little bit of contact for more game power. He skipped a level and didn't perform in full-season ball in 2019, which felt fine because of his age and the hitting environment in the Midwest League. Then we had no minor league season last year and Roederer's 2021 was interrupted by an elbow strain that cost him all of June and persisted through list publication. It's made his statistical output difficult to contextualize. Ultimately, I think Roederer projects as the larger half of a corner outfield platoon à la David Peralta, Seth Smith, Matt Joyce and the like. He sees righty pitching well and pulls it with power. He's played a lot of center field but most big league clubs have a superior defender on their roster, so I have Roederer projected in left.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: I'll speculate that the Royals and Guzmán came to some kind of mutual agreement regarding his roster status, since last winter Kansas City exposed him to free agency in order to clear a 40-man spot but re-signed him to a minor league deal only a week later. He didn't hit during sporadic big league spring training at-bats but has looked fantastic during minor league play this spring, especially on defense. The Royals added Guzmán to the 40-man after his age-20, 2019 season even though he was overmatched at A-ball that year. In the year and a half since then, he has become considerably more physical without really compromising his defensive ability, and he was still making rangy, acrobatic plays this spring. With the strength has come added power, enough that Guzmán is a real threat to do damage when he makes contact. An expansive approach and grooved pair of swings mean he'll likely max out with a 40-grade hit tool, but a plus-gloved infielder with mistake power is still a desirable role-player, and also describes a lot of low-end shortstop regulars. (Alternate site, LIDOM)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Tabor was once again parked in the 90-93 range during 2020 instructs, so while he's quite athletic and has a good frame, it seems the velocity explosion he experienced late in high school will be the only one he enjoys. Though his arm slot looks like it creates backspin on his heater, his fastball's spin axis is actually closer to the dreaded 1:30 mark, a no-man's land for creating movement, but his fastball also has a ton of spin and slightly above-average measured run and rise. I think it's a viable big league pitch but not an impact one. Instead, Tabor will need to lean on his secondary stuff (and command thereof) to miss big league bats. I've seen plus changeups and average breaking balls from Tabor. He'll need to hit the command grade I have projected for him, but he is tracking like a low-variance No. 4/5 starter. Several arms with greater relief risk (but better stuff) are behind him in this system and might pass him if they prove capable of starting. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had a run of college infielders in the 2019 Draft led by Quintana, a converted shortstop turned third baseman at the University of Arizona, who slugged his way into becoming one of the more productive hitters in the Pac-12 Conference. His 77 RBIs as a junior ranked fifth among NCAA Division I hitters in 2019 to go with a .342 average, 15 home runs and a .626 slugging percentage. After signing for $1.58 million in the second round, Quintana had an encouraging first week as a pro at Class A West Michigan before slumping to a .155 average and 36 strikeouts in July. Once the offensive struggles followed him into the infield, the Tigers pushed him to Short-Season Connecticut to regain his bearings as the season ended. Quintana generates a surprising amount of power for his size. It also leaves him susceptible to all-or-nothing outcomes, which seemed to amass around him in his introduction to pro ball. After hitting his first home run in his fifth pro game, he went 17-for-98 (.173) with 38 strikeouts over his next 106 plate appearances, including an 0-for-12, nine-strikeout stretch over three games in late July. Ironically, both of his home runs at West Michigan and Connecticut came in games in which he didn’t strike out. Defensively, his quick first step and sure hands made him a plus defender in college, with arm strength when needed. The Tigers drafted Quintana early hoping for an eventual quality two-way player for the hot corner. If he’s going to make it, he’ll have to learn to separate the two sides of his game and keep his defense out of slumps. He’ll approach the 2020 season with a fresh start.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Quintana was a high school prospect of repute from Las Vegas, then hit .317/.424/.565 during his career at Arizona, squaring up everything but well-located breaking balls, which he tends to swing over top of. His track record of hitting and the likelihood that he'd stay on the dirt had him in teams' late first, early second round mix. He really struggled after the draft, then had no 2020 season to rebound. Quintana is also one of those prospects who had trouble working out and doing baseball activities throughout 2020 because of the safety measures in place in Vegas, and this impacted his fall look. He's still in a holding pattern on this list but could have an average hit/average power combo and play every day at third base. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 There was obvious excitement when the Twins aggressively pursued Javier, one of the top prospects in the 2015-16 international class, and signed him for $4 million in July 2015. Since then, however, there have only been glimpses of what he can do. The talented infielder missed most of his first summer, in 2016, because of a hamstring injury, then re-set a high bar by being one of the best prospects in the Appalachian League in his United States debut in 2017. Momentum was halted when a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder kept him off the field for all of 2018. Because the injuries have limited his time on the field, Javier is a bit of a wild card. Once he can shake the rust off, there is confidence he'll once again show his considerable offensive upside. He makes consistent hard contact with a natural feel to hit and while as a young player without that many reps, he'll need to refine his approach. He does work counts and draw walks. As he fills out, his bat speed and potential plus hitting tool could lead to at least average power. Fortunately, Javier's injury wasn't to his throwing shoulder, so his plus arm should be just fine. Whether he outgrows the position remains to be seen. With a clean bill of health and no setbacks from his injury, Javier should be ready to show what he can do over the course of a long season. Getting at-bats and reps in the field is priority number one for now.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There are instances when knowing less about a prospect actually improves the industry's view of them. There's space to dream and fill in the gaps in the profile with optimism, as we may not know about relevant underlying issues lurking beneath the surface. Such was the case with Javier, who signed for a IFA franchise record $4 million back in 2015 and basically missed two of his four pro seasons due to quad and hamstring injuries, along with labrum surgery. Finally (mostly) healthy in 2019, Javier went to full-season ball, struck out a ton, and hit .177. His bat-to-ball ability and pitch recognition were not great, but part of that was surely because he hasn't seen a lot of pro pitching due to the injuries. Then 2020 happened and Javier lost yet another year of actual development. Twins instructs included nothing but intrasquads against pitchers who were about the same age as Javier, and according to teams that watched video from those in preparation for the Rule 5, he continued to struggle from a bat-to-ball standpoint in the Fall. In the last year we've gone from not knowing much about Javier's contact/approach to knowing it's either not good or lags way behind because of the lack of reps. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had Packard on an aggressive track after drafting the reigning American Athletic Conference Player of the Year out of East Carolina in the fifth round in 2019. He tore up Midwest League hitting that summer at Class A West Michigan, then had a brief stint of High-A play. The cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season cost him a chance to build upon that momentum and potentially work his way toward the upper levels. Packard has a bat-first profile with a pure, polished left-handed swing and a disciplined approach that keeps him from wandering outside the strike zone. His big frame allows him to produce power without too much vulnerability to strikeouts. His extra-base power beyond home runs is more from exit velocity than his slow foot speed. He has worked on his instincts in left field but has limited range and athleticism, leading some to wonder whether he could eventually shift to first base. The Tigers have found few productive hitters beyond early Draft picks in recent years, but Packard has the skill set and work ethic to potentially contribute at the big league level. His upside will be almost entirely determined by his bat.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Packard was an interesting buy-low guy in the 2019 draft. His power output dipped during his junior year at East Carolina because of injuries (back and wrist), but he had a stock-up summer after the draft, slashing .296/.392/.422 across three levels. He is patient, swings with verve, has above-average raw power, and looks like a potential Lucas Duda type from a body and swing standpoint. He's sometimes guilty of simply swinging through the center of the zone rather than guiding his barrel to the pitch location, but his hands are really loose and fast. The shaky feel for the barrel slides him below some other role-player types in the system from a certainty standpoint. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown already has overcome more adversity than most players will face, losing his mother to cancer when he was 13, blowing out his elbow and having Tommy John surgery as a high school sophomore, and fathering a daughter born with Down syndrome and life-threatening heart defects when he was a Vanderbilt freshman. His toughness translates to the mound, where he set a school record with 17 saves in 2019, including three in Omaha as the Commodores won their second national championship. He wasn't as sharp in the shortened 2020 season but still should be one of the first relievers drafted. Brown usually attacks hitters with a 91-94 mph fastball with running action that misses bats up in the strike zone, topping out at 96, and an 83-86 mph slider. Both pitches were more solid than plus this spring but have shown better in the past. He also mixes in a mid-70s curveball with more depth than power to give batters a different look, and he can throw them off balance with a decent low-80s changeup. As with his stuff, Brown's control and command were a tick down this year but he usually pounds the zone. With his four pitches, strike-throwing ability and a strong 6-foot-4 build, some scouts think he has the ingredients to start and could get the opportunity to do so in pro ball. Other evaluators believe his delivery and mentality are better suited for late-inning relief.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Brown was mostly 91-93 during the abbreviated 2020 college season but was more 92-95 the season before, when he struck out 65 and walked just nine in 49 innings of relief work. If he can reclaim that comfy mid-90s range, he is very likely to be a quick-moving middle relief piece with a vertical action fastball/curveball combo. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels were limited to signing players for $300,000 during the 2015-16 international signing period after going over their limit the previous year. But they were still active, and the top six bonuses they handed out were all to pitchers. Only two got more than Yan’s $80,000 bonus and Reyember Mendoza is out of baseball while Wilkel Hernandez is with the Tigers. It took Yan awhile to get going, spending three summers in three different Rookie-level leagues, but he dominated once he got to full-season ball, finishing second in the Midwest League in strikeouts in 2019 and earning a spot on the 40-man roster. There were two very tangible things that led to Yan’s step forward in 2019. His fastball velocity once again ticked up, averaging a bit over 93 mph all year, up from 92 mph in 2018. And his curve got even better, with added velocity and more depth to it, giving it a chance be a plus pitch eventually. His changeup is definitely his third pitch, but he has shown some feel for it, something that will have to keep improving to give him a chance to start. Yan has a very deceptive delivery which leads to uncomfortable at-bats for hitters, but it’s also tougher to repeat and has led to control issues. He did cut his walk rate down considerably while seeing his strikeout rate soar, perhaps a sign of things to come.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Yan's velo has regressed and he now has 40-grade arm strength after he was up to 96 in 2019 and struck out so many hitters that the Angels felt they needed to put him on the 40-man. In the past I've compared him to a mirror image of Freddy Peralta, a long-armed side-armer with a cross-bodied delivery, except left-handed rather than right. His fastball dominates lefties because it's being released so far behind their heads that they struggle to see the ball, while it has weird angle in on the hands of righties, making at-bats against Yan awkward for them as well. The rest of the repertoire isn't great. Yan's slider lives almost entirely off of his arm slot and really only works against left-handed hitters, and he doesn't throw his changeup with conviction yet. That his velo has regressed is a real problem since he needs to feast off his fastball to succeed. Yan worked as a starter early in 2021 but I think a bullpen move is coming both because he's struggling and because that's his likely long-term destination. He'd be an interesting buy-low guy for teams looking to balance rental deals with the Angels since his 40-man occupancy is a dead weight for the Halos to carry right now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 28 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2018-19 signing period, Valdez, with his big body and power potential, was viewed by scouts as one of the more physically advanced players in his class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. In the past, he's been overly aggressive and pull-happy, leading to some swing-and-miss issues, but scouts were pleased with how he improved his overall approach this past year. He's solid athletically, earning at least average grades as a runner, and the Mets view him as a pure center fielder that should stay up the middle. Earning high praise for his makeup, scouts like the way Valdez competes and his joy for the game. That should help him deal with the long road ahead through the Mets' Minor League system, with enough offensive potential to carry him to Citi Field.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Valdez is an absolute behemoth of a corner outfield prospect who is likely to end up in the Franmil Reyes size/strength area at maturity, though right now he's built a little more athletically than that. This guy makes the bat look like a toothpick in his hands and he has thunderous raw power with pretty crude feel for contact coming from a swing that scouts don't really like. His 2019 exit velos are below what you'd probably guess from someone this big and strong who performed the way he did in the 2019 DSL (certainly they're below what I'd guess). I think that's more an in-game contact quality indicator, but a front office source from a team that seems to like contact-oriented players told me they thought Valdez should be higher here. I'm more inclined to move a guy like this after he performs on paper and I think Valdez is physically mature enough to be tested in full-season ball this year. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendoza was a highly regarded prospect in the 2016 Draft, but a strong commitment to Florida State led to him being taken by the Tigers in the 36th round. Three years later, after batting .298 with 31 homers and 124 RBIs in 160 games with the Seminoles, he became the Nationals’ third-round pick and signed for above slot value. A successful pro debut at Class A Hagerstown came next, with Mendoza flashing his power potential while making a smooth transition as a first baseman. As a 6-foot-5, 230-pound left-handed hitter, it is easy to dream on Mendoza’s potential at the plate. He gets good leverage in his swing and knows how to impact the baseball, showing plus raw power that should improve as he adds strength. He is still figuring out how to get to that power consistently, though, with swing-and-miss issues and a passive approach currently holding him back. Though he does work his share of walks, the Nationals would like to see him be more aggressive early in the count, viewing it as key for unlocking both his hitting ability and power. Mendoza’s defense at the hot corner with the Seminoles drew mixed reviews from scouts, with most of the concerns stemming from his size and actions. The Nationals immediately moved him to first base in pro ball and have been pleased with the early results, noting that his feet and hands both work well there. They may still offer him reps at third base, where his above-average arm fits well, but their hopeful that Mendoza’s bat will flourish now that he no longer has to focus on improving defensively at third base.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Mendoza had some first round buzz early in his high school career because he had at least 70-grade raw power projection, but he struck out a lot and his stock fell a bit down the stretch while his price tag did not, so he ended up at Florida State. There he continued to strike out while posting relatively modest underclass statlines before exploding as a junior in 2019. He still struck out a ton, but also slugged just shy of .600 and walked 23% of the time. Some scouts describe his approach as more passive than patient, which contributes to a healthy heaping of true three outcomes. There's real risk that Mendoza's hit tool is just a binary "no," and that he ends up flaming out in Double-A. But he also has so much raw power that his swing might be made so simple that he can cut down on the K's and become a viable role player. Because the power here is so titanic, we suppose there's more ceiling than that, but a good realistic outcome for Mendoza would be to become a 1B/DH platoon partner and high-leverage bench bat. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
