He also needs to perform immediately to stay on it. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Scott was neither at the alt site nor instructs, so his report is the same. He was a 2018 fourth round senior sign, then spent most of his first pro season all the way up at Double-A. He was in the 88-92 range that year but his stuff ticked up in 2019, sitting 90-94 and touching 95 with the fastball, while locating his wipeout slider to his glove side. He's tracking like a quick-moving reliever, at least. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Nothing new on Ovalles, who was one of the pieces in the Nate Lowe trade: Ovalles is a smaller-framed first base and corner outfield prospect whose build and limited raw power are the sorts normally found in the honorable mention section of this list. But I've seen him do some precocious defensive stuff at first base and I think he has a chance to be plus there while also making enough contact to offset his limited raw juice. He's a long-shot, but I value him more than is typical because of the bat-to-ball and projected defense. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Maldonado's report, pending how he looks coming off a drug suspension: Eighteen-year-olds who touch 95 don't exactly grow on trees. Maldonado was handed a 72-game suspension for testing positive for Stanozolol in December of 2019, so he didn't pitch in 2020. He didn't turn 17 until July of 2019 and, at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-4, was already sitting 89-93. Obviously the drug suspension lends doubt to the arm strength. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: I stood next to Bautista near the Rangers backfield bullpens before he threw this spring and he's about the size of Darren Sproles. But he has incredible arm speed and came out sitting 94-96 and touched some 7's and 8's that day, and in the following weeks when I saw him again. He'll flash a plus breaking ball, but it's inconsistent, as is Bautista's overall command. He has a long arm action and brings it from a low, three-quarters slot that screams relief. He's rather rough around the edges but has big lefty stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change here as Gavilan was not at instructs: Gavilan was the Pirates' top July 2 signee from 2018 at $700,000. He's an average runner (he ran a 7.1 60-yard-dash in workouts) with good instincts in center field, and he'll stay there if he speeds up as he matures as an athlete. His current swing is somewhat long but again, Gavilan has advanced feel to hit, enough to compensate for his mechanical maladies right now. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Once a little infielder in the D-backs system, Ozuna was released and moved to the mound on his own. He was sitting in the mid-90s immediately, was signed by the Rangers, and pitched just 12 innings in the 2018 DSL before he blew out and needed TJ, the second of his career. Back in 2021, Ozuna is once again showing impact velocity. He was 94-97 when I saw him this spring and has a really athletic drop-and-drive delivery. His power changeup will come in at about 90 mph and his slider, which is typically a 45-grade pitch but flashes better, is also hard. Conversion arms tend to move quickly if things work out. Ozuna has a middle relief look.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Irizarry is a compact, short-levered second baseman whose stroke is so short that he's capable of catching fastballs at the top of the zone. He has just enough pull pop to threaten the right field fence when he does. I think Irizarry has a chance to be a role-playing infielder purely based on his ability to get around on velocity.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: No new info here. A short, athletic righty with a high arm slot, Lugo pairs a mid-90s fastball and power curveball in a two-pitch relief profile. Of all the hard-throwing arms in this tier of the system, Lugo has the best combination of stuff and athleticism. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: No change here as Whittle was not seen in 2020: A Rubenesque junior college righty, Whittle signed for $100,000 as a 2018 23rd rounder and had a velo spike in 2019. He's now 89-92 with heavy sink (he had an over 60% groundball rate in 2019) and a good splitter, as well as a passable slider. He's quite athletic and gets down the mound well for a 5-foot-11 guy, and he lives around the zone. It's probably important that Whittle's stuff keep improving, but it's trending up enough now that he's popped onto the radar. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Gonzalez was once a rangy shortstop prospect with Colorado who was traded to Texas for Jonathan Lucroy back in 2017. He kept growing and eventually had to move to the outfield, where after some promising seasons his feel for contact was exposed. Gonzalez's swing-and-miss issues stem from his lever length, and the industry sees it as enough of a problem that it has passed him over during the last couple of Rule 5 drafts. He hit 23 homers and stole 14 bases at Low-A in 2019, and I'm still betting on his tools and frame to some degree, the same as Seise and Thompson except in an outfield corner rather than up the middle.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Cortorreal's velocity took a huge leap in 2019 when he improved his conditioning. It appears that conditioning has regressed a bit but his velocity has not. He still needs to find a secondary weapon, and fast. (DR Instructs)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bannister is a sushi raw athletic marvel who needs as many reps as the Rangers can give him to polish his feel to hit. His route to pro ball was unique. Bannister was born in the Bahamas and grew up there, then moved to Maryland and played at West Nottingham High School until 2017 when he moved to the Dominican Republic to train, before going back to the Bahamas during the summer of 2018. I've only ever seen him swing right-handed, including against righty pitchers, so I think his roster status as a switch-hitter is now obsolete. He's a physically gifted developmental project.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Gonzalez was acquired from Kansas City for international pool space back in 2018. He's a power bullpen arm with a mid-90s fastball and two quality secondaries that both have similar downward action. I was told he won't pitch this year due to Tommy John, but I don't know the exact date of the surgery.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: 2020 was going to be a big year for Arias, who likely would have gone to Double-A and either earned a 40-man spot or not based on his offensive performance, which to this point in his career has been strong. I like him as a contact-oriented infield bench piece who plays all four spots, but he's slowed down a little bit and now fits best as a 3B/1B and shift-enabled second baseman.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Rodriguez-Cruz is a veyr projectable righty who was just shy of 18 on 2021 draft day. He showed a loose, whippy, but inconsistent delivery on the showcase circuit and was sitting mostly 91-92 while topping out at 94. His curveball has shape but lacks power, and he has pretty crude feel for creating action on ihs changeup, but ERC is a premium arm talent developmental prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Rivera earned a spot on the in-season 2021 Angels list based on the strength of his Extended Spring Training look, even though he was a little older than the other prospects there. He has a very projectable frame, he's super loose and has a whippy, athletic swing. He struggled once the actual lower-level season began, though.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Once an arm-strength lotto ticket (who worked to reshape his body just to become one), Scherff has developed a plus changeup and now projects as a good middle reliever. His strikeout rate has nearly doubled above his career norms in 2021.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Valera is a body beautiful shortstop with power, and serious swing and miss issues created by poor pitch recognition. He's a high-variance prospect who may never hit enough to be anything at all, but he has rare power for a shortstop.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A late-round, cold-weather high school flier who signed for $290,000, Bush played in some of the big prep showcases during his final amateur summer and was clearly overmatched against the better pitching. But he put on an absolute show during batting practice and has one of the best raw power projections among potential future Sox. He had a strong pro debut on paper and continued to look good with the bat during the spring of 2019, then struggled during the summer. The general scouting consensus is that Bush will not stay at his current third base and will have to move to an outfield corner or to first, which immediately makes his whiffs troublesome. He's a high-risk, long-term developmental prospect with some of the louder offensive tools in the system. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Thomas has an ideal baseball frame and huge raw power. He's also performed fairly well in the best college conference in the country. His approach leads to concerningly walk and strikeout ratios and his wristy swing is atypical, but there's very exciting raw material to work with here. Thomas is a high-variance college prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Ulloa's skillset compares closely to Michael Chavis' at the same age. He's a compact-framed power hitter who takes a very athletic, high-effort swing, and though he plays shortstop right now he's likely to funnel down the defensive spectrum, maybe as a fringe 2B or as a 3B/1B type. He showed a roughly even BIP/whiff split during summer showcase play, in which Ulloa participated  heavily.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Manzardo plays first base and he hasn't produced big, over-the-fence power, but he's one of the few college hitters from the 2021 draft who had a good shortended 2020 season and complete 2021 campaign on paper. He also had among the highest average exit velocities in college baseball at a whopping 98mph. Manzardo is short to the ball and squares it up. He sprays hard line drives everywhere. He may end up with a 60 or 70 hit tool and fit as an everday first baseman even without procuding big home run numbers.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Smith-Shawver was a two-sport star in high school and was committed to Texas Tech for football (QB) and baseball. He's a long-term project with a big frame (6-foot-3, 205), present arm strength (up to 95 last summer), and the looseness of his arm action portends secondary pitch development.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Spence went from the college postseason to Cape Cod, where he played for Harwich for about a week leading up to the draft. He is of Aussie descent, spent two years at an Arizona JUCO, and walked more than he struck out as a 23-year-old senior with Tennessee. He might have more upside than most seniors because of his background.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: A senior, Bates ws the backbone of a great 2021 LA Tech team, and is a lefty-hitting OF with good plate coverage and average power.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Low-to-mid-90s, wild, flashes above-avg slider but is very erratic, in general.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star out of the high school ranks in Ohio who played wide receiver at football powerhouse St. Edward outside of Cleveland, Wainwright could have headed to college on the gridiron but committed to Ohio State for baseball. Wainwright wasn’t as strong on the Draft radar because an injury (fractured tibia) had interfered with much of his summer showcase work before his senior year. The team he was supposed to play for at East Coast Pro Showcase was run by Reds scouts, and the relationship they forged with the young outfielder, not to mention a return to health that fall and before the shutdown this spring, gave the Reds confidence to take Wainwright in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft and sign him for full pick value. After signing, Wainwright stood out with his all-around tools and work ethic in his introduction to the club at instructs. He’s strong with an athletic frame, and while it might take some time for his tools to sharpen given his dual-sport focus and living in a cold-weather state, there are some serious skills that show up now. He has excellent bat speed and solid raw power, though he’ll need some reps to learn to catch up to premium velocity and recognize breaking stuff. While he’s not a burner, Wainwright does run well and provides a solid arm to go along with strong defense. He’s a center fielder now and could be given the chance to stay up the middle, though some evaluators feel he’ll outgrow the position and end up in a corner spot, where he could eventually develop into a prototypical athletic run-producing right fielder.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There were fewer prospects like Wainwright taken in the 2020 draft because there were fewer rounds, less overall bonus pool space, and less time to iron out deals for mid-six-figure high schoolers on Day Three. Wainwright is a typical version of this sort of prospect, a big-framed kid from the Midwest who's a little less polished than the Southern kids, and a little less projectable than some of the skinnier kids. But Wainwright was young for the group and is really physical for how young he is, he's shown feel for lifting the ball in BP, and he's a high-ceilinged developmental prospect in a system that is short of this kind of developmental depth. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A few really strong 2020 undrafted free agents have emerged and one of them is curly-locked Brzykcy, who was a power reliever at Virginia Tech. He quickly went from sitting 94-95 out of the Hokies bullpen in his first 2020 appearance to sitting 96-98 and touching 99 in his last few. Brzykcy does not have good fastball control; he's a grip-and-rip type of guy whose heaters often sail to his arm side. His low-80s power curveball flashes plus and he buries it just beneath the strike zone with much more regularity than he locates his fastball. A pure relief prospect, Brzykcy's ultimate role is dependent on his fastball command becoming a little more precise. He has obvious middle relief stuff with an up/down reliever's control at present. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The Blue Jays used most of the international pool space they acquired for Kendrys Morales and Dwight Smith to sign Zululeta just before the 2018-19 signing period ended in June of '19. They did so knowing he'd need Tommy John, which he had shortly after signing. Finally back in the Fall of 2020, Zululeta was topping out in the 94-96 at Toronto's facilities in Florida. He worked with four pitches during his time in Cuba but it sounds like he only threw one breaking ball variation in the Fall. He's really well-built and athletic, has a good arm action, and obviously has requisite big league velocity coming out of rehab. The rest is very hazy, but because of when he signed, Zululeta has a long developmental runway. He's a high-priority 2021 eval. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A big-bodied, lefty power prospect, Aguilar had among the most present raw power in the 2021 international signing class, but because of how big he is already, there's a real possibility that he ends up at first base. The Mariners know this and want Aguilar to work on his conditioning to give himself the best possible shot to stay at third base, but he's still pretty soft-bodied at the moment. He does have above-average bat speed from the left side and is a fairly short-levered hitter with relatively advanced feel for contact, but the list of hitters who have been in this realm before (Joe Rizzo, Tyler Keenan, Austin Shenton, Keegan McGovern, etc.) have all either been stagnant or regressed physically, so there's no example of these sorts ending up on a more favorable end of the defensive spectrum. (International Signee)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brown pitched to uneven results during his three seasons at the University of Kentucky while working as both a starter and a reliever. Intrigued by his untapped potential, the Brewers made him their third-round pick in 2016, signing him for a shade over $400,000. After reaching Class A Wisconsin in his pro debut, Brown excelled in his return to the Midwest League in 2017 and received a late-season promotion to Class A Advanced Carolina, where he put a bow on his first full season with four solid outings. Moving up to Double-A in 2018, Brown broke out as he garnered honors as the Southern League's Most Outstanding Pitcher after he posted a circuit-best ERA (2.44) and finished second in WHIP (1.06) and BAA (.210). Brown confidently attacks hitters on both sides of the plate with a 92-95 mph fastball and holds his velocity deep into starts. He adeptly manipulates the pitch as dictated by the situation, as he'll either turn it over to create sinking action to induce weakly hit ground balls -- something he did at a 55.6-percent clip in 2018 -- or reach back for some extra velo to get whiffs with his four-seamer. His curveball is his best offering, a plus pitch, and he also has feel for a promising changeup that contrasts nicely against his heater. The Brewers have long been impressed with Brown's competitiveness on the mound and, more importantly, his ability to make adjustments and improve the deeper he worked into games. His delivery isn't the cleanest but also doesn't cost him control or command, so he should be able to remain a starter. If not, Brown's fastball-curveball combo and deceptive delivery could make him a late-inning weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After being limited by injury to just nine games as a Florida freshman, McConnell rebounded in 2019 as a Draft-eligible sophomore to hit .332/.385/.576 with 15 home runs. His performance in college baseball’s best conference (Southeastern) and the fact that McConnell was a highly regarded prep prospect prompted the Royals to draft him in the second round and offer him first-round money ($2,222,500) to sign. A quick stop in the Rookie-level Arizona League to begin his pro debut was followed by a promotion to the Pioneer League, where McConnell produced uneven numbers (.667 OPS, 39.1% K%) before suffering a concussion in late August that kept him off the field during fall instructional league. McConnell's offensive profile stands out the most. The 6-foot-3 infielder has a knack for barreling up the baseball from the right side of the plate, with power that has begun to emerge in concert with his physical gains. He will need to refine his approach and trim some of the swing-and-miss from his game to reach his ceiling, but club officials believe he has the physical tools and remaining projection needed to become an average hitter with at least average power. He is a good athlete and plus runner but is unlikely to steal many bases as a pro due to a lack of explosiveness. The jury is out on whether he can stick at shortstop, and a 16-error pro debut didn’t help to sway opinions in his favor. Some scouts believe he’ll eventually move over to second base, while those who think his actions and hands are what's holding him back believe he'd be best off in center field, where his athleticism would play well. The Royals sent him out as a shortstop and will likely give him every opportunity to stick there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Armenteros was one of the top international prospects according to MLB Pipeline in 2016 and the A's liked him enough to go over the spending threshold, incurring penalties when he signed with the A's for $3 million. He had a solid pro debut making his way to the United States and the rookie-level Arizona League in 2017, then showed glimpses of his tools during a full-season debut that was interrupted by injury. Armenteros has the chance to have four at-least average tools at the Major League level. He has plus bat speed that makes it easy to project the ability to hit for average with potentially plus power down the road. He's not afraid to see pitches and draw walks, though he needs to continue to refine his overall approach and pitch recognition in order to cut down his strikeout rate, which was 33.8 percent in 2018. While he does have excellent speed, he is expected to slow down some as he matures. He's largely played left field, likely his long-term home given his fringy arm strength. That puts pressure on him to be a corner outfield type bat, but he has the potential to easily fit that profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery is never thought of as a positive achievement, despite it becoming almost commonplace among young pitchers these days. But there might be a silver lining in having needed the surgery in 2018 for Aquino, the 6-foot-6 right-hander who got $100,000 to sign in Dec. 2016. Yes, he missed development time on the mound by being out for all of 2018, but the strength and conditioning that went along with rehabbing the injury could help him take a big step when he returns to the mound. Before Aquino went down with injury, he had already improved strength-wise enough to add velocity to his fastball. What was a 90-91 mph heater when he first signed was touching 96 mph at instructs in the fall of 2017 with excellent spin and riding life. He's filled out even more now, so dreaming about more velocity once he gets his feet under him isn't unrealistic. He can really spin his breaking ball, giving him the chance for a second plus pitch, and he'll continue to work on what could be a decent changeup. With his size, Aquino will have to work at repeating his delivery. He'll get a chance to do that as he puts his rehab in the rearview mirror and hopefully gets a full season of work in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 After three years pitching out of the University of Alabama bullpen, Burrows left as the school's career leader in saves with 30. Seeing him as a future left-handed big league reliever, the Mariners took him in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He spent just one summer with Seattle as he was sent to the Braves in January 2017, along with Luiz Gohara in return for Mallex Smith and Shae Simmons. He reached Double-A in 2018, his second season in the organization, then capped things off in the Arizona Fall League. Burrows' calling card is his breaking ball, and it's a real weapon against left-handed hitters but nasty enough to miss right-handed bats as well. He throws it with deception with late, sharp break, and hitters don't see it. It's the main reason why he carries a 12.2 K/9 ratio into the 2019 season. His fastball sits in the low-90s coming from a low three-quarters slot, allowing it to play up beyond the velocity. Burrows' progress has been slowed a bit by a lack of consistency and command, though it's clear his two-pitch mix is plenty to get big league hitters out. At the very least, he's a left-handed specialist. At the top end, he's a seventh-inning type reliever, with an Eric O'Flaherty career path.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz came up as a shortstop in the Dominican Republic before converting to pitcher and signing with the Cubs for $85,000 in 2012. He broke out as one of their top pitching prospects when he made his U.S. debut in 2015 but he worked just 39 innings in 2016 because of forearm soreness and just 56 2/3 last year with a pectoral strain. He stayed healthy in 2018, though his season came to an end in early July when he drew an 80-game suspension after testing positive for a banned diuretic and masking agent. When healthy, De La Cruz operates with a pair of plus pitches and flashes a changeup with at least solid potential. His 91-97 mph fastball has plenty of velocity and is even harder to hit because of its movement and the angle he creates with his 6-foot-4 frame. His curveball combines power and depth and he's improving the consistency of his arm speed with his changeup. De La Cruz has a strong, athletic frame -- he weighs more than his listed 200 pounds -- that should lend itself to durability. He has good body control for his size, repeats his delivery well and never has had any problems throwing strikes. If he can do a better job of staying on the mound, he can become at least a No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dyson was viewed as potential first-round pick going into his junior year at Florida before some early struggles cost him a spot in the Gators’ rotation. His stuff was impressive even when he struggled, though, and he pitched with more velocity while working in shorter bursts in relief. The Nationals saw untapped potential and value in Dyson as a potential starter and went nearly $150,000 over slot value to sign him after selecting him in the fifth round. He rewarded the organization with a strong debut, posting a 1.14 ERA over eight starts at Class A Short Season Auburn. Dyson’s plus fastball carried over into pro ball as the Nationals hoped it would, with the right-hander sitting in the mid-90s and locating it well in the New York-Penn League. Dyson’s heater jumps on hitters due to his clean arm action and easy delivery, though it can be hittable when he misses his spot due to a lack of movement. Dyson’s slider lacks depth but should be an average pitch once developed, and he’ll need to make similar gains with a changeup that currently is below average. Though the Nationals think Dyson can remain a starter and were encouraged by his strong pro, club officials also acknowledge that the 6-foot-3 righty has some major hurdles to clear in his development. If that doesn’t work, Dyson has the type of stuff that could play up in shorter bursts in relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Nova Scotia high schooler, Sanford drew no scouting or recruiting interest and his only college offer was to play volleyball at Dalhousie University in his home province. He walked on at McCook (Neb.) CC, where he hit 23 homers in two years with wood bats, then transferred to Western Kentucky in 2019 and won the first regular-season triple crown in Conference USA history. After he went undrafted the previous three years, the Yankees made him a third-round pick. One of the best power prospects in the 2019 Draft, Sanford creates well-above-average raw pop with plenty of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-2, 215-pound frame. Some scouts worry about the deep load in his left-handed swing and his tendency to get off balance at the plate, though New York believes his hand-eye coordination and quick stroke can make it work. He struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances while batting .238/.289/.411 in his pro debut at short-season Staten Island, so he has adjustments to make. In addition to his big power, Sanford features plus speed and can flash even faster running times, though he's not much of a basestealer. A first baseman in junior college, he made a nice transition to right field at Western Kentucky. The Yankees deployed him in center field to see how his quickness played there during his first pro summer, and his fringy arm strength likely will land him in left field if he shifts back to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Primarily a pitcher in his first two seasons at Gonzaga, Jones didn't become a full-time starter at first base until he was a senior in 2016, when he set a school record and placed second in NCAA Division I with 27 doubles. Signed for $2,500 in the 19th round that June, he didn't start to realize his power potential until he slammed 18 homers in Double-A in 2018. He encored with 22 more last year while enhancing his versatility in Triple-A. Though Jones has plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-7 frame, he only began tapping into his power once he did a better job of staying back on pitches and stopped diving so much at the plate. He's driving the ball in the air more often and to all fields. While his size results in a naturally long right-handed swing, he does a good job of making contact and draws walks with a patient approach. Part of a Washington state 4-A basketball championship team at Kentwood High -- where his baseball teammates included future big leaguers Reese McGuire and Austin Voth -- Jones is athletic for his size. He's a below-average runner but not a baseclogger, and he's a quality defender with a strong arm at first base. He also can provide adequate defense on the outfield corners and looked fine in his initial exposure to third base in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round pick out of a Virginia high school in 2017, Perry spent most of his first two pro seasons in Rookie ball before breaking out in the New York-Penn League in 2019. He finished second in the short-season circuit in homers and won MVP honors at the New York-Penn all-star game, where he went deep in his lone at-bat. He was slated to finally make his full-season debut in 2020 before the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season. Perry stands out with his strength and plus raw power, most of which comes to his pull side. He has a short left-handed stroke with natural loft and enjoyed more success once he realized he didn't need to sell out for home runs. He still needs to make more consistent contact, but he's willing to work counts and draw walks. While Perry shared time behind the plate in the New York-Penn League, that was in deference to 2019 first-rounder Korey Lee, and the Astros believe he can stick at catcher. He has improved as a receiver since turning pro and does a nice job of framing pitches, though he can look a bit stiff at times. He has average arm strength, a quick transfer and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former multi-sport star from the Rhode Island high school ranks, Reed showed off his raw tools and athleticism in spurts during three years at the University of Florida. The Padres liked his very high ceiling enough to take him in the second round of the 2016 Draft. Following a rough first full season, Reed broke out in 2018, played in the Futures Game and advanced to Double-A. His struggles there carried over to his 2019 season back in the Texas League and he wasn’t protected from, nor was he selected in, the Rule 5 Draft. He was then sent to the A’s as the player to be named later for Jurickson Profar. The A’s are hoping a change of scenery, some new instructors and new ideas might be just what is needed to unlock Reed’s treasure trove of raw tools more consistently. The switch-hitter can make loud contact and drive the ball from both sides of the plate, though his right-handed swing is a bit better. He had changed his swing path to be shorter to the ball with more extension, leading to his breakout to start 2018, but his strikeout rate soared once he got to Double-A. Reed’s speed is close to top of the scale and he’s a major basestealing threat, swiping 51 bags in 2018. It also helps him cover a ton of ground in the outfield, where he’s a plus defender in center and has an arm that works really well in the corners. He still has 20-20 potential if he can refine his approach enough to make more contact with his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brady went from his high school in southern New Jersey to East Carolina University, but after not seeing much mound time as a freshman in 2016, he returned to the Garden State and Mercer Community College. A standout season there in 2017 landed him in the seventh round with the Angels. Some arm issues slowed him early on in his career -- he amassed just 144 2/3 innings over his first two-plus seasons, but he’s healthy now and would have been ready to go for a full 2020 season had it transpired. The 6-foot-1 right-hander has a three-pitch mix and an idea of what to do with it, giving him some starting pitcher qualities. His fastball sits in the 92-93 mph range, and he can reach back for 95 mph on occasion. Depending on who sees him and how he’s throwing it, Brady has either a hard curve or a slider, and a decent slurvy breaking ball that he has a good feel to spin while adding to and subtracting from it. He’ll mix in a changeup that flashes average as well. Despite not having wow stuff, Brady has done a nice job of missing bats while filling up the strike zone fairly consistently. The lack of an out pitch or premium velocity kept him off the radar enough to not be selected in the 2020 Rule 5 Draft, even though he was left unprotected. After a solid showing at instructs this fall, the Angels are intrigued to see what Brady can do in a full healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at the University of Georgia, Elliott pitched as a reliver and a swingman. He got a chance to be a part of the Bulldogs’ rotation as a junior and had a breakthrough season, establishing himself as the best midweek starter in the nation. The Mariners were hunting college pitching in the 2019 Draft and made Elliott the fifth of five college arms they took to kick things off, signing him for a below-slot $400,000 and sending him out for a solid pro debut in the short-season Northwest League. Elliott was a lean 6-foot-1, 170 pounds when he began his college career, but was up to 200 lbs by the time he began his pro career, allowing his stuff to play up. He throws his fastball in the 89-94 mph range and showed he can maintain that velocity deep into starts. He does a nice job mixing in three secondary offerings. His changeup is the best of the lot, an above-average offspeed pitch, and he makes good use of his average slider and even his fringy curve. Command has been an issue for Elliott at times, though he did much better in the strike-throwing department as a starter during his junior year. If he can continue that, with his repertoire, he has the chance to eventually develop into a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter at California Baptist University, Rinehart pitched well in relief in the Cape Cod League and continued to impress out of the bullpen in his professional debut. After the Mariners grabbed the right-hander in the 16th-round of the 2019 Draft, he pitched his way to full-season ball, where he posted a 3.52 ERA over 10 appearances. Listed at 6-foot-3, 185 pounds, Rinehart showed up to Spring Training in exceptional shape and appeared ready to put together a breakout campaign. Of course, COVID-19 shut down the 2020 Minor League season so Rinehart didn’t get a chance to compete against other organizations, but he did impress at Seattle’s alternate site. The right-hander throws his fastball in the 94-96 mph range and complements it with a trio of secondary offerings. Rinehart has plus control of a changeup that he throws in the upper 70s, a stark separation from his fastball, and also throws both a sweeping slider and a downer curveball that is used as an out pitch early in counts. Rinehart has thrown strikes as a pro, but the improved velocity and usage of the zone has helped him miss more bats. While the Mariners plan to let him start for now, he needs to continue to refine his breaking stuff to remain in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017 Cape Cod League MVP, Jenista's strong summer likely helped his stock avoid falling too much after an uneven junior season at Wichita State, as he landed in the second round with the Braves. He did make it to Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in his first full year of pro ball, but didn’t swing the bat very well and didn’t get any official reps in 2020. The power showed up a bit more in 2021, though he wasn't added to the Braves' 40-man roster in the offseason. There is some juice in Jenista’s left-handed bat, but there are questions as to whether he’ll be able to get to it at the highest level. The power has shown up at times, including hitting 19 homers in a tough hitters' park in 2021. But while he does draw some walks, the swing-and-miss is a real concern, as he has struck out in more than 32 percent of his plate appearances in his first two full seasons of pro ball. Jenista runs well enough for his size and has the athleticism and arm strength needed to play right field well. He saw time at first base in the AFL to close out 2019 and continued to do so in 2021. In the end, though, it will be Jenista’s ability to unlock his offensive potential that will determine his future value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last catcher from the Southern Indiana to make it to the big leagues was Kevin Brown, a Rangers second-round pick who spent parts of seven seasons in the Majors as a backup. His son Logan followed in his footsteps to USI, starting for the Division II school for two years and eventually being taken in the 35th round by the Braves in 2018. The defensive-minded backstop was a South Atlantic League All-Star and earned a promotion up to the Florida State League in his first full season of pro ball. While Brown hit well in Rome, it’s still his defense that stands out. He has excellent catch and throw skills, throwing out 40 percent of potential basestealers in 2019. He also receives very well and gets high marks for his game-calling, working with pitchers and leadership behind the plate. The left-handed hitter makes a ton of contact, though he doesn’t walk a ton, and hasn’t shown much ability to impact the baseball. The Braves think there’s more bat to come, which would help him develop into a very good glove-first backup catcher at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out a $2.5 million bonus to shortstop Luis Garcia. Six months later, and at the other end of the bonus spectrum, they inked Martinez for $10,000. Martinez put up pedestrian numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and while he pitched sparingly in his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, he created some buzz with his size, stuff and upside potential. The 6-foot-2 left-hander is lanky and loose and has a legitimate three-pitch mix at his disposal. He can throw his fastball in the 91-96 mph range, throwing it with good late life. His slider has the chance to be a true out pitch, and he has surprisingly good feel for his changeup at a young age, selling it well with good arm speed. Martinez has shown the ability to throw strikes with a clean, easy and relatively effortless delivery that also provides some deception, with an idea of how to mix his pitches. It’s been a very small sample size of performance thus far, but scouts are excited to see what he can do with more time on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed a pair of promising 16-year-old Dominican outfielders at the outset of the 2018-19 international period, signing Marte and Jeremy De La Rosa for $300,000 apiece -- the maximum amount allowed without incurring a penalty -- on July 2. Though both players flashed a collection of intriguing tools during the pro debuts in the 2019 Dominican Summer League, it was Marte who led the team in home runs (tied, 5), slugging (.448) and total bases (94) at age 17, and he was one of Washington’s most impressive prospects during fall instructional camp in 2020. Marte possesses a blend of athleticism and physicality that has already earned him comparisons to an NFL running back. His projectable frame is ideal for adding more strength, and club officials do not expect those physical gains to detract from the plus speed that also enables Marte to play a quality center field. The Nationals believe he has a chance to remain at the position long-term, but his strong arm would more than suffice if he’s forced to move to an outfield corner. Marte’s development as a hitter will be key in unlocking his overall potential. He can do damage from the right side of the plate, combining strength and bat speed into an explosive swing, and Marte already showcases plus raw power to his pull side that should begin to play to all fields more consistently as he gains experience. Marte’s approach and pitch selection will both require considerable refinement (as is the case with most teenage hitters), but the raw ingredients are all there for him to become an impact talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Nationals for $35,000 out of Panama in 2013, Fuentes pitched to mixed results in multiple roles early in his career but began to put it all together in 2018. He built upon that success during a breakout age-22 campaign in 2019, excelling as a reliever at Class A Advanced Potomac and then as a starter at Double-A Harrisburg. But after compiling a 2.23 ERA with 89 strikeouts and 22 walks in 80 2/3 innings between the two stops, Fuentes was slapped with a 50-game suspension in early August after testing positive for Heptaminol, a banned stimulant. Fuentes succeeds with an intriguing blend of stuff and pitchability. His fastball can touch 95 mph and sits in the low 90s with heavy sinking action that fuels the right-hander’s extreme ground-ball tendencies. He posted a 58 percent ground-ball rate in Double-A before the suspension and has induced grounders at 54.2 percent clip since the start of the 2017 season, his first in full-season ball. Both his average slider and his above-average changeup improved when he moved into the rotation, and he generated whiff rates of 41 and 40 percent, respectively, with the two pitches in the Eastern League. He can throw all three pitches for strikes and doesn't hurt himself by issuing many free passes. Fuentes' ability to work effectively in various roles is an asset, and club officials view him as a potential multi-inning reliever much like former Nats hurler Yusmeiro Petit. At the same time, it wouldn't surprise anyone in the organization if Fuentes were to continue to excel as a starter en route to a spot in the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international class, Parra was also one of its more physically advanced prospects, showing a promising mix of strength and hitting ability as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers signed him for $210,000 on Aug. 30, 2018, Parra’s 16th birthday, and he rewarded the organization by having a successful 2019 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he was nearly two years younger than the circuit’s average player. Listed at 6-foot-2, 184 pounds, Parra has present strength and plenty of room still to grow into his projectable frame. He has impressive natural hitting ability for a young player, with an impactful right-handed swing that already yields hard contact as well as raw power. Parra’s swing can get long at times, resulting in some and miss, though the Brewers think that will be less of an issue once the teenager adds strength and has more experience under his belt. He split time between second and third base in his pro debut but profiles better at the latter position, where his plus arm and below-average speed are fits. Parra offered an early glimpse of his offensive potential when he went 5-for-5 with two home runs, two doubles and five RBIs in his third game as a professional. He improved as the season unfolded, batting .329/.451/.573 with 19 RBIs in July, and finished the year with 23 extra-base hits and a .770 OPS in 65 games. The Brewers are understandably excited about the 17-year-old’s bat and view him as someone who could one day hit in the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his high school career in New York, Fletcher transferred to Maine and reclassified into the 2019 Draft, where the Cardinals selected him 58th overall. The second-round selection secured Fletcher’s status as the highest position player ever selected out of a Maine high school. (The Tigers’ eighth-round selection of Kurt Hall in 1977 previously held the record.) The Cardinals signed him for an above-slot bonus, which led Fletcher to forgo his Vanderbilt commitment and join the professional ranks, where he hit .244 with four homers over two levels of Rookie ball (43 games) in 2019 and then repeated the level in 2021. Fletcher’s raw tools are exciting, though they don’t always show up in games. He struck out in roughly 44 percent of his plate appearances in his professional debut, prompting the Cardinals to work with Fletcher on eliminating his big leg kick. While he needs to improve his contact rate, Fletcher does hit the ball hard and has plus power when he connects. Fletcher participated in St. Louis’ alternate training site during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic, which provided him with valuable reps against advanced pitchers. There’s 20-20 potential if everything goes well, but the tools haven’t translated to on-field production so far. A good athlete with plus speed, Fletcher has the tools -- including an arm that used to fire 93-mph fastballs from the mound -- to play center field, but needs to improve upon his reads and jumps to stay there long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prater was part of a loaded weekend rotation for an Oklahoma squad that also featured 2020 first-round pick Cade Cavalli (Nationals) and fourth-rounder Dane Acker (A’s). However, Prater had the best ERA (3.42) of the bunch and struck out 33 in his 23 2/3 innings before the coronavirus pandemic halted the 2020 season and the Cardinals selected him with the 93rd overall pick (third round) that June. In a more complete sample size, the lefty was named to the 2019 All-Big 12 Second Team and led Sooners’ starters that year with 97 strikeouts and a 3.26 ERA in 80 innings. While there’s still room for growth, Prater did show an ability to miss bats in his professional debut, racking up 83 strikeouts over his first 52 1/3 innings in Low-A. A deceptive, crossfire delivery helps Prater’s stuff play up and makes him hard to hit. He throws his fastball with armside run in the low 90s and sits around 80 mph with his slider. He also throws a changeup around 80 mph that flashes plus, but isn’t always consistent. The development of that pitch, as well as his overall command, will likely go a long way into determining his future role. The Cardinals are giving Prater an opportunity to start as he begins his professional career and he’ll be able to remain there if he’s able to improve upon his control. His delivery features some effort, which may push Prater into a reliever role. He profiles well as a middle reliever and may ultimately wind up in the bullpen, depending on how he develops that third pitch. If he is able to put everything together, his ceiling is likely that of a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best position player to come out of Loyola Marymount to date has to be Angels infielder David Fletcher, a sixth-round pick back in 2015. Three years later, it was Decolati’s turn to represent the Lions in the sixth round when the Rockies took him. After a very successful debut in 2018, a broken hand kept him out until June '19, and he wasn't able to match his production from the summer prior. Decolati might have been one of the players in the Rockies system to suffer the most from the shutdown as he needs reps to turn his athleticism into consistent performance. He was rusty during instructional league play, though it started to come together by the end of the fall. The right-handed hitter can make loud contact and has plenty of raw power, but his overly aggressive approach was exposed in 2019 and led to a high strikeout rate. With plus speed, Decolati can steal a base and cover a lot of ground in the outfield. He’s shown he can handle center field and his above-average arm works well from right field. He might settle in as a fourth outfielder type, but more than anything, he just needs to go out and play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets for an over-slot $150,000 in the 18th round of the 2015 Draft, Humphreys was breaking out during his full-season debut two years later when he blew out his elbow, requiring Tommy John surgery in August 2017. A second operation to address an ulnar nerve issue in his elbow delayed his return until June 2019 and he pitched only two innings in Rookie ball last year, but he allowed just one run in 11 2/3 Arizona Fall League frames and landed a spot on New York's 40-man roster. He was designated for assignment twice in 2020 and changed organizations each time, going to the Giants in a trade for Billy Hamilton in July and to the Indians via waivers in November. Humphreys' best pitch is his fastball, which plays better than its 90-94 mph velocity because of its riding life and his ability to command it to any quadrant of the strike zone. Both of his secondary pitches presently grade as average but show flashes of becoming better than that. He has a tight upper-70s curveball with promising spin rates and a changeup that he sells well with fastball arm speed. Humphreys pounded the strike zone before he got hurt, averaging just 1.6 walks per nine innings in his first three pro seasons before issuing five in 13 2/3 innings in 2019. He offers the upside of three solid pitches with plus control, though he's also 24 years old and has worked just 11 innings above low Class A. Cleveland probably won't know exactly what it has in Humphreys until he returns to game action in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at UConn in 2018, Feole collected the second-most strikeouts in school history. When he followed that up with 11 shutout innings for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team, he looked poised to be one of the more intriguing college lefties in the 2019 Draft class. But a forearm issue slowed him early as his velocity dipped, hurting his stock considerably, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in July after the Padres took him in the 11th round. After completing his rehab process, Feole appeared physically stronger and operated with better stuff when he returned to mound in San Diego’s fall instructional camp. At his best, Feole leans heavily on his fastball-curve combination. The former will sit in the low 90s and was touching higher during instructional league, while the breaking ball serves as his out pitch, flashing plus at times. Feole has a third-pitch changeup that is below average. An unorthodox delivery that includes a head snap makes it difficult for Feole to find the strike zone consistently and portends a full-time move to the bullpen, where his two-pitch repertoire could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres’ fabled 2016-17 international spending spree is bearing fruit across the system, and they used the entirety of that window to haul in top-tier prospects. Case in point: Osvaldo Hernandez. The Friars inked the then-18-year-old to a $2.5 million contract out of Cuba in March 2017, three months before the window closed. Hernandez pitched at three different levels during his debut season, but his breakout came in ’18 at Class A Fort Wayne where he posted a 1.81 ERA, which would’ve led the Midwest League with a few more innings to qualify. Injuries prevented Hernandez from building upon that performance much in 2019, though he did pitch well in the California League during the second half before losing all of ’20 to the pandemic. Hernandez fits the mold of a crafty and deceptive southpaw, even if he doesn’t boast big-time velocity. His fastball sits in the low 90s but can reach the mid 90s. He’s got a put-away curveball, and he pairs it with a serviceable slider and changeup. What stands out most about Hernandez is his savvy on the mound. He constantly changes speeds and varies his delivery, and he routinely induces weak contact from opposing hitters. Hernandez is athletic, and he boasts an easy, smooth delivery. There’s no one trait that jumps off the page, but his creativity and pitchability could make him a solid middle-to-back-of-the-rotation starter in the Major Leagues.
